title: JUPITER AI Factory kooperiert mit NVIDIA, um Startups und SMEs zu unterstützen
content:
JUPITER AI Factory kooperiert mit NVIDIA, um Startups und SMEs zu unterstützen
Mit ihrer Rechenleistung auf Exascale-Niveau bietet die JUPITER AI Factory (JAIF) einzigartige Möglichkeiten zum Training von KI-Modellen in Europa. Sie eröffnet Start-ups und KMU sowie Forschenden und der Industrie einen kostenlosen, schnellen und einfachen Zugang zu Rechenzeit. Nun erweitert JAIF ihre Infrastruktur und ihr Leistungsspektrum durch die Zusammenarbeit mit dem NVIDIA Inception-Programm für Start-ups.
JAIF basiert auf JUPITER, Europas erstem Exascale-Supercomputer. Indem JAIF mit NVIDIA Inception zusammenarbeitet – das Start-ups ebenfalls Zugang zu Entwicklertools, Schulungen und einem Netzwerk aus Investoren und technischen Experten bietet – bringt sie ihre enorme Rechenleistung direkt in ein größeres, rasch wachsendes Ökosystem für KI-Innovation ein. Damit erhöht sie ihre Sichtbarkeit bei Start-ups und KMU im deutschen und europäischen KI-Umfeld.
Diese Kooperation ergänzt die bestehenden Partnerschaften von JAIF und erweitert das Angebot an offenem, herstellerneutralem Zugang zu europäischen KI- und HPC-Ressourcen.
>>Wissenstransfer und Kompetenzaufbau für KI und HPC
Von der Zusammenarbeit profitieren soll die gesamte JAIF-Forschungs- und Entwicklungs-Community, bestehend aus Wissenschaft, Start-ups und KMU. Im Rahmen der geplanten Initiativen werden gezielte Schulungs- und Mentoring-Angebote über Programme von NVIDIA Training für Entwickler:innen und Administrator:innen, das NVIDIA AI Technology Center sowie die Open-Hackathon-Initiative bereitgestellt. Diese Aktivitäten sollen den Wissensaustausch fördern und praktische Kompetenzen für die Entwicklung von KI- und HPC-Anwendungen vermitteln.
Zudem werden durch die Kooperation die Rechenressourcen und Serviceangebote von JAIF über das NVIDIA Inception-Portal noch sichtbarer. Start-ups und KMU steht eine leistungsstarke, hochmoderne KI-Infrastruktur offen – sowohl über die regulären Antragswege von JAIF als auch über das NVIDIA Inception-Portal als ergänzenden Zugangsweg. Durch diese Kombination sollen für das JAIF-Ökosystem neue Nutzergruppen gewonnen und bestehende Dienstleistungsangebote stärker genutzt werden. JAIF-Anwender erhalten ergänzende Expertise im Wissenstransfer und in den jeweiligen Fachdisziplinen, was die effektive Nutzung der vorhandenen Rechenkapazitäten fördert. Die Verknüpfung eines größeren Ökosystems für KI-Innovation mit europäischen KI- und HPC-Ressourcen soll dazu beitragen, den Einsatz und die Skalierung von KI-Anwendungen in zahlreichen Feldern voranzutreiben – darunter im Gesundheitswesen, in der Energieversorgung, der Fertigung, in den Bereichen Klima und Umwelt, Bildung, Kultur und Medien sowie im öffentlichen Sektor und im Finanz- und Versicherungswesen.
>>JUPITER – Schlüsselinfrastruktur für KI und Hochleistungsrechnen
Integriert in eine breitere, herstellerneutrale Dienstleistungslandschaft ergänzen diese neuen Angebote das Fachwissen der deutschen und europäischen Partner von JAIF. Gleichzeitig treiben sie die KI-Innovation mit JUPITER, Europas erstem Exascale-Supercomputer, voran. Das im September 2025 eingeweihte EuroHPC-System wird von rund 24.000 NVIDIA Grace Hopper-Superchips angetrieben und bildet das zentrale technologische Rückgrat des JAIF-Ökosystems. JUPITER stellt eine Schlüsselinfrastruktur für KI und Hochleistungsrechnen in Deutschland und Europa dar. Um Training und praktische Anwendungen nahtlos miteinander zu verbinden, umfasst das JAIF-Ökosystem zudem JARVIS, eine spezialisierte Cloud-Plattform für fortschrittliche KI-Inferenz und skalierbare Nutzerdienste.
>>Langjährige Zusammenarbeit im Bereich Hochleistungsrechnen und GPU-gestützter Forschung
Das JSC arbeitet in den Bereichen Hochleistungsrechnen und GPU-gestützter Forschung seit vielen Jahren eng mit NVIDIA zusammen. Dazu gehören Entwicklungs- und Optimierungsarbeiten für KI- und HPC-Anwendungen sowie der Betrieb von Forschungs- und Entwicklungslabors, darunter ein NVIDIA Application Lab am Standort Jülich.
Diese Zusammenarbeit trägt dazu bei, JAIF als eines der führenden KI-Innovationszentren Deutschlands zu stärken und fördert die wirtschaftliche Entwicklung in Nordrhein-Westfalen, Hessen, Deutschland und Europa.
»JAIF hat das Ziel, Dienstleistungen anzubieten, die Start-ups und KMU den Zugang zu KI-Anwendungen in großem Maßstab erleichtern. Unsere Zusammenarbeit mit NVIDIA und dessen Inception-Programm trägt maßgeblich dazu bei. Die Partnerschaft stellt sicher, dass die Stärken von JUPITER einerseits und die Flexibilität von JARVIS andererseits voll ausgeschöpft werden können«, so Prof. Dr. Dr. Thomas Lippert, Jülich Supercomputing Centre (JSC), Koordinator von JAIF.
»Deutschlands Forschungseinrichtungen bringen Gründer hervor, die ihre eigenen Modelle trainieren wollen, und dieser Anspruch stößt schon früh an infrastrukturelle Grenzen«, sagt Tobias Halloran, Direktor für EMEAI-Start-ups bei NVIDIA. »Durch diese Zusammenarbeit erhalten Start-ups und KMU im NVIDIA Inception-Programm über JAIF ebenfalls Zugang zu JUPITER für das Training und zu JARVIS für die Inferenz sowie fachkundige Unterstützung bei deren Nutzung. Damit erweitert JAIF seinen Nutzerkreis unter Start-ups und KMU weiter.«
>>Über das Jülich Supercomputing Centre (JSC) am Forschungszentrum Jülich
Das Jülich Supercomputing Centre (JSC) betreibt Systeme für das Hochleistungsrechnen und stellt Wissenschaft und Industrie in Deutschland und Europa Zugang zu modernster Supercomputing-Infrastruktur bereit. Als eines der führenden Supercomputing-Zentren Europas ermöglicht das JSC Forschenden, komplexe wissenschaftliche und gesellschaftliche Herausforderungen mit innovativen Methoden aus Simulation, Data Science und Künstlicher Intelligenz anzugehen. Mit seinen Systemen – darunter Europas erster Exascale-Supercomputer JUPITER – unterstützt das JSC interdisziplinäre Forschung in einer Vielzahl wissenschaftlicher Felder und entwickelt Methoden für Recheninfrastrukturen der nächsten Generation. Darüber hinaus betreibt das JSC JUNIQ, eine europäische Quantencomputer-Infrastruktur, die Zugang zu modernsten Quantencomputern bietet und die frühe Erforschung sowie den Einsatz von Quantentechnologien unterstützt. Das JSC ist Teil des Forschungszentrums Jülich (FZJ), Mitglied der Helmholtz-Gemeinschaft.
>>Über die JUPITER AI Factory (JAIF)
Die JUPITER AI Factory (JAIF) ist Teil eines Netzwerks von KI-Fabriken in ganz Europa, das von der EuroHPC JU kofinanziert wird. Im Rahmen dieser Initiative betreut die EuroHPC JU den Aufbau von 19 KI-Fabriken, ergänzt durch 13 KI-Fabrik-Antennen, um die Einführung künstlicher Intelligenz in Start-ups, KMU, der Industrie, der Forschung und im öffentlichen Sektor zu beschleunigen. Basierend auf JUPITER, Europas erstem Exascale-Supercomputer, der von EuroHPC beschafft wurde und vom JSC betrieben wird, bietet JAIF Zugang zu hochmoderner KI-Infrastruktur für Training und Inferenz sowie fachliche Unterstützung, Schulungen und Innovationsangebote, die Organisationen bei der Entwicklung, Skalierung und dem Einsatz von KI-Lösungen unterstützen. Als zentrale Anlaufstelle für KI-Innovation ermöglicht JAIF Anwendungen in Bereichen wie Gesundheit, Energie, Klima, Fertigung, Finanzen, Bildung, Medien und dem öffentlichen Sektor.
Die JUPITER AI Factory wird vom FZJ koordiniert und vereint die RWTH Aachen University, das Fraunhofer-Institut für Angewandte Informationstechnik FIT, das Fraunhofer-Institut für Intelligente Analyse- und Informationssysteme IAIS, hessian.AI sowie AI Factory Antennas in Belgien und Ungarn, um die KI-Innovation und -Anwendung in Europa zu unterstützen.
>>Förderung
JAIF wird durch das EuroHPC Joint Undertaking (JU) finanziert, mit Kofinanzierung durch die Bundesregierung sowie die Länder Nordrhein-Westfalen und Hessen. Das Gesamtvolumen der Förderung für die AI Factory beträgt 25 Millionen Euro. Zusätzlich wird das mit JAIF verbundene KI-Inferenzsystem JARVIS mit 30 Millionen Euro durch die Bundesregierung und das Land Nordrhein-Westfalen finanziert.
JUPITER, der »Joint Undertaking Pioneer for Innovative and Transformative Exascale Research«, wird zur Hälfte von der europäischen Supercomputing-Initiative EuroHPC Joint Undertaking (EuroHPC JU) und zu je einem Viertel vom Bundesministerium für Forschung, Technologie und Raumfahrt (BMFTR, vormals BMBF) sowie dem Ministerium für Kultur und Wissenschaft des Landes Nordrhein-Westfalen (MKW NRW) finanziert.

Auswertung von Ultraschalldaten am Prüfgerät und am Computer: KI soll Prüfpersonal dabei unterstützen, Schäden z.B. in Schweißnähten zu erkennen und zu bewerten.
| Copyright:
Download
Berlin, 28.10.2026. Die Bundesanstalt für Materialforschung und -prüfung (BAM) entwickelt gemeinsam mit Partner*innen eine menschenzentrierte KI-Assistenz, die Prüfpersonal bei der Erkennung und Bewertung von Schäden in Schweißnähten unterstützen soll. Im Forschungsprojekt UltrasonAIc, das jetzt seine Arbeit aufgenommen hat, werden dafür Ultraschalldaten mithilfe künstlicher Intelligenz ausgewertet. Ziel: Fehlbewertungen reduzieren und Prüfungen beschleunigen – damit sicherheitsrelevante Schäden an kritischen Infrastrukturen und technischen Anlagen frühzeitig erkannt werden können.
Zerstörungsfreie Ultraschallprüfungen können dazu beitragen, die Sicherheit kritischer Infrastrukturen und technischer Anlagen wie Brücken, Pipelines oder Kraftwerken zu gewährleisten. Dazu werden hochfrequente Schallwellen durch das Material geleitet und ihre Reflexionen ausgewertet. Hierdurch lassen sich beispielsweise Risse oder eingeschlossene Fremdstoffe im Inneren eines Bauteils erkennen, ohne es zu beschädigen. Die Prüfergebnisse helfen, den Zustand zu bewerten, notwendige Reparaturen frühzeitig zu planen und das Risiko von Ausfällen und Unfällen zu verringern.
Mit der zunehmenden Digitalisierung wachsen jedoch die bei diesen Prüfungen anfallenden Datenmengen erheblich, während qualifiziertes Prüfpersonal zunehmend fehlt. Hier setzt das Gemeinschaftsprojekt UltrasonAIc an, in dem die BAM, die deeplify GmbH und die DGZfP Ausbildung und Training GmbH KI-gestützte Assistenzsysteme entwickeln, die Prüfende künftig bei der Auswertung großer Datenmengen unterstützen sollen. Die BAM bringt hierbei ihre Expertise in Ultraschallsimulation, Zuverlässigkeitsbewertung und Mensch-KI-Zusammenarbeit ein.
„Ein Schwerpunkt liegt auf der realitätsnahen Simulation von Ultraschallprüfungen. Die dabei erzeugten Daten dienen dem Training von KI-Modellen und ermöglichen leistungsfähige Algorithmen auch dort, wo reale Prüfdaten nur begrenzt verfügbar sind“, sagt Thomas Heckel, BAM-Experte für angewandte Ultraschallprüfung.
UltrasonAIc kombiniert verschiedene Ultraschallverfahren in einem gemeinsamen KI-Modell. Dadurch sollen Defekte präziser erkannt und Fehlbewertungen deutlich reduziert werden. Das Besondere bei UltrasonAIc: Der Ansatz ist konsequent menschenzentriert. Die KI unterstützt Prüfende als Assistenzsystem, ersetzt sie jedoch nicht.
„In sicherheitskritischen Prüfaufgaben muss KI nicht nur leistungsfähig, sondern auch vertrauenswürdig und praxistauglich sein. Deshalb untersuchen wir bei der BAM systematisch, wie KI für die zerstörungsfreie Prüfung menschenzentriert gestaltet werden kann: von der sinnvollen Aufgabenteilung zwischen Mensch und KI bis hin zu Benutzerfreundlichkeit, Nachvollziehbarkeit und Akzeptanz durch das Prüfpersonal“, erklärt Marija Bertović, BAM-Expertin für menschliche Faktoren und Mensch-Maschine Interaktion.
Die Technologie bietet insbesondere für die Energie- und Wasserstoffwirtschaft, die chemische Industrie, den Anlagen- und Maschinenbau sowie die Luft- und Raumfahrt großes Potenzial. Neben einer benutzerfreundlichen Softwareplattform entstehen Schulungs- und Weiterbildungskonzepte für den Einsatz KI-gestützter Prüfsysteme. Die Trainingsdaten werden in einem offenen Format bereitgestellt und können für weitere Forschungs- und Entwicklungsarbeiten genutzt werden. Die Ergebnisse sollen dazu beitragen, die Sicherheit kritischer Infrastrukturen zu erhöhen und Prüfpersonal bei anspruchsvollen Prüfaufgaben zu entlasten.
Das Projekt wird von der deeplify GmbH, einem deutschen Software- und KI-Unternehmen mit Sitz in Düsseldorf, koordiniert, das KI-Lösungen für Asset Integrity und industrielle Inspektionen, insbesondere für sicherheitskritische Anlagen und Prozesse entwickelt. Die DGZfP Ausbildung und Training GmbH bringt ihre Expertise in der Qualifizierung von Prüfpersonal ein. So verbindet das Projekt KI-Entwicklung, Sicherheitsforschung und berufliche Praxis, damit die Assistenzsysteme zuverlässig funktionieren und im Prüfalltag sinnvoll eingesetzt werden können.
Das Vorhaben wird im Rahmen des Europäischen Fonds für regionale Entwicklung (EFRE/JTF NRW, Förderkennzeichen EFRE-20801446) über 33 Monate mit rund zwei Millionen Euro gefördert.
UltrasonAIc ist in den BAM- Aktivitätsfeldern Anlagensicherheit und Prozesstechnik sowie Degradation von Werkstoffen verankert. Hier entwickelt die BAM u.a. Verfahren, mit denen sich Schäden erkennen und die Sicherheit technischer Bauteile über ihren Lebenszyklus bewerten lassen. Das Projekt soll diese Bewertung durch verlässliche KI-Unterstützung verbessern und leistet damit einen Beitrag zur übergeordneten BAM-Mission Sicherheit in Technik und Chemie.

Professor Jean Pierre Bergmann und sein Forschungsteam von der Technischen Universität Ilmenau haben den Thüringer Forschungspreis 2026 in der Kategorie „Angewandte Forschung“ gewonnen. Mit den Forschungsarbeiten zum Schweißen mit Hochleistungslasern gelang es dem Team des Fachgebiets Fertigungstechnik, den durch ungewollte Spritzer verursachten Masseverlust eines Werkstücks um über 90 Prozent zu reduzieren, was für verarbeitende Betriebe weniger Ausschuss, niedrigere Kosten für die Nacharbeit und eine nachhaltigere Produktion bedeutet. Der Thüringer Forschungspreis wird seit 1995 vom Freistaat Thüringen in den Kategorien „Grundlagenforschung“ und „Angewandte Forschung“ vergeben.
Die Photonik-Industrie ist in Thüringen ein wirtschaftliches Schwergewicht. Kein anderer Standort in Deutschland bietet eine vergleichbare Dichte an Spezialisten für Optik, Lasertechnik, Produktionstechnik und Präzisionstechnologien. Mit 195 Unternehmen, einen Umsatz von vier Milliarden Euro und fast 20.000 Beschäftigten in Industrie und Forschung zählt die Photonik zu einem der wichtigsten Wirtschaftsbranchen in Thüringen. Doch beim Schweißen mit Hochleistungslasern – etwa in der Automobil- oder Medizintechnik – gab es für die Industrie bislang ein großes Problem: Will man schneller schweißen, um effizienter zu produzieren, steigt die Zahl der Fehler sprunghaft an. Besonders gravierend: Spritzer. Diese winzigen, flüssigen Metallpartikel werden aus dem Schmelzbad geschleudert, zerstören die Oberfläche des Fertigungsteils und machen aufwändige und teure Nacharbeiten nötig.
Dem Forscherteam um Professor Jean Pierre Bergmann, Leiter des Fachgebiets Fertigungstechnik an der TU Ilmenau, gelang es mit einem neuartigen Schweißverfahren, den Masseverlust durch Spritzer um über 90 Prozent zu reduzieren. Für die kleinen und mittleren Betriebe des verarbeitenden Gewerbes, die Thüringen prägen, bedeutet das weniger Ausschuss, niedrigere Kosten und eine nachhaltigere Produktion.
Um Spritzer beim Laserschweißen zu verhindern, musste das Forscherteam der Ilmenauer Fertigungstechnik zunächst verstehen, was während des Schweißvorgangs im Inneren des Werkstücks passiert, dort, wo das Auge nicht hineinschauen kann. Aber modernste Techniken wie Hochgeschwindigkeitskameras, Bildverarbeitung und Simulationen – und der Teilchenbeschleuniger der European Synchrotron Radiation Facility im französische Grenoble, eine europäische Forschungseinrichtung, die wie ein riesiges, extrem starkes Mikroskop funktioniert. Mit hochenergetischer sogenannter Synchrotronstrahlung – dem weltweit intensivsten Röntgenlicht, das milliardenfach heller ist als herkömmliche Röntgengeräte – kann sie Materie durchleuchten und die Struktur von Atomen und Molekülen bis ins kleinste Detail sichtbar machen.
In hochauflösenden Scans bekamen die Ilmenauer Forscher die extrem schnellen Vorgänge im Inneren der Dampfkapillare, der winzigen, mit Metalldampf gefüllten Kanäle, die beim Tiefschweißen entstehen, in Echtzeit zu sehen. Die Aufnahmen zeigten: Spritzer entstehen durch ein komplexes Zusammenspiel von Metalldampf, Schmelzbadwellen und instabilen Kapillaren. Mithilfe von computergestützten Strömungssimulationen gelang es dem Forschungsteam erstmals, ein vollständiges Modell dieser Mechanismen zu entwickeln.
Dieses tiefe Verständnis der Prozesse, die sich beim Laserschweißen im Innern des Werkstücks abspielen, erlaubte es den Forschern, gezielte Gegenmaßnahmen gegen die Spritzerbildung zu entwickeln. Intelligente Strahlprofile, etwa mit überlagerten Strahlenformen, verlangsamen die Schmelzbadströmungen und erleichtern so das Entweichen von Metalldampf, eine der Ursachen für die ungewollten Spritzer. Zudem positionierten sie Gasdüsen so präzise, dass die Wechselwirkung zwischen Gas und Schmelze zu einer Reduzierung der Spritzer führte.
Die Ergebnisse der Forschungsarbeiten und ein daraus abgeleitete Patent „made in Thüringen“ wurden bereits in Fachzeitschriften veröffentlicht, sodass High-Tech-Laser in der Industrie weltweit präziser, effizienter und kostengünstiger arbeiten.

title: Pairing industrial AI autonomy and human control
content:
In partnership with
Industrial intelligence
Living digital twins are helping industrial plants run more like living systems, and setting the stage for industries that work in sync.
Most people associate industrial environments with cold steel and clockwork machinery. Functionally, though, a plant or factory is more like a living thing: It has a pulse, even a metabolism. It goes through wear and tear as it ages, and signs of deteriorating health often show up as barely perceptible irregularities.
Digital twin technology has long aimed to mirror that dynamism and model anomalies that may be symptomatic of larger problems. But earlier implementations were a few beats behind physical reality; they were incapable of real-time analysis and unable to proactively address any issues detected. They focused more on simulation, observation and what-if scenario planning, rather than closed-loop execution. Rather than serving as a digital mirror of reality that can spot anomalies or suggest optimizations, a living digital twin combines a dynamic, high-fidelity digital representation of complex operations with the capacity to intervene in the physical world through operations and control systems.
AI is at the center of this change. Rob McGreevy, chief product officer at AVEVA, likens newer, AI-infused digital twins to organisms that grow and evolve. These “living” versions are adaptive, evergreen models of a plant’s assets and processes. Because they keep pace with live conditions and connect systems that once ran in isolation, they provide a previously missing layer of visibility and orchestration that better reflects the organic rhythms of the facility itself.
Now, agentic AI is also enabling industrial systems to move beyond diagnostics or suggestions and act of their own accord. As the technology progresses toward greater autonomy, it’s starting to develop the reflexes for a kind of industrial homeostasis, in which small, constant adjustments keep a plant or factory healthy and humming.
All that said, human judgment and operator oversight still play an instrumental role by defining what healthy looks like to begin with—and flagging when AI systems are falling out of alignment. Living digital twins provide the means for human engineers to monitor what AI is doing and ensure execution is on track.
technologies
Living digital twins link engineering and design information with real-time operational data through a digital thread, or a connected record of an asset that follows it through its lifecycle. A couple of notable technological shifts have helped string this thread together: Sensors (which have gotten more affordable in recent years) now stream telemetry from IoT devices and industrial control equipment, and software platforms bring that information into user-friendly interfaces. Predictive and physics-based models can also provide AI-enriched insights into how a machine or process might behave.

The lenses through which operators view digital twins have evolved in turn. “You can look at the digital twin through the lens of sustainability: What are my emissions?” says McGreevy. “Or, through the lens of maintenance: Is this asset performing in a healthy way? Or, through a performance metric: Is it producing the number of widgets I need?”

survey of manufacturers
(opens in new tab)
, 66% said they are using or plan to use agentic AI in their operations, and 40% expect some degree of factory autonomy by 2030. At the same time, they’re wary of the potential risks: In

(opens in new tab)

“There is a lot more refinement to be done, a lot more proof points, testing, and validation needed,” McGreevy says about the ongoing process of making AI autonomous. In the near term, McGreevy expects agentic AI to follow the path seen in other industrial technologies like SCADA systems. “The ‘S’ in SCADA means supervisory, and supervisory means there’s a human in the middle,” he says. He sees AI working mostly in that advisory mode for the foreseeable future, with full autonomy limited to narrow, highly repetitive tasks.
As for the role human operators play, the day-to-day is evolving. Workers who once specialized in a single process line or maintenance task can now take on multiple disciplines. They can spend less time and effort approving routine actions one by one, and more on defining acceptable operating limits. Because AI can reinforce patterns in the data it receives, catching missteps early is a core part of the job. Human knowledge and experience in interpreting what AI is seeing and doing is instrumental.
Governance on a company- and industry-wide scale, too, needs to adapt to the times. Organizations must establish clear guardrails for which decisions AI can make on its own and how its actions are monitored and audited. Still, many have yet to set up comprehensive safeguards: In a recent study from
AVEVA and IMD
(opens in new tab)
, 43% of organizations said AI has changed decision-making and accountability across ecosystem partners only slightly or not at all, while just 23% reported a significant or fundamental change. (Only 27% reported sharing data substantially or extensively with partners.)
In the meantime, regulators are starting to define some of the rules. The EU AI Act classifies certain AI safety components used in critical infrastructure as high-risk and imposes requirements for human oversight. Companies are setting up their own structures as well; AVEVA, for one, has a responsible AI governance board and a published set of principles for how AI is developed and deployed.
Real-world
Inside the semi-autonomous systems already running, that oversight looks different from one deployment to another. In some cases, an operator approves every action; in others, AI acts on its own while people oversee and define the boundaries it can operate within. McGreevy cites several examples of what machine autonomy and human-plus-machine collaboration looks like among AVEVA customers:
At Saudi Aramco’s Yanbu refinery, optimization algorithms adjust production in a closed loop, with operators overseeing as needed. At its Ras Tanura refinery, the algorithms recommend changes, and operators decide whether to implement them.
Nestlé uses AI optimization at Nesquik plants to tune the industrial dryers used to produce powdered beverage ingredients. In a landmark test, this tuning reduced energy use by 16%, while improving quality and yield.
At Thailand’s SCG Chemicals, an AI-supported digital twin spanning engineering, operations, and maintenance monitors asset health and flags potential failures. The company reports 99% plant reliability and a ninefold return on investment within six months.
The National Laboratory of the Rockies in the U.S. has built a generative AI model for grid control rooms to provide oversight at scale. The model supports operators with renewable energy forecasting and estimates of grid conditions.
The same synchronization that was once missing from individual plants’ technology systems has also been lacking on a larger scale. “Manufacturing and critical infrastructure have operated as siloed systems for the last 50 years,” says McGreevy. But certain emerging technologies, he suggests, are creating opportunities for more holistic coordination.
On an enterprise level, this might involve the integration of physical AI: systems that pair robotics and sensing technologies with AI-powered decision-making. Drones that fly over pipelines and power lines, for instance, can feed visual inspection data to algorithms that spot gas leaks and other hazards. Not only does this create a more accurate and interconnected flow of information, but it spares humans from needing to physically enter potentially dangerous environments. “The robotics-meets-software convergence will mean fewer incidents, fewer outages, and a more sustainable way of operating,” McGreevy predicts.

A bigger-picture version extends beyond any one plant or process to entire industrial networks, something McGreevy dubs the “integrated value chain.” “Living digital twins make digital manifestations of the entire value chain possible,” he says. “This allows companies to react quickly to supply chain changes, demand changes, tariffs, and material availability.”
Amid today’s realities of turbulent geopolitics and shifting regulatory demands, such resilience will be “an absolute necessity,” adds McGreevy. “Without it, it will be very hard to run an effective business.”

title: The Download: dead startups fueling AI and interspecies communication
content:
The Download: dead startups fueling AI and interspecies communication
Plus: Hackers have disrupted the US Federal Election Commission’s website.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
AI labs are buying data from dead startups to train their models
When Keelan Miskell began winding down his crypto startup, he didn’t think its data was worth much. But he’s since turned the company’s digital archives into tens of thousands of dollars, selling its codebase and workspace data.
He’s part of a growing market in which companies that help shut down startups sell their data to AI labs. Demand has grown as training labs hit the limits of public and synthetic datasets, with buyers seeking real-world records to help train AI agents. But the sales raise legal and ethical questions.
Read the full story on the AI labs buying up the remains of failed startups.
—Matthew King
Are we there yet? Interspecies communication
Humans are far from the only species with a gift for gab, and our furry, feathered, and finned friends could have a lot to tell us.
Decoding how animals communicate with one another could reveal the inner lives of other species—and give humans a window onto how they see the world. A growing arsenal of devices and advances in AI have made it easier to study their howls, squeaks, and clicks, but making sense of it all remains complex.
Find out how close we are to interspecies communication.
—Cassandra Willyard
This story is part of “Are we there yet?”, our series that takes stock of six technologies that have long promised to change the world—and scores them on a progress meter. We’re exploring each one in The Download, so stay tuned, and subscribe to read the rest of the stories in our new Impossible issue.
MIT Technology Review Narrated: what it would take to build a city on the moon
The US and China are racing to build bases on the moon, with NASA hoping to establish a small lunar city by the end of the century. But the moon is a tremendously hostile place to set up camp.
A sprawling lunar base must be safe for its inhabitants, protected from falling asteroids, endless cosmic radiation, razor-sharp lunar dust, and torturous temperature swings. It also must be somewhat self-sustaining.
That will require autonomous robots, nuclear power, and a way to use the moon’s resources to keep the base operating. But the chief obstacle may be one of political will.
This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts. Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released.
The must-reads
I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.
1 Hackers have disrupted the US Federal Election Commission’s website
The FEC filing system went offline a week before the midterms. (Reuters $)
+ The attack is hiding spending data during the costliest midterms ever. (Gizmodo)
+ Social media platforms are struggling to contain AI election lies. (Guardian)
+ Software flaws in US voting machines threaten election security. (Axios)
+ A blueprint for using AI to strengthen democracy. (MIT Technology Review)
2 Starlink restrictions have driven US allies to rethink their dependence
Restrictions in Ukraine have spooked officials across Europe. (Bloomberg $)
+ And given European firms a new pitch for their rival services. (Axios)
+ An Israeli spy firm allegedly targeted Starlink users. (Reuters $)
+ Stratospheric internet could take off this year. (MIT Technology Review)
3 Greenhouse gas levels keep reaching new records worldwide
Carbon dioxide, methane, and nitrous oxide are all on the up. (New Scientist $)
+ Trump is making it easier for fossil fuel companies to leak methane. (Verge)
+ The IPCC is fighting for survival. (Nature)
+ How to study a swiftly melting climate disaster. (MIT Technology Review)
4 Monkeys’ brains have revealed new clues about consciousness
Their neural activity encodes images that escape their awareness. (Nature)
+ Bees’ feelings are also changing views of consciousness. (New Scientist $)
+ Debates over AI consciousness are a trap. (MIT Technology Review)
5 Chinese scientists have developed a catalyst to make Mars rocket fuel
It converts Martian atmospheric carbon dioxide into liquid methanol. (SCMP)
6 Tech billionaires have teamed up against California’s wealth tax
Sergey Brin, Eric Schmidt, and others have funded a major campaign. (NYT $)
7 Delaware plans to let AI agents run entire businesses
The proposal could let owners evade responsibility for harm. (Ars Technica)
+ A better web for AI agents could hurt humans. (MIT Technology Review)
8 Palmer Luckey has unveiled plans for American-made military laptops
Anduril will build rugged PCs in Ohio using Qualcomm chips. (WSJ $)
9 Gen Z is turning away from the social media it grew up with
Young people are fueling a boom in digital detox tools. (Guardian)
10 Trump now wants to ban the term “artificial intelligence”
He’s demanding we all start using “Super Intelligence.” (Gizmodo)
Quote of the day
“For the next two years, we’re going to be living in a state where, on average, every week there is a critical, internet-wide vulnerability.”
—Matthew Prince, Cloudflare’s chief executive, tells the New York Times that AI is currently finding software vulnerabilities quicker than they can be patched.
One more thing
Inside the controversial tree farms powering Apple’s carbon-neutral goal
In 2020, Apple set a goal to become net zero by the end of the decade. To hit that target, the company is offsetting its emissions by planting millions of eucalyptus trees in Brazil.
Apple is betting that the strategy will lead to a greener future. But critics warn that the industrial tree farms will do more harm than good.
Here’s why the plans have sparked a backlash.
—Gregory Barber
We can still have nice things
A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line.)
+ Ugly shoes have become beautifully mainstream.
+ Scientists have built a stunning new simulation of the early universe.
+ Guitarist Kent Nishimura has stripped Thriller back to a mesmerising acoustic performance.
+ A photographer who snapped punks and mods in 1980 has tracked them down for an emotional reunion 46 years later.

title: 【奋斗100天】重庆青山电控升压快充技术实现突破：800V车型充电效率再提升
content:
近日，重庆青山电控升压快充技术实现突破应用并在多款车型搭载。该技术让800V高压平台车型接入400V充电桩时，也能实现满功率稳定充电，填补了企业在新能源车辆升压充电板块的技术空白。
快充要“快”，先看充电桩。当前国内直流快充网络仍以400V电压平台为主，约70%以上的公共直流充电桩额定电压在750V以下，难以满足800V高压车型对大功率快充的需求。当800V车型接入400V充电桩时，充电功率往往受限于桩端电压平台，实际只能达到额定功率的40%—60%，快充体验大打折扣。
行业常规做法是增设独立的Boost升压模块，但需额外配置升压电感器、独立散热回路、高压线束等部件，单套系统会增加约1.5-2升体积和金钱成本，还因额外磁性元件损耗使系统效率下降1-2个百分点。
重庆青山EDS3项目团队给出创新解决方案
团队基于“充电时电机定子绕组复用为Boost电感”的思路，从PCB结构、布局与控制策略等多维度优化，
创新采用三环控制、跳桩检测、转子抑制等技术，实现在不新增独立升压模块的前提下完成高效升压充电，
并兼容国标、欧标等不同电压平台的充电桩。
从技术细节看，方案通过抽头（Tap）技术重构绕组，从电机绕组引出抽头，把负责驱动的电机电控，改造为高效的升压电源；基于两相绕组构成的两相交错Boost并联结构，可降低母线侧的合成电流纹波，再以三环级联控制精准稳定充电过程，并以跳桩检测与转子抑制技术应对充电异常、稳定车辆姿态；同时配合热管理模块，把温度控制在安全区间，实现安全高效升压充电。
该方案实测升压充电效率可达98%-98.5%，
较传统方案提升0.5-1个百分点；充电电流纹波可降至5%以内，母线电容纹波电压下降60%以上；峰值充电功率可达120kW，支持250A以上充电电流。
目前，该方案已在多款车型搭载运用。
这是公司在电控核心技术上坚持自主创新、补齐产品能力短板的一次突破。未来公司将围绕客户需求和市场趋势，持续拓展该技术应用场景，加快电驱电控技术迭代升级，以更具竞争力的产品服务客户。

title: 四国合作落地，小鹏集团加速布局中东非及西巴尔干市场
content:
近日，小鹏集团全球化布局迎来重要进展：相继与尼日利亚、阿曼、科威特、阿尔巴尼亚四国本地合作伙伴达成经销合作，完成四国市场落地。
本次落地市场横跨海湾、西非与西巴尔干区域。小鹏携手本土合作伙伴，持续织密跨区域合作网络，为后续车型导入、品牌建设、销售及售后服务体系搭建夯实基础。
小鹏将稳步推进全球化战略，拓展全球智能出行边界，以创新科技为各地用户带来智能、便捷、绿色的出行体验。
织密本地化布局网络
9 月至 10 月，四国经销合作协议陆续完成签署：9 月 1 日，阿尔巴尼亚合作协议于广州小鹏总部签约；9 月 21 日、9 月 24 日，尼日利亚、阿曼合作协议在迪拜完成签署；10 月 26 日，小鹏与科威特合作伙伴在当地小鹏展厅签约落地。
尼日利亚经销协议签约现场
阿曼经销协议签约现场
科威特经销协议签约现场
阿尔巴尼亚经销协议签约现场
四个市场区位各异，各有看点。阿曼与科威特同为海湾合作委员会（GCC）成员国，阿曼正积极推进经济多元化，科威特经济发展水平较高，为高端汽车市场提供了发展空间，两国合作将进一步完善小鹏在海湾地区的布局。尼日利亚是非洲人口第一大国，消费群体庞大、长期增长潜力突出，是小鹏拓展西非的重要一步。阿尔巴尼亚位于西巴尔干地区，合作的落地进一步拓展了小鹏在这一区域的市场布局。
依托本地合作伙伴，小鹏将循序渐进地推进品牌建设、车型导入与渠道布局，逐步完善当地的销售与售后服务体系。
中东非及西巴尔干多点并进
迈入 2026 年，小鹏中东非市场的拓展全面提速。在品牌上市方面，摩洛哥、突尼斯、巴林、毛里求斯四个市场相继上市，其中毛里求斯是小鹏中东非区域首个右舵车市场，进一步适配当地法规与用户习惯；在经销合作方面，科威特、尼日利亚、阿曼、阿尔巴尼亚四个市场陆续推进经销协议签署，上市与签约双线并行。
后续，小鹏将与各国合作伙伴同心同行，把智能座舱、智能辅助驾驶等核心技术带到当地，并逐步完善售后服务体系，让更多用户感受智能出行的魅力。
助推全球化发展进程
中东非市场的持续突破，是小鹏集团全球化战略的生动实践。小鹏自挪威起步，稳步深耕欧洲，并拓展至中东、东南亚等区域，目前销售网络已覆盖全球 83 个国家和地区。
以技术为帆，以伙伴为舟。未来，小鹏集团将继续稳步推进全球化布局，持续拓展全球出行边界，用创新科技，为世界各地用户带来更智能、更便捷、更绿色的出行新体验。

title: 安森美：面向无人机嵌入式系统的先进电源、控制和连接解决方案 | 上篇
content:
现代无人机已不再是简单的无线电遥控飞行器，而是集成了推进、电源转换、传感、实时控制、通信、成像、诊断和安全功能的紧凑型机电系统。在工业级无人机领域，核心工程目标是在最大限度减轻重量、降低热损耗和布线复杂度的同时，尽可能延长飞行时间和提升有效载荷能力。因此，配电和内部通信构成了系统架构的基础。推进、传感、通信及有效载荷电子设备均须依靠同一电池电源实现高效可靠的运行。
本文为安森美（onsemi）《面向无人机嵌入式系统的先进电源、控制和连接解决方案》白皮书上篇，将聚焦无人机的动力与感知中枢，深度剖析如何通过高能效功率开关、精密栅极驱动及稳健传感接口，夯实飞行控制与云台稳定的底层基石。
随着无人机在基础设施巡检、精准农业、建筑测绘、应急响应、环境监测、物流和安防等应用中展现出切实价值，无人机市场正在持续增长。针对不同的任务，需要采用不同的平台。多旋翼无人机更适用于悬停、垂直起降和空间受限的作业。固定翼无人机在远距离任务中具备更优的巡航效率和更广的区域覆盖能力。单旋翼平台虽支持更高的有效载荷，但增加了机械复杂度；混合垂直起降 (VTOL) 系统则兼具垂直起飞与固定翼续航优势。
尽管存在上述差异，大多数无人机平台的电子需求基本相似。推进系统需要大电流开关和精确的电机控制，而飞行控制器则依赖稳定的低压轨、低噪声时序、存储器、保护电路及传感器接口。相机、激光雷达、雷达、热传感器和通信模块等有效载荷需要纯净的电源和可靠的数据传输。电池保护和电流监测同样至关重要，可防止子系统故障波及整机。随着无人机向超视距 (BVLOS) 飞行、AI 辅助导航和多传感器自主化方向发展，高效电源转换和确定性通信的重要性日益凸显。
在许多无人机中，推进级消耗了大部分可用能量，而周边电子设备决定了能量的利用效率。无人机不仅需要高效的 DC-DC 转换来为飞控和机载电子设备生成稳定电压轨，也需要紧凑的电机驱动电路在尽量降低额外热损耗的同时管理无刷直流 (BLDC) 功率级，还需要精确的位置反馈来稳定云台或执行器驱动机构等运动子系统。如果上述功能块实现效果不佳，后果不仅是效率降低， 还会导致控制质量下降、热应力增加、任务可靠性降低等问题。
因此，行业不再将无人机简单视为“电池 + 电子调速器 (ESC)”的组合。随着高端无人机平台拓展至商业和防务相关任务，对环境适应性、能效和控制精度的要求显著提高。无人机设计人员因此有充分理由选用功能不止于基础电气能力的辅助器件。有效的器件有助于简化电源架构、减少外部元件数量、改善热性能并增强整体系统弹性，且不会增加不必要的设计复杂度。
低压 MOSFET 与栅极驱动器用于推进系统和功率开关
低压 MOSFET是多个无人机子系统中的关键器件，涵盖电子调速器 (ESC)、电池开关与保护电路、DC-DC 转换器、负载开关及有效载荷配电单元。在推进系统中，此类器件用于驱动 BLDC 电机的三相半桥级，其导通损耗和开关损耗直接影响效率、发热量和飞行时间。在电源架构中，MOSFET 用于电池路径控制、反极性保护、热插拔功能，并向传感器、相机、激光雷达和通信模块提供稳压电源。
安森美低压MOSFET 产品组合（包括T10、T8、T6 和PTNG 系列）具备低RDS(on)、高电流承载能力和高效散热封装。低 RDS(on) 可最大限度减少大电流运行时的导通损耗，而低栅极电荷则可降低 PWM 电机控制和电源转换级中的开关损耗。这一特性在多旋翼无人机中尤为重要，因为多个 ESC 通道同时运行时，即便单个开关效率仅有微小提升，也能显著降低总发热量和电池功耗。Power 33、Power 56、Power 88、TCPAK 和 TOLL 等封装改善了电流处理能力和散热性能，对于 PCB 面积和散热能力受限的紧凑型无人机设计极具价值。
MOSFET 性能与栅极驱动器密切相关。NCV51511、NCP51513、NCP81075、FAN8811T 和 NCD83591 等器件为电机驱动器和电源转换器提供高侧和低侧栅极驱动控制。栅极快速充放电可减少转换损耗，而精确的死区时间控制有助于防止半桥电路直通。在紧凑型无人机电子设备中，此举提高了开关效率，简化了 PCB 设计，并增强了动态负载条件下的可靠性。
用于位置反馈、力反馈和压力反馈的传感器接口
精确传感在提升无人机系统飞行稳定性和有效载荷性能方面发挥着关键作用。在 BLDC 电机驱动中，精确的转子位置反馈可改善换向质量，尤其在低速运行、高扭矩工况及快速瞬态机动期间效果显著。NCS32100电感式位置传感器利用转子和定子 PCB 布局实现非接触式角度测量。与光学编码器相比，电感式传感在严苛的无人机运行环境中更具稳健性，因为灰尘、湿气、振动和污染物可能损害光学编码器的长期可靠性。
NCS32100 提供适用于电机换向和闭环速度控制的高分辨率位置反馈。在推进应用中，精确的转子角度测量有助于减小扭矩脉动、改善相位对齐并提高整体电机效率。凭借高角度精度和高速运行能力，NCS32100 非常适合无人机推进系统中常用的紧凑型电机和高转速旋转组件。
针对负载、力和压力测量，NCV7192 桥式信号调理接口支持从电阻式惠斯通电桥传感器（包括应变片和压阻式传感器）采集低电平差分信号。NCV7192 集成了低噪声可编程增益与偏移级、温漂与传感器非线性数字补偿、基于 EEPROM 的配置存储、内置诊断功能，并支持比例模拟输出或 SENT 数字输出。在无人机平台中，NCV7192 可连接相应的桥式传感器，实现有效载荷称重、着陆力测量、结构应变监测、推力相关力检测或压力测量等功能。通过将模拟前端调理、补偿和诊断功能集成于单一器件，NCV7192 减少了外部元件数量，提高了全温区测量一致性，并简化了传感器模块设计。
无人机云台控制与稳定
云台是一种精密机电子系统，可在偏航、俯仰和横滚方向上稳定相机，最大限度减少由振动、机身运动和快速姿态变化引起的图像模糊。在无人机应用中，有效的云台控制不仅取决于精确的位置反馈和平滑的电机换向，而且依赖于能以极小抖动和发热产生精细扭矩校正的高效功率级。
采用 NCS32100 绝对编码器、NCD83591 三相栅极驱动器和 NTMFS0D9N04XM MOSFET 可构建紧凑的三轴解决方案。NCS32100 为各轴提供精确角度位置反馈，无需启动归零即可实现快速准确的稳定控制。NCD83591 支持平滑的 BLDC 电机控制并集成电流检测，有助于维持稳定扭矩并减少可见的相机抖动。NTMFS0D9N04XM MOSFET 以低导通损耗和高效开关完善了逆变级，有助于降低紧凑型有效载荷模块的热应力。上述器件协同工作，可在严苛的无人机环境下实现精确的相机定位、平滑的三轴稳定，并保障云台的可靠运行。
优秀的动力与电机控制是无人机飞得稳、控得准的前提，但当机载传感器与外设呈几何级增长时，机身内部的“神经网络”与配电架构又该如何应对？

title: 村田亮相SAECCE 2026：以高可靠性元器件构筑智能移动出行的坚实底座
content:
中国苏州，2026年10月28日——在刚刚启幕的第三十三届中国汽车工程学会年会暨展览会（SAECCE 2026）上，村田制作所（以下简称“村田”）携面向智能驾驶、人形机器人及低空经济的高可靠性元器件与系统级解决方案亮相（展位号：C馆C308），并将于“舱驾融合软硬件协同与中央计算架构”论坛发表《精准之源，稳健之基：村田IMU与EMC技术赋能智能驾驶》主题演讲。依托车载级高可靠性产品线，村田重点展示了应对智能汽车与新兴移动出行工具在供电稳定、信号完整与精准感知方面共性挑战的技术实践。
当前，汽车产业正加速向CASE趋势演进。随着Zonal（区域）架构与中央计算架构的普及，传感器融合、OTA升级、48V系统导入以及大数据处理带来了系统功耗与传输数据量的激增，这对元器件的频率特性、噪声抑制、散热及安装空间提出更高需求。在这一逻辑下，村田展示的重点并非单一器件的参数竞赛，而是围绕稳定供电与高速信号完整性的系统级支撑能力。
电容器：面向SoC供电的封装内与主板协同方案
随着智驾SoC算力的指数级跃升，芯片功耗激增导致电源分配网络（PDN）的阻抗控制与瞬态响应难度陡增，单纯堆砌电容数量已无法满足大电流、高频率下的供电稳定性诉求。针对这一痛点，村田的电容器方案同时覆盖芯片封装内部（In-PKG）与主板两个层面：主板侧以高容值密度和低ESL方案保证供电稳定性，可以支持小型高容以及三端子低ESL MLCC 实现SoC板极PDN阻抗优化；封装内侧也可提供多种形态电容方案，实现芯片更高性能和高可靠性的同时，满足小尺寸、高容值、低ESL、薄形化等规格需求。此外，村田还提供无偿的PI（电源完整性）仿真支持，协助客户在设计阶段完成阻抗优化与电源瞬态仿真。
电感器：PoC方案保障SerDes高速链路稳定传输
面对车载网络高速化趋势，村田的一站式PoC电感解决方案助力汽车、机器人乃至 eVTOL，实现高精度系统性能与高可靠传输。村田提供覆盖ADP、ASA、FPD-LINK、GMSL、HSMT、MIPI A-PHY、R-IRC等主流SerDes标准的PoC电感产品阵容，通过有效隔离电源噪声，确保复杂电磁环境下的信号保真。同时提供PoC回路参考设计、仿真模型及多据点SerDes仿真与实测支持，帮助客户降低试错成本与量产风险。此外，村田拥有完整的大电流、小尺寸磁珠，和全协议覆盖的信号线共模电感产品线，有效抑制电源与信号线的干扰，保障系统稳定运行。
IMU传感器：以“一芯多域”支撑功能安全与OTA升级
针对L2+及以上自动驾驶对高精度位置检测的需求，村田IMU提供六自由度（6DoF）运动测量能力，加速度计22ug、陀螺仪0.4°/h的零偏不稳定性典型值，以及加速度2mg、陀螺仪0.05-0.15°/s的典型值全温温漂，并具备优秀的全寿命性能一致性和振动下性能稳定性。在系统层面，村田通过硬件指标前置规划支持OTA远程升级辅助驾驶等级，以一颗高性能IMU覆盖AD/ADAS、ESC、底盘控制、大灯调节等多个系统，帮助客户降低总成本。此外，村田在中国的销售与技术支持网络，正与IMU模组厂、OEM、SoC厂家及算法公司形成紧密协同，贴近本土ADAS供应链的迭代节奏。
新兴版图：将车载级可靠性平移至人形机器人与低空经济
智能移动出行技术边界正从汽车向人形机器人与低空经济延伸，两者对小型化、高可靠性及稳定传输的需求与车载场景高度同源。在人形机器人领域，村田依托严苛车载验证的品质体系，提供涵盖MLCC、电感、IMU、无线模块、电源等多元产品组合，此外3D力传感器、电机散热等前瞻性方案，将支撑关节模组、感知系统等在狭小空间内的高频可靠运行。面向eVTOL，村田以符合AEC-Q200的车规级陶瓷电容、高温静噪滤波器、DLW系列高速共模扼流圈、耐高温高可靠性电源滤波电路用电感器及IMU传感器，满足飞控、航电与动力系统对耐高温、抗振动及信号完整性的极致要求，将车规级可靠性平移至低空经济核心系统，助力新兴移动出行安全稳健发展。
开放协作：以元器件为支点，缩短下一代技术的“验证到量产”路径
村田围绕OEM、Tier1及IC厂商构建早期介入的深度协同模式，在新项目定义阶段即导入元器件提案，将适配前移至共同定义。在高速链路领域，其PoC电感方案已获多家主流SerDes芯片厂商验证，助力客户缩短研发周期；在本土智驾生态中，亦与IMU模组厂、SoC及算法公司紧密协作，贴合中国市场节奏。面对架构演进与应用场景拓展，村田始终以稳定供电、完整信号与可信赖感知为核心，依托扎实材料工艺、严密工程验证及开放生态协作，为下一代智能移动出行提供可靠的基础硬件保障。

title: ImportGenius: AI, Trade Intelligence and Supply Chain Risk
content:
ImportGenius: AI, Trade Intelligence and Supply Chain Risk
Prioritise Us
on Google
ImportGenius offers a source of customs and bill-of-lading information covering more than 25 countries, with data sourced from government customs agencies and other public trade records. Credit: ImportGenius
ImportGenius executives James Orr and Daniel Mikhail explain how AI, customs data and global supply chain visibility are reshaping trade intelligence
The pressures for supply chain leaders to identify potential supply chain risks, whether those are from
geopolitical
disruption or shifts in the competitiveness of individual suppliers, have never been greater than at present.
Data has become an increasingly important element of competitive advantage. But supply chain leaders understand that the strength of the data they are relying on to identify
disruption
, assess competitors and explain strategic decisions is a key variable.
ImportGenius is a supplier of international trade and supply chain intelligence. Through advanced data management technologies, the firm is able to help its clients make sense of hundreds of millions of shipping manifests and customs records from government agencies and private companies around the world.
Artificial intelligence
can be used to improve trade data quality, support supplier discovery, improve shipment analytics and sharpen supply chain mapping. However, the successful application of AI relies on its use as a support for human decision-making, rather than when it operates without controls.
AI moves beyond the chatbot
James Orr, Chief Product and Technology Officer at ImportGenius, says the company is applying AI across its data infrastructure rather than treating it solely as a conversational interface.
“The opportunity is not simply to put a chatbot on top of trade data. It is to use AI inside the data pipeline, where it can improve classification, correct anomalies and help customers work with information they can trust,” James adds.
ImportGenius describes its platform as a source of customs and bill-of-lading information covering more than 25 countries, with data sourced from government customs agencies and other public trade records.
The platform’s use cases include:
Competitor shipment monitoring to identify who companies buy from and sell to.
Supplier discovery based on shipment history, product descriptions and trade relationships.
Trade volume analysis using shipment counts, weight and estimated TEUs.
HS code enrichment for US maritime records that do not publish standard classifications.
Supply chain mapping across Tier 1, Tier 2 and further supplier relationships.
Tariff and country-of-origin analysis to assess exposure to changing trade conditions.
Lead generation based on importers, exporters, products and shipping lanes.
Multilingual trade-data search across datasets published in languages such as Spanish, Hindi and Russian.
Data governance is the foundation of AI
Orr stresses that trade data is inherently imperfect. Customs records may be supplied in different formats, languages and standards. Some information is entered manually, while other records may originate in scanned documents.
For enterprise users, this creates a governance challenge. A dataset can be faithfully reproduced from its source and still produce misleading results if errors are aggregated across millions of records.
ImportGenius said its data governance approach includes: data lineage, chain of custody, data quality monitoring, data preservation, transparent corrections and model confidence controls.
Orr gave an example involving US maritime data for the Port of Baltimore. A single declaration reportedly included an implausible weight of three trillion kilograms. When aggregated, the error suggested that Turkey represented 91% of trade through the port by weight.
The example illustrates why data quality matters. A single abnormal record may have little effect on a shipment search, but it can distort a market analysis, country comparison or supply chain forecast. The solution favoured by ImportGenius is to preserve both versions: the original source value and a corrected estimate designed for aggregate analysis.
Shipment data needs correction before analysis
One of the distinctions that James draws is between data cleansing and data imputation.
Data cleansing identifies and corrects errors in information already present. Data imputation adds a new value based on available signals, historical patterns and a defined model.
The company described several applications:
Weight correction: identifying values that are materially above or below a reasonable range.
TEU estimation: calculating twenty-foot equivalent units where volume information is incomplete.
Container-size validation: identifying impossible or inconsistent container descriptions.
Text parsing: extracting useful signals from unstructured shipment descriptions.
HS code imputation: predicting product classifications from descriptions and related evidence.
ImportGenius said its Lighthouse analytics environment contains approximately 170 million US maritime import records covering the previous decade. That scale makes manual review impractical and increases the importance of system-level modelling.
The TEU model must account for different cargo types, including: containerised cargo, less-than-container-load shipments, breakbulk cargo, grain and oil and inconsistent container-size descriptions.
The company said its estimates can also be compared with macroeconomic and government statistics, including data from the Bureau of Transportation Statistics, to assess whether the aggregated picture is consistent with national trade activity.
AI adds HS codes to US maritime data
Harmonised System Codes classify traded goods internationally. The first six digits - HS6 - provide a globally standardised product classification, while additional digits may vary by country.
One complicating factor is that US maritime import and export records do not consistently publish HS codes. In order to circumvent this, ImportGenius has developed a machine-learning model to infer classifications from shipment descriptions and other signals.
The model uses a confidence-based approach. If an HS code appears directly in the product description, it can be extracted. Approximately 17% of relevant records contain an HS code directly in the product description, providing a particularly strong classification signal, according to ImportGenius. If the product description supports a specific classification, the model may assign an HS6 code.
Where a description supports a broad classification, the model may assign an HS2 or HS4 code.
However, there are cases where the description is ambiguous or unreadable, in which the record may remain unclassified. Finally, multiple HS codes may be returned where a shipment record contains several products.
The company’s public HS code materials state that its system combines a product-sanitising process with an AI classifier and applies an 80% or higher confidence threshold to displayed predictions.
The approach is most useful for aggregate analysis, such as comparing product categories across countries or suppliers. For highly specific searches, ImportGenius advises combining HS codes with keywords and other shipment fields.
Approximately 17% of relevant records contain an HS code directly in the product description, providing a particularly strong classification signal, according to ImportGenius.
Key uses for HS codes
Tariff assessment
Product searches
Customs compliance
Market analysis
Country-of-origin research
Import and export trend reporting
Global search connects trade datasets
Daniel Mikhail, Enterprise Sales Lead at ImportGenius, offers the example of a global search for coffee. The search combined product descriptions with HS code 0901, the 4-digit HS classification code for coffee.
The platform can use a single search to examine: product categories, HS codes, importers, exporters, countries of origin, shipping relationships, shipment volumes, date ranges and supplier networks.
Mikhail showed how analysts could use shipment data to understand whether goods are entering a market as one-off transactions or through consistent supply relationships.
The platform can reportedly present results by year, month, week or day, depending on the search and date range. Results can also be exported for further analysis in spreadsheets, customer relationship management systems or business intelligence tools.
Daniel Mikhail, Enterprise Sales Lead at ImportGenius, demonstrated a global search using coffee as an example. Credit: Daniel Mikhail/LinkedIn
Company profiling links shipments to business intelligence
ImportGenius introduced its Genius Company Profiler as a research tool combining web information with trade records. By accessing a company profile, clients can access information such as shipment history, company address, industry sectors, business model, value proposition, suppliers and countries of origin.
This meets the different needs of both supply chain professionals, who might need shipment intelligence to investigate a competitor, and sales professionals who need commercial research to identify active importers or potential customers.
The same workflow can support supplier vetting by showing a supplier’s customers, sourcing countries and apparent trade activity.
Key technology, data and ecosystem partners
1. US Customs and Border Protection (CBP)
Commissioner: Rodney S. Scott
Headquarters: Washington DC
US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) is the largest federal law enforcement agency within the US Department of Homeland Security. CBP is the primary source for US maritime import and export data. The records are delivered digitally and updated daily. The data includes bill-of-lading information used to analyse shipment activity, importers, exporters, ports and cargo descriptions.
2. Bureau of Transportation Statistics
Director: Rolf Schmitt (acting)
Headquarters: Washington DC
The Bureau of Transportation Statistics (BTS), part of the US Department of Transportation (DOT), is the US agency responsible for compiling, analysing, and publishing statistics on commercial aviation, multimodal freight activity, and transportation economics. BTS data is a source for macroeconomic and transport-level data, which is used by ImportGenius to help identify anomalies in weight, volume and shipment calculations.

title: The Returns Value Gap: ReBound’s Circularity Concerns
content:
The Returns Value Gap: ReBound’s Circularity Concerns
Prioritise Us
on Google
ReBound explores how retailers can tackle the returns value gap. Credit: Getty
Though circularity is becoming more of a sustainability strategy, ReBound explores the returns value gap and how to protect operational margins
As customers are buying online more and more, the returns and recommerce markets are growing.
With this comes a particular challenge for retailers, as they need to find value from returned stock – can it be resold, can it be recycled, does it need to be written off?
ReBound is a global returns management specialist, helping brands as they simplify the returns process with increased efficiency, resilience and profitability.
Rising supply chain priorities
In September, ReBound Returns and Advanced Supply Chain conducted a study, revealing a major gap between
retailer’s circularity ambitions
and the value they are generating from returned items.
The Circularity Index was conducted using research from 150 senior leaders at mid-to-large UK and European retailers. The study found that 86% of retailers have a policy in place that focuses on
circularity in returns
, looking at resale, repair, refurbishment and recycling. Circularity is a core priority in returns management for 27% of leaders.
Despite this, there is a major gap when transforming these strategies into commercial value. Out of all returned items, as many as 12% generate no value, and only 9% of retailers resell more than half of their returned products at full price. Half of retailers state that between 6% and 40% of all returned items are written off, destroyed or discarded.
However, leaders are consistently looking for opportunities to unlock value, with 82% of retailers thinking that enhanced recommerce strategies could generate additional value for up to half of their returned stock. Though efforts are already being made to recover value from 62% of retailers, value recovery is lacking behind – but ReBound explores solutions in its Circularity Index.
At a glance
90% of customers say they would buy again after a positive return experience
1 in 3 customer purchases will end in a return
67% of shoppers explore the return policy before purchasing an item
12% of returned items generate no value
62% of retailers make efforts to recover value from goods that cannot be resold
ReBound Returns processes more than one million items every month
Closing the gap
Value recovery is a difficult task, with transport, processing and technology integration all proving to be an added cost. There are also challenges of whether the stock is returned in good condition or not, as well as the risk to brand reputation if quality is not maintained.
Disconnected data on condition, location, environmental impact and more means that the most effective option is often overlooked. Instead, it becomes a question of whether the item gets written off, rather than if time and resources are going to be spent extracting value from it.
end-to-end visibility and automation
, leading organisations are gaining more value from their returns. It is helping them plan a solution and measure compliance, delays and value much more efficiently.
Other leaders are building a recommerce ecosystem, with 98% of leading
retailers running an integrated strategy
. These include specialist partners for repair, refurbishment, donation and recycling.
“Collaboration comes up again and again,” explains Inge Baars, Head of Sustainability at ReBound.
Inge Baars, Head of Logistics at ReBound
“Not just because the challenges are too big for any one organisation to solve, but because we also need each other to keep the energy and motivation going.
“There’s still so much improvement needed, and sometimes simply staying hopeful and keeping the momentum matters.”
Out of the retailers, 28% have achieved a Leading circularity score, driven by consistency, speed and follow-through. These organisations have seen greater value recovery than their peers, demonstrating that the gap can be closed.
Returns are rising in today’s market, but the leading retailers are approaching these returns as an
opportunity for circular and profitable
supply chains.
There’s still so much improvement needed, and sometimes simply staying hopeful and keeping the momentum matters.
Inge Baars, Head of Sustainability at ReBound
Key partners
CEO: Graham Best
HQ: Dewsbury, United Kingdom
ReBound is a returns management specialist providing
reverse logistics solutions
for retailers and brands. The company handles product returns, refurbishment, quality control, and redistribution services across fashion, beauty, and consumer goods sectors. They process millions of returned items annually, helping brands maximize value recovery while minimizing waste. Their operations focus on sustainable practices, extending product lifecycles through resale channels and recycling programs, supporting the circular economy.
Advanced Supply Chain
Managing Director: Keith Lawrence
HQ: Stoke-on-Trent, United Kingdom
Advanced Supply Chain Group provides end-to-end logistics solutions including warehousing, distribution, fulfillment, and freight management. They serve fashion, retail, and e-commerce sectors with technology-driven supply chain services. Their operations span multiple UK facilities offering scalable solutions from storage to last-mile delivery. The company emphasizes innovation through automation and data analytics, helping brands optimize inventory management and customer experience while maintaining flexibility for seasonal demand fluctuations.
Pretty Little Thing
CEO: Pretty Little Thing
HQ: Manchester, United Kingdom
PrettyLittleThing is a fast-fashion online retailer targeting young women aged 16-35. Founded in 2012, it's part of the Boohoo Group, offering trend-led clothing, accessories, and beauty products at affordable prices. The brand leverages social media marketing and influencer collaborations extensively. Known for rapid product turnover with hundreds of new styles weekly, PLT has expanded internationally while facing scrutiny over sustainability practices and labor conditions common to fast-fashion business models.
CEO: Andrew Rees
HQ: Broomfield, Colorado, USA
Crocs manufactures and markets casual foam footwear known for distinctive clog designs. Founded in 2002, the brand experienced viral popularity, decline, then remarkable resurgence through collaborations with celebrities, designers, and brands like Justin Bieber and Balenciaga. Their proprietary Croslite material offers comfort and functionality. Beyond classic clogs, they produce sandals, slides, and boots. The company emphasizes sustainability initiatives and has achieved significant growth through successful digital marketing and personalization via Jibbitz charms.

JD Sports Fashion is a leading multichannel retailer of sports, fashion, and outdoor brands. Operating over 3,400 stores globally across multiple fascias including JD, Finish Line, and Size?, they specialize in exclusive products and limited-edition releases from Nike, Adidas, and other premium brands. Strong in athleisure and sneaker culture, JD has expanded internationally through acquisitions. The company combines physical retail presence with growing e-commerce operations, targeting youth-oriented consumers.

Columbia Sportswear Company designs and manufactures outdoor and active lifestyle apparel, footwear, accessories, and equipment. Founded in 1938, the family-run business owns brands including Columbia, Mountain Hardwear, SOREL, and prAna. Known for innovative technologies like Omni-Heat thermal reflective warmth and OutDry waterproofing, they serve hikers, skiers, and outdoor enthusiasts globally. The company emphasizes functional performance, durability, and value across diverse price points in outdoor recreation markets.

Known for accessible on-trend styles at mid-market prices, River Island collaborates with influencers and designers while maintaining own-brand focus. They emphasize fast fashion responsiveness with new product launches weekly.

title: AMG Lithium opens test laboratory for solid electrolytes in Frankfurt - electrive.com
content:
AMG Lithium has commissioned its new Performance Lab "PerLa" in Frankfurt, Germany. The company aims to test sulfide solid electrolytes under more realistic conditions in complete laboratory cells and further develop them with customers.
AMG Lithium's laboratory in Frankfurt for solid electrolytes.
Image: AMG Lithium
AMG Lithium
is expanding its development activities for solid-state batteries with a new laboratory at its Frankfurt site. The laboratory space is increasing by 250 to around 1,100 square metres. The centrepiece is a glovebox line that can replicate the entire manufacturing process of laboratory cells under controlled, inert atmospheric conditions.
This includes the production of electrode pastes, coating, cell assembly and, finally, packaging as pouch cells. The company says more than 200 test stations are available for electrochemical investigations.
The real advancement, however, lies less in the additional laboratory space and more in the ability to test its own materials under application-relevant conditions. AMG Lithium can now not only characterise its solid electrolytes at the material level but also examine them in complete battery cells using standardised test protocols.
This is intended to facilitate joint development projects with customers in particular. AMG Lithium is thus positioning itself more strongly at the interface between material development and cell validation, although this does not include industrial cell production.
The new Glovebox-Linie enables the production of complete laboratory cells under inert atmosphere.
Focus on sulphide solid electrolytes
AMG Lithium is developing sulphide solid electrolytes for future solid-state batteries in Frankfurt. Such materials are intended to replace the liquid electrolytes in today’s lithium-ion cells. The technology fundamentally promises advantages in energy density and safety but continues to face challenges in material stability, cell integration and industrial manufacturing.
This is precisely why validation in complete cells is crucial. Material properties that can be demonstrated well on a laboratory scale must also prove themselves in interaction with electrodes, interfaces and real-world manufacturing processes.
With PerLa, AMG Lithium now aims to represent this step more strongly in-house. The company describes this step as an important building block for the market entry of its solid electrolyte technology. However, AMG Lithium has not yet provided specific details about its customer projects, offtake agreements or a potential production ramp-up for solid electrolytes.
In parallel, the company is expanding its industrial base for battery materials in Germany. In Bitterfeld-Wolfen, AMG Lithium is increasing its capacity for producing battery-grade lithium salts. For this undertaking, the company has been granted €36 million from the German federal funding initiative
as part of a total investment of €180 million. The plan is to achieve an annual capacity of 20,000 tonnes of battery-grade lithium compounds at the facility. According to the Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs, this theoretically corresponds to battery production of around 34 GWh per year.

title: 110 Chinese humanoid robots dance in sync to set Guinness World Record
content: China has set a Guinness World Records title after 110 humanoid robots performed synchronized dance routines. The robots, developed by Chinese robotics company AGIBOT, demonstrated coordinated movements in a large-scale public performance. The event highlights China’s efforts to advance humanoid robotics and expand the commercial deployment of robots across different industries. In August, AGIBOT won 46 medals, including 18 gold, at the second World Humanoid Robot Games, competing in athletics, manipulation, hotel services, and emergency response.Robots create recordA group of 110 humanoid robots developed by AGIBOT has set a Guinness World Records title after performing synchronized dance routines in Jinan, Shandong Province.According to reports, the performance took place on October 24 at the Yellow River International Convention and Exhibition Center. The robots, identified as full-size Expedition A3 models, danced in formation, jumped, and carried out coordinated movements while repeatedly changing positions.During the demonstration, the robots created wave-like patterns and arranged themselves into different formations, including the number 2026. Their movements were coordinated to maintain synchronization as the group transitioned between dance sequences.A hundred AGIbot A3 pic.twitter.com/JF0319qXa7— Eren Chen (@ErenChenAI) October 25, 2026A Guinness World Records adjudicator attended the event to verify the number of participating robots and present an official certificate recognizing the achievement. The record was for the most humanoid robots dancing simultaneously.According to AGIBOT, all 110 robots were standard production models rather than machines specially modified for the event. This detail highlights the company’s use of commercially produced humanoid robots in a large-scale coordinated performance.The demonstration showcases the ability to coordinate a large number of humanoid robots during a complex group activity. It also highlights the role of communication systems and centralized control in managing multiple robotic platforms simultaneously. However, synchronized dancing is a controlled demonstration and does not, by itself, establish how reliably the robots can perform complex tasks in industrial or other real-world environments.Synchronizing robot fleetFor the Guinness performance, AGIBOT robots used the firm’s LinkBots platform, which is designed to coordinate multiple robots through swarm scheduling and cluster control. LinkBots combines communication networks, positioning technology, and control software to manage the movements of multiple robots. Its integration with ultra-wideband (UWB) positioning technology enables centimeter-level tracking of the robots’ relative positions, helping them maintain spacing as they move through different formations.This positioning capability is especially important when robots move in coordinated proximity. Accurate location information helps the system organize formation changes and reduce the risk of collisions during complex sequences.The platform also supports coordinated scheduling, allowing robots to execute assigned movements as part of a larger routine. Rather than requiring operators to control every robot individually, the system is designed to manage group activities through centralized coordination and information about each machine’s state.LinkBots uses 5G and Wi-Fi connectivity to support communication between the robots and the control infrastructure. These networks provide channels for transmitting instructions and coordination data across the fleet.The platform’s reported capabilities also include adjusting formations and planning movements around obstacles. However, publicly available technical details do not fully establish how these functions operate or how extensively they have been tested outside controlled demonstrations.According to experts, the performance highlights AgiBot’s efforts to coordinate commercially produced humanoid robots at scale. It also demonstrates the role of swarm-control systems in managing multiple robotic platforms performing synchronized tasks.

title: 5-MW swappable nuclear reactor prepares for offshore ship integration
content: Nuclear-powered offshore vessels have moved a step closer to reality. A Norwegian project has secured fresh state funding to build and test atomic engines for commercial ships.The Research Council of Norway has awarded $2 million to the Marine Nuclear Propulsion System (MarNuPS) project. The consortium plans to develop and deploy small, modular nuclear reactors designed specifically to replace fossil fuels in offshore shipping. The reactors are intended to deliver high power output and long operating range without frequent refueling stops.Engineers will not start by placing active nuclear materials straight onto the water. Instead, the team is building an integrated land-based testing facility at Stette, near Ålesund, with trials scheduled to begin in 2027.The Stette facility will run a full-scale replica of a ship’s power plant. To assess safety and performance without radiation risks, engineers will heat the system with electricity rather than atomic fuel. “Testing will cover normal operation, rapid changes in power demand, transient and stress conditions, system performance and crew interaction,” explained the company.Using the Gem microreactorThe system will use the Gem Microreactor. It is a 5-megawatt unit developed by Emerald Nuclear. The design uses TRISO fuel pellets, which coat enriched uranium in layers of ceramic and carbon. “The MarNuPS Pilot will integrate Emerald Nuclear’s 5 MWe Gem Microreactor technology with energy storage, power conversion, vessel power management, automation and bridge control systems,” noted the firm. This structure withstands extreme heat without melting, preventing the radioactive releases associated with older reactor technologies. The reactor will convert heat into electricity through specialized power conversion systems supplied by Peregrine Turbine Technologies.Under the current plan, the reactor operates inside a sealed unit that is swapped out every five to 15 years, avoiding the need for complex refueling procedures inside ports.Commercial sea deploymentNorwegian shipowner Island Offshore intends to be the first operator to take the system to sea. The company plans to install an operational Gem reactor aboard an offshore service vessel between 2031 and 2032, paving the way for commercial atomic shipping across the North Sea.“Nuclear energy has the potential to provide a new route to decarbonizing offshore vessels without compromising the power, endurance and operational flexibility these ships require,” said Tommy Walaunet, CEO of Island Offshore.“Our role is to ensure that the system is developed around real offshore operations and the people who will ultimately use it.”Leading the industrial consortiumEmerald Nuclear Norway leads the industrial consortium alongside several prominent European maritime and engineering organizations. Shipbuilder VARD Group will manage vessel design and naval architecture, while Vard Electro handles power distribution and control networks.Academic partners are running the underlying simulations. The Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU) is modeling reactor physics and thermal hydraulics, while Imperial College London examines structural integrity under dynamic sea conditions. Engineering firm Maskindynamikk will oversee condition monitoring and system diagnostics.Partners have committed substantial private capital alongside the state award. The initial development phase carries an estimated budget of $15.6 million.

title: Anduril, Qualcomm plan rugged US-made laptop with 90% local components
content: A computer made entirely in the United States, down to its display and smallest components, is the ambition behind Anduril’s latest project.The defense technology company announced a partnership with Qualcomm on Tuesday to develop BlueChip, a rugged laptop that will open for preorders in 2027.The first model will target military personnel, government agencies, first responders, and law enforcement, combining an Arizona-made processor with hardware built for demanding environments. About 90 percent of its components will initially come from the U.S. or allied countries, with founder Palmer Luckey aiming to move the entire supply chain onto American soil eventually.An American chip at the coreBlueChip will use a Qualcomm Snapdragon X Series processor manufactured at Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company’s facility in Arizona. Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon said the chip shares its architecture with processors used in other laptops, including Microsoft’s Surface devices.However, Anduril has not finalized contracts with every component supplier, and detailed specifications remain unavailable.“As of right now, the laptop’s bill of materials is about 90 percent U.S. and allied [ally countries], and we have a technical roadmap to get to 100 percent domestic over time,” Luckey said.That ambition extends beyond processors and final assembly. Luckey is aiming for produce displays, metal parts, magnetic components, and everything else inside the machine domestically.Some pieces are already falling into place. He said he has identified an American supplier for the glass covering the screen. The display itself remains among the components he says are currently manufactured only in China.Built for government demandsBlueChip’s first customers are expected to value durability and supply-chain transparency over portability. Engineering the laptop to withstand rain, dust, and harsh conditions will add weight and limit battery life.Anduril is positioning the computer for agencies that must purchase U.S.-made equipment. Customers would be able to trace and audit its components, providing greater visibility into where their hardware originates.“These computers are the anti-surveillance computer. You fully control it,” Luckey said in a recent interview. “You know everything that is in it, every single component, and you know every software component that is running on it,” he added.Software compatibility is another priority. Anduril is working to ensure the Arm-based machine supports Windows applications, software built for certain government-used Linux distributions, and older programs that agencies continue to operate. That work will be important for buyers whose existing systems depend on aging applications.A premium for domestic productionAnduril has not announced a price, though Luckey estimates BlueChip could cost about 20 percent more than a typical high-end PC.Consumers will be able to order one, and the company may set up a waiting list. Still, Luckey acknowledged that an ordinary buyer without a specific need for its capabilities would likely find better value elsewhere. He nevertheless sees the laptop as the beginning of a broader BlueChip computer lineup, potentially reaching beyond its initial institutional audience.For now, the challenge is turning that manufacturing ambition into a finished product while securing suppliers for components that remain outside the proposed domestic supply chain.

title: Artificial channels separate lithium up to five times more selectively
content: Researchers in the US have developed artificial channels that are up to five times more selective for lithium than other recently developed lithium transporters, potentially offering a simpler way to extract the critical battery material.The nanoscale channels, developed at the University of Texas at Austin, allow lithium ions to pass through while restricting competing elements commonly found alongside them. The researchers say the channels are among the most selective developed so far.The technology takes inspiration from biological channels that control the movement of ions and molecules across living cell membranes. By recreating this function in artificial structures, the team aims to separate lithium without relying on conventional extraction methods that can consume substantial energy and produce chemical waste.Lithium is essential for batteries used in electric vehicles, smartphones and energy storage systems. However, extracting it from underground brines, hard rock and recycled batteries remains challenging because it is often mixed with sodium, potassium, magnesium and calcium.Tiny channels filter lithiumThe researchers developed nanoscale pores designed to favor the movement of lithium ions over other dissolved substances.The channels use two features to achieve this separation: chemical groups positioned near their entrances and a confined internal structure that influences how ions move through them.As ions approach the opening, they interact with the chemical groups. These interactions, combined with the restricted space inside the channel, help determine which ions can pass through more easily.In laboratory experiments, the artificial channels demonstrated lithium selectivity two to five times higher than other recently developed lithium transporters, according to the researchers.The findings build on the team’s earlier work developing similar technology to separate rare earth elements used in industrial applications.Manish Kumar, a professor of civil, architectural and environmental engineering and chemical engineering at UT Austin, said the goal is to simplify the recovery of lithium from complex mixtures.“Our goal is a process that is faster, cleaner and easier to run,” Kumar said.The researchers believe the approach could eventually reduce the need for harsh solvents in lithium separation. However, the current results demonstrate selective ion transport rather than a complete industrial extraction process.Scaling membranes for extractionThe next challenge is incorporating the channels into larger membranes capable of processing significant quantities of lithium-containing solutions.The team is exploring a previously developed membrane material made from interconnected, cell-like layers. These structures can be assembled using lipids or polymer materials and could provide a framework for integrating the selective channels.The researchers envision a continuous separation system in which lithium-rich solutions pass through membranes that preferentially transport lithium ions.Such a process could potentially improve lithium recovery from underground brines while reducing the chemical demands of conventional separation methods.However, further testing is required to establish whether the channels can maintain their performance when exposed to real brines containing multiple dissolved salts.The researchers also need to determine how effectively the technology can operate at industrial scale. The announcement did not provide commercial-scale recovery rates, energy consumption figures, or operating costs.Beyond mining, the team sees possible applications in recovering lithium from spent batteries and developing improved separators for future battery designs.The research was published in the Journal of the American Chemical Society.
