title: New flywheel design could eliminate power converter for grid connection - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
A research team has built a fixed-speed flywheel prototype that uses a wire-rope mechanism to move weights inward and outward during discharge and charge. The system briefly supplied power to the electrical supply, but steady-state losses prevented net electrical energy discharge over the complete operation.
Lior Kahana
28 Oct 2026
Research & Development
Batteries
Energy Storage
System Integration
Clockwise from left: the experimental setup, the flywheel in its open state, and the flywheel in its closed state
A research team at
Tokyo University of Science
in Japan has developed and tested a prototype fixed-speed flywheel energy storage system (FESS). Flywheels store energy as rotational motion and suit short-duration applications that require rapid charging and discharging, such as grid frequency regulation. Conventional systems use a power electronic converter to vary the flywheel’s speed while exchanging electricity with the grid. The proposed system moves weights within the flywheel instead of changing its speed, potentially eliminating the converter and reducing costs.
“The main novelty is the development and experimental evaluation of a flywheel mechanism that enables charging and discharging through active changes in its moment of inertia while maintaining an approximately constant rotational speed,” corresponding author Ryoga Sugata told
pv magazine
. “To our knowledge, experimental studies of such mechanisms remain limited, particularly those that deliberately reduce the moment of inertia to extract stored rotational energy.”
The researcher added that his team developed the design to address losses in their earlier winch- and ball-screw-based mechanisms. “A potential future application is to add controllable active-power storage capability to synchronous condensers. Our longer-term objective is to investigate whether a synchronous condenser can combine its usual reactive-power and inertial support with fast, controllable active-power exchange enabled by the variable-inertia flywheel,” he added.
To test the concept, the researchers built a prototype using a modified centrifugal brake as the flywheel, with two 0.856 kg weights attached to pivoting arms. They added wire ropes, pulleys, bobbins, gears, an electromagnetic clutch, and a brake to control the weights’ position. A shaft connected the flywheel to a 0.75 kW, three-phase induction machine that acted as both a motor and a generator.
The team tested charging and discharging at synchronous speeds of 400, 450, and 500 rpm using a regenerative variable-frequency power supply, with voltage and frequency held constant during each test. For charging, they released the clutch, allowing centrifugal force to move the weights outward. For discharging, they activated the brake to drive the reeling mechanism and pull the weights inward.
They measured voltage, current, shaft torque, rotational speed, and clutch and brake voltages, and calculated electrical and mechanical power and energy. They then compared the results with theoretical values, subtracting steady-state power consumption to isolate the energy associated with moving the weights. The analysis excluded the energy consumed by the clutch, brake, and control circuitry.
“The most surprising finding was that charging and discharging efficiencies showed different trends as rotational speed increased,” Sugata said. “Over the tested range of 400–500 rpm, charging efficiency decreased slightly, whereas discharging efficiency increased. For example, after subtracting the steady-state mechanical power input, mechanical charging efficiency decreased from approximately 51% to 49%, while mechanical discharging efficiency increased from approximately 40% to 53%.”
The team attributed the difference to the distinct loss characteristics of the two operations, the academic said. During charging, frictional losses increase with centrifugal force, limiting the benefit of higher speeds. During discharging, the main losses appear to increase more slowly than the available stored energy, reducing their relative impact. The researchers said that improving efficiency would require addressing the specific loss mechanisms of both operations.
More according to the results, at 500 rpm, the researchers calculated a theoretical storage capacity of 36.61 J. After subtracting steady-state power consumption, the prototype consumed 84.1 J during charging and discharged 16.4 J, corresponding to electrical efficiencies of 43.3% and 45.1%, respectively.
“We demonstrated electrical power delivery to the grid without a power electronic interface for frequency conversion, although steady-state losses still prevented net electrical energy discharge over the complete discharge operation,” Sugata added. “In follow-up research, we plan to improve the mechanical design to reduce friction and losses associated with clutch and brake operation. We also plan to investigate replacing the induction machine with a synchronous machine and evaluate the effects on electrical losses and charging and discharging performance.”
The article “
Charging and discharging performance of a fixed-speed flywheel energy storage system with a reeling-type inertia control mechanism
” has appeared in the
Journal of Energy Storage.

title: Qvantum launches 50 kW propane heat pump for residential, commercial applications - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
The Swedish heat pump manufacturer said its the QA50 heat pump delivers a maximum heating capacity of 50 kW and a COP of up to 3.12. The system uses propane (R290) as a refrigerant, operates at outdoor temperatures ranging from -25 C to 43 C, and can be integrated into low-temperature ambient heat networks.
Emiliano Bellini
28 Oct 2026
Technology & Products
Commercial & industrial
Heat pumps
Residential
The QA50 heat pump system
Swedish heat pump manufacturer
has launched a new air-to-water heat pump designed for multi-residential developments and light commercial buildings.
“With a wide operating window, the QA50 is ideal as the primary energy source for low-temperature ambient loop systems. Its compact dimensions and modular design allow multiple units to be combined, creating a scalable solution that can be tailored to project requirements while maximising available plant room space,” the company said in a statement.
The new unit measures 1,195 mm × 980 mm × 1,900 mm and weighs 363 kg. It can reportedly operate at outdoor temperatures ranging from -25 C to 43 C.
According to the manufacturer’s technical datasheet, the QA50 delivers a maximum heating capacity of up to 50 kW and a coefficient of performance (COP) of up to 3.12. Its seasonal coefficient of performance (SCOP) reaches 4.52 at 35 C and 3.26 at 55 C, corresponding to A+++ and A++ energy efficiency ratings, respectively. The unit has a rated heating output of 25.56 kW at 35 C and 25.53 kW at 55 C. It offers a maximum heating-water flow temperature of 70 C, a cooling capacity of 51.93 kW at A35/W25 and a heating capacity of 30.3 kW at A-10/W55.
The heat pump features two refrigerant circuits containing 1.5 kg of propane (R290) each, for a total refrigerant charge of 3 kg. It has a maximum electrical input of 24 kW, a maximum operating current of 30 A and a three-phase electrical supply of 380 V to 415 V. The unit has an IPX4 protection rating and its declared sound power level is 75 dB(A), while its sound pressure level at a distance of 1 m is 70 dB(A).
The heat pump’s modular design allows multiple units to be connected in cascade configurations to meet higher heating and cooling demands. It can be integrated with existing building energy infrastructure and supports communication with building management systems via Modbus.
Qvantum said the QA50 has been developed primarily for use in fifth-generation district heating and cooling networks, also known as ambient heat networks, which typically operate at temperatures between 10 C and 30 C.
In these applications, the QA50 can be combined with the company’s QG water-to-water apartment heat pump to provide space heating, domestic hot water and cooling at the individual apartment level. The low-temperature network configuration is designed to reduce distribution heat losses compared with conventional high-temperature heating networks.
The QA50 can also operate as a standalone heating and cooling solution for offices, leisure facilities and mixed-use buildings.
The system incorporates Qvantum’s QC PRO controller, which enables centralised management of multiple heat pumps and associated heating and cooling components. Other features include remote monitoring and diagnostics through the company’s Q Service platform, over-the-air software updates and compatibility with flexible electricity tariffs.

title: Ricoh announces GW-scale perovskite solar cell production in Japan - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Japan’s Ricoh plans to begin producing perovskite solar cells by 2030, initially targeting annual capacity of several hundred megawatts. The company will use its proprietary inkjet printing technology to streamline manufacturing and reduce production costs.
Emiliano Bellini
28 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Asia-Pacific
Perovskite solar cells manufactured with Ricoh’s inkjet technology
Japanese imaging and electronics company
has announced plans to begin producing perovskite solar cells in Japan by 2030.
The factory will be located at Ricoh Industry Co., Ltd.’s Tohoku site in Shibata, Miyagi prefecture, northern Japan, and will use a manufacturing process based on Ricoh’s proprietary inkjet technology. “With future expansion to GW-scale production in mind, Ricoh aims to establish annual production capacity of several hundred MW by 2030,” the company said in a statement.
Ricoh said its inkjet technology enables precise control over microscopic droplets, allowing materials to be deposited in the required quantities at specific locations. By using the technology to pattern-print all functional layers of perovskite solar cells, the company aims to improve material utilization, simplify manufacturing processes, increase productivity and reduce production costs.
“Ricoh has pursued research and development of organic solar cells based on organic photoconductor technologies developed through the innovation of its multifunction printers,” the company said. “Technologies cultivated through these efforts are now being applied to perovskite solar cells.”
Ricoh said the combination of inkjet printing and substrate transport technologies developed for commercial printing enables continuous, high-speed processing of roll-to-roll substrates, increasing production throughput while reducing manufacturing costs.
In November 2025, Ricoh
announced
that its perovskite solar cells would undergo testing aboard the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency’s (JAXA) unmanned HTV-X1 cargo spacecraft. The two-month demonstration was designed to assess power generation, electrical performance and durability under space conditions. Ricoh has been developing perovskite solar cells for space applications in collaboration with JAXA since 2017.
The company previously tested its perovskite solar technology aboard the Denden-01 satellite, launched in 2024 for a six-month evaluation. Ricoh has identified low-light performance, resistance to cosmic radiation and the potential for lightweight, flexible designs as key advantages of perovskite solar cells for space applications.
In September 2025, Ricoh also
joined a five-year research project
with Daiwa House Industry and NTT Anode Energy to develop perovskite solar technology for building-integrated and building-attached PV applications. The project, backed by Japan’s New Energy and Industrial Technology Development Organization (NEDO), focuses on improving manufacturing processes and developing installation solutions for rooftops of logistics facilities and exterior walls of data centers.
Ricoh’s move follows that of Japanese electronics manufacturer Panasonic, which last week began
commercial sales of its glass-based perovskite solar panels
, ahead of the planned launch of full-scale mass production in April 2029.
The commercialization efforts come as the Japanese government seeks to establish a domestic perovskite solar industry. In November 2024, the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI)
announced a target
of deploying around 20 GW of perovskite solar capacity by 2040.
The government also outlined plans to support domestic manufacturing and reduce production costs to JPY 14 ($0.09)/W by 2030 and JPY 10/W by 2040. In September 2025, the Ministry of the Environment
introduced subsidy programs
to support early deployment of perovskite solar cells and their integration with battery storage systems.
Japan has since stepped up its support for the technology. In May 2026, NEDO
opened a supplementary funding call
under its Green Innovation Fund to advance mass-production technologies for single-junction perovskite solar cells.
In September, the Ministry of the Environment
announced plans
to exclude conventional silicon solar panels from newly introduced subsidy programs starting in fiscal 2027, prioritizing perovskite and other next-generation solar technologies. The policy shift is intended to strengthen Japan’s industrial competitiveness and accelerate the commercialization of emerging photovoltaic technologies.

title: Sunkean advances copper-to-aluminum jumpers for PV DC systems - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
The manufacturer has developed a copper-to-aluminum jumper solution for PV DC-side applications, addressing conductor material costs, field installation efficiency, and the long-term reliability of copper-to-aluminum connections in utility-scale solar projects.
Sunkean Cable
28 Oct 2026
Technology & Products
Utility-scale
For utility-scale PV plants, DC-side cabling often spans considerable distances, making conductor selection an important factor in overall material costs. SUNKEAN’s copper-to-aluminum jumper solution uses a dedicated transition structure that allows aluminum conductors to be used in selected sections of the DC-side circuit, reducing copper consumption while maintaining the required connection performance. Project experience indicates that, under suitable application conditions, the copper-to-aluminum approach can deliver cost savings of nearly 50%. For cable runs exceeding 20 meters, the economic advantage of aluminum becomes increasingly significant.
Installation efficiency is another consideration behind the jumper design. SUNKEAN supplies the copper-to-aluminum jumper as a pre-assembled cable harness, with the copper-to-aluminum connector assembled before delivery. At the project site, installers only need to crimp the copper connector to the copper cable, eliminating the need for complex copper-to-aluminum conversion work in the field. For utility-scale projects involving large numbers of repeated DC connections, this prefabricated approach can reduce field operations and improve installation consistency.
The copper-to-aluminum connector is central to the solution. The challenge in adopting copper and aluminum conductors is not simply replacing one material with another but ensuring a stable connection between dissimilar metals over the operating life of the system. SUNKEAN’s copper-to-aluminum terminals use solid-state friction welding, in which heat generated by high-speed friction, combined with applied pressure, creates a solid-state bond between copper and aluminum without melting the materials.
Compared with conventional fusion welding, the process avoids key manufacturing challenges associated with the different melting points and thermal expansion characteristics of copper and aluminum. The terminals also feature a high-performance multilayer protective coating to enhance environmental resistance at the connection interface and reduce the impact of moisture, heat, salt spray, and other environmental factors. Contact resistance is controlled at ≤0.3 mΩ, with current ratings of 46 A, 55 A, 70 A, and 95 A available for different applications.
As utility-scale PV projects continue to focus on reducing BOS (Balance of System) costs and improving construction efficiency, copper-to-aluminum conversion is emerging as an option for optimizing conductor materials on the DC side. SUNKEAN’s copper-to-aluminum jumper applies this approach through a prefabricated DC-side harness, offering a way for PV projects to reduce copper consumption while simplifying field installation.

title: Togo opens consultation on large-scale solar tender - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
Togo is inviting stakeholders to provide feedback on draft documents relating to development of a large-scale solar project, ahead of launching a competitive tender. Comments can be submitted until November 9.
Patrick Jowett
28 Oct 2026
Applications & Installations
Markets & Policy
Utility-scale
The government of Togo is asking stakeholders to comment on documents covering the development of a large-scale solar project ahead of issuing a competitive tender.
The Nangbéto solar PV project, with a planned capacity between 70 MW and 110 MW, represents the first tranche of a planned 400 MW clean power program in Togo.
Earlier this year, Belgium-headquartered clean energy non-profit RELP entered into an agreement with the Togolese government to support the development of a government-led renewable energy program.
A social media post published by RELP explains that before the government opens the competitive tender for the Nangbéto project, it is asking the market to
review the draft documents
. Documents available for comment include the concession agreement, power power agreement, tender dossier and technical requirements.
Togo’s Minister Delegate to the Minister of Economy and Finance, Robert Koffi Messan Eklo, explained during the launch of the public consultation why Togo was requesting the feedback.
“If I sign at the wrong price, we’ll be paying for it for 25 years,” the minister said.
Independent power producers, contractors, suppliers and financiers are invited to give feedback on the documents. The deadline to submit comments is November 9.
RELP says the feedback will help make the final documents “clear, balanced and bankable, ahead of the tender launch expected by year-end.”
“Togo is starting something that matters for investors: a multi-year programme and a transparent, competitive process will give developers and lenders a credible pipeline and will provide the government good value,” Andrea Bertello, RELP Regional Director for Africa and Asia, told
pv magazine
RELP is also working with other West African nations to develop similar government-led renewable energy procurements, including Ghana, Senegal and
The Africa Solar Industry Association (AFSIA) has tracked 656 MW of operational solar in Togo, according to figures available in its project database, 496 MW of which is identified as commercial and industrial projects.

title: UK government approves nearly 2 GW of co-located solar in October - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Four projects in nationally significant infrastructure project planning pipeline granted planning permission by secretary of state. All four projects include battery energy storage systems.
Matthew Lynas
28 Oct 2026
Applications & Installations
Markets & Policy
Utility-scale
The 373 MW Cleve Hill Solar Park project was the largest UK PV plant when commissioned in summer 2025.
Four utility-scale projects have secured planning permission through the UK government’s pipeline for large infrastructure projects in October, including a co-located plant expected to have 1.12 GW DC installed solar capacity.
Great North Road Solar and Biodiversity Park and Frodsham Solar were both issued development consent orders (DCO) on Oct. 27, while Steeple Renewables Project and Green Hill Solar Farm were granted DCOs on Oct.9 and Oct. 8 respectively.
Developed by Elements Green, Great North Road Solar will be one of the largest in the United Kingdom when commissioned at its site northwest of Newark on Trent, England. The 1.12 GW project has secured a grid connection for import and export of 800 MW and will be built with a co-located 440 MW/880 MWh battery energy storage system.
Frodsham Solar is being developed by Cubico and project documents list the capacity as “around 150 MW”. The project near Chester, England, has a connection agreement with SP Energy Networks to supply up to 100 MW to the existing Frodsham substation.
Steeple Renewables Project in Nottinghamshire is being developed as a 450 MW solar generation project with approximately 150 MW of BESS in power output terms. The project is being developed by RES and is expected to use grid capacity made available from the decommissioning of the adjacent West Burton power station.
Green Hill Solar Farm is being developed by Island Green Power at a site north of Northampton. The project is expected to have a capacity of “up to 500 MW” and will also have a BESS installation.
All four projects were approved through the UK government’s Nationally Significant Infrastructure Project (NSIP) process, continuing a 100% success rate for solar in the NSIP pipeline. Run by the UK Planning Inspectorate, the NSIP process is used to approve or reject large-scale projects across industries – including solar projects in England with capacity greater than 100 MW. The first UK solar project approved through the NSIP process, the
376 MW Cleve Hill Solar Park,
was approved in 2020 and entered commercial operations in July 2025.

title: Avaada unveils 745 W TOPCon solar module with 23.98% efficiency - pv magazine Global
content:
Avaada Group has unveiled a 745 W domestic content requirement (DCR)-compliant n-type TOPCon solar module at Renewable Energy India (REI) Expo 2026.
The module was unveiled by Heeralal Nagar, Minister of State (Independent Charge), Energy Department, Government of Rajasthan.
The glass-to-glass module delivers a power output of up to 745 W and a module efficiency of 23.98%. According to the company, it features a 132 half-cell configuration and an 18-busbar architecture, designed to increase power density and energy generation while supporting long-term performance.
“India’s clean-energy transition is being supported by advances in solar technology, energy storage and decentralised power solutions. It is encouraging to see companies such as Avaada Group bring advanced solar modules, rooftop solar solutions and storage technologies to the market. Such innovations can help expand renewable-energy adoption and contribute to strengthening energy security,” said the minister.
Vineet Mittal, Chairman, Avaada Group, said, “India should not just be one of the world’s largest consumers of solar technology. India must become one of the world’s leading creators and manufacturers of solar technology. Our 745 W DCR TOPCon module reflects this ambition—to manufacture high-performance, globally competitive solar products on Indian soil.”
At the three-day REI exhibition, Avaada also showcased its ready-to-install rooftop solar kits, developed to simplify solar adoption for households, shops, farms and commercial establishments.
The kits bring together key installation components, including solar inverters, electrical protection systems, earthing equipment and connectors.
Complementing the rooftop offering was Avaada HALO, the company’s integrated battery energy storage system designed to help customers store electricity and use it when needed.
Combining a hybrid inverter, lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery technology and smart monitoring through the Avaada mobile app, HALO supports backup power, improved utilisation of rooftop solar generation and greater control over electricity consumption.
The modular system supports configurations of up to four stacked units and delivers up to 10 kW of continuous power. Output can reach up to 11.5 kW with solar support during power outages, subject to operating conditions.
Avaada has 8.5 GW of operational solar module manufacturing capacity. Its solar cell manufacturing capacity stands at 6 GW, comprising 3 GW of operational capacity and an additional 3 GW production line at an advanced stage of commissioning.

title: Climate change could boost Swedish PV generation by 5% - pv magazine Global
content:
Researchers in Sweden have investigated how climate change could affect the country’s solar power generation potential throughout the 21st century, aiming to provide more accurate projections of PV output in high-latitude regions. The study accounts for factors such as panel orientation, temperature and snow cover, which are often overlooked in conventional assessments of PV potential, potentially leading to inaccurate estimates in cold climates.
“We found that the combined effects of air temperature and snowfall are as crucial as solar radiation for PV production in high-latitude regions,” corresponding author Wujun Wang told
pv magazine
. “This is quite different from the case in low- and mid-latitude regions. In Sweden, climate change will lead to an approximate 5% increase in PV generation, which means global warming might be positive for PV generation.”
The researchers assessed PV generation from 1951 to 2100 in four Swedish cities: Malmö in the south, Gothenburg on the west coast, Stockholm on the east coast, and Kiruna in the far north. Malmö recorded the highest temperatures and solar radiation levels and the least snowfall, while Kiruna had the coldest conditions, lowest solar radiation levels and approximately twice as much snowfall. Stockholm and Gothenburg represented intermediate climatic conditions. The team combined an hourly snow-PV model with climate projections from the HCLIM43-ALADIN regional climate model at a spatial resolution of 12.5 km.
The researchers considered two climate scenarios: a low-emissions scenario involving strong climate action (SSP1-2.6) and a high-emissions scenario involving limited climate action (SSP3-7.0). Their model calculated direct, diffuse and reflected solar radiation reaching the modules, accounting for incidence-angle and snow-related losses. It also estimated cell temperatures based on ambient temperature, irradiance and nominal operating cell temperature, before calculating electricity generation using module efficiency and its temperature coefficient. For south-facing modules, the researchers tested tilt angles ranging from 0 degrees to 90 degrees in 0.1-degree increments. They compared projected yields with a historical baseline covering 1951 to 2014 and a reference tilt angle of 15 degrees.
“The projected trends depend on both location and scenario,” the researchers said. “Under SSP1-2.6, annual generation increases by 1.52–2.60 kWh/kW per decade, corresponding to less than 0.5% per decade. Under SSP3-7.0, PV output increases in Stockholm and Kiruna; however, it decreases in Gothenburg and Malmö. Nevertheless, the net change remains within approximately 30 kWh/kW by 2100.”
Compared with the historical period, annual PV output variability is projected to decrease in the three southern cities but increase in Kiruna. The frequency and duration of consecutive periods with zero generation are also generally expected to decline, potentially reducing energy storage requirements.
“In the future, an installation tilt of approximately 35° is suitable for all selected cities and can increase annual generation by about 3–6% relative to the commercial angle currently used,” the researchers said.
“The findings provide valuable insights into photovoltaic potential in a changing climate,” the researchers concluded. “It provides a powerful tool for a wide range of stakeholders, including researchers, policymakers, PV plant owners, power grid operators, investors, and engineers, to estimate the impacts of local climate change on PV generation, particularly in high latitude cold regions with long snow seasons.”
The findings are presented in “
Impact of climate change on the photovoltaic power potential in Sweden across 21st century
,” published in
Communications Earth & Environment
. The research team included scientists from Sweden’s
KTH Royal Institute of Technology
Swedish Meteorological and Hydrological Institute
, as well as China’s
Zhejiang University of Technology

title: Enerparc attracts non-binding offers in insolvency sale - pv magazine Global
content:
Enerparc AG has been in provisional insolvency proceedings since early September, following a failed financing process. The proceedings also affect sister companies Pvwerk and Sonnen Tiefbau, which handle project implementation, but not marketing subsidiary Sunnic Lighthouse or Enerparc Service.
The company and provisional insolvency administrator Stefan Denkhaus, a partner at law firm BRL, said more than 10 non-binding offers had been submitted. A small number of bidders are being selected for the second phase of the investor process, taking into account Enerparc’s limited staffing and organizational capacity to conduct due diligence. Bidders will assess the company and its assets before submitting binding offers.
Denkhaus said the sale of Enerparc’s solar park portfolios, project pipeline and stakes in non-insolvent subsidiaries, including Sunnic Lighthouse and Enerparc Service, is still expected to be notarized in December 2026. The transaction is also intended to include the workforce.
In early October, Denkhaus told
pv magazine
that the process would prioritize interested parties seeking to acquire the company as a whole. Enerparc is one of Germany’s largest independent power producers (IPPs) in solar energy. Its vertically integrated business spans photovoltaic project development and construction through to electricity marketing.
Enerparc and Denkhaus also reported progress in parallel negotiations with suppliers and lenders aimed at resuming work on solar parks under construction. Work had been interrupted following the insolvency filing.
On Oct. 26, 2026, Hamburg District Court ordered a so-called “strong” provisional insolvency administration at the provisional administrator’s request, with the support of Enerparc’s management board. The measure is intended to provide greater legal certainty for all parties, particularly when construction work resumes.
Under the order, legal transactions conducted during the insolvency application process have the same binding force as those carried out after formal insolvency proceedings open. The opening of proceedings is expected on Dec. 1, 2026.
Enerparc and Denkhaus said cooperation between the management board and the provisional insolvency administrator and his team would continue.

title: Itaipu studies up to 1 GW of solar to support Paraguay’s power grid - pv magazine Global
content:
Binational hydropower operator Itaipu has presented a study examining the integration of 100 MW to 1,000 MW of solar photovoltaic capacity into Paraguay’s electricity system to meet rising demand and improve grid stability.
The research, titled “Use of photovoltaic generation to meet Paraguayan electricity demand and dampen inter-area electromechanical oscillations,” was recently presented by Manuel Sosa Ríos, an engineer in Itaipu’s Technical Directorate, at the Cigre Energy Forum 2026 in Calgary, Canada.
The study draws on forecasts of rising electricity consumption in Paraguay. The country currently has 8,800 MW of hydropower capacity, comprising Itaipu’s 7,000 MW 50 Hz system, Yacyretá’s 1,600 MW and Acaray’s 200 MW. According to planning studies cited by the researcher, this capacity could become insufficient around 2029.
Solar photovoltaic generation is among the alternatives considered, with Paraguay recording average annual daily global horizontal irradiation of 5.08 kWh/m².
Grid oscillations
The research also examines stability issues associated with Paraguay’s electrical interconnection with Argentina, which has operated under the current configuration since December 2022. The system experiences inter-area electromechanical oscillations at frequencies of 0.33 Hz to 0.41 Hz.
Itaipu’s power system stabilizer (PSS) is currently the main mechanism used to dampen these oscillations, but its response can be limited under certain low-frequency conditions.
To assess potential solutions, the researchers incorporated a power oscillation damping (POD) controller into photovoltaic plant models, tuning it using the damped Nyquist method. Simulations examined three connection points: the 500 kV Villa Hayes substation, the 220 kV Villa Hayes substation and the 220 kV Acaray substation. The locations were selected for their ability to observe inter-area oscillations.
In a scenario with Itaipu’s PSS out of service, the model showed an unstable 0.4 Hz inter-area mode with negative damping of 4.96%. Adding photovoltaic generation equipped with the POD controller stabilized the modeled electricity system at all three connection points.
The researchers concluded that controlled solar generation could complement the damping function currently provided by Itaipu.
The study also recommends installing battery energy storage systems (BESS) alongside photovoltaic plants to maintain an appropriate response during transient events and reduce the effects of changes in solar irradiance.
The research used generic solar plant models implemented in the Anatem power system simulation program. The authors propose evaluating additional connection locations and control signals in subsequent work.
The study was presented to Study Committee C4 of the International Council on Large Electric Systems (Cigre), which focuses on the technical performance of power systems.

title: Portugal makes grid-forming mandatory for large battery storage plants - pv magazine Global
content:
Few battery plants connected to Portugal’s transmission grid, or rated at 45 MW or more, must provide grid-forming capability and synthetic inertia under a new
regulatory ordinance
. Plants of 500 kW or more must also switch automatically from charging to discharging when grid frequency falls.
The rules took effect on Oct. 23 and apply to connection requests filed from that date. Existing plants are covered only if they undergo a significant expansion, modernization or equipment replacement.
The ordinance, signed by Jean Paulo Gil Barroca, Portugal’s secretary of state for energy, applies the requirements for generating units under the EU network code on requirements for generators to storage, whether plants are discharging, charging or powering their own auxiliary systems.
The grid-forming obligation also covers plants connected at 110 kV or above, on terms the grid operators will set. The ordinance extends it to plants of 10 MW to 45 MW, although its technical annex ties the obligation for that class to provisions in grid capacity titles, permits or tender documents.
Smaller plants must provide grid-forming capability only where those documents require it. Plants on the distribution grid must also be able to operate in grid-following mode, with the operator deciding which mode applies.
The technical parameters are based on a joint report by the European transmission and distribution operator bodies ENTSO-E and the EU DSO Entity, industry associations SolarPower Europe, WindEurope and Energy Storage Europe, and the standards body CENELEC. Plants must hold additional power and energy to provide synthetic inertia during frequency deviations between 47.0 Hz and 52.5 Hz and rates of change of up to 2 Hz per second.
The mechanical starting time, which sets the level of inertia a plant emulates, must be adjustable from 1 to 20 seconds, with a default of 12 seconds. Plants must also achieve a damping ratio of at least 10% for power oscillations between 0.1 Hz and 10 Hz. Pumped hydro and other storage that provides synchronous inertia is excluded from the grid-forming requirements.
All plants of 1 MW or more must be technically able to provide frequency containment and restoration reserves, as well as voltage and reactive power control. For the automatic switch to discharging, the default underfrequency relay setting is 49.2 Hz while charging.
Plants must ramp load changes outside reserve activation over 10 minutes unless the system operator instructs otherwise. Plants above 1 MW must give the system operator real-time monitoring and remote control. Grid operators can issue power instructions during congestion or supply-demand emergencies, but the ordinance does not require plants to hold back state of charge to respond.
The government said it is setting the requirements now, while the
European Union’s generator connection code is under revision
, because of the storage growth expected from Portugal’s national storage strategy and from storage funding calls under its EU-backed recovery plan, which together cover more than 1 GW of projects. It said the ordinance does not prevent the revised EU rules from being implemented once they are published.
Portugal’s draft national storage strategy, put to
public consultation
in August, targets 6.9 GW of storage by 2030 and highlights grid-forming inverters as a tool for the stability of the Iberian power system. The government has also said it plans a
dedicated auction
for 750 MVA of battery storage capacity, and in June
scheduled it for September
alongside a 300 MW round for storage paired with renewable energy projects.
The rules arrive while Portugal’s battery fleet is still small. The country had
20 MW of battery storage
in operation at the end of 2025, according to renewable energy association APREN, which expects deployment to accelerate from that base. In January 2025, the government awarded €100 million ($112 million) to 43 storage projects totaling about 500 MW.

title: UNSW study finds bushfire risks to PV assets extend far beyond direct fire damage - pv magazine Global
content:
A research team from the
University of New South Wales
(UNSW) has investigated the impact of bushfires on PV power generation and long-term module reliability, finding that their effects extend well beyond fire-affected areas.
“Using 20 years of atmospheric and satellite data (2003–2024), we quantify the impact of bushfire smoke transport, elevated operating temperatures, and associated degradation, focusing on Australia’s major Black Summer and Black Saturday bushfires,” corresponding author Bram Hoex told
pv magazine
Black Summer bushfires
of 2019–2020 and the Black Saturday bushfires of 2009 were among Australia’s most devastating natural disasters. Black Summer burned more than 24 million hectares, destroyed thousands of homes, and killed or displaced billions of animals. The Black Saturday fires in Victoria claimed 173 lives and destroyed more than 2,000 homes. Both disasters caused widespread environmental damage and loss of life, highlighting the risks associated with extreme heat, drought, and climate change.
The researchers explained that bushfire smoke contains aerosols, including fine particulate matter (PM2.5), which reduce air quality and attenuate sunlight. These particles scatter and absorb solar radiation, significantly reducing PV electricity generation. Aerosol deposition on solar panels also causes soiling, reducing efficiency and potentially creating hotspots, while elevated temperatures during bushfires can accelerate module degradation and shorten their service life.
The scientists used the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts’ ERA5 reanalysis dataset to obtain hourly meteorological data and the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) to assess smoke pollution using aerosol optical depth (AOD) data. They also used observations from the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) to identify active bushfire hotspots with a detection confidence greater than 75%.
To isolate aerosol effects, the researchers selected clear-sky conditions using a daily clear-sky index (DCI) greater than 0.95. They defined solar generation lulls as periods when irradiance remained below 180 W/m² for at least two consecutive hours. The Python Photovoltaic Library (pvlib) and PVWatts model were used to simulate electricity generation under clean and smoke-polluted conditions, while the Sandia temperature model estimated PV module temperatures based on solar irradiance, ambient temperature, and wind speed.
The researchers also assessed thermal degradation by analyzing temperature fluctuations and cyclic thermal stress in PV modules. They used the Hybrid Single-Particle Lagrangian Integrated Trajectory (HYSPLIT) model to track smoke dispersion and evaluate its impact on solar power generation across different regions.
The analysis showed that during the Black Summer bushfires of 2019–2020, AOD exceeded 1.7 near fire hotspots, several times higher than typical levels. Solar power generation declined by up to 70% near the fires and by 30% to 40% in areas more than 150 km away. The researchers also found that smoke-related low-generation periods averaged up to three hours per day in affected areas and reached eight hours per day in the most severely affected locations. PV module temperatures increased by 10 C to 20 C compared with climatological levels, contributing approximately 0.15% additional thermal degradation.
During the Black Saturday bushfires of 2009, smoke reduced solar generation by up to 18% near fire hotspots, while areas more than 100 km away experienced generation losses of 5% to 10%, demonstrating the long-range effects of smoke transport. Module temperatures increased by approximately 18 C, contributing around 0.12% additional thermal degradation.
“The study demonstrates that bushfire risks to PV assets extend well beyond direct fire damage, as long-range smoke transport can significantly affect energy generation, system reliability, and grid operations,” Hoex said. “It also emphasizes the importance of incorporating bushfire-related aerosol impacts into solar resource assessments, energy yield forecasting, and long-term reliability modelling.”
The researchers recommended several mitigation measures, including improved smoke forecasting, vegetation management, regular module cleaning, thermal monitoring, and predictive maintenance.
“The findings also provide a framework for evaluating bushfire exposure during solar farm site selection and strengthening operational resilience in fire-prone regions,” Hoex said.
The researchers said the findings could also be relevant to other bushfire-prone regions, including California, southern Europe, and South America.
The research work was presented in “
Understanding non-localised impacts of bushfires on photovoltaic performance, reliability, and management strategies
,” recently published in
Solar Energy
Other UNSW researchers have also investigated the impact of bushfires on solar power generation. In a
2023 study
, they found that smoke from the Black Summer bushfires caused significant PV generation losses, resulting in estimated financial losses of up to AUD 29 million ($20.4 million). The researchers also
demonstrated
that rooftop PV systems could serve as early bushfire warning and monitoring tools by detecting changes in electricity generation caused by smoke.

title: US state opens $200 million solar-storage grant program - pv magazine Global
content:
The Maryland Energy Administration (MEA) has officially
launched Megawatts for Maryland
, a multi-phase competitive auction program aimed at expanding in-state renewable generation and energy storage capacity while putting downward pressure on regional electricity rates.
Backed by up to $100 million for Fiscal Year 2027, with an additional $100 million anticipated for FY 2028, the initiative draws funding from the state’s Strategic Energy Investment Fund. The program targets grid-scale deployment to tackle climbing electricity demand and regional transmission cost pressures.
The launch comes as state leadership works to expand a mid-Atlantic solar and storage footprint that currently stands at 3,440 MWdc of installed solar capacity across 119,137 individual installations, representing $7.7 billion in total investment and generating 8.77% of Maryland’s electricity.
While solar currently powers over 408,000 homes, the state’s battery storage capacity remains modest at just 35 MWh, underscoring the need for near-term grid-scale storage incentives. With a robust local footprint of 200 solar companies including 17 manufacturers and 100 installers and developers supporting nearly 5,000 jobs, current market forecasts project Maryland will add 2,637 MW of solar capacity over the next five years.
The initiative utilizes a strict two-stage competitive bidding process designed to weed out speculative proposals and back projects capable of reaching commercial operation. Developers must establish baseline eligibility by November 30, 2026, through a preliminary application where MEA will evaluate initial project parameters, real estate control, and interconnection standing.
Applicants cleared in this first stage must then submit their final bid price per megawatt-hour alongside comprehensive financial models and documentation by January 22, 2027. MEA anticipates issuing grant decisions in Spring 2027, with selected projects required to achieve commercial operation within seven years of funding allocation.
MEA is casting a wide net for asset classes, opening eligibility to Tier 1 renewable energy generation projects not participating in net energy metering, energy storage systems encompassing standalone battery energy storage systems as well as systems co-located with net-metered or non-net-metered Tier 1 renewables, and hybrid assets coupling generation and storage directly. Rather than relying on fixed incentives, MEA will award grants to eligible developers requesting the lowest price per megawatt-hour through the closed-bid auction format.
Renewable energy and energy storage projects are the quickest, cleanest, lowest cost option to develop local energy supply, according to MEA Director Kelly Speakes-Backman. Developers can review the complete Funding Opportunity Announcement, financial model templates, and submit proposals through the online My MEA portal.

title: Western Australia to allow balcony solar-plus-storage - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
In an Australian first, Western Australia is on the path to legalise plug-in solar panels and batteries based on
standards, which can plug in to a household wall outlet, offering clean energy for homes and apartments/units unable to benefit from rooftop solar installations and can also be moved when a resident changes address.
WA Energy and Decarbonisation Minister Amber-Jade Sanderson said the benefits of cheap solar have been out of reach for anyone who doesn’t own their roof.
“That isn’t fair, and the Cook Labor Government is doing something about it,” Sanderson said.
“I’m proud that our State is leading the nation on this issue – millions of European households already use these systems every day, and WA families should be able to do the same.”
The WA department of Energy and Economic Diversification (DEED) and Local Government, Industry Regulation and Safety’s Building and Energy Division (LGIRS) are consulting on the proposed legalisation pathway and a new technical standard.
The proposal would mean plug-in systems are classed as standard electrical appliances through a new Technical Bridging
Standard
(TBS), which proposes to enable plug-in systems with solar panel combinations up to a rated capacity of 2 kW (DC), and with inverters up to a rated capacity of 800 VA (AC).
The TBS does not propose to set an upper limit on plug-in battery storage capacity.
Balcony solar advocacy organisation Solar Citizens Chief Executive Officer Heidi Lee Douglas said it agrees it isn’t fair that the
benefits
of cheap solar are out of reach for anyone who doesn’t own their own roof.
“WA’s announcement starts a ‘race to the top’, and puts a rocket up the need for the federal government to announce a nationally coordinated approach for the release of this money-saving technology across Australia by July next year,” Douglas said.
“We support the Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen announcing a date for the legal safe sale of these money saving devices that are already legally and safely available in the United Kingdom, Germany and 10 states of
America.
“Plug-in solar and batteries are an anti-inflationary energy reform. They put downward pressure on household electricity bills, allow more Australians to use cheap solar power, and can reduce demand for expensive electricity during peak periods,” Douglas said.
According to the WA plug-in solar and
batteries
consultation website, DEED and LGIRS will continue to work with safety experts, other states and territories, and the Australian Government to support nationally consistent requirements for plug-in systems.
“For this reason, the final TBS is likely to have two separate parts, one each for product-specific requirements and another for installation requirements. This would make the TBS more consistent with AS/NZS technical documents,” the site says.
The department will also work on other changes that might be needed to support renter access to the systems once they are available.

title: A New Chemistry Breakthrough Could Change How Scientists Build Quantum Computers
content:
Chemistry
Diamond is one of the materials currently being investigated to make quantum computers and sensors. When nitrogen is added to diamond in a very specific way, the material has certain properties that could be ideal for quantum computers and sensors. Such diamond typically looks pink. Credit: Michael Livingston / PPPL Communications Department
Most materials being considered for quantum technology can hold a stable quantum state only when chilled to extreme temperatures. Diamond-based materials can work at room temperature, but their usefulness depends on defects in the crystal that have been difficult and computationally demanding to simulate.
At the U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE) Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL), staff research scientist Mark Martirez has developed a far faster way to calculate how those defects respond to light and microwave pulses. The approach has identified promising boron- and oxygen-based defects that could serve as qubits, the basic information-processing units of quantum computers and sensors. The research was recently published in
ACS Central Science
and has already attracted
attention
Diamond’s flaws can store quantum information
Pure diamond consists entirely of carbon atoms, but storing and processing quantum information requires a disruption in that structure. A carbon atom might be missing from its usual position, an atom of another element might take its place, or both changes might occur together. The cluster of atoms closest to the defect forms the qubit.
Scientists use laser light and microwave pulses to read information stored in these qubits. Most quantum diamond research has focused on the nitrogen-vacancy defect, in which a nitrogen atom replaces a carbon atom and a nearby position normally occupied by another carbon atom is empty. When illuminated by a laser, this qubit emits red light if it is in a particular quantum state. Calculating how other defects respond to light and microwaves helps researchers assess whether they, too, could be useful.
Molecular models identify new qubit candidates
Martirez simplifies those calculations by computationally “carving out” a cluster of just 16 to 30 atoms around a defect and considering it in isolation. This makes highly accurate tools that chemists have used for decades to study simple compounds available for studying defects inside a solid.
“Because we’re treating the qubits as molecules, the cost of calculating these defects is equivalent to the cost of just modeling a simple molecule,” Martirez said. “This method really opened the floodgates” in terms of how qubits can be assessed.
The calculations identified oxygen-based defects that shine blue and boron-based defects that emit ultraviolet light. These defects, known as color centers, could potentially serve different roles within a single quantum device.
“One could imagine, then, combining different qubits of different responses, so you can basically probe one qubit but not the other,” Martirez said.
Chemistry’s path to custom qubits
Understanding the chemistry could also change how researchers conceive of a qubit’s structure. Diamond-based qubits are often treated as a physics problem, but Martirez’s work shows that chemistry offers another way to understand them. A fuller chemical understanding could let scientists design and build qubits for specific purposes, much as chemists design custom molecules, such as a new medication.
Martirez encouraged other chemists to bring their expertise into solid-state physics. “At this moment in time, there’s a great emphasis on building the first state-of-the-art qubit computer,” he said. “But it’s not just physicists who should be participating in this research. Chemists have decades of developed intuition about chemical systems that could be easily translated into understanding defects in solids as well.”
Practical quantum devices could eventually support sensors with greater sensitivity and accuracy than those currently available, along with computers capable of tackling highly complex problems far faster than today’s conventional supercomputers. Developing these future technologies is among the strategic national priorities PPPL works to advance.
For quantum chemistry, that progress could create a useful cycle. The field could help develop tools that allow it to “enrich itself” in the decades ahead, Martirez said. He expects a practical system containing multiple qubits to greatly improve the accuracy of quantum chemistry calculations.
“We could describe larger molecules, biomolecules, proteins, and everything like that in a more accurate way, and that could improve all the chemical-adjacent industries, such as pharmaceutical science and materials science. Even our fundamental understanding of molecular systems could be enriched.”
Reference: “A Chemist’s Guide to Solid-State Qubits: Diamond Color Centers as Embedded Vacancy-Centered Molecules” by John Mark P. Martirez, July 27, 2026,
ACS Central Science
DOI: 10.1021/acscentsci.6c00548
Funding for this research comes from PPPL’s Laboratory Directed Research and Development under prime contract number DE-AC02-09CH11466, as well as additional support from DOE Office of Science, Office of Fusion Energy Sciences.

title: A Routine Blood Test Could Predict Dementia Risk 15 Years in Advance
content:
A routine blood test measuring hemoglobin levels may offer clues about a person’s risk of developing dementia up to 15 years later, according to a large study. Credit: Shutterstock
A large study tracking more than 316,000 adults for up to 15 years suggests that a routine blood test may reveal important clues about future dementia risk.
A standard blood test taken during a routine health check could offer clues about dementia risk more than a decade later. In a study of more than 316,000 adults, researchers found that people with unusually low or high levels of hemoglobin were more likely to develop dementia, although the risks varied depending on the type of disease.
Hemoglobin is the oxygen-carrying protein in red blood cells. Low levels are commonly associated with anemia, while unusually high levels can result from smoking, dehydration, or certain heart and lung conditions. The findings suggest that this familiar blood measurement may also reflect broader aspects of physical health associated with brain aging.
Tracking Dementia Risk for Up to 15 Years
Researchers analyzed health records from 316,542 Korean adults aged 40 and older who underwent national health screenings in 2004 and 2005. Participants were divided into five groups based on their hemoglobin levels, from the lowest 20% to the highest 20%. National health insurance records were then used to track new dementia diagnoses through the end of 2019.
Compared with the group that had the lowest dementia rate, participants in the lowest hemoglobin category had a 16% higher risk of developing dementia from any cause. Those in the highest category had a 7% greater risk.
The findings, published in the
Journal of Alzheimer’s Disease
and presented at the 39th ECNP Congress in Munich, also identified differences between Alzheimer’s disease and vascular dementia.
Alzheimer’s and Vascular Dementia Show Different Patterns
For Alzheimer’s disease, the increased risk was concentrated among people with the lowest hemoglobin levels. Participants in this group were 14% more likely to develop the disease than those in the reference group.
The relationship was different for vascular dementia (caused by reduced blood flow to the brain). People in the lowest hemoglobin category had a 19% higher risk, while those in the highest category had an 18% higher risk. However, the association did not follow a consistent pattern across all five hemoglobin groups. The researchers also observed clearer and more consistent relationships among women than men.
What Hemoglobin Levels May Reveal About Brain Health
Lead researcher Dr. Hyun Soo Kim, an assistant professor at Dong-A University College of Medicine in Busan, South Korea, emphasized that the results do not establish a direct causal relationship.
“The findings do not show that hemoglobin itself causes dementia, but suggest that abnormal hemoglobin levels may be a visible marker of wider physical vulnerability relevant to brain health.”
Kim added, “Dementia is one of the fastest-growing health challenges in aging societies, and there are not many treatments and no cure. Identifying simple, accessible markers of future risk could help researchers and clinicians better understand how whole-body health relates to brain health over time.”
Could Routine Blood Tests Help Identify Future Risk?
Hemoglobin is already measured in standard blood tests around the world, making it considerably more accessible than specialized brain imaging or newer dementia biomarkers. The researchers suggest that existing blood test results could potentially help scientists investigate connections between general physical health and long-term cognitive decline.
Kim explained, “A blood test most people already get at a routine check-up may say something about their brain health many years later. In this large Korean cohort, people with unusually low hemoglobin, and, to a smaller degree, those with unusually high hemoglobin, were more likely to develop dementia. This does not prove that hemoglobin causes dementia, but it supports the idea that general physical health, including the body’s ability to carry oxygen, matters for long-term brain health.”
Why the Findings Do Not Prove Cause and Effect
Because the study was observational, it cannot determine whether abnormal hemoglobin levels contribute directly to dementia. Other medical conditions could influence both hemoglobin measurements and brain health. Early dementia processes might also affect nutrition, body weight, frailty, or anemia before the disease is formally diagnosed.
“We want to emphasize that the findings should not be interpreted as advice to take iron supplements, to raise hemoglobin levels, or to lower high hemoglobin levels in order to prevent dementia. An abnormal hemoglobin result should instead be discussed with a doctor, because it may point to underlying health issues that deserve attention,” Kim said.
More Research Is Needed Across Different Populations
The study drew on health records from South Korea, leaving questions about whether the same relationships apply to people from other ethnic, geographic, and medical backgrounds. Further research is also needed to establish whether identifying abnormal hemoglobin levels can meaningfully improve dementia risk assessment or prevention.
Dr. Lindsey Sinclair (University of Southampton), who was not involved in the research, commented:
“There is a growing body of evidence that physical health and brain health are intertwined. We are also increasingly aware that changes supporting better brain health, be they medical or lifestyle changes, are important in mid-life to reduce the risk of later dementia. While this study shows a possible link between hemoglobin levels and dementia risk, more work is required to understand if this link is present in people from a wider range of backgrounds; and what can best be done to reduce dementia risk in people with the lowest and highest levels of hemoglobin.”

title: Aging’s “Zombie Cell” Problem May Have a Solution, Scientists Discover
content:
Senescent cells, often called “zombie cells,” are cells that have stopped dividing but remain alive and metabolically active. Although they play important roles in wound healing and tissue repair, they can accumulate with age, releasing inflammatory substances that damage surrounding tissues and contribute to age-related diseases. Credit: Shutterstock
“Zombie cells” become harder to clear with age, and a new study reveals why the immune system struggles to remove them.
Researchers at Albert Einstein College of Medicine have identified a breakdown in protein recycling that helps explain why senescent cells, often called “zombie cells,” accumulate in aging tissues. In experiments involving older mice, restoring that process reduced senescent-cell buildup, inflammation, and tissue scarring. The findings, published in
Nature Aging
, suggest a possible way to help the immune system clear these cells more effectively.
Senescent cells remain alive after they stop dividing, but their activity changes. Although they can support tissue repair, their prolonged presence can fuel chronic inflammation and age-related disease. Most of the new experiments involved mice, with human lung samples providing evidence that the biological changes may also occur in people.
“In older animals, age-related changes in both senescent cells and the immune cells responsible for removing them allow these zombie cells to accumulate and play a role in disease,” said study leader Ana Maria Cuervo, M.D., Ph.D. “By restoring cellular recycling, we may be able to help the body’s own defenses clear these cells more effectively.”
Dr. Cuervo, study leader, distinguished professor of developmental & molecular biology and of medicine, and co-director of the Institute for Geroscience at Einstein. Credit: Albert Einstein College of Medicine
When Helpful Cells Overstay Their Welcome
Some injured cells enter senescence and release substances that recruit other cells to support repair. Once that work is done, immune cells called macrophages normally remove the senescent cells.
Macrophages also fight infection, dispose of dead cells, and regulate inflammation and tissue repair. The researchers found that their ability to remove senescent cells depends partly on chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA), a recycling process that uses specialized “chaperone” molecules to select damaged or unnecessary proteins for breakdown.
When the team genetically altered mice so their macrophages lacked CMA, senescent cells lingered at wound sites, and healing slowed compared with control animals. The experiment showed how a defect inside immune cells can turn a temporary repair response into a lingering obstacle to recovery.
Cuervo, a leading CMA researcher, is a distinguished professor of developmental & molecular biology and medicine, the Robert and Renee Belfer Chair for the Study of Neurodegenerative Diseases, and co-director of Einstein’s Institute for Geroscience. Her
earlier research
established that CMA declines with age. Subsequent work linked
the resulting buildup of cellular waste
to Alzheimer’s and other neurodegenerative diseases, as well as atherosclerosis and diabetes.
Old and Young Zombie Cells Behave Differently
The age-related decline in CMA also affects senescent cells themselves. To examine this, the researchers collected fibroblasts, cells found in connective tissue, from young and old mice. They then used drugs to stop the cells from dividing and induce senescence in the laboratory.
Cells from young mice responded by increasing CMA activity. Cells from old mice failed to increase their already low activity, allowing certain proteins to escape proper breakdown. They consequently released harmful substances that encouraged neighboring healthy cells to become senescent and interfered with macrophages’ ability to recognize and remove them.
At the same time, macrophages from older animals had lower CMA activity than those from younger animals and were less able to engulf senescent cells. Aging therefore disrupted both the cells awaiting removal and the immune cells responsible for clearing them.
Age-related changes in senescent cells could affect drug development. Researchers are developing senolytics to eliminate these cells, but testing them on cells taken from young animals and induced to become senescent in the lab may not accurately predict their effects in older bodies.
Restoring the Body’s Cleanup Process
The findings pointed toward another possibility: improve cellular recycling so senescent cells release fewer harmful substances and macrophages can recognize and engulf them more effectively. The team tested a compound it had previously developed, a small-molecule CMA activator called CA77.1.
Aged mice given CA77.1 orally every day for five months accumulated fewer senescent cells in several organs. They also showed fewer signs of inflammation and fibrosis, the buildup of scar tissue.
In a separate experiment, the researchers treated macrophages collected from aged mice with CA77.1. Their ability to engulf particles recovered to levels comparable to those of macrophages from young mice. That result demonstrated improved engulfing capacity, while the experiments in living animals showed reduced senescent-cell accumulation.
Testing A Link to Lung Fibrosis
The researchers next investigated idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), an aging-associated disease in which scar tissue progressively builds up in the lungs, making breathing increasingly difficult. People diagnosed with IPF have a median survival of three to five years.
Lung samples from patients with IPF showed markedly reduced CMA activity, prompting the researchers to test whether boosting it with CA77.1 could help in a mouse model of lung fibrosis. Treatment with CA77.1 soon after lung injury reduced scarring, senescence, and inflammation.
“Our research connects two major drivers of aging—declining CMA and cellular senescence—and shows for the first time how their interaction allows senescent cells to evade clearance by the immune system in old organisms,” said Dr. Cuervo. “We’ve also found that instead of trying to kill zombie cells, we may be able to restore their interaction with the immune system so that the body can clear them naturally. The next challenge is determining whether this approach can eventually be developed into a safe treatment for age-related diseases in people.”
Reference: “Decline of chaperone-mediated autophagy in aging impairs macrophage clearance of senescent cells” by Rebecca Sereda, Kristen Lindenau, Antonio Diaz, Zhaohui Liu, Olaya Santiago-Fernández, Rabia R. Khawaja, Ronald Cutler, Jazmin Calyeca, Mericka McCabe, Sylvére Durand, Fanny Aprahamian, Natalia Del Pilar Vanegas, Hu Chen, Felipe Vilicich, Bhakti Chavda, Yair Botbol, Guido Kroemer, Toren Finkel, Evripidis Gavathiotis, Simone Sidoli, Ana L. Mora, Mauricio Rojas, Susmita Kaushik and Ana Maria Cuervo, 5 October 2026,
Nature Aging

title: Beyond Bad Cholesterol: Scientists Uncover a Hidden Driver of Heart Disease
content:
Researchers have uncovered unexpected molecular similarities between two types of blood lipoproteins, pointing to inflammatory pathways that could reshape heart disease prevention. Credit: Shutterstock
Protein patterns linked to TRL and Lp(a), two types of fat-carrying particles, suggest shared inflammatory pathways that could offer new targets for heart disease prevention.
Lowering “bad” cholesterol substantially reduces the risk of a heart attack, yet some people still develop coronary heart disease after treatment brings their LDL cholesterol down to a recommended level. Other particles that carry fats through the blood can contribute to the risk that remains. Understanding how they affect blood vessels could help researchers find more precise ways to prevent heart disease.
Coronary heart disease develops when cholesterol accumulates in the blood vessels supplying the heart and can lead to a heart attack if untreated. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), cardiovascular diseases kill nearly 17.9 million people worldwide each year, with heart attacks and strokes accounting for more than four out of five of those deaths.
Researchers at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden measured almost 3,000 proteins in blood samples from around 35,000 UK Biobank participants without previous heart disease, to see if differences in blood proteins could give any clues as to why a risk of heart disease still prevails in some people after bad cholesterol levels are brought down to a healthy level. Credit: Wikimedia Commons
Cholesterol carriers are not equally harmful
Researchers at
Chalmers University of Technology
in Sweden have now identified blood protein patterns that offer clues to what happens beyond cholesterol buildup. Two types of fat-carrying particles, triglyceride-rich lipoproteins (TRL) and lipoprotein(a), or Lp(a), shared many protein patterns and signs of potentially harmful biological effects. The pattern associated with LDL, or low-density lipoprotein, was mainly linked to cholesterol accumulating in artery walls.
All three types of particles can deposit cholesterol in artery walls, and LDL is the most abundant. But abundance does not tell the whole story. A
previous study
Clemens Wittenbecher, Assistant Professor of Precision Medicine and Diagnostics, at the Department of Life Sciences, Chalmers University of Technology, Sweden. Credit: Chalmers University of Technology | Martina Butorac
“For this study, we wanted to understand what happens beyond the accumulation of cholesterol in artery walls, whether different fat-carrying particles can damage the blood vessels differently and why the remaining risk of heart disease still occurs,” says Jakub Morze, lead author and a postdoctoral fellow at Chalmers University of Technology.
Protein patterns point to shared inflammation
The team used proteomics, the study of proteins, to examine how the three types of particles affect the body. Proteins carry out essential functions, and their levels can change with diet, stress, aging, or disease. Measuring them provides a snapshot of how the body is functioning at that moment. The researchers combined measurements of almost 3,000 blood proteins with genetic data and long-term health records to identify patterns that might help explain how the particles damage arteries.
The overlapping protein patterns associated with TRL and Lp(a) appeared to be linked to the later development of heart disease. These particles also contained proteins that attract immune cells, which could contribute to inflammation and changes in the structure of blood vessel walls. Although TRL and Lp(a) are different types of particles, the findings suggested that some of their harmful effects may involve shared biological pathways.
A graphic showing three types of fat-carrying particles (lipoproteins) which can deposit cholesterol in the blood vessel walls. Their common feature is apolipoprotein B particle on their surface. Credit: Chalmers University of Technology | Jakub Morze
“The overlap for TRL and Lp(a) is one of the most interesting findings,” says Morze. “It suggests that these particles may affect some of the same inflammatory and vascular processes. This could help identify targets for more precisely directed prevention in the future.”
“Lowering LDL cholesterol remains a cornerstone of prevention,” says Clemens Wittenbecher, who led the study and is Assistant Professor of Precision Medicine and Diagnostics at Chalmers. “Our findings point to biological processes that may help explain some of the risk that remains beyond LDL. The next step is to establish whether measuring or targeting these processes can improve prevention alongside existing treatments.”

title: Drinking Tea May Lower Your Risk of Vascular Disease – but There’s a Catch
content:
Tea is one of the world’s most widely consumed beverages, enjoyed for its diverse flavors and potential health benefits. Rich in natural compounds such as polyphenols and antioxidants, tea has attracted scientific interest for its possible effects on heart health, metabolism, and overall well-being. Credit: Shutterstock
Not all tea-drinking habits were associated with the same health benefits. Researchers found that tea type, strength, and temperature were linked to notable differences in vascular disease risk.
People who regularly drank tea had a lower risk of diseases affecting the heart and blood vessels in a large study in China. However, the pattern varied with the type, strength, and temperature of the tea, with “burning hot” tea associated with elevated risk.
The study, published in the
Journal of Internal Medicine
, followed 485,934 adults for a median of 9.05 years. Researchers recorded 14,863 cases of cardiovascular disease, cerebrovascular disease, pulmonary heart disease, and peripheral artery disease. These conditions involve the heart and circulation, including blood vessels in the brain, heart problems related to lung disease, and reduced blood flow through arteries supplying the limbs. Regular tea consumption was associated with an 11% lower risk of these outcomes compared with not drinking tea.
Tea drinking was also considered alongside smoking and physical activity, providing context for how it fit into a broader pattern of habits.
“Joint analyses showed that tea consumption, smoking status, and physical were collectively associated with vascular risk, with the favorable combination of habitual tea consumption, non-current smoking and high physical activity associated with the lowest risk,” the authors wrote.
Tea type, strength, and temperature matter
Among weekly tea drinkers, the lowest risk was estimated at approximately 6 to 8 cups per day. Black tea showed more consistent associations with lower vascular disease risk than green tea, while moderate-strength tea was associated with the lowest risk. These findings describe associations, rather than establishing that a particular amount or preparation of tea prevents disease.
The elevated risk associated with “burning hot” tea contrasts with the lower risk linked to regular tea consumption overall. Temperature therefore matters when interpreting the findings, but the reported results do not explain why very hot tea was associated with higher risk or establish that heat itself caused the increase.
