title: Hubble Finds a Stunning Twist in How the Universe Emerged From Darkness
content:
This painting shows massive stars emitting ionizing radiation, but gas swept up by supernova-driven galactic winds can prevent that radiation from escaping the galaxy. Credit: Siyi Wang
Hubble observations of nearby starburst galaxies challenge the idea that supernova winds helped reionize the early universe, suggesting young stars may have enabled radiation to escape before those winds formed.
Powerful winds from exploding stars were thought to clear paths for ultraviolet radiation to escape early galaxies. A new study of nearby galaxies suggests those winds may instead make escape more difficult, challenging a leading explanation for how the universe emerged from a fog of neutral hydrogen.
Within the first billion years after the Big Bang, that fog made the universe opaque to ultraviolet light. It began to clear during an era called reionization, which started about 13 billion years ago. Energetic radiation from early galaxies struck neutral hydrogen atoms, separating them into charged protons and electrons.
“Eventually, when it ionized the majority of hydrogen filling intergalactic space, that was the end of reionization and we see the universe today,” said Cody Carr, a postdoctoral researcher in the Department of Astronomy at the University of Michigan. “We call reionization the last major phase transition of the universe.”
For radiation to transform the gas between galaxies, it first had to get out of the galaxies that produced it. Astronomers proposed that supernovae, or large exploding stars, helped by generating winds powerful enough to reshape galaxies and clear routes through the surrounding gas.
“Basically, how these galaxies were leaking ionizing radiation isn’t what we thought,” Carr said.
Faster winds, less escaping radiation
Carr led and carried out the study as a postdoctoral scholar at Zhejiang University in China before joining Michigan. The international team, which includes University of Michigan researchers, used the Hubble Space Telescope to observe nearby starburst galaxies, where stars form at exceptionally high rates. These galaxies resemble some of those thought to have helped reionize the early universe, giving researchers a way to investigate how radiation escapes.
The team analyzed the galaxies’ spectra, which separate their light into different wavelengths, to measure the speeds of their galactic winds. Gas moving in those winds absorbs light at specific wavelengths, leaving dips whose positions and widths reveal how the gas is moving. Galaxies with the fastest winds allowed the smallest fraction of ionizing radiation to escape.
“It appears that energy input from supernovae has stirred up the surroundings and increased, rather than decreased, the coverage of neutral gas and dust that suppresses ionizing radiation escape,” said Stephan McCandliss, a senior author of the study and director of the Center for Astrophysical Sciences at Johns Hopkins University.
Young stars may help radiation escape
The findings, published in
Nature Astronomy
, strengthen an alternative explanation centered on activity from young stars. Radiation and smaller winds operating in the neighborhoods of these stars could help light escape.
“Our observations show that these photons are escaping before galactic winds form,” Carr said.
The researchers are working to secure more Hubble observing time to examine additional galaxies and further test the role of these smaller winds. Hubble is a NASA mission launched with contributions from the European Space Agency. The telescope also supported the study through a grant administered by the Space Telescope Science Institute.
Connecting the behavior of nearby galaxies to the universe’s early transformation remains an unfinished task. “We don’t know exactly what objects caused reionization or how it evolved,” Carr said. “We know that it took place, but we don’t have complete answers to those questions.”
The observations can already inform computer simulations that astronomers use to investigate reionization, particularly how stellar activity changes the gas through which radiation must travel.
“Supernovae play a central role in cosmological hydrodynamic simulations that explain how ionizing radiation escapes from galaxies,” said Renyue Cen, a senior author of the study and professor and director of the Center for Cosmology and Computational Astrophysics at Zhejiang University. “Our findings highlight the need to examine how radiation and winds from young stars shape the surrounding gas before the first supernovae explode.”

title: Obesity Could Disable a Key Defense Against Breast Cancer, Study Finds
content:
Scientists have discovered that fat cells in breast tissue may play an unexpected role in protecting against cancer. Credit: Shutterstock
A hopeful new direction in the fight against breast cancer may lie in the body’s own defenses, as mouse experiments suggest that protection weakened by obesity could be restored.
Breast cancer develops in tissue surrounded by fat cells, and those cells may play a greater role in controlling tumor growth than previously understood. Researchers have discovered that fat cells in lean breast tissue produce a molecule that helps destroy cancerous cells. In obesity, production of this protective molecule drops, potentially removing one of the body’s natural defenses against breast cancer.
The finding comes from researchers at Huntsman Cancer Institute at the University of Utah (the U), who identified a previously underappreciated way obesity may contribute to breast cancer. Rather than simply creating conditions that encourage cancer growth, obesity may also weaken a biological process that normally helps eliminate dangerous cells.
The research was led by Keren Hilgendorf, PhD, a Huntsman Cancer Institute investigator and assistant professor of biochemistry at the U, and first author Meghan Curtin, a doctoral candidate in molecular biology at the university. Their findings were published in the journal
Keren Hilgendorf, PhD. Credit: Huntsman Cancer Institute
Lean fat cells promote cancer cell death
Much of the breast consists of fat cells called adipocytes. These cells become larger with obesity, changing the surrounding tissue environment in ways that can affect cancer cells. By studying preclinical models, including breast tissue from donors, the researchers identified a key difference between lean and obese adipocytes involving a fatty acid known as 9S-HODE.
Lean adipocytes produced substantially more 9S-HODE than obese adipocytes. This molecule helps promote ferroptosis, a form of cell death involving iron-dependent damage to cellular fats. Ferroptosis is one of the processes through which the body can eliminate old or damaged cells, including those that could become cancerous.
“We found that the lean adipocytes produce much more 9S-HODE than obese ones. This means that cancerous cells die more readily in lean tissue,” says Curtin. “By producing more 9S-HODE, our bodies are actively protecting us, under lean circumstances, in a way it cannot with obesity.”
Boosting 9S-HODE suppresses tumor growth in mice
The researchers also tested whether restoring this molecule could change tumor growth. In preclinical mouse models, increasing 9S-HODE levels in obese adipocytes suppressed breast cancer tumor growth. This suggests that the reduced production of 9S-HODE associated with obesity may contribute directly to the loss of a protective mechanism.
For Hilgendorf, the results offer a different way to understand the relationship between obesity and cancer.
“We uncovered the role of a molecule that normally appears in lean tissue that restrains breast cancer growth but is less present with obesity,” says Hilgendorf. “We know obesity is often a driver of breast cancer, and researchers in our field usually consider how obesity is promoting the disease. But we hadn’t really considered that obesity could also be the loss of something that naturally protects us.”
Meghan Curtin, Doctoral Candidate. Credit: Huntsman Cancer Institute
Could 9S-HODE become a cancer therapy?
That distinction could have implications for treatment. If 9S-HODE helps limit tumor growth, researchers may eventually be able to develop therapies that restore its protective activity. The mouse experiments provide early evidence supporting this possibility, although further research is needed to determine whether the approach could work in patients.
“From a clinical perspective, this discovery is incredibly empowering. Because 9S-HODE is naturally present in the body but is lost with obesity, we may be able to restore this protection by putting it back,” says Hilgendorf. “That could become a very feasible therapeutic approach to slow breast cancer growth.”
The researchers emphasize that obesity is only one of several factors contributing to breast cancer, which can also develop for unrelated reasons. Their findings suggest that 9S-HODE is produced primarily by fat cells in the breast, although fat cells elsewhere in the body may provide similar protection. Whether this mechanism operates in other tissues remains an open question.
“We believe this shift in the understanding of the roles of lean and obese adipocytes is the start of something. This is just one discovery, and it’s not the end of the road,” says Curtin. “This opened our eyes to new ways to think about science, and hopefully we can harness what our bodies are already doing to make progress against this disease.”
Reference: “Lean adipocyte oxylipin signaling restrains breast cancer through ferroptosis” by Meghan C. Curtin, Abigail E. Jackson, Mark D. Lee, Elisabeth A. Brown, J. Alan Maschek, David H. Lum, James E. Cox, Alana L. Welm and Keren I. Hilgendorf, 10 September 2026,
DOI: 10.1126/science.aea4287

title: Scientists Discover a Hidden Weakness in Cancer Cells That Could Transform Treatment
content:
Cell experiments revealed that the cancer drug target Wee1 also helps healthy cells copy DNA, a previously overlooked role that could explain treatment toxicity and guide safer therapies. Credit: Shutterstock
A new study reveals a previously overlooked weakness in certain cancer cells that could help researchers refine targeted treatments and reduce harmful side effects.
Cancer cells that have lost one safeguard against DNA damage can become dependent on another, an enzyme called Wee1. Drugs that block Wee1 aim to exploit that weakness, but serious side effects are disrupting clinical trials and threatening their adoption in the clinic.
One of the cell’s main safeguards is the tumor-suppressor protein p53, which can halt the cell cycle when DNA damage is detected. In around half of all cancers, p53 is inactive, allowing damaged cells to continue growing. Wee1 provides a second line of defense, acting as a backup brake that prevents cells with damaged DNA from entering cell division. Cancers with mutated p53 rely on this remaining safeguard, making Wee1 an attractive drug target.
Blocking Wee1 may stall healthy cells
A study published in
has now revealed that Wee1 also helps healthy cells begin copying their DNA, much earlier in the cell cycle. Researchers from the MRC Laboratory of Medical Sciences (LMS), the University of Oxford, and UCL found that this role involves a protein degradation complex, a group of proteins that breaks down molecules needed for DNA replication. Wee1 helps switch off the complex so replication can begin. Without Wee1, the complex remains active, delaying or preventing cells from progressing through the cell cycle.
“We think what’s happening in patients is that when they’re being treated with these Wee1 inhibitors, it’s stopping their normal fast proliferating cells, like you get in the colon and the blood system, from starting to replicate,” says Alexis, head of the Cell Cycle Control group at the LMS. “And so those cells are stuck, unable to generate new cells, and that could be causing some of the toxic side effects.”
Cell experiments challenge the Wee1 model
The discovery grew out of an effort to test the established understanding of Wee1’s activity early in the cell cycle. The team built a mathematical model based on the scientific literature to predict what would happen when the enzyme was inhibited.
“Wee1 has been very intensely studied in the later stages of the cell cycle, where targeting its activity for cancer treatment makes sense,” says Alexis. “However, the side effects of Wee1 inhibitors in patients were hard to explain based on these functions so we started to wonder if this Wee1 enzyme had some other function that we hadn’t appreciated that could explain these. We wanted to look earlier in the cell cycle to see if there was something we had missed.”
Human epithelial cells labelled for a Wee1 target (phosphorylated CDK; in yellow) and DNA (in blue). Credit: Cell Cycle Control Group, MRC Laboratory of Medical Sciences
The researchers then tested the model’s predictions in healthy and cancerous cells. Alexis says, “We quickly found out that the model we had based on the literature on Wee1 was wrong because that was not what we saw in cells. What had been missed was an early function of Wee1 that people hadn’t looked at.”
Matching Wee1 inhibitors to vulnerable cancers
If the side effects are linked to Wee1’s role in controlling the protein degradation complex, the findings could help identify patients most likely to benefit from treatment. The researchers suggest that cancers with reduced activity of this complex may be particularly susceptible to Wee1 inhibitors. That could create a therapeutic window in which lower doses kill cancer cells while limiting damage to healthy cells and reducing side effects.
“We’re also starting to think about if there are different ways we could inhibit Wee1 that get round this early cell cycle function,” says Alexis, “though how this might be achieved is a work in progress.”
The researchers now want to test the work’s predictions further in preclinical models and in patients currently enrolled in Wee1 inhibitor clinical trials. Those tests could help determine whether the newly identified function explains the toxic effects and how that understanding might guide safer treatment.
“Now we’ve uncovered this new function for Wee1, are there other functions that we haven’t appreciated? What else is it doing that we have not seen since we’ve not looked at the right stage?” asks Alexis.

Weston, Jade-Ellen Brown, Emma Graham, Leelou Moulin, Ivan Andrew, Georgia Roumelioti, Alex Montoya, Laurence Game, George R. Young, Keshava K. title: The Ocean’s Mysterious “Snow” Could Be Hiding a Powerful Climate Secret
content:
Viscous marine snow particles (white) colonized by bacteria (orange) transport carbon to the deep ocean. Credit: Must credit Bryce Inman
A new imaging technique reveals how bacteria interact with the microscopic structure of marine snow.
A surprising property of the tiny particles sinking through the ocean could help determine how much carbon is stored in the deep sea. Scientists have discovered that the stickiness of marine snow affects how easily bacteria can break it down, potentially changing how much carbon reaches the ocean depths.
Researchers at UC San Diego’s Scripps Institution of Oceanography and the University of Lincoln found that particularly gooey marine snow resists bacterial degradation. Their findings, published October 8 in
, suggest that highly viscous particles can transport more than six times as much carbon to the deep ocean as less viscous particles.
The Ocean’s Never-Ending Snowfall
Marine snow consists of tiny clumps of dead plankton, waste, mucus, minerals, and other debris that continuously descend through the water column. As these particles sink, they carry carbon from the sunlit surface ocean toward deeper waters, where some of it can remain stored for hundreds or thousands of years.
Scientists estimate that marine snow transports more than 10 gigatons (11 billion U.S. tons) of carbon away from the surface each year. However, only about 2 gigatons (2.2 billion U.S. tons) reach depths where the carbon can remain stored for extended periods. Much of the sinking material is broken down or recycled before reaching those depths.
The new research identifies particle viscosity, a measure of resistance to flow, as an important factor in this process. Marine snow particles vary in composition and consistency, and those differences influence how bacteria colonize and consume them.
Scientists Find a Way to See Inside Marine Snow
Understanding these interactions required a technique that had previously been unavailable: directly observing individual living bacteria as they navigate the microscopic structure of mucus.
“Observing individual bacteria interacting with the physical structure of mucus had never been possible,” said Bryce Inman, who began investigating the problem in 2021 while working as a postdoctoral scholar at Scripps Oceanography.
After four years of unsuccessful attempts, Inman and his colleagues, including Scripps microbiologist and professor emeritus Farooq Azam, developed a working approach in 2025. By combining 3D confocal microscopy with specialized fluorescent molecules, they could map the intricate physical structure of marine snow and track how bacteria interacted with it. The imaging technique is described in a companion study published in
Nature Communications
Why Stickier Marine Snow Carries More Carbon
The images showed that bacteria colonize less viscous regions near the surface of marine snow particles more easily than the thicker, more resistant material inside. These internal regions present a physical barrier that bacteria must gradually break down before penetrating farther into the particle.
“Bacteria can latch on to less viscous portions of each particle, but cannot reach more viscous regions until they break it down,” Inman explained. “Think of it like a worm in an apple: the flesh is easy to penetrate, but the core is tough to chew through”
Laboratory experiments confirmed that more viscous marine snow takes longer for bacteria to degrade and fragment. Computer simulations further suggested that these resistant particles can sink to greater depths before breaking apart. Together, the findings indicate that viscosity can substantially influence how much carbon escapes recycling in shallower waters and reaches the deep ocean.
What Ocean Slime Could Reveal About Other Ecosystems
The newly developed imaging method could also help researchers investigate interactions between bacteria and mucus in other environments. Similar relationships occur in coral reefs, kelp forests, plant root systems, and the digestive tracts of humans and other animals.
“Mucus, slime, whatever you want to call it, has a surprising amount of structure,” Inman said. “There are bulges, crevasses, all this sort of structure to it that we really had no idea about at a scale smaller than bacteria. This is the first time we’re really examining this physical habitat.”

title: This Alien Planet Should Have Lost Its Atmosphere Billions of Years Ago
content:
Artist’s concept of the lava world TOI-561 b and its star, whose surface churns with hot, bubbling gas. Webb observations show the planet reflects most of its starlight, and models suggest bright silicate clouds above its magma ocean may be the reason. Credit: CryoDragon Inc
James Webb Space Telescope observations suggest that exotic mineral clouds may be shielding a distant lava planet from its star.
A rocky planet exposed to extreme heat from its star appears to reflect nearly three-quarters of the starlight that reaches it. Astronomers suspect silicate-mineral clouds could act as a protective sunscreen, helping the planet maintain temperatures far below those expected for an exposed surface of molten rock.
The planet, TOI-561 b, lies about 280 light-years from Earth and was previously considered too hot to retain a substantial atmosphere. New observations from the
James Webb Space Telescope (JWST)
suggest that it has a significant envelope of gas that reflects incoming radiation and redistributes heat around the planet. The findings, published in
The Astronomical Journal
, challenge existing theories about how atmospheres survive on intensely irradiated rocky worlds.
Webb Observations Reveal an Unusual Temperature Pattern
An international research team, including University of Birmingham astrophysicist Dr. Anjali Piette, monitored TOI-561 b for 37 hours, covering nearly four complete orbits around its star. By measuring changes in the planet’s brightness and thermal emission throughout its orbit, the researchers investigated how heat is distributed between its permanently illuminated dayside and its dark nightside.
Earlier observations had shown that the dayside was unexpectedly cool for a bare, dark rocky surface. Scientists considered whether winds might be transporting the missing heat to the nightside or whether the planet was reflecting much of the incoming starlight. Webb’s first measurements of the nightside showed that it was not warm enough to account for the difference. The results indicate that TOI-561 b reflects approximately 75% of the starlight it receives, a proportion comparable to Venus.
Professor Lisa Dang, the project’s lead researcher at the University of Waterloo in Ontario, Canada, explained: “We measured how the planet’s brightness and heat changed throughout its orbit. This technique, known as a phase curve, revealed that the planet reflects a significant amount of light from its star, and that heat is being redistributed around the planet instead of only on the sunlit side. Together, these point to the presence of an atmosphere.”
Could Clouds Made of Rock Protect the Planet?
To investigate the planet’s unusual reflectivity, the researchers compared their measurements with computer simulations of its climate. The models suggest that clouds containing silicate minerals, including silicon dioxide (SiO2) and magnesium silicate (MgSiO3), could form on the dayside. These clouds might reflect substantial amounts of stellar radiation before it can heat the surface, much as a sunscreen reduces the amount of sunlight absorbed by skin.
The atmosphere’s chemical composition remains unknown. One possibility is a dense layer of carbon dioxide, resembling the atmosphere of Venus but exposed to much more extreme conditions. Another is an atmosphere rich in sulfur dioxide, a volcanic gas also released by Jupiter’s moon Io. Neither scenario would produce habitable conditions.
Why Hasn’t the Atmosphere Disappeared?
The evidence for a substantial atmosphere raises questions about the planet’s history. Intense stellar radiation should have stripped much of the gas from a rocky world like TOI-561 b over billions of years. Yet the new measurements strengthen
earlier findings
suggesting that the planet still possesses a thick atmosphere, potentially replenished by gases escaping from its molten interior.
Dr. Piette, Assistant Professor in Astronomy at the University of Birmingham, said: “Our discovery challenges current theories. We would expect a heavily irradiated rocky planet like TOI-561 b to have lost its atmosphere billions of years ago.”
“Instead, the evidence suggests it still has a significant atmosphere today. This raises major questions such as whether the planet started with an unusually large supply of gases or if the ocean of molten rock covering its surface, acts as a planet-wide volcano that is constantly feeding its atmosphere.”
The Next Question: What Is the Atmosphere Made Of?
Determining which gases surround TOI-561 b could help researchers understand how its atmosphere has persisted under such extreme conditions. Additional Webb observations at longer wavelengths may provide the spectral information needed to distinguish between competing atmospheric models and investigate whether volcanic activity is continually replacing gases lost to space.
Professor Dang added: “The next big question we will seek to answer is whether TOI-561 b’s atmosphere resembles Venus or an extreme version of Io. Observing the planet at longer wavelengths with JWST could give us insights and help explain how a planet this hot has held on to an atmosphere for billions of years.”

title: This Giant Planet Orbits Its Star Every Two Days – but Something Is Very Wrong
content:
After around 2033, planet TOI-1355 b will disappear from view as it must pass between the star and Earth to be seen. There would be no major changes for the planet itself. But astronomers will become unable to observe its transits to characterize the planetary nature for hundreds of years. © ESA/Hubble, N. Bartmann CC-BY Credit: ESA/Hubble, N. Bartmann CC-BY
Astronomers have discovered an unusual planet with an extremely hot host star and a highly eccentric orbit that challenges expectations for its class.
A giant planet racing around an unusually hot star has caught astronomers’ attention because of its highly elongated orbit. Known as TOI-1355 b, the planet completes one revolution in roughly two Earth days, following a path that differs sharply from the nearly circular orbits typical of many hot Jupiters.
Researchers from the
University of Tokyo
and their international collaborators believe the planet’s unusual trajectory could help explain how giant planets migrate toward their stars. However, its changing orbit is expected to limit observations after approximately 2033, leaving scientists a relatively short window to investigate its behavior.
An Unusual Orbit Around an Extremely Hot Star
TOI-1355 b belongs to a class of exoplanets called hot Jupiters, massive gas giants that orbit exceptionally close to their host stars. Its star, TOI-1355, has a surface temperature of approximately 8,400 degrees Celsius (15,152 degrees Fahrenheit), compared with about 5,500 degrees Celsius (9,932 degrees Fahrenheit) for the Sun.
Although astronomers have discovered thousands of planets around stars similar to or cooler than the Sun, planetary systems surrounding hotter stars remain less thoroughly explored. Project Researcher Noriharu Watanabe and Professor Norio Narita of the University of Tokyo’s Graduate School of Arts and Sciences are investigating these systems to better understand the diversity of planets beyond our solar system.
“Planet surveys around stars as hot or cooler than the sun are flourishing, and thousands of planets have been discovered around such stars. But planet surveys around hotter stars are still not advanced,” said Watanabe. “In this project, we hunted for planets around hot stars to examine the diversity of exoplanets more broadly. When we investigated the change in brightness of TOI-1355 from prior data, we found that the secondary eclipse, a phenomenon in which a planet passes behind a star, occurred faster than the timing assumed for a circular orbit. This was unusual for hot Jupiters around hot stars, and this is why we began to research this planet in detail.”
How Changes in Starlight Exposed the Planet’s Orbit
NASA’s Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) first detected periodic decreases in TOI-1355’s brightness. Narita’s team identified these dips as planetary transits, which occur when a planet passes in front of its star from Earth’s perspective and temporarily blocks a small fraction of its light.
The researchers also examined the secondary eclipse, when the planet passes behind its star. Its unexpected timing indicated that TOI-1355 b was traveling along an elliptical rather than circular orbit. By analyzing brightness variations recorded by TESS, the team determined the planet’s mass and orbital eccentricity, a measurement of how far an orbit deviates from a perfect circle. Calculating the mass required more complex mathematical models to account for the planet’s elongated trajectory.
Clues to a Planet’s Turbulent History
One possible explanation for TOI-1355 b’s orbit involves gravitational encounters with other massive planets or celestial bodies. Such interactions can dramatically alter a planet’s trajectory, sending it into a highly eccentric orbit. Over time, tidal forces from the host star can shrink and gradually circularize that orbit, potentially producing the close, nearly circular paths observed in many hot Jupiters.
“It is considered that the planetary orbit had become highly elliptical, initially due to the gravitational interaction with other celestial bodies, such as other giant planets, and shrunk gradually later due to the tidal effect of its host star,” said Watanabe.
The discovery supports theoretical predictions that hot Jupiters around hotter stars may undergo dramatic orbital migration. Researchers have not established which interactions shaped TOI-1355 b’s particular orbit, but its pronounced eccentricity is consistent with a history of gravitational disturbances followed by tidal evolution.
The team is now investigating how the planet’s orbital plane is tilted relative to the star’s rotation, another measurement that could help reconstruct its past. The researchers are preparing a separate paper on this work and planning an observation proposal involving NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope. With the planet’s evolving orbit expected to prevent the same transit and eclipse observations after around 2033, the opportunity to collect these measurements is limited.
Reference: “Discovery of an eccentric hot super-jupiter leaving the transiting geometry of the early-A-type star TOI-1355” by Noriharu Watanabe, Norio Narita, Akihiko Fukui, Bun’ei Sato, Keisuke Isogai, John H Livingston, Jerome P de Leon, Daniel Huber, Yugo Kawai, Yuya Hayashi, Masashi Omiya, Hideyuki Izumiura, Akito Tajitsu, Keivan G Stassun, Eric Girardin, Giuseppe Marino, Antonio Frasca, Giovanni Catanzaro, Javier Alonso-Santiago, Manfred Raetz, Stephanie Striegel, Nobuhiko Kusakabe and Motohide Tamura, 18 September 2026,

title: Ultra-Processed Foods May Be Changing How Children’s Brains Respond to Food
content:
Scientists have uncovered a potential connection between ultra-processed diets, the brain’s reward system, and changes in children’s body composition. Credit: Shutterstock
A yearlong study of 46 children suggests that brain responses to tempting food images may partly explain the link between ultra-processed diets and increasing body fat.
Ultra-processed foods account for about
67% of the daily calories
consumed by children in the United States. Although these products have been linked to weight gain and other health problems, scientists are still trying to understand how they may interact with the developing brain. New research suggests that children who eat more ultra-processed foods show stronger brain responses to appetizing food images, and those responses are associated with increases in body fat one year later.
Ultra-processed foods (UPFs) include products such as certain breakfast cereals, packaged breads, and instant soups. They are manufactured to be appealing, convenient, and shelf-stable, often containing artificial sweeteners, colors, and other ingredients not typically used in home cooking. Previous studies have linked UPF consumption to weight gain, type 2 diabetes, and cardiovascular disease, but the role of the brain’s reward system in these associations remains unclear.
Childhood may be an especially important time to investigate this relationship because the brain is still developing and food preferences are taking shape.
“Children’s brains are still developing, habits are still forming, and food preferences are still being made. It’s an important period where the brain is very sensitive to food and the food environment,” said study senior author Kathleen A. Page, MD, professor of medicine and pediatrics and co-chief of the Division of Endocrinology and Diabetes at the Keck School of Medicine of USC. “We’re particularly interested in understanding these processes in children, because we believe that intervening early could make a real difference.”
Brain scans reveal stronger reward responses
To explore how UPF consumption relates to brain activity and weight gain, researchers studied 46 children between the ages of seven and 10 who were enrolled in the long-term
BrainChild study
, which investigates diabetes and obesity risk. All participants began at a healthy weight, allowing the team to examine potential early signs of increased risk.
At the beginning of the study, researchers used magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to monitor the children’s brain activity while they viewed pictures of appealing foods, including cookies and French fries. The team also collected information about each child’s diet, body mass index (BMI), body fat percentage, and waist circumference. BMI is a measurement based on height and weight. One year later, researchers measured BMI, body fat percentage, and waist circumference again.
The brain scans revealed that children who consumed more UPFs had stronger responses to food pictures in the dorsal striatum, a brain region involved in reward and motivation. Children with stronger responses in this region also tended to experience greater increases in BMI and body fat percentage over the following year.
Brain responses may help explain weight gain
When they statistically accounted for how strongly each child’s dorsal striatum responded to food images, the association between UPF consumption and BMI weakened by 31%. The association with body fat percentage weakened by 44%. These findings suggest that the brain’s sensitivity to appealing food cues may help explain part of the relationship between UPF consumption and changes in body composition.
“This study goes beyond just understanding that UPFs affect weight gain,” Page said. “It actually gives us insight into the neurobiological underpinnings by which these foods may be linked to body composition over time.”
The findings, published in
JAMA Network Open
, provide evidence of a possible connection between diet, reward-related brain activity, and subsequent changes in body fat. The research was funded in part by the National Institutes of Health.
Whether diet changes the brain remains unknown
However, because the study was observational, it cannot establish that eating UPFs directly changes brain activity or causes weight gain. The results also do not determine whether stronger brain responses lead children to consume more UPFs or whether their diets influence how the brain responds to food.
To investigate cause and effect, Page hopes to conduct an intervention study in which children who regularly consume UPFs are provided with more minimally processed foods. Researchers could then examine whether changing their diets alters their brain responses to food images over time and whether those changes are associated with less weight gain.
The researchers also emphasize that improving children’s diets cannot depend entirely on individual families. Ultra-processed foods are often among the most affordable, convenient, and accessible options, making dietary changes difficult without broader improvements in food availability.
“Changing the food environment to help people access healthier, more minimally processed foods is an important part of the solution,” Page said.
Meanwhile, the BrainChild study will continue following participants through puberty and into young adulthood. By tracking changes in brain activity, body composition, diet, and overall health, researchers hope to better understand how eating habits during childhood relate to health later in life.
Reference: “Ultraprocessed Food Intake, Striatal Response to Food Cues, and Adiposity Gain in Children” by Jasmin M. Alves, Ella Morgan, Brendan Angelo, Kianna Le, Jared Smith, Ting Chow, Kay Jann, Anny H. Xiang and Kathleen A. Page, ,

title: Amazon Hedges Against AI Shopping Agents With 250 Million Outside Listings
content: For more than a year, Amazon has blocked outside shopping agents from its site while finding ways for its own customers to shop elsewhere. Now a new wave of AI assistants like Meta’s Muse is raising the stakes. In recent months Amazon has stepped up its Shop Direct initiative, which promotes products from brands that don’t sell on Amazon’s site, potentially giving shoppers less reason to turn to outside AI tools that can buy across retailers. The company now has 250 million listings that link to products sold elsewhere, about 2.5 times as many as in March, and is highlighting the goods more prominently through curated style edits and other displays on its site. Amazon says it’s continuing to innovate on how and where it’s showing outside products to customers. As part of that, Amazon has added items from big brands such as Alo Yoga and Warby Parker and introduced dedicated pages for showcasing outside listings from brands. It’s also started showing more product details on its own site before shoppers click through to an outside retailer. Amazon has been testing new placements since March. Combined with the surge in Shop Direct listings, the moves represent a significant expansion that mixes in brands’ off-site product listings across Amazon’s selection. Earlier on, the Shop Direct products had mostly appeared in Amazon’s search bar and suggestions in its Alexa shopping chatbot. “Amazon is increasingly a destination where customers can find and buy products not just from our store,” an Amazon spokesperson said. “Tens of millions of customers have discovered hundreds of millions of unique products from other stores through Shop Direct since the program launched, and Shop Direct products are appearing in hundreds of millions of searches monthly. We’re pleased with the foundation we’re building—broad selection, quality search results, and a growing customer response that reinforces our commitment to making every product discoverable, no matter where it’s sold.” Listings on Amazon from non-Amazon websites. Yet for all that growth, the effort remains a mystery to many online merchants. Eleven people who run e-commerce sites or work with merchants, representing hundreds of sellers overall, said they have little insight into when or why outside products show up on Amazon. Those whose products do appear say they’ve seen few sales as a result. Several also said they haven’t heard much from their own Amazon reps in the past six months about Shop Direct. Earlier this month, for instance, e-commerce agency Nectar noticed Amazon listings for products sold on two of its clients’ direct-to-consumer sites, according to Co-CEO Jason Landro. Amazon didn’t tell Nectar or its clients ahead of time that it would be listing the products, and Nectar found out only when the listings went live. Katharine McKee, founder of Morphology Consulting, an e-commerce consultancy that works with around 50 brands across six clients, said Amazon started showing links to buy some clients’ products on other retailers’ sites sometime between late July and October, though she wasn’t sure exactly when they first went live. The listings can come and go on Amazon without notice. Jason Boyce, CEO of e-commerce agency Avenue7Media, said he noticed Amazon showing listings that linked to other retail sites at the end of 2025 that disappeared sometime in the second quarter of this year. Some merchants also say they’ve noticed issues with listings on Amazon that show product information that doesn’t match what they’re actually selling on their sites—the same kind of errors Amazon cited when it blocked outside AI shopping bots last year. CEO Andy Jassy has said outside technology doesn’t offer a good customer experience, though Amazon is open to letting outside shopping tools in if they improve and offer attractive economics. The product links also don’t always go to the brands’ own direct-to-consumer sites. For one wellness brand, Amazon directed shoppers to a page from a retailer that isn’t an authorized reseller of the products, McKee said. Scaling up Shop Direct could represent a big change for Amazon, which has long moved cautiously with major changes to its retail site, the heart of its $588 billion commerce and ads business. The company launched outside product listings in Amazon in February 2025 and two months later added a Buy for Me feature, which uses agents to complete outside purchases without leaving Amazon’s site, moves that came as OpenAI and Google were gearing up to add AI checkouts. AI shopping has had false starts before, with OpenAI scrapping a high-profile ChatGPT checkout push in March, and using AI to buy things is far from a mainstream consumer habit. Still, signs are emerging that the latest crop of AI consumer apps is starting to actually generate orders—and could represent an eventual threat to Amazon’s dominant role in how people shop online. Omar Qari, CEO of e-commerce software seller Logicbroker, said his clients have seen a handful of Muse orders in the past few weeks while not seeing many Shop Direct–driven sales since the Amazon program began. “I was just surprised that anybody” was shopping via an agent, Qari said. Amazon’s Reach Amazon has pushed beyond its own site before with services like Buy with Prime, which lets outside merchants offer Amazon’s checkout and speedy delivery, features they actively select. With Shop Direct, merchants have to opt out of inclusion. Amazon says the technology powering its AI shopping features crawls publicly available data, much as other tools do, and abides by websites’ robots.txt instructions on what bots are allowed. Merchants are considered for Shop Direct unless they ask to be excluded, an option Amazon says has been in place since the program first launched. The features sparked blowback early this year from some merchants who complained that they were included without a heads-up, and who said the feature pulled incorrect product details that led to erroneous orders. Still, some who work with online brands, including ones that sell on sites powered by e-commerce giant Shopify, saw potential benefits in features that provided visibility on Amazon. “If you’re going to put our Shopify listings on Amazon in front of a billion people, great, more money for us. [Amazon has] much better reach than our Shopify site,” said McKee, the e-commerce consultant. At the same time, Amazon has had to grapple with the same challenges other agentic shopping efforts face. Retail sites, rife with features like pop-up windows and promo codes for new shoppers, are hard for AI tools to navigate , and pricing and in-stock information can quickly go stale. Early on, Amazon’s shopping agent software, built around Anthropic models, had trouble navigating some retail websites, according to people with knowledge of the project. Amazon also had to direct the agent to check sites frequently to get current product data, and engineers needed to confirm the AI’s findings, one person with knowledge of the project said. In March, Amazon announced more integrations with a number of e-commerce feed providers, which compile retailers’ product information in real time. Those included Feedonomics, owned by Shopify competitor Commerce (formerly BigCommerce), as well as Salsify and CedCommerce. Amazon recently added another provider, VersaFeed. Amazon says it’s choosing which products to show through Shop Direct based on the quality of the product listing and whether something is in stock, among other factors. It has received requests from large and small brands alike asking to be included. Amazon is also laying the groundwork for brands to better track the sales Shop Direct drives. The company says that, based on URL tags added to links to show where visitors come from, companies can see what traffic Shop Direct is driving to their sites. Amazon is also building more reporting capabilities to track the benefits of showing up in Shop Direct.

title: Bumble Founder Whitney Wolfe Herd Explains Decision to Take Company Private
content: Bumble cofounder and CEO Whitney Wolfe Herd said on Tuesday a sale of her 12-year-old dating app was important for the “for the longevity of Bumble’s mission” given the way the public markets had treated the company, whose stock had dropped to near $2. Herd said she would “disassociate” watching the stock price but was newly optimistic about Bumble’s future after new tech investment firm Ithaca Holdings agreed to take the company private in a $1.3 billion deal announced earlier this month. “I felt like I was stuck under a wave for like five years,” she said at The Information’s WTF Summit , in her first interview since Bumble agreed to a sale. “But now I’m on the beach.” Herd said she expected the company to take advantage of AI to modernize a product she said had become disconnected from the “revolutionary technology at the tips of your fingers today,” such as Anthropic’s Claude. She said Bumble could use AI to introduce more people to relevant events and groups of people, feeding what she termed as an “absolute craving of meeting people out in the world again.” As part of the deal, Wolfe Herd will step down as CEO, ceding the role to Ithaca Holdings founders Ravi Gupta, a former Sequoia Capital general partner, and former Meta Platforms executive John Hegeman, who will serve as co-CEOs. Wolfe Herd, who founded the company in 2014 with the unique feature that women would send the first message to a potential date, said she will remain involved and an “active shareholder.” She said she plans to continue being involved in the brand. “I’m not a technologist,” she said. “This is not my area of expertise. Like, you want me to build you a brand? Call me. I got you.” Wolfe Herd abstained from voting on the deal, which was unanimously approved by the rest of Bumble’s board. Still, she was optimistic about the sale, which she described as “the best outcome for the way the public markets were viewing our business.” Bumble went public in 2021 at a roughly $14 billion valuation. Its market cap has since sunk to less than $1 billion amid a decline in revenue and a drop in paying users. As for why the company has struggled in recent years, Wolfe Herd blamed fatigue among users in their 20s and 30s, who she said have just gotten “really, really overexposed to technology.” But she maintained there is still demand for dating apps, even as the broader industry has struggled. “Fundamentally speaking, the demand for love and connection I would argue is stronger today than when I started the company,” she said. The company has been making changes to its core features. Earlier this year, the company announced it was rethinking its core swipe feature (Wolfe Herd said “swipe is still breathing” though suggested it is being rethought) and introducing a new AI assistant called Bee that would help with the matchmaking process. According to Wolfe Herd, the company will also focus on using AI to improve the quality of suggested matches and for improving safety on the platform. “This can be a company that outlives me and that’s why I’ve hung on so long. And I don’t say that in some weird, delusional founder narrative,” she explained. “I just really do believe in this.”

title: Chipmaker Onsemi in Talks to Buy Startup for About $1 Billion
content: Semiconductor component maker Onsemi has been discussing an acquisition of 16-year-old chip startup Ferric for close to $1 billion, say people familiar with the matter—a deal that reflects growing demand for technology that can manage the intense energy needs of AI chips. Onsemi’s talks with Ferric follow a similar acquisition by rival Analog Devices, which in May agreed to pay $1.5 billion to buy Empower Semiconductor, a 12-year-old startup whose devices help AI chips manage electricity more efficiently. It isn’t clear how the Onsemi deal is being structured. It could include payments to Ferric based on performance targets. An Onsemi deal for Ferric could come together in the coming days, though discussions are ongoing and deal terms could change or fall apart, the people said. Onsemi is scheduled to report quarterly earnings on Monday. A spokesperson for Onsemi didn’t respond to requests for comments. A spokesperson for Ferric declined to comment. Onsemi, which has a market cap of about $30 billion, designs and makes semiconductors that manage the power needs of cars, factories and, increasingly, AI data centers. As the demand for electricity from these data centers grows, chipmakers are on the hunt for new technologies that can deliver energy to a chip with less waste. Traditionally, chip designers such as Onsemi and Analog Devices have handled power consumption by placing power management chips next to the processor on a circuit board and running electricity horizontally across the circuit board. These chips act as a central system to monitor and distribute electrical power. Startups like Ferric make so-called integrated voltage regulators and their devices can funnel power directly to thin, small chips underneath or inside the AI chips. The design cuts the distance the electricity needs to travel, reducing the energy lost along the way. Scottsdale, Ariz.-based Onsemi, which generated $6 billion in revenue last year, has been trying to expand its business lines.  This month, it agreed to buy publicly-traded Synaptics for $5.7 billion in cash, a deal that could help it to expand its sales of sensors and processors in smart devices. Founded in 2010, New York-based Ferric raised venture funding from New Science Ventures and received grants from the federal government, according to PitchBook. A price tag of close to $1 billion would be a steep price for a startup generating little revenue.

title: Foundry Raises $100 Million for Autonomous Factories
content: Large companies have learned over the past couple years that they can get more mileage out of AI agents by rethinking their processes from scratch, rather than merely automating the existing ways of doing things. Manufacturers are beginning to learn the same lesson as they adopt robots powered by physical AI models. One such manufacturer is Foundry , a startup that was founded less than a year ago, which has raised a new round totaling $100 million to build automated factories, the company told The Information exclusively. Marlinspike Partners led the Series A funding round, and Khosla Ventures , which led Foundry’s seed round, participated. Foundry is designing its factories around AI-powered robots, rather than slotting robots into existing production lines. Those robots are organized into work cells that focus on skills such as cabling, fastening and precise placement, rather than making a particular product. Due to that flexibility, Foundry can produce a variety of products for its customers within a single factory, following a manufacturing-as-a-service business model. It currently has a handful of customers in industries including military, energy, autonomous vehicles and telecommunications. “The value of autonomous facilities is that you can build many things under one roof,” said co-founder and CEO Adarsh Kulkarni . “The same model that has really learned fastening can work on satellites and drones and robot dogs and autonomous submarines,” he said. “We build drones on Monday, batteries on Tuesday, satellites on Thursday.” That flexibility comes at the cost of some inefficiency, Kulkarni acknowledged, but he said versatility that enables fast iteration is more valuable to customers. “One mass producing automatic facility is highly efficient, but it's highly efficient in only one axis, which is building a million of exactly the same thing,” he said. “You have basically no design flexibility.” Specialized factories will still make more sense for some mass manufacturing, such as producing iPhones or cars, at least for the next several years, Khosla Ventures founder Vinod Khosla said in an interview. But Foundry’s approach allows it to change the products it makes “rapidly based on market demand in very short cycles,” which opens an opportunity for factories in the U.S. to compete against cheaper labor in China, he argued. “American factories have to be done differently: much more capex efficient, much more product flexible, much more demand responsive, and closer to the demand. You can't have 60-day shipping times,” he said. Kulkarni previously ran the robotics division at Scale AI , the data-labeling startup part-owned by Meta , where he led work on third-party robotics data. His co-founder, Emmanuel Lamacchia , previously ran the Model Y program at Tesla . Foundry recently moved to its first factory in Emeryville, Calif. The facility is about 130,000 square feet. Foundry is still setting it up, but it is already shipping products to paying customers. The factory will eventually hold thousands of robots: primarily industrial arms wielding tools that Foundry develops, in addition to a fleet of vehicles to shuttle partially assembled products from one work cell to another. One type of robot is conspicuously absent at the facility: humanoid robots that walk on two legs. The potential for such machines to automate manufacturing tasks has lifted the valuations of humanoid companies to astronomical heights in recent years, but Foundry’s aversion to humanoids indicates that the market for humanoids could be smaller than some proponents have suggested. “I‘ve done my time with legged robotics, and I love it, and it’s amazing, but humanoids are very inefficient in a lot of ways,” said Kulkarni. “Deploying a humanoid in an existing manual facility might make sense, but if you’re building the building from the ground up, there is no reason you need to depend on that.” (Khosla, who expects highly capable humanoids in the next two years, said he foresees humanoids becoming a “key component” of Foundry’s operations in the future.) Foundry’s robots have their own limitations. Even after being trained for specific manufacturing jobs, AI-powered robots still struggle with some tasks, such as those requiring “micron-level precision,” Kulkarni said. For those tasks, Foundry employs hundreds of human technicians. Data collected from their work will feed into and improve its AI models. The ability to hold onto data from making a wide variety of products is one advantage that Foundry has over companies that sell robots to factories and warehouses, some of which are reluctant to allow an outside company to collect data from their facilities. “It‘s pretty easy for us to negotiate that we own the data,” Kulkarni said. “All of this training data is a byproduct of making our customers’ manufacturing lives easier.” Khosla said that the ability for Foundry’s robots to learn more over time is key. “These are learning factories, so if they learn on assembling defense gizmos, they will apply it to assembling alarm clocks too.” Here’s what else is going on… Big Number Meta Platforms is slightly increasing the size of its planned stock sales to fund AI investments to a total of $97.5 billion from $95 billion, the company said. title: Google is Having a TPU Moment
content: Get ready to hear Google brag about TPUs on Wednesday. When Alphabet, Google’s parent company, reports third-quarter earnings tomorrow, the company’s in-house AI chips, tensor processing units, are sure to be on the lips of Google executives and Wall Street analysts. That’s because we got a bunch of new  signs this week of the swelling customer demand for TPUs. Earlier today, Google said that Oracle will become the first major cloud provider outside Google itself to begin offering TPUs to customers through its own data centers. And a short while ago, Ryan Barwick published a scoop for us that says OpenAI—a major customer for Nvidia’s AI chips—plans to buy Google’s TPUs. But perhaps the juiciest details on TPU demand came on Monday courtesy of Anthropic’s IPO prospectus. In that filing, Anthropic chronicled the enormity of the financial commitment it has made to the Google chips, including a plan to spend $114.5 billion with Google Cloud (it didn’t specify how much of that will be for TPU-based compute). Anthropic also estimated it could spend an additional $125 billion to $150 billion on TPUs with Google and other providers. And the AI company will pony up $161.2 billion for TPU compute with Broadcom, which co-designs TPUs with Google. TPUs, you’ll recall, began as chips that Google used only internally starting over a decade ago. The company began allowing outside customers to use them via Google Cloud in 2018. More recently, Google has begun striking agreements with companies like Fluidstack and now Oracle to run TPUs in their own data centers. Google only began recognizing revenue from the sale of TPUs to outside data centers last quarter, though Chief Financial Officer Anat Ashkenazi said on an earnings call then that only a small portion of the revenues from its TPU agreements were reflected during that period. The “vast majority of revenues” from those agreements will kick in next year, Ashkenazi said. Analysts are predicting something of a windfall for Google when that happens. In a report earlier this month, TD Cowen’s John Blackledge estimated that TPUs will generate $9.4 billion in sales during the second half of this year, about 13% of the roughly $70 billion in revenue he was forecasting for Google Cloud during that period. By 2028, Blackledge thinks TPUs could be a $138 billion business, accounting for 34% of Google Cloud’s estimated revenue that year. While big, that figure would still be a fraction of the $692 billion in revenue that analysts, on average, are expecting Nvidia, the dominant provider of AI chips, to report in its fiscal year ending January 2028. Still, Google’s TPU growth has not gone unnoticed at Nvidia. Today, we got further evidence of Nvidia’s efforts to keep marquee companies in its tent. The chipmaker announced an expansion of its partnership with Meta, which said it would increase its deployment of Nvidia chips. As part of the agreement, Nvidia will invest $3 billion into the nearly $100 billion in stock offerings that Meta announced this week. We reported earlier this year that Meta struck a deal to rent TPUs from Google. Nvidia isn’t going to let Google invade its turf without a fight. In Other News Meta increased the size of its planned stock sales to $97.5 billion from $95 billion. The offerings will help the company raise money for its AI investments. Anthropic said it has begun working with Bristol Myers Squibb, BigHat Biosciences and other pharmaceutical companies to use AI in drug discovery. Anthropic also said it acquired a small company, Mithril Medicine, working on treatments for rare forms of muscular dystrophy. Anduril and Qualcomm said they’re working together to build rugged laptops in the U.S. aimed at government, defense, first responders and other customers. The companies are calling the line of computers BlueChip. title: Is Anduril Worth $120 Billion?
content: Some senior employees at Anduril Industries have indicated to investors that the autonomous weapons maker hopes to raise a new funding round in the first quarter next year, I’ve learned. It has considered doing so at a valuation of around $120 billion, according to people with knowledge of the conversations. Given that the prospective round is months away, though, it’s too soon to know it will happen for sure at this price. “No decisions have been made about any future financing, and anyone claiming knowledge of its terms, structure, pricing or timing is speculating or misinformed,” an Anduril spokesperson told me. “As a private company, we regularly evaluate opportunities to fund the growth of the business.” If Anduril does raise at a $120 billion valuation, it would be a steep increase to an ongoing employee share sale at a $90 billion valuation and about double the valuation of its most recent funding round, a $5 billion financing announced in May at $61 billion . It’s also higher than the $100 billion valuation Reuters reported the munitions maker was discussing in July. Recent contract wins could justify such a sizable valuation jump: In September, the U.S. Army awarded Anduril a nearly $163 million contract to expand the use of its software platform, Lattice, within the Army. That contract could become as large as $1.8 billion over the next five years. More contracts like these would help boost Anduril’s revenue, which is still small compared to that of large defense contractors: The company earlier this year forecast that its revenue will rise to $4.3 billion this year, more than double last year—just a sliver of the more than $80 billion Lockheed Martin, which has a market cap of about $144 billion, expects to generate this year. Now on to Anthropic… When Spark Capital first invested in Anthropic in early 2023, the model maker had only raised money from wealthy investors like Sam Bankman-Fried, FTX co-founder, and Jaan Tallinn, Skype co-founder. The older OpenAI had more cash and talent, and Anthropic was barely generating any revenue, we reported at the time . But Spark General Partner Yasmin Razavi—alongside Factorial Funds, started by Sol Bier, a former Cruise Automation engineer, and Sound Ventures—figured there was room for another large language model maker. Spark invested about $75 million, its biggest single investment at the time, leading Anthropic’s Series C that year. If Anthropic’s initial public offering values it at $1.5 trillion, those shares would have been worth 80 times what Spark paid. But Anthropic’s IPO filing, made public on Monday , showed just how aggressively the 21-year-old venture fund has added to its investment since the first check. Spark came into every funding round after the C, snapping up a total of 12.2 million shares for just under $777 million, according to the securities filing. Over 56% of that money is from Spark’s investment in Anthropic’s $65 billion Series H in May, raised on the heels of Claude Code’s breakout success. That round valued the model maker at $965 billion including the investment, and Spark sunk nearly $440 million into it (That huge check didn’t even earn Spark a mention in Anthropic’s press release , where it focused on co-leads like Sequoia Capital, which invested more than $2 billion into the round.) If Anthropic debuts at a valuation of $1.5 trillion, Spark’s slice of Anthropic could be worth over $11 billion, according to our estimates. At a cost basis of under a billion, plus a little IPO dilution, Spark could haul in $9 billion or more—a windfall its limited partners, such as the Orange County Employees Retirement System, will certainly be pleased with. (Spark was already making plans to raise a $3 billion fund, in part off the Anthropic momentum, we reported in March.) Most of the investments seem to come out of Spark’s fourth, fifth and sixth growth funds, according to the footnotes in Anthropic’s S-1. It’s also possible that Spark, like many venture capital firms that have coughed up hundreds of millions of dollars to invest in one round, may have tapped other capital vehicles, such as limited partner co-investment pools, which I wrote about last week . These vehicles are similar in structure to a traditional fund but make fewer, and bigger, investments—often at a discounted fee to their limited partners. In 2023, investing in a foundation model company was somewhat new for Spark. The generalist firm had cut its teeth with breakout consumer tech bets such as Postmates, Discord and Twitter as well as fintech startups like Plaid and Deel. Razavi, who led the firm’s investment in Deel in 2020, is enthusiastic about the wide-ranging use cases for Anthropic’s tech. “The speed of adoption and breadth of applications—across law, medicine, accounting, software development, mining, agriculture, and beyond—are unlike anything we’ve seen before,” Razavi wrote in a Medium post that announced the firm’s Anthropic investment in 2023. “At the heart of all of this lies helpful, harmless, and honest technologies like Anthropic’s AI assistant Claude.” Razavi’s conviction in the company also clinched her a coveted board seat. She is still the only venture capitalist on Anthropic’s board. title: OpenAI, a Longtime Nvidia Customer, Plans to Buy Google’s AI Chips
content: OpenAI plans to buy Google ’s AI chips, according to a person familiar with the matter, in a boost for a rising competitor to OpenAI backer Nvidia. Financial terms and other details of OpenAI’s planned purchase couldn’t be learned. But any deal for it to buy tensor processing units would be a big win for Google’s chip business, which is a growing challenger to the Nvidia graphics processing units that have dominated the market for AI computing power. OpenAI has been one of the most valuable customers for Nvidia, which in turn has invested tens of billions of dollars in the startup. In August, Nvidia also agreed to provide more than $100 billion in credit support for a massive Ohio-based data center project planned for OpenAI and built exclusively using Nvidia’s chip stack. At the time, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang wrote in a blog that OpenAI had committed to spending roughly $600 billion to use Nvidia servers through 2030. OpenAI’s plans for Google chips come as it seeks to hire an engineer to “lead the optimization” of OpenAI’s state-of-the-art frontier models on TPUs. Google, meanwhile, scored a separate win for its chip business with its announcement Tuesday that Oracle will become the first major cloud provider outside Google to rent out TPUs to customers. A person familiar with that agreement said that Oracle is purchasing the chips and that large mutual customers of the two companies will be the TPUs’ users. The customers’ identities couldn’t be learned. OpenAI is a major cloud customer of Oracle and last week announced plans to make its models available through Google Cloud. OpenAI also has been renting Nvidia chips from Google Cloud. Google developed its TPUs more than a decade ago and says they are more efficient than Nvidia’s GPUs. Google has rented TPUs out of its own cloud facilities for years to customers including Anthropic (which trained its models on the chips) and Apple as well as trading firms such as Citadel Securities and startups. Google more recently began selling its TPUs to other data center operators and users starting with neoclouds such as Fluidstack. Last year, The Information reported that OpenAI had begun using Google’s TPUs, lessening the company’s reliance on Nvidia’s chips. That prompted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to spring to action, and Nvidia and OpenAI then worked on a new deal. An OpenAI spokesperson later said the company did not have “current plans to use TPUs specifically.” The OpenAI job listing indicated that OpenAI’s efforts to optimize its models for TPUs are at an early stage, saying the position will have “broad technical ownership” of the effort. “We welcome experience gained through either training or inference, with a strong foundation in optimizing real workloads on TPUs,” the listing said.

title: Why Cheaper Models Won't Win OpenAI the Enterprise
content: OpenAI is trying to chip away at Anthropic’s lead with enterprises by fashioning itself as a cheaper, more flexible provider, Steph and I reported this weekend . But Anthropic's impressive prospectus for an initial public offering , filed Monday, shows OpenAI will need to do a lot more than that to really move the needle. To be sure, OpenAI has done a great job getting companies like Rippling to switch to its cost-efficient models from Anthropic’s. In fact, compared to Google and Anthropic, OpenAI has released the least expensive models this year when it comes to completing tasks in evaluations run by research firm Artificial Analysis. For instance, the most cost-efficient model OpenAI released in 2026, GPT-6 Luna with a low reasoning setting, was 45% less expensive than Google’s cheapest model, Gemma E4B, and 80% less than Anthropic’s Claude Haiku 5.5. But as we noted in our piece this weekend, the aftermath of Anthropic’s release of a not-cheap but very capable model, Opus 5.5, in late September took some of the wind out of OpenAI’s sails, at least among customers of OpenRouter, a service businesses use to access different models from one place. That’s a not-so-surprising signal that model capabilities still remain a dominant factor in customers’ eyes. And it adds more urgency to the all-hands-on-deck effort at OpenAI to launch its next major model safely . While Anthropic’s prospectus only covered the first half of the year and didn’t include the third quarter, it showed off strong business metrics. (We already know its growth rate slowed considerably between the second and third quarters , though it was still excellent. And Anthropic is almost certainly at least 40% bigger than OpenAI in terms of revenue.) For instance, Anthropic said that as of Sept. 30, its net revenue retention was 900%, meaning it’s generating nine times more revenue from existing customers, on average, compared to the same period a year ago. (That figure excludes fixed-price Claude Pro and Max subscriptions, which Anthropic says don’t capture changes in spending the way usage-based products, which account for the vast majority of its revenue, do). In addition, the number of enterprises that spent $100,000 or more on Anthropic products in the past 12 months rose more than 12 times to around 11,900. Anthropic is looking to lock in its lead by getting customers to sign longer contracts. The company said in its filing that more enterprise customers are signing non-cancelable, annual or multiyear contracts with minimum spend commitments. Right now, Anthropic doesn’t have such contracts with many of its top customers. Given Anthropic’s commitment to leasing $657 billion in computing capacity over the next seven to 10 years, it may want to lock in some long term contracts with its customers. Fighting the Narrative While OpenAI turns itself into a budget option for enterprises, Anthropic is fighting the narrative that it’s a budget buster . Anthropic lately has taken steps to show its models are also getting cheaper to use. It said last month that Opus 5.5 cost 40% less to complete a task than an earlier version of the model, Opus 5, and it said Monday that the model motivated “many” customers to switch to using that model rather than older Anthropic models. And earlier this month, Anthropic said its newest Haiku model was 75% cheaper to run, compared to an earlier version of the same model. Also in its prospectus, Anthropic said its most capable model, Fable 5.1, was 25% cheaper to use than its earlier flagship, Fable 5. For all the hype around the technology, Anthropic showed that the market has barely taken off. In its prospectus, Anthropic said its products account for less than 1% of the expenses of its largest Fortune 500 customers, and therefore their spending has a lot of room to grow. For other Fortune 500 clients that spend at least $100,000, but less than the top customers, Anthropic products account for less than 0.1% of their total expenses. This represents an opportunity for OpenAI and other AI providers too. But first, these companies have to show that AI can take a share of a company's labor budget, not just replace legacy software or applications. While Anthropic itself has said its engineers are five times more productive now than they were just six months ago, due to Claude, the vast majority of companies won’t be able to match Anthropic’s efficiency for some time. Here’s what else is going on… Ex-GitHub CEO Launches Competitor After GitHub experienced several months of prolonged outages earlier this year, many customers bemoaned the fact that there were so few viable alternatives, we reported this spring . Now, former GitHub CEO Thomas Dohmke—who left the Microsoft-owned developer services firm last summer—has officially launched a competitor to GitHub. Dohmke’s company, Entire , on Monday announced a new coding repository product where customers can upload and collaborate on code, similar to how people work together in a Google Doc. But unlike GitHub, Entire, which has raised $60 million from Felicis and other backers—says it was purpose-built for AI agents, including features that make it easier to track what AI coding agents are doing and explain why they took specific actions. Whether Entire can take a bite out of GitHub’s pie remains to be seen, but Dohmke is betting that his former employer is ripe for disruption. —Aaron Holmes Upcoming Events Monday, November 9 — Intimate Dinner with The Information and EY Consulting in San Francisco Trust is quickly becoming the defining question of the AI era. title: ‘Nobody’s Ready’: AI-Found Bugs Spark a Corporate Security Spending Spree
content: A week ago, Vijay Rayapati, CEO of enterprise software startup Atomicwork, gathered his team of roughly 30 software engineers and told them to drop everything and prioritize cybersecurity. A series of cybersecurity incidents over the prior 48 hours demanded the company’s immediate attention: eMudhra, a so-called root certificate authority, which websites and software makers rely on to prove their identity to users, had been hacked; LiteLLM, a popular open-source tool for routing requests to different AI models, was compromised; and a security vulnerability had been found in PHP, a programming language used by roughly 70% of websites. While the startup ultimately verified that it wasn’t directly impacted by the threats, the fact that it was scrambling last week “shows nobody’s ready,” Rayapati said. He is planning to hire one cybersecurity engineer for every three technical hires his company makes, and projects the number of cybersecurity-focused engineers will roughly triple to 27 in the year ahead. Atomicwork is hardly alone. Half a dozen cybersecurity executives in different industries say they’re planning to increase their spending on cybersecurity in the year ahead, including on headcount and software, such as AI agents that aim to be on guard around the clock. The explosion of new vulnerability scanning tools powered by large language models poses a competitive threat to more established products that have been around since before LLMs The scramble stems largely from AI models that are finding software flaws far faster than companies can fix them. Bigger, regulated enterprises have even more to worry about. Bank of America, for instance, recently disclosed it’s hiring 1,000 contractors to work on patching gaps in its software using AI such as Anthropic’s Mythos. Atomicwork CEO Vijay Rayapati, credit: Helen Shanthi, Atomicwork. Other big financial institutions are boosting spending too. Goldman Sachs has been using models like Mythos and OpenAI’s Astra heavily to hunt for bugs in its own software, and Goldman executives have discussed how the firm could soon be on track to spend as much or more on AI for security than it spends on AI coding tools, which has been its biggest AI-related expense, according to someone who spoke to Goldman leadership about it. The firm spends in the millions annually on AI, though its total spending couldn’t be learned. A Goldman spokesperson declined to comment. In another example, a major U.S. energy provider is expanding its roughly $30 million cybersecurity budget by more than 10% this year compared to last year, according to its chief information security officer, who wasn’t authorized to speak publicly about their firm’s strategy. The additional spending is going towards AI like Mythos as well as AI-powered add-ons in security tools it was already using from vendors like Proofpoint, which it used for email protection, and Cisco’s Splunk, which it used to monitor data, this person said. The two security vendors charge extra to use AI that continuously monitors the tools, which this executive said was necessary to prepare for more persistent, AI-powered attacks by hackers, which are fast becoming the norm . The energy firm pulled next year’s cybersecurity budget forward to pay for the additional features, its CISO said. Global IT services firm Diversified experienced a chaotic sprint to respond to the PHP flaw and a new vulnerability reported in Brotli, a widely used open-source library for compressing web traffic, according to Viral Trapathi, its chief information officer. The company directed most of its roughly 100 IT staff, including analysts and engineers who typically don’t work directly on cybersecurity, to investigate which of its cloud applications and webpages could be vulnerable, and to install patches. “These are massive efforts to do the remediation, so it’s a much wider impact than just a straightforward patch. This is taking time away from actual day to day operations,” Tripathi said. Diversified is planning to hire at least three new full-time cybersecurity staff, Tripathi said, and is budgeting roughly 20% more on cybersecurity software in the coming year, including on AI that automates app monitoring. Cybersecurity vendors, whose revenues have already accelerated this year as AI became more useful for cybersecurity, are licking their chops. “This is part of the new norm. Don’t think of this as an emergency one-off, think of this as something you’ll have to do basically every day going forward,” said Lee Klarich, chief product and technology officer at Palo Alto Networks, the biggest standalone provider of cybersecurity. The company’s growth rate doubled in the past two reported quarters, to more than 30%, compared to prior quarters. The increased spending on security software has implications for many companies. OpenAI and Anthropic are each betting on cybersecurity demand to drive their sales in the coming year, thanks in part to companies such as Palo Alto Networks, which use them in their products. And cybersecurity startups that also utilize such models to automate various cybersecurity roles are fielding takeover interest, The Information has reported . “It’s clear that the next three to five years are going to be the most important in the history of the security industry,” said Alex Stamos, who previously led Facebook’s cybersecurity and last month joined AI startup Cognition in the same role. “Defenders had a headstart at getting ready for AI-related risks, in part because we [corporate defenders] have more money. But attackers are already catching up.” An Explosion in Vulnerabilities Even if hackers weren’t using AI in droves right now, the sheer number of vulnerabilities that good-guy security researchers have found this year using AI has put a strain on cybersecurity staff tasked with patching newly discovered gaps. Palo Alto Networks’ Klarich illustrated the scope of the problem. When Anthropic first gave a dozen tech and cybersecurity companies access to its Mythos model in May, the total number of vulnerabilities in open source software that had been reported across the globe that month was roughly 1,500. One month later, the number of new open source vulnerabilities discovered by just those 12 companies using Mythos exceeded 37,000, he said, though not all of the vulnerabilities are severe and not all have been confirmed or publicly reported. And in August and September alone, the number of so-called high-severity vulnerabilities—those that could pose serious threats to sensitive data—that were reported exceeded the total number found in the entirety of 2025, according to research firm Epoch AI. Cybersecurity executives say their spending on AI like Mythos ballooned earlier this year and they’re seeking cost-effective alternatives. UiPath Chief Information Security Officer Scott Roberts, for instance, said the enterprise software firm has recently cut such spending by using cheaper open source models.
