title: Räume erleben, bevor sie gebaut sind
content:
Räume erleben, bevor sie gebaut sind
Neues IEQ-Lab am Hermann-Rietschel-Institut der TU Berlin verbindet Klimaraum und Virtual Reality und erforscht, wie sich Energieeffizienz, Gesundheit und Komfort in Gebäuden zusammenbringen lassen
Wie warm soll ein Raum sein, wie viel Licht brauchen wir und wann empfinden wir die Luft als angenehm? Im neuen IEQ-Lab des Hermann-Rietschel-Instituts (HRI) der TU Berlin können solche Fragen unter genau kontrollierten und zugleich realitätsnahen Bedingungen untersucht werden. Das Labor verbindet dafür einen hochflexiblen Klimaraum mit Virtual Reality. Temperatur, Luft, Licht und die visuelle Gestaltung eines Raumes lassen sich gezielt verändern und miteinander kombinieren. So können Forscher*innen untersuchen, wie unterschiedliche Bedingungen auf Gesundheit, Wohlbefinden und Leistungsfähigkeit wirken – und wie Gebäude künftig zugleich komfortabel, gesund und energieeffizient geplant werden können.
Virtuelle Räume, reales Klima
Die Besonderheit des Labors liegt in der engen Kopplung von Virtual Reality und real erzeugten Raumbedingungen. Versuchspersonen sehen durch eine VR-Brille beispielsweise einen Büroraum mit bestimmten Fenstern, Lichtverhältnissen oder Raumgeometrien. Gleichzeitig erzeugt der Klimaraum genau die dazu passenden thermischen Bedingungen. Öffnet eine Versuchsperson in der virtuellen Realität beispielsweise ein Fenster, spürt sie unmittelbar den damit einhergehenden Luftzug – und zwar aus genau der Richtung, aus der er auch im virtuellen Raum kommt.
54 einzeln regelbare Oberflächenmodule an Wänden und Decke können dafür geheizt oder gekühlt werden. Elektrische Heiztextilien und wassergeführte Kapillarrohrmatten ermöglichen schnelle Temperaturänderungen. Innerhalb von nur 30 Sekunden können sich die Oberflächentemperaturen um bis zu fünf Kelvin verändern. Eine leistungsfähige Klimaanlage erlaubt darüber hinaus die präzise Einstellung von Lufttemperatur, Luftfeuchtigkeit und Luftströmung. Auch unterschiedliche Lüftungsformen wie Misch- und Quelllüftung können nachgebildet werden.
Parallel dazu erfassen zahlreiche Sensoren unter anderem Luft- und operative Temperatur, Luftfeuchtigkeit, CO₂-Konzentration und Beleuchtungsstärke. Auf diese Weise können thermische, visuelle und lufthygienische Einflüsse sowohl einzeln als auch in ihrem Zusammenspiel untersucht und mit der Wahrnehmung der Proband*innen verknüpft werden.
„Der große Vorteil des IEQ-Labs ist, dass wir Innenräume unter genau kontrollierten Bedingungen realitätsnah untersuchen können. Thermische, visuelle und akustische Bedingungen sowie die Luftqualität lassen sich gezielt und reproduzierbar verändern – und mit ganz unterschiedlichen virtuellen Raumkonzepten kombinieren. Das ist in Feldstudien nur eingeschränkt möglich. So können wir systematisch untersuchen, wie verschiedene Raumkonzepte auf den Menschen wirken und wie sich dabei zugleich die Energieeffizienz optimieren lässt“, sagt Lukas Schmitt.
Wann ist ein Raum wirklich gut?
Das Labor ist Teil eines grundlegenderen Forschungsansatzes des Projekts EnOB: GEnEff (Neuartige Bewertung der Gebäudeenergieeffizienz). Bislang wird die Energieeffizienz eines Gebäudes vor allem daran gemessen, wie viel Energie es im Betrieb benötigt. Welchen Komfort und welche Innenraumqualität dieser Energieeinsatz für die Menschen tatsächlich erzeugt, wird dagegen nur eingeschränkt berücksichtigt. Das Forschungsteam am HRI hat deshalb einen Ansatz entwickelt, der beide Seiten miteinander verbindet. Die sogenannte GEnEff-Kennzahl setzt die Wahrscheinlichkeit, dass Nutzer*innen das Innenraumklima akzeptieren, ins Verhältnis zum dafür notwendigen spezifischen Energiebedarf.
Energieeffizienz soll damit nicht mehr allein anhand des Verbrauchs beurteilt werden, sondern auch anhand des tatsächlich erzielten Nutzens für die Menschen im Gebäude.
Wie wichtig diese Perspektive ist, zeigte bereits eine Befragung in zwei nachhaltig zertifizierten Bürogebäuden. Zwischen dokumentierten Zertifizierungswerten und der tatsächlichen Wahrnehmung der Nutzer*innen fanden die Forschenden teilweise Abweichungen von bis zu 50 Prozent – insbesondere bei der Raumluftqualität und den Möglichkeiten, das Raumklima selbst zu beeinflussen.
Temperatur verändert auch die Wahrnehmung der Luft
Im IEQ-Lab wurde der neue Ansatz bereits in einer Studie mit Proband*innen erprobt. Dabei kombinierten die Forschenden unterschiedliche operative Temperaturen zwischen 20 und 28 Grad Celsius mit verschiedenen Beleuchtungsstärken, während Luftqualität und Akustik konstant gehalten wurden.
Die Ergebnisse zeigen, wie eng die einzelnen Faktoren der Innenraumqualität miteinander verbunden sind. So wurden warme Räume von den Versuchspersonen als Räume mit schlechterer Luftqualität wahrgenommen – unabhängig davon, wie hoch der tatsächliche CO₂-Gehalt war. In der Untersuchung hatte die thermische Behaglichkeit mit 33 Prozent den größten Einfluss auf die Gesamtbewertung des Raums. Es folgten die wahrgenommene Raumluftqualität mit 26 Prozent, die visuelle Behaglichkeit mit 23 Prozent und die Akustik mit 18 Prozent.
Eine anschließende Feldstudie an 16 Arbeits- und Wohnorten bestätigte, dass sich die im Labor gewonnenen Erkenntnisse auch auf reale Gebäude übertragen lassen. Die im IEQ-Lab entwickelte Komfortfunktion sagte die Bewertung der Innenraumqualität in 81 Prozent der untersuchten Fälle richtig voraus.
Energie sparen, ohne an Raumqualität zu verlieren
Mit dem IEQ-Lab steht der TU Berlin nun eine Forschungsinfrastruktur zur Verfügung, mit der sich das Zusammenspiel von Mensch, Gebäude und Energieverbrauch wesentlich differenzierter untersuchen lässt. Künftig können weitere Einflussgrößen der Innenraumqualität integriert und unterschiedliche Gebäudekonzepte bereits unter Laborbedingungen erprobt werden.
Die Forschung ist insbesondere mit Blick auf Klimawandel und steigende Anforderungen an die Energieeffizienz von Gebäuden relevant. Denn ein möglichst niedriger Energiebedarf allein macht noch kein gutes Gebäude. Entscheidend ist vielmehr, mit möglichst wenig Energie eine hohe Qualität des Innenraums zu erreichen. Die im Projekt entwickelten Methoden könnten deshalb langfristig auch für Zertifizierungsverfahren, Normen und Richtlinien interessant werden. Ziel ist eine Gebäudeplanung, bei der Energieeinsparungen nicht zulasten von Gesundheit, Komfort und Zufriedenheit der Nutzer*innen gehen.
Auch über das GEnEff-Projekt hinaus soll das IEQ-Lab für Forschungs- und Entwicklungsprojekte sowie in der universitären Lehre eingesetzt werden. Es schafft damit neue Möglichkeiten, die Gebäude der Zukunft aus der Perspektive der Menschen zu entwickeln, die sich täglich in ihnen aufhalten.
Das IEQ-Lab ist im Forschungsprojekt „EnOB: GEnEff“ entstanden, das vom Bundesministerium für Wirtschaft und Energie (BMWE) gefördert wurde. Beteiligt war neben dem Hermann-Rietschel-Institut der TU Berlin das Fachgebiet Versorgungsplanung und Versorgungstechnik der Universität der Künste Berlin unter Leitung von Prof. Dr. Christoph Nytsch-Geusen.

Blut abnehmen, ins Labor schicken, auf Ergebnisse warten: Wer wissen will, wie es um seinen Stoffwechsel steht, braucht häufig aufwendige Untersuchungen. Zwei Masterstudenten der Universität Duisburg-Essen wollen das ändern: Mit ihrem Projekt VitaMetis entwickeln sie ein tragbares Sensorsystem, das künftig mehrere Stoffwechselwerte kontinuierlich und ohne Eingriff in den Körper erfassen soll. Mit dieser Idee haben sich Abdulmohaimen Algamoudi und Abdullah Osman Gwela für den bundesweiten COSIMA-Wettbewerb qualifiziert. Am 12. und 13. November stellen sie ihr Projekt auf der Elektronikmesse electronica in München vor.
Harnstoff, Vitamine oder sogar Hormone: Solche Stoffwechselwerte sollen sich eines Tages genauso einfach beobachten lassen wie heute schon Puls oder Bewegung mit einer Smartwatch. Daran arbeiten Abdulmohaimen Algamoudi (27) und Abdullah Osman Gwela (28) von der Universität Duisburg-Essen (UDE), die im Master Elektrotechnik studieren. ‚Wenn der Körper spricht und die Technologie zuhört‘ – dieser Gedanke steckt hinter ihrem Projekt VitaMetis, an dem sie seit über einem Jahr tüfteln. In München werden sie nun einen funktionsfähigen Demonstrator vorstellen.
So soll VitaMetis funktionieren: Ein kleiner Sensor-Patch auf der Haut misst kontinuierlich verschiedene Stoffwechselwerte. Dafür nutzt er ein optisches Verfahren, das bestimmte Substanzen im Schweiß erkennt und ihre Konzentration bestimmt. Möglich macht das eine Sensortechnologie mit winzigen Kohlenstoffröhrchen, sogenannten Carbon Nanotubes (CNTs), die am Duisburger Fraunhofer IMS zur Anwendungsreife gebracht wurde. Mit einer Art Handscanner lassen sich die Daten dann aus dem Patch auslesen – ganz ohne Blutabnahme oder sonstigen Eingriff in den Körper.
Bis zur Marktreife ist es noch ein weiter Weg. Doch die beiden Studenten haben ein klares Ziel: „Wir möchten eine Technologie entwickeln, die möglichst vielen Menschen zugutekommt. Das können gesunde Menschen, Sportler:innen, Schwangere, aber auch Nierenpatient:innen sein“; erklärt Abdulmohaimen Algamoudi. „In Ländern mit schlechter Gesundheitsversorgung wie Libyen, wo wir herkommen, wäre ein tragbares Sensorsystem wie VitaMetis ein Segen“, ergänzt Abdullah Osman Gwela.
Für die Umsetzung konnten die Studenten bereits Sponsoren gewinnen. Auch von der Universität und ihrem Betreuer Prof. Dr. Karsten Seidl aus dem Fachgebiet Elektronische Bauelemente und Schaltungen erhalten sie Unterstützung. Und das Ziel für München steht fest: „Wir fahren nach München“, betont Algamoudi, „um COSIMA zu gewinnen!“
COSIMA als Sprungbrett
Der vom Verband der Elektrotechnik, Elektronik und Informationstechnik (VDE) ausgerichtete COSIMA-Wettbewerb richtet sich an studentische Teams, die innovative Anwendungen der Mikrosystemtechnik entwickeln. Den drei bestplatzierten Teams winkt u.a. die Qualifikation für einen internationalen Wettbewerb.

KI-Leuchtturmprojekt GreenTwin zeigt Virtual Reality-Demonstrator und Prof. Dr. Stefan Naumann diskutiert in Berlin auf dem Podium über den ökologischen Gesamtwert von KI.
„Green AI neu denken“ lautete das Motto der AI CONFERENCE 2026, zu der das Bundesumweltministerium (BMU) am 6. Oktober nach Berlin eingeladen hatte. Ausgerichtet von der Zukunft - Umwelt - Gesellschaft (ZUG) gGmbH und eröffnet von Bundesumweltminister Carsten Schneider, diskutierten Fachleute aus Forschung, Wirtschaft und Politik, wie sich der Energie- und Ressourcenverbrauch von Künstlicher Intelligenz messen und senken lässt. Der Umwelt-Campus Birkenfeld der Hochschule Trier war gleich doppelt vertreten.
Am Showcase-Stand stellten Kristof Ueding, Paul Rübenich und Max Dengler das KI-Leuchtturmprojekt GreenTwin vor. Das vom BMU geförderte Verbundprojekt mit der Rheinisch-Westfälischen Technischen Hochschule Aachen, dem Deutschen Forschungszentrum für Künstliche Intelligenz (DFKI) und der Firma PSI Logistics hat für die Region Birkenfeld einen KI-gestützten Marktplatz entwickelt, der Einkäufe, Lieferungen und Mitfahrten an Menschen vermittelt, die ohnehin unterwegs sind und so Autofahrten auf dem Land einspart. Mitgebracht hatte das Team seinen VR-Demonstrator und Besucherinnen und Besucher konnten durch einen virtuellen Dorfladen gehen und erleben, wie Nahversorgung im Dorf künftig aussehen kann.
Auf dem Podium diskutierte Professor Stefan Naumann im Panel mit dem Titel „KI-Nutzen versus Emissionen“ gemeinsam mit Felix Behrens (Öko-Institut) und Anita Schüttler (Bundesverband Green Software), moderiert von Larissa Holzki (Handelsblatt), wie sich der Nutzen von KI gegen ihren ökologischen Fußabdruck aufrechnen lässt. Naumann leitet am Umwelt-Campus die Arbeitsgruppe Umwelt- und Nachhaltigkeitsinformatik und beschäftigt sich damit, den Energie- und Ressourcenverbrauch von Software messbar zu machen. So wurden die Kriterien des Umweltzeichens Blauer Engel für Software maßgeblich in Birkenfeld mitentwickelt. In die Diskussion brachte er die Sicht der Green Software-Forschung ein: Ob KI der Umwelt unterm Strich nützt, lässt sich nur dann belastbar beantworten, wenn auch der Verbrauch der KI selbst gemessen und transparent gemacht wird.
Die Delegation des Umwelt-Campus Birkenfeld freute sich sehr, GreenTwin am Showcase-Stand und die Birkenfelder Forschung bei einer so hochkarätig besetzten Konferenz präsentieren zu können. Weitere Forschungsprojekte in diesem Umfeld laufen bereits und in den Studiengängen am Campus, unter anderem Angewandte Informatik und KI sowie Umwelt- und Nachhaltigkeitsinformatik, werden solche Themen auch in der Lehre vermittelt.

title: Our climate models have a big, dangerous blind spot
content:
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
Climate change itself is increasingly fueling climate change. Rising concentrations of greenhouse gases are driving up global temperatures, setting off dangerous feedback loops that we have not fully accounted for in our climate models—or our emissions-reduction goals.
Scientists have long warned that warming would propel further warming in various ways, but a growing number of observations and studies are at last providing a sharper sense of just how powerful these cascading effects could be. And, by extension, they’re showing how much faster the planet may warm in this century.
A study in
Environmental Research Letters
in September, synthesizing the results of previous papers, found that the additional carbon dioxide and methane released from thawing permafrost, intensifying wildfires,
hotter lakes and reservoirs
, and wetter, warmer wetlands alone could drive global average temperatures up 0.2 °C to 0.4 °C this century. That would come on top of the
2.6°C of warming
above preindustrial levels that modelers are already expecting through 2100. The additional heat could subject many of the world’s cities to
monthslong heat waves
and expose
hundreds of millions
of people to flooding.
None of the models that inform the major UN climate reports, which assess how much the planet will likely warm under various emissions scenarios, account for all these feedback effects. Many of them don’t incorporate any. That leaves a huge blind spot in our understanding of how much the world could actually warm in the coming decades—and how rapidly nations will need to slash emissions to stay within critical boundaries.
A separate
analysis published in
One Earth
in March
, which examined what the feedback problem means for our international climate goals, concluded that the world may be much further off track than is widely believed. It found that just three regional sources of warming-driven emissions—thawing permafrost, increasing fires in boreal forests, and warming tropical wetlands—may shorten by as much as 25% the time before the planet consistently breaches the 1.5 °C and 2 °C warming thresholds.
Our climate models and the UN’s reports clearly need to be updated to better represent these effects. Nations must also step up their efforts to reduce emissions to reflect this improving understanding of the dangers we face, says Sam Abernethy, the lead author of the paper and a climate scientist at Spark Climate Solutions, a San Francisco–based nonprofit research group.
At least some of this is starting to happen. Spark kick-started an initiative, called the
Warming-Induced Greenhouse Gas Emissions Model Intercomparison Project
, through which more than 20 international teams are running the same set of analyses on different models to develop greater understanding of feedback effects’ potential power. Researchers involved hope that the UN will incorporate those results into its next major climate assessment, due out in 2029. That report will update estimates of the remaining emissions that can be released before the world crosses key temperature thresholds.
But what is already clear is that the planet is rapidly warming and that nations haven’t done nearly enough to cut fossil-fuel pollution. And even if we did manage to halt it, warming-driven emissions could continue.
So a number of the research groups involved in the recent studies have started to explore what nations could do to get feedback emissions under control. Scientists at the Woodwell Climate Research Center in Massachusetts are, for example, investigating the possibility of preventing fires or rapidly detecting them and putting them out when they threaten to burn the vegetation and soil that help insulate particularly carbon-rich wedges of permafrost (a subject I explored at length in
a recent feature story
). In addition, the Environmental Defense Fund’s Climate Innovation Initiative has
backed lab research
on the potential of adding sulfate, iron, or other compounds to wetlands to counteract fast-rising methane emissions.
Several startups are also exploring possibilities. They’re looking into
suppressing the lightning strikes
that are igniting more and more fires in high latitudes, placing synthetic mats above permafrost to prevent it from melting, and deploying autonomous drones to quickly suppress potentially high-emissions fires before they burn out of control.
Investigating all these ideas is worthwhile. But researchers are only in the earliest stages of figuring out how big a dent in emissions any such efforts could achieve across sprawling global ecosystems undergoing massive transformations.
The surest path to reducing the effect of warming-driven warming remains the one we’ve known all along: breaking society’s addiction to fossil fuels.

title: We urgently need to monitor AI agents’ actions in real time
content:
This summer, hundreds of OpenAI agents tried to
on a cybersecurity test. They broke out of their test environment and successfully hacked Hugging Face, a site that they believed held clues about how they’d be graded. Around the same time, another OpenAI agent
accessed
private files from an Australian government website. It’s a problem that’s by no means confined to OpenAI. In the months since, Anthropic, Google, and Meta have also disclosed incidents in which their agents have gone off track. And worryingly, in many cases the agents eluded the very researchers and safety teams tasked with monitoring them.
AI agents are taking unauthorized actions, and the companies building and running them are mostly relying on luck and hindsight to mitigate any harmful impacts. They must do more to ensure safety. That’s why
EU regulators
US agencies
are rightfully calling for agent developers and deployers to monitor agents in real time. But these rules assume that companies can see what their agents are doing and why—when in reality, they lack sufficient visibility.
Imagine a bank hiring a thousand new employees who can access customer accounts and sensitive information, but the employees’ ID badges change every day, it’s not clear whether a manager ever reviewed or authorized their work, and nobody logs the changes employees make to approval processes. That lack of visibility is where we are with agents today.
As agents roll out across critical sectors, from
government
medicine
, we must be able to monitor them in real time to prevent wide-ranging and potentially devastating consequences.  And while safety depends on monitoring, monitoring requires
observability
: the capacity to capture what the system did, process it into signals, and present those to humans or automated oversight systems. In other words, we need to know what the agent did and why it did it. And as our recent
research
shows, current agent frameworks—the software that runs agents— do not reliably generate the crucial observability records we need to ensure that agents are deployed safely.
Agents present new kinds of problems that generative AI alone does not. They inherit the unpredictability of the LLMs they are built on, but where a generative AI system produces a single output for a human to act on, an agent performs longer tasks—it plans, picks tools, spawns sub-agents, and takes actions. So an agent’s course can take shape in a multitude of different ways, and no tests before launch can fully anticipate the risks. This makes observing the agents while they work even more challenging, and even more important.
With colleagues from academia, civil society, and industry, we
the four most widely used agent frameworks to see what signals they actually emit. We found major gaps that made it hard to achieve key safety goals, like noticing policy violations, unauthorized actions, and even human oversight failures. Key observability requirements were missing—like Agent IDs that persist over time, and records about which humans approved agent tasks. This made it hard to tell which agents did what or assess whether they were taking unauthorized actions.
The good news is that these gaps, once identified, can be closed. Doing so starts with capturing two types of records: those that reveal what happened in an agent’s run and how the agent made its decisions. The “what happened” records identify the agent (while preserving privacy) and log how humans intervened and whether agent permissions or “memory” shifted, while the “decision” records show an agent’s reasoning and levels of confidence in the actions it’s taken.
Take, for example, agents working to process a bank’s mortgage loans. The system examines an application and recommends denying it, and then a human loan officer signs off on the decision. In a later audit, or perhaps even in real time, a bank or regulator needs to be able to reconstruct which agent made the call, which officer approved it, and how long they took. And the bank must also analyze records of how the agent arrived at its refusal decision in order to ensure it did not use off-limits information, like details about the neighborhood the applicant is from.
Recording “what happened” and “how the agent decided” require different approaches, but both are feasible. The current lack of “what happened” records is mostly a software plumbing problem that can be addressed through OpenTelemetry, an open observability standard maintained by engineers across the industry and by the agent frameworks adopting it.
OpenTelemetry has launched a working group drafting shared formats for tracing agents, but they have
yet to be finalized
. The group should urgently incorporate standards for maintaining persistent agent identity and for recording human interventions and changes to agents’ permission or memory. And it should be done before these systems can scale, all the while attending to the
privacy implications
of agent ID that links to real people.
Preserving “how agents decided” records is more challenging. The issue raises open research questions for model providers and researchers: Does the step-by-step reasoning a model displays, known as chain of thought, reflect how the model actually made a decision? And do we have reliable ways to measure how confident the agent is in that decision? These questions need answers before anyone sets standards for how such observability records are used.
No single organization or sector can close the observability gaps on their own, but together, they can support the infrastructure required to prevent dangerous incidents and support safety.
AI developers building agent frameworks, like OpenAI, Anthropic, CrewAI, and LangChain, must integrate telemetry signals recording an agent’s persistent identity, any human interventions, and any changes to an agent’s permissions and memory. Meanwhile, enterprises adopting these agent frameworks have an influential role to play; enterprises in regulated industries, like banks and hospitals, can put pressure on the agent developers to supply these missing observability records where standards do not yet exist.
Enterprises must also define policies, permissions, and roles that set out what agents can safely do, since telemetry alone cannot assess whether agents broke specific rules. Finally, regulators and AI standards institutes must specify the observability records required for high-stakes AI deployments while leaving the technical details to industry. We have already seen initial momentum here:
NIST’s agent standards initiative
in the US is working on agent identity, one of the most salient gaps we found in our research.
No bank would let a thousand unbadged employees loose on customer accounts and hope to piece together what happened when something goes wrong. Yet that’s how we’re deploying AI agents. Making their behavior observable is the first step toward fixing this. And by building the regulatory and policy ecosystem that makes it possible to act on what we see, we can hold organizations accountable. Until then, every task we hand to an agent hands over our agency, too.
Madhulika Srikumar is the Head of the AI Safety Program at the Partnership on AI, a global non-profit partnership of leading industry, academic, and civil society organizations, advancing best practices in AI governance.
Claire Leibowicz is the Director of AI, Trust, and Society at the Partnership on AI and a doctoral candidate at Oxford University.

title: Wolfspeed 与博格华纳签署多年期碳化硅器件协议，助力电动汽车未来发展
content:
该长期供应协议将依托 Wolfspeed 业界领先的碳化硅技术，支持博格华纳下一代 800V 碳化硅逆变器平台
美国东部时间 2026 年 10 月 28 日，美国北卡罗来纳州达勒姆市 —— 全球碳化硅技术引领者 Wolfspeed, Inc.（美国纽约证券交易所上市代码：WOLF）宣布签署一项多年期供应协议，将作为战略合作伙伴向博格华纳（BorgWarner）供应 Wolfspeed 碳化硅（SiC）器件，支持博格华纳（BorgWarner）下一代 800V 碳化硅（SiC）基逆变器平台。该协议进一步巩固了双方长期以来的合作关系，同时为博格华纳（BorgWarner）在下一代电动汽车（EV）及功率转换应用方面提供可靠、长期的高性能碳化硅（SiC）技术供应保障。
该协议的签署正值全球电动汽车（EV）市场持续扩大之际。2025 年，电动汽车（EV）占全球新车销量的 25%。据国际能源署（IEA）预测，到 2035 年电动汽车有望占全球汽车销量的约一半。随着汽车制造商加速推进下一代电动汽车（EV）平台，碳化硅（SiC）在实现先进汽车架构所需的效率、功率密度和性能方面正变得愈发关键。
Wolfspeed 全球销售高级副总裁兼首席营销官 Matthias Buchner 表示：“我们的战略是将技术领先优势与深厚的长期客户合作关系紧密结合。我们与博格华纳（BorgWarner）的供应协议正体现了这一战略。Wolfspeed 先进的碳化硅（SiC）技术、久经验证的质量与可靠性、规模化的 200mm 制造能力，将为博格华纳（BorgWarner）的下一代电动汽车（EV）平台提供所需的性能表现和供应保障信心。”
Wolfspeed 第五代（Gen 5）碳化硅（SiC）技术旨在满足下一代汽车电力电子产品对效率、性能和可靠性的要求。博格华纳（BorgWarner）正依托 Wolfspeed 1200V 碳化硅（SiC）技术，用于其 800V 碳化硅（SiC）基逆变器平台。
该协议旨在为博格华纳（BorgWarner）提供持续、稳定的 Wolfspeed 碳化硅（SiC）器件供应，并进一步巩固 Wolfspeed 作为稳定、长期供应合作伙伴的地位。该协议也与 Wolfspeed 规模化的北美制造能力相契合，目前该制造能力已全面转型至 200mm 晶圆。
Wolfspeed 与博格华纳（BorgWarner）共同致力于保障车规级品质。Wolfspeed 的碳化硅（SiC）解决方案针对在严苛的高热、高电压环境中实现稳定运行而设计。这种性能、可靠性与长期供应保障的结合，为汽车制造商推出日益精密复杂的电动汽车（EV）平台提供了有力支持。

title: 上海发布新政策：到2028年，推动8000台人形机器人进工厂
content:
2026年10月28日，人员从上海市经信委获悉，为深入贯彻落实国家关于加快发展新一代智能制造的战略部署，推动上海市制造业全要素全环节全流程智能化转型升级，《上海市加快发展新一代智能制造行动方案》近日正式发布。
新一代智能制造是人工智能与制造业深度融合形成的先进生产方式。行动方案提出，按照“场景牵引、模型驱动、装备升级、能力溢出”总体思路，以AI与制造业全链条融合为主线，以智能工厂为关键载体，夯实智能技术底座，强化智能产品和服务供给。到2028年，实现全市重点制造企业智能工厂全覆盖，推动AI在智能工厂应用普及全覆盖，培育500家先进级智能工厂，AI在制造业应用场景突破2000个，开发10个先进适用的垂域大模型，推出300个以上高水平智能体，建成满足新一代智能制造需求的新型基础设施，工业机器人密度达600台/万人，推动8000台人形机器人进工厂，推动AI赋能的新型智能制造装备产业规模突破2000亿元，智能制造系统集成产业规模达1000亿元，完成“54321”目标。
上海市经信委介绍，新一代智能制造“54321”目标指的是：累计培育500家先进级智能工厂，50家卓越级智能工厂，5家领航级智能工厂；形成基础级、先进级、卓越级和领航级梯度分明的4级智能工厂培育体系；按照“单点实施型、系统集成型、智能引领型”打造新一代智能制造综合服务商3层阶梯；建设功能强大、辐射全球的智能制造供需对接和智能制造出海赋能2大服务平台；布局1个具备智能制造装备验证、工业大模型测试、标准符合性检测等功能的智能制造中试验证平台。
上海市加快发展新一代智能制造行动方案
新一代智能制造是人工智能与制造业深度融合形成的先进生产方式。为深入贯彻落实国家发展新一代智能制造战略部署，推动制造业全要素全环节全流程智能化转型升级，制定本行动方案。
按照“场景牵引、模型驱动、装备升级、能力溢出”总体思路，以AI与制造业全链条融合为主线，以智能工厂为关键载体，夯实智能技术底座，强化智能产品和服务供给。
到2028年，实现全市重点制造企业智能工厂全覆盖，推动AI在智能工厂应用普及全覆盖，培育500家先进级智能工厂，AI在制造业应用场景突破2000个，开发10个先进适用的垂域大模型，推出300个以上高水平智能体，建成满足新一代智能制造需求的新型基础设施，工业机器人密度达600台/万人，推动8000台人形机器人进工厂，推动AI赋能的新型智能制造装备产业规模突破2000亿元，智能制造系统集成产业规模达1000亿元，完成“54321”目标。
新一代智能制造“54321”目标
核心载体：累计培育500家先进级智能工厂，50家卓越级智能工厂，5家领航级智能工厂。
梯度培育：形成基础级、先进级、卓越级和领航级梯度分明的4级智能工厂培育体系。
供给体系：按照“单点实施型、系统集成型、智能引领型”打造新一代智能制造综合服务商3层阶梯。
公共平台：建设功能强大、辐射全球的智能制造供需对接和智能制造出海赋能2大服务平台。
中试验证：布局1个具备智能制造装备验证、工业大模型测试、标准符合性检测等功能的智能制造中试验证平台。
二、实施新一代智能制造供给引领工程
（一）攻关突破核心技术和基础部件。聚焦智能制造“感知-控制-执行-互联”关键环节共性领域，攻坚分布式传感、多模态融合治理、高动态运动规划与控制、超精密加工工艺提升、工业无线实时通信、边缘智能集成等核心技术。重点攻关高端传感器、高转矩密度伺服电机、高精度重载关节模组、高性能伺服驱动器、高可靠性减速器等基础部件。
（二）研制推广新型智能制造装备。支持将AI技术与装备深度融合，推动智能制造装备升级为装备智能体。研制推广物理AI装备，研制具备自主感知和决策能力的机器人、工业母机、检测装备等智能制造装备，以智能工厂建设需求推动装备升级与规模应用。支持人形机器人、协作机器人、高精度重载机器人等机器人创新突破；加快AI赋能的超精密磨床、大型五轴机床、高速双五轴镜像铣等工业母机迭代升级；推动X射线光子能谱仪、残余气体质谱、工业CT等检测装备自主化能力构建。
（三）加快打造工业智能控制系统。加强高性能容错运行时引擎、大规模节点并发处理等技术攻关，完善协议栈、数据中间件、标准化接口、动态工具等配套能力。加快打造高水平可编程逻辑控制器（PLC）、集散控制系统（DCS）、数据采集与监视控制系统（SCADA）、安全仪表系统（SIS）等智能控制产品。围绕汽车、高端装备、新材料等重点行业，引导企业分阶段推进工业控制系统升级，打造典型应用。
（四）打造新一代智能制造服务商。以场景开放强化新一代智能制造服务商培育。推动研发设计、质量检测、供应链服务等生产性服务业智能升级。培育语料服务、数字孪生、AI Agent等单点实施型服务商；培育具备工艺、装备与软件全域贯通能力，开展跨环节创新的系统集成型服务商；强化工业AI原创引领，培育懂工艺、懂装备、懂软件、懂AI的智能引领型服务商。支持制造企业提升“产品+服务+解决方案”综合能力，发展服务型制造新模式新业态。
三、实施“人工智能+制造”筑基创新工程
（五）夯实工业网络和算力基础设施。支持制造企业开展新型工业网络改造，推动控制系统、工业网络、算力设施一体演进。推进工业5G/EUHT独立专网试点，支持部署5G-A、万兆光网等高质量网络。加快突破AI高性能芯片。加快构建“枢纽-区域-边缘”算力设施体系。强化智算资源统筹调度，加快国家算力互联互通节点建设，推动算力资源标准化接入和按需调用。推进算力服务普惠供给行动，推动工业智算云平台提级增效。
（六）打造工业模型赋能新引擎。面向高端装备、船舶海工、工业软件等行业打造10个以上垂域大模型，提升大模型对物理规律、工业图纸、时序数据、代码等的理解；针对辅助设计、生产自适应调整、预测性维护等高价值场景上线300个以上智能体或专业模型；构建多层次工业模型体系，提升大小模型协同效率。引导智能工厂率先开展工业模型应用试点，推动模型在研发设计、中试验证、生产制造、营销服务、运营管理全链条应用。
（七）打造高价值工业数据集及专业服务平台。支持制造企业与服务商、高校科研院所协同，将工艺机理与专家经验转化为异构工艺语义统一的工业知识库和知识图谱。加强数据合成、语义对齐、多模态融合等技术攻关，围绕高端装备、电子信息、核电等组建10个市级制造业高质量数据建设联合体。打造结构完整、标注准确、模型适配的高质量工业数据集，围绕设计校审、缺陷判定、设备诊断等经验密集场景，沉淀10类“老师傅”经验数据集。推动通专融合工业语料服务平台建设。
（八）推动人工智能与工业软件融合创新。推动传统工业软件向软件智能体演进，推动软件智能体深入生产制造核心环节应用。支持制造企业开放场景，鼓励AI和软件企业与高校科研院所协同，围绕研发设计、生产控制、设备运维、质量检测等打造链式应用场景。实施AI+工业软件“百企百项”，聚焦AI原生工业软件开发、AI赋能工业软件智能化升级等方向，开展技术和产品协同攻关。
（九）筑牢工业网络安全防护能力。开展网络安全攻防演练和应急处置演练，增强网络安全事件应急处置能力。推动安全大模型、安全智能体等AI安全产品在制造业落地，打造智能渗透测试、AI安全运营中心等10个标杆场景，推出20个深度应用大模型的网络安全产品，构建“以模制模”新型防护范式。推动10%以上优质工业企业实现工业互联网安全分类分级管理。加强数据分类分级管理和安全防护，推动50家以上优质企业开展重要数据识别、分级防护和风险评估等工作。
四、实施智能工厂梯度培育工程
（十）广覆盖建设基础级智能工厂。引导制造企业合理部署必要的智能制造装备、软件和系统，实现核心数据实时采集、关键生产工序自动化、生产与经营管理信息化。各区推动本区域制造业企业开展基础级智能工厂“自评估自建设”工作。到2028年实现基础级智能工厂累计达1600家。
（十一）系统化建设先进级智能工厂。推动基础级智能工厂广泛部署智能制造装备、软件和系统，实现生产经营数据互通共享、关键生产过程精准控制、生产与经营协同管控，瞄准典型场景加快AI应用，形成区域示范，加快向先进级智能工厂升级。各区建立先进级智能工厂“潜力库”。到2028年实现先进级智能工厂累计达500家。
（十二）集优化建设卓越级智能工厂。推动先进级智能工厂开展产品全生命周期和供应链全环节综合优化，推动多场景系统级应用，实现设计生产经营数据集成贯通、制造装备智能管控、生产过程在线优化，深化AI多场景协同应用，稳步向卓越级智能工厂跃升。到2028年实现卓越级智能工厂累计达50家。
（十三）标杆化建设领航级智能工厂。推动卓越级智能工厂加快垂域模型、工业智能体深度融合应用，探索未来制造模式，带动产业模式和企业形态变革，奋力向领航级智能工厂迈进。引导领航级智能工厂对外输出新技术、新工艺、新装备和新模式，引领研发范式、生产方式、服务体系和组织架构变革。到2028年培育领航级智能工厂累计达5家。
（十四）规模扩大场景创新应用。聚焦研发设计、生产制造、运维服务、营销服务、供应链管理等全环节，按照“单场景试点、多场景集成、工厂级重构”推动基础级智能工厂AI普及率100%，先进级、卓越级、领航级智能工厂AI应用场景比例分别达10%、30%、70%，智能工厂AI应用场景突破2000个，推动企业生产效率有效提升、研发周期稳步缩短。
（十五）打造“AI+制造”样板企业。建设10家以智能体高密度分布、多场景集成为特征的“AI+制造”样板企业，推出标志性智能产线、标志性智能产品，推动人形机器人进工厂，探索改变制造底层逻辑并实现质效跃升的路径，形成行业内可复制推广的全流程数智化转型示范。
五、实施新一代智能制造生态营造工程
（十六）促进大中小企业协同转型。支持链主企业带动上下游企业“链式”转型。面向中小企业转型需求，研发推广专业化“小快轻准”解决方案，降低转型门槛。支持不同行业、不同所有制企业基于现有基础，加快形成各具特色的智能化转型路径。
（十七）构筑智造标准创新高地。完善智能制造标准体系建设，聚焦工业智能体、装备数智升级、智能场景与新技术融合等优先开展标准制修订工作。深化国际合作，推动国际先进标准转化、本地标准走出去。
（十八）搭建新一代智能制造公共平台。搭建智能制造供需对接平台，整合本市场景建设需求、服务商产品能力，建立“技术攻关—场景落地—模式复制”的闭环生态。搭建智能制造出海赋能平台，推动智能制造服务商优质产品及高水平解决方案加速出海。支持优质企业联合产业链上下游共建智能制造中试平台，开展数据模拟、工艺改进、样品试制、测试验证、示范应用等中试服务。
（十九）合力打造智能制造引领区。深化市区协同，支持各区聚焦主导产业制定新一代智能制造“一区一策”方案。支持建设一批智能制造引领区，加强对优质企业和项目的精准对接，推动优势产业加速集聚，引导各区在生产组织范式、新型制造模式、产业链协同等方面引领示范，形成特色鲜明、多点支撑、全域联动的新一代智能制造发展格局。
加强人才培养。构建智能制造复合型人才梯度培育体系，实施智能制造前沿部署工程师、智能工厂持续运营工程师等培育计划。深化产教融合，健全覆盖智能制造多层次人才的培训课程体系，加大对产业工人和技能人才的培训。加强统筹协调。加强部门协同，市、区、优质企业建立专班机制，建立责任明确、协调有序、监管有力的工作体系，加强任务统筹，开展动态评估。加强政策支持。加快重大项目谋划，积极承担国家“两重”等重大专项，统筹用好促进产业高质量发展等政策。鼓励各区结合实际进行政策支持。

title: 上海：拟依法有序推动自动驾驶技术在出租汽车行业的应用
content:
财联社10月29日电，《上海市出租汽车条例（草案）》近日公开征求意见。其中提出，依法有序推动自动驾驶技术在出租汽车行业的安全应用。交通、公安等部门依法加强指导和服务。另外，运用大数据、区块链、人工智能等现代信息技术，拓展开发应用场景，提升出租汽车服务与管理的数字化、智能化水平。推进出租汽车行业的绿色低碳转型，鼓励和支持新技术、新能源、新装备在出租汽车行业的创新应用。

title: 中科海钠 | 循环超3000次！电解液助力 270 Ah 大容量钠离子电池取得重大突破
content:
近日，中国科学院物理研究所研究员、中科海钠董事长胡勇胜团队在大容量钠离子电芯长循环技术方面取得进展。采用多阴离子协同电解液的270 Ah方形电芯，在1 C条件下循环3333次后容量保持率达89.2%，实现了大容量电芯长循环性能。相关成果为钠离子电池面向规模化储能应用的产品开发与制造验证提供了新的技术支撑。
此次测试覆盖两种大容量方形电芯。73174207型270 Ah电芯在1 C条件下循环3333次后容量保持率为89.2%，连续循环时间超过一年；54173207型210 Ah电芯常温循环1670次后容量保持率为92.7%，在45 ℃条件下容量保持率为88.6%。电芯能量密度达168 Wh/kg，工作温域覆盖-40 ℃至60 ℃。在-40 ℃、0.33 C条件下，放电容量保持率为92.8%；在25 ℃、3 C条件下，充电和放电容量保持率分别为94.3%和99.1%。
大容量电芯对材料体系的长期稳定运行提出了更高要求。随着单体容量提升，电极与电解液界面反应可能引发产气和内阻增长，进而影响电芯寿命与运行表现。针对这一问题，团队开发了多阴离子协同电解液方案，在常规1 M碳酸酯溶剂体系中组合使用NaPF6、NaFSI、NaDFOB和NaDFP，并添加FEC、PS成膜添加剂。所用原料为电池级工业化常规产品，供应链成熟。研究表征显示，该方案有助于在正负极形成稳定界面，抑制循环过程中的副反应和阻抗增长。
该成果的一个重要特点，是在210 Ah和270 Ah方形电芯上开展了长循环及宽温域性能验证，将电解液设计与大容量电芯产品验证相结合，通过层状氧化物||硬碳体系的高能量密度、长循环寿命与大容量单体制造“三位一体”，真正把钠离子电池的低成本优势从原料端落到了产品端。
相关研究以“Manufacturing large-format practical Na-ion battery with over 200 Ah and 3 000 cycles”为题，发表于《极端制造》International Journal of Extreme Manufacturing (IJEM，IF 25.1) 期刊上。

title: 大众汽车调整中国战略
content:
大众汽车集团正在调整其中国战略。正如该集团在中国东部合肥市宣布的那样，沃尔夫斯堡方面正从以往的“在中国，为中国”（In China, for China）口号，转向以“在中国，超越中国”（In China, Beyond China）为目标，开始瞄准中国以外的市场。
从长远来看，大众汽车希望与其在中国的合资企业共同服务东南亚、南部非洲和南美洲的更多市场。今年4月，该集团在中国车展期间曾暗示过相关计划。据称，目前大众汽车已经将中国生产的汽车出口到中东、哈萨克斯坦和乌兹别克斯坦等地。
除了中国品牌带来的激烈竞争和价格压力外，目前中国疲软的汽车市场也带来了挑战。中国乘用车市场信息联席会（CPCA）最新数据显示，今年前九个月，中国整体汽车市场销量下降了21.7%。
对大众汽车而言，在华业务同样举步维艰：第三季度销量下滑38.5%，降至40.58万辆。中国市场的销量下滑占其全球总降幅的80%以上。
因此，通过这一战略转变，大众汽车不仅希望在其他市场抵御竞争对手，还希望开拓新的国家市场。集团内部人士表示：“竞争压力增大。”单靠欧洲生产的产品很难应对这种局面，这也是大众希望从中国出口的原因。

title: 大底盘与联合电子达成战略合作  共筑智能悬架产业新生态
content:
当前汽车产业电动化、智能化变革持续深化，智能底盘已成为整车核心竞争力的关键制高点。为聚力关键技术协同攻关，深化产业链创新协同，加速智能悬架技术规模化落地，10月28日，大底盘‑联合电子战略合作签约仪式隆重举行。
上海汇众、联创汽车电子总经理芦勇，上海汇众副总经理邱海漩，联创汽车电子副总经理鲍时明，联合电子第一副总经理郭晓潞、跨域控制业务部总经理曹海平、销售部总监郝利君、变速箱与悬架业务控制部总监王骞等双方核心管理层出席本次签约活动。
仪式正式开始前，邱海漩陪同联合电子团队实地参观大底盘实验室与智能底盘展厅，系统介绍上海汇众在智能底盘领域的技术积淀、产品矩阵与研发成果，全面展示上汽大底盘战略建设阶段性成效。
与会人员移步厂区道路，现场观摩全主动液压悬架共创展车动态演示。实车的功能表现，直观印证智能悬架技术对整车舒适性、操控性、安全性的综合赋能，充分彰显底盘智能化升级巨大的技术价值与市场潜力。
随后双方开展深度座谈研讨。围绕上汽大底盘整体战略布局，上海汇众底盘构型部总监张元伟介绍大底盘业务体系、核心产品与中长期发展规划；联合电子变速箱与悬架业务控制部总监王骞分享联合电子在汽车电子领域的技术能力与业务布局。通过充分交流研讨，双方进一步明晰各自核心优势与业务契合点，凝聚联合创新共识，为后续全方位、深层次技术共研、项目落地筑牢坚实基础。
座谈结束后，战略合作签约仪式正式举行。在全体与会领导嘉宾共同见证下，双方代表签署战略合作协议，并集体合影留念，标志双方战略协作开启全新篇章。
签约完成后，双方围绕后续业务落地路径开展务实交流。联合电子第一副总经理郭晓潞在发言中指出，智能底盘产业蓬勃发展，为汽车电子技术迭代与场景拓展开辟广阔蓝海。本次战略合作是强强联合、优势互补、资源共享的重要里程碑。未来双方将聚焦主动悬架核心应用场景，深化软硬件联合开发，协同推进产品验证迭代与量产落地，以硬核技术创新助力上汽集团“二次创业”。
上海汇众、联创汽车电子总经理芦勇表示，本次战略合作，是上汽体系内深化产业协同、攻坚智能底盘自主创新的重要实践。大底盘将依托智能悬架系统研发与整车工程化应用能力，强化与联合电子跨领域技术协同，持续提升智能底盘系统集成与工程落地能力，提速智能悬架产业化进程，合力打造具备行业领先竞争力的自主智能底盘整体解决方案。
站在战略合作的全新起点，双方将打通技术、资源、业务链路，强化联动协同，为上汽集团夯实智能底盘产业版图、培育全新业务增长极注入强劲动能。面向行业未来，双方将坚持自主创新，携手攻坚底盘关键核心技术，助力国内汽车产业向智能化、高端化加速迈进，为中国汽车工业高质量发展贡献上汽力量。

title: 宁德时代计划在欧洲再建电池工厂
content:
宁德时代（CATL）显然希望进一步扩大其在欧洲的电池生产版图。据该公司评估，现有的产能不足以长期覆盖市场的结构性增长。
宁德时代在欧洲已经启动了多个项目。在德国，一座产能为14吉瓦时（GWh）的工厂正在运营；在匈牙利，一座100吉瓦时的工厂正在产能爬坡；在西班牙，正与Stellantis集团合作建设一座50吉瓦时的工厂。尽管如此，欧洲区负责人沈锋认为这仍然不够。
新建工厂的关键要素
对于进一步的扩张， 沈锋 主要将预期的市场增长视为驱动力。他看到了三波电气化浪潮：首先是纯电动乘用车，其次是储能电池，最后是商用车。新的选址尚未确定，但对宁德时代而言，靠近客户以及拥有良好的物流和能源基础设施至关重要。
人才短缺阻碍扩张步伐
目前最大的障碍被认为是人员问题。沈表示，欧洲电池行业缺乏熟练的技术工人和工程师。这些人才必须进行培训，这可能会额外增加扩张所需的时间。

title: 宇树Q3净利润同比下降17%
content:
10月28日，宇树科技发布2026年第三季度报告。第三季度，公司实现营业收入6.65亿元，同比增长69.93%；归属于上市公司股东的净利润1.13亿元，同比下降17.37%；扣除非经常性损益后的归母净利润1.05亿元，同比下降17.42%。公司称，产品创新和业务拓展带动了收入增长。
第三季度，宇树研发投入1.27亿元，同比增长249.58%，占当季营收的19.10%，较上年同期提高9.82个百分点。前三季度累计研发投入2.63亿元，同比增长191.48%，占同期营收的14.47%。
宇树表示，研发投入增长主要来自具身大模型研发及算力投入增加，以及研发团队扩充和新产品研发。
前三季度，公司实现营收18.17亿元，同比增长55.71%；归母净利润3.87亿元，同比增长270.54%；扣非归母净利润3.49亿元，同比下降18.78%。公司解释，收入增长带动毛利额增加，去年一次性确认的较大金额股份支付费用也影响了同比基数。
前三季度，宇树营业成本为8.36亿元，上年同期为4.70亿元；毛利率约54.02%，较上年同期的59.75%下降5.73个百分点。销售费用由上年同期的7600.85万元增至2.30亿元，同比增长约202.45%。管理费用从3.81亿元降至7350.10万元。
公司前三季度经营活动产生的现金流量净额为1.94亿元，同比下降54.69%。宇树称，采购、职工薪酬及销售、研发相关现金支出随收入增长而增加。
同期，销售商品、提供劳务收到的现金为20.22亿元，上年同期为12.56亿元。购买商品、接受劳务的现金支出从6.23亿元增至13.52亿元；职工相关现金支出也由1.18亿元增至2.24亿元。

title: 新锋龙锚定具身智能硬件研发和制造平台，多款产品已实现量产
content:
随着优必选完成对锋龙股份的收购，双方产业协同持续深化。依托优必选在具身智能技术及落地应用优势，结合自身精密制造积累，锋龙股份成立了全资子公司新锋龙，持续推进具身智能核心硬件自研与规模化制造业务，致力于为全行业提供标准化硬件产品与解决方案，支撑不同整机厂商的产品开发与量产需求。
新锋龙构建了三大产品矩阵：一是核心零部件，包含仿生人面部舵机、高密度舵机（行星、谐波、摆线、直线）、冷却模组、电子皮肤；二是末端执行器，涵盖二指夹爪、灵巧手、超拟人仿生灵巧臂；三是周边配套部件，包含换电柜、充电支架等。
目前，新锋龙已实现二指夹爪和仿生人面部舵机的研发和量产，产品性能优于市场同类产品。计划于2027年量产高功率密度舵机、灵巧手、超拟人仿生灵巧臂，并同步开展液冷模组、电子皮肤等前沿技术的研发。
依托打造的人形机器人核心硬件底座，新锋龙还将逐步整合优必选旗下的优世界、优医疗等具身智能机器人业务，覆盖家庭消费、医疗赛道：
优世界（UWORLD）是优必选旗下的消费级人形机器人品牌，致力于打造能与人类建立深层情感连接的超仿生人形机器人。首款产品为U1系列全尺寸超仿生人形机器人，于2026年6月30日正式发布，可广泛应用于情绪支持、日常陪伴、养老陪伴、迎宾接待、文旅展览等民生与商用场景，为人形机器人普惠化落地奠定坚实基础。
优医疗是优必选旗下聚焦医疗健康赛道的具身智能品牌，以脑科学、类脑人工智能研究为基础，依托人工智能与新型传感器技术，开展脑、心、认知等相关核心技术与产品研发，提供脑健康医疗器械、医康养智能产品、大数据平台及相关服务。

title: 日本寻求欧盟调整EV优惠政策，但阻力巨大
content:
日本首相高市早苗与德国总理默茨在会谈后召开的联合人员会结束后握手（10月28日，首相官邸）
欧盟《工业加速器法案》公布后，日本产生危机感，认为该法案“势必会对汽车产业造成影响”。日本政府和企业正加大力度游说德法以及其他成员国政府和欧洲议会议员……
10月28日，日本首相高市早苗与德国总理默茨举行会谈，要求修正欧盟（EU）的纯电动汽车（EV）优惠政策。如果将日本产汽车排除在外的现行方案最终获得通过，那么日本车企的销量势必会大幅减少。虽然该政策影响着日本车企在欧洲的战略布局，但政策修正的难度很大。
欧盟执行机构欧盟委员会3月公布了《工业加速器法案》（IAA）。该法案要求汽车制造商在欧盟境内组装汽车和生产零部件，以换取针对EV的补贴及公共支持。
德法两国于10月16日就“欧盟境内”的定义明确指出，除欧盟的27个成员国外，在满足一定条件的情况下，还包括“截至2020年1月1日参与欧盟单一市场的伙伴国家”。预计英国将被纳入欧盟境内这一范围，但并未出现日本和韩国的名字。
IAA法案公布后，日本政府与企业界均产生危机感，认为该法案“势必会对汽车产业造成影响”。尤其是丰田，在欧洲（包括英国）销量中，EV超过5万辆，占比约5%。包括丰田在内的日本车企，一直和日本政府共同呼吁，应该将日本纳入相关政策的适用范围。
2026年6月，在法国东部城市埃维昂举行的七国集团（G7）峰会期间，高市早苗与欧盟委员会主席冯德莱恩举行会谈，直接表达了对IAA草案将日本汽车排除在外的关切。
5月，日本经济产业相赤泽亮正在布鲁塞尔要求欧盟委员会执行副主席塞茹尔内（分管产业战略，法国籍）修改法案内容。
日本车企未能形成统一阵线
但是，事前游说并未奏效。除丰田以外，日本其他车企在欧洲的销售规模较小，民间企业未能形成统一阵线，这也是一大课题。
尤其是坚持追求“欧洲制造”的法国。与德国相比，雷诺等法国汽车企业的业务以欧洲境内的内需为主，法国更倾向于保护欧盟境内的本土产业。未来，除了德国之外，日本也必须对法国施加相应影响。
在欧洲，有一种被称为“公司车”的惯例。企业将租赁车辆作为实物福利，算作薪酬的一部分发放给员工，这类车辆还可以享受税收优惠与购置补贴。该类车型占到欧洲市场的6成，也是日本车企的销售主力。
有预测称欧洲市场9成以上将是EV
丰田计划2028年在捷克工厂生产EV，但目前主要依靠从日本本土出口。有预测认为，到2030年代，欧洲市场新车中9成以上将是EV。
丰田欧洲子公司CEO中田佳宏强调：“丰田在欧洲不是‘客人’，而是欧洲汽车产业重要的贡献者”。
日本车企从1960年代开始向欧洲出口汽车，丰田于1968年就和葡萄牙当地企业合作，开始组装生产“卡罗拉”。1980-90年代，丰田、日产、本田陆续在英国建厂，铃木则在匈牙利设立工厂。
日本车企在欧洲合计创造约17万个就业岗位，拥有长达50余年的供应链与销售网络积淀。
或将波及整条供应链合作
日欧之间的合作并不局限于汽车领域。日本与欧盟在2025年7月达成共识，启动名为“日欧竞争力联盟”的合作框架。
该框架以2019年生效的经济伙伴关系协定（EPA）为基础，携手促进投资与贸易、强化供应链。双方认为，有必要步调一致，应对美国的保护主义倾向、以及中国产能过剩等问题。
在德法达成共识的基础上，欧盟各大核心机构接下来将着手敲定最终方案。除欧盟委员会之外，立法机构欧洲议会、由成员国组成的欧盟理事会也将正式开启磋商。在这一过程中，法案仍存在部分修改的可能性。
日本政府和企业正加大力度游说德法以及其他成员国政府和欧洲议会议员。但德法在欧盟内部话语权很强，想要推翻二者已经达成的共识难度极大，最终结果尚不明朗。一旦确定将日本产品排除在外，很有可能对日欧在供应链领域的合作造成冲击。

title: 杭州首个商业综合体“低空云驿”启用：无人机10分钟配送商圈，时效提升30%
content:
10月27日，一架搭载着定制伴手礼的无人机从杭州城北万象城广场平稳升空，飞往杭州东站万象汇方向。这标志着杭州市首个复合式商业综合体低空配送起降点——杭州城北万象低空云驿正式启用，杭州低空基础设施与大型商业综合体完成首次深度“并网”。
“空中驿站”进商场：时效提升30%
与以往设在公园、产业园区的起降点不同，此次“低空云驿”直接嵌入商业综合体，让低空消费场景更贴近普通市民的生活。
运作模式：消费者只需在微信闪送小程序正常下单，后台会自动匹配空中运力，实现无感运输。目前，城北万象低空云驿可辐射周边约3公里商圈，空中配送时长约10分钟，时效比地面运输提高约30%。
空间设计：起降点采用双层空间复用设计。上层为标准化无人机起降平台，满足常态化物流配送的全流程作业；下层为开放式公共空间，现阶段作为低空科普体验窗口，向市民展示低空配送的运作流程与安全标准。
对杭州万象商业体系而言，低空云驿的接入不仅提升了跨商圈货品调运的效率，也为商场打开了全新的立体流量入口；对市民来说，通过“帮我买”等线上服务，可以跨区高效选购万象系商圈好物。
从“产业端”切入“消费端”
“低空云驿首次落地商业综合体，是杭州低空经济从产业端切入大众消费场景的标志性突破。”杭实集团党委委员、副总经理陆舞鹄在启幕仪式上表示。
活动现场，杭州城北万象城、杭州东站万象汇正式加入由杭州低空产业发展有限公司牵头打造的“低空飞友圈”，拉开了杭州万象商业体系全域接入低空网络的序幕。
“过去起降点大多设在园区，这次接入商业综合体，叠加了商业运营空间，让更多商场打开了低空飞行的新场景。”杭州低空公司副总经理杜颂兰表示。
杭州低空商业化版图持续扩容
以低空云驿为锚点，杭州的低空商业化网络正在快速铺开。
截至2026年底，杭州低空公司将在全市建成投用20余个公共起降场及多个起降点。从即时配送闪送试点、跨江航线打通，到吴山广场飞行咖啡业态落地，杭州低空经济的应用场景正持续丰富。
杜颂兰透露，后续计划开通更多飞行线路，低空云驿也将在科普功能基础上，引入匹配商业调性的多元业态，探索更多“低空+商业”的新玩法。

title: 精进电动北美公司配套美国新客户的全新电驱系统批量投产
content:
美国密西根州法明顿山市（Farmington Hills），2026年10月28日 ─ 精进电动北美公司今天宣布，公司为又一核心美国客户配套的全新三合一电驱动系统正式批量投产。新产品、新客户，这是精进电动多年耕耘美国市场迎来的全新里程碑。
自精进电动2008年创建以来，北美市场就是公司的核心市场之一。精进电动北美公司的电驱工厂位于美国的汽车城底特律附近，是美国汽车工业的核心区域。工厂已经投产多款电机、电控和电驱系统产品，也培养了一支高素质、熟练的员工队伍，以及面向北美市场的成熟的物流和售后保障体系。
精进电动北美公司总经理Scott Taylor先生表示：“今天我们迎来了一个新的里程碑。这款新电驱系统特别适合北美的小型皮卡，产品批量和营业收入也比以往的项目更高，将把精进电动北美公司的运营推向全新的高度。”
这款全新的三合一电驱系统将配套核心客户的电动皮卡。系统包含一台高效扁线电机，一台高功率密度控制器和一个高效、低噪音减速器，峰值功率超过150kW，输出扭矩超过3200Nm。系统采用了精进电动首创的无泵油水复合冷却技术，持续功率高，适合高速和拖车等工况，同时配备了北美市场需要的电子轮爪式驻车系统，功能安全达到行业最高的“ASIL-D”等级。

title: 纳芯微推出Mini SBC NCA1169V-Q1系列，助力汽车电子控制单元高集成度升级
content:
纳芯微近日推出集成CAN收发器、LDO稳压器的Mini SBC产品NCA1169V-Q1系列。该系列产品满足ISO 11898-2:2024 标准要求，为汽车电子控制单元提供集成化的电源管理与CAN FD通信支持，可应用于汽车车身控制、智能座舱、车载照明、底盘转向及安全传感器等多种应用场景。凭借高集成度与低功耗设计，NCA1169V-Q1系列有助于简化外围电路设计，兼顾汽车电子系统对成本及可靠性的综合需求。
搭配看门狗保障系统稳定运行
NCA1169V-Q1集成两路内部LDO稳压器，提供强大的带载能力，支持灵活的负载配置。其中，主LDO（V1）提供350mA的电流驱动能力，辅LDO（V2）提供100mA的电流驱动能力。同时，NCA1169V-Q1内置看门狗功能，支持窗口模式、超时模式和自主模式三种工作模式，可根据不同系统运行状态与应用场景灵活配置，为MCU运行状态监控及系统异常管理提供支持，进一步提升系统运行的可靠性。
凭借双路LDO稳压器的集成设计，NCA1169V-Q1系列能够有效简化系统架构，减少外围器件需求，助力汽车电子控制单元实现更紧凑的设计，为整车电子系统的小型化与集成化发展提供支持。
图-1：NCA1169V-Q1功能框图
集成CAN FD满足最新标准
自研振铃抑制电路助力高速稳定通信
NCA1169V-Q1集成的CAN FD满足ISO 11898-2:2024 标准要求，CAN FD通信速率达5Mbps，在特定应用条件下最高可达8Mbps，充分满足汽车电子系统对高速数据传输的需求。
在CAN总线信号传输过程中，阻抗不匹配等因素可能会引发信号反射，形成振铃现象，影响信号完整性，并对高速通信的稳定性带来挑战。NCA1169V-Q1集成纳芯微自研振铃抑制电路，有效抑制总线信号振荡，改善信号质量，提升高速数据传输的稳定性，为汽车电子系统实现高速、可靠的CAN通信提供支持。
低功耗待机与多种唤醒机制
兼顾能耗与响应需求
NCA1169V-Q1具有极低功耗设计，在睡眠模式下电流仅34.3μA，待机模式下电流仅49.6μA，有效降低车辆非活跃状态下的静态能耗，为整车低功耗管理提供有力支持。
此外，NCA1169V-Q1支持标准唤醒、WAKE引脚本地唤醒及选择性唤醒等多种唤醒机制，并具备唤醒源识别功能，可根据系统需求灵活配置唤醒策略，在降低功耗的同时实现快速响应，助力汽车电子系统兼顾低功耗运行与高效响应的需求。
提升汽车电子系统运行可靠性
面对复杂多变的汽车电子应用环境，NCA1169V-Q1集成多种保护功能，为芯片及外围电路提供多层次的安全保障。在总线故障保护方面，器件可承受最高±58V的电压，有效应对总线短路及异常电压冲击；在热保护方面，支持过热预警与关断机制，可在芯片温度过高时及时采取保护措施，防止器件损坏；在ESD防护方面，CDM静电放电耐受能力达±2000V，并针对CAN引脚提供相应的ESD防护，增强器件在装配及使用过程中的静电耐受能力。
NCA1169V-Q1系列产品采用DFN20封装，满足AEC-Q100汽车级要求，与市场主流器件P2P兼容。收发器的I/O电平可根据需要调整为微控制器的I/O电平，包括1.8V、3.3V和5V，灵活适配各类微控制器。NCA1169V-Q1系列现已支持送样，预计今年年底量产。
快速响应定制开发需求
纳芯微在通信接口领域布局已久，通过平台化IP和自研专利的协同，实现了快速的产品迭代，并且在CAN/LIN/RS485/I2C/I3C/SerDes接口等方面完成了全面的产品布局。技术层面，纳芯微在EMC增强的CAN/LIN接口技术、专有协议接口技术、高速接口技术等方面不断突破，达到业内领先的水平。
在技术迭代的同时，纳芯微全面落地全国产供应链体系，打通晶圆制造、封装测试、核心物料配套的全链路国产化。目前，纳芯微车载CAN/LIN/SerDes等汽车通信接口芯片，均已实现全国产供应链落地，精准匹配新能源汽车等领域的国产化替代需求。高度自主可控的本土供应链，不仅大幅提升了产品交付稳定性与成本可控性，还能快速响应客户定制开发与批量供货需求，为终端客户提供安全可靠、高适配的国产化接口芯片解决方案。

title: DHL Group Strengthens Asia Pacific Healthcare Supply Chains
content:
DHL Group Strengthens Asia Pacific Healthcare Supply Chains
Prioritise Us
on Google
Did you know?
You can read this and more in the magazine
DHL commits €2bn globally to life sciences and healthcare logistics. Credit: DHL
As demand for reliable healthcare logistics increases, DHL is investing in its Asia Pacific operations to increase compliance and efficiency
DHL Group is strengthening its
Life Sciences and Healthcare (LSHC) capabilities in Singapore
, following the opening of its Pharma Hub in 2025.
As the company continues to
grow its investments
, the region will see expanded capacity across its medical supply chains, driving greater efficiency and security across the industry.
In a critical sector like healthcare, a reliable supply chain saves lives.
Through these investments, DHL is making better healthcare accessible for more people, resulting in patient satisfaction and supply chain resilience.
Demand for logistics
Healthcare supply chains
are incredibly complex, brought into the light during the COVID-19 pandemic when vaccines were being brought out,
was in high demand and non-critical surgeries were being pushed back.
Since this period of disruption, organisations have been examining their supply chain and logistics capabilities, exploring where issues occurred and what demonstrated resilience.
Healthcare supply chains have been seeing greater investments in recent years, driven by a new understanding of their importance.
Key Stats
€2bn – DHL Group announced a €2bn (US$2.29bn) global investment into LSHC
€500m – the amount DHL is investing in the Asia Pacific Health Logistics expansion
US$239bn – Asia Pacific’s pharmaceutical logistics market is expected to grow to US$239bn by 2031
12,000 – DHL Supply Chain’s Singaporean footprint will accommodate 12,000 pallet positions
These supply chains require careful strategies, temperature-controlled carriers and efficient handovers. The smallest error can result in high amounts of monetary and product waste – and put lives at risk.
“In healthcare logistics, precision is non-negotiable. A temperature excursion of just a few degrees can compromise the integrity of high-value medicines, biologics and other critical healthcare products,” explains
Praveen Gregory
DHL Global Forwarding
Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia.
“That is why building an end-to-end, unbroken cold chain is essential. Beyond protecting products, it gives healthcare companies the confidence that life-saving therapies can move safely, compliantly and reliably across increasingly complex global supply chains.”
Praveen Gregory, CEO of DHL Global Forwarding Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia. Credit: DHL
DHL, therefore, is further developing its LSHC capabilities in Singapore, growing its capabilities across transport, storage and distribution, medical devices and clinical trial materials across Asia Pacific.
The investments prioritise infrastructure, specialist expertise and strategic partnerships.
Temperature-controlled carriers are vital to safe healthcare supply chains Credit: DHL
DHL’s investment
In 2025, the Asia Pacific
pharmaceuticals market
was valued at US$163bn.
Following an ongoing demand for vaccines, biologics and temperature-controlled products, it is expected to reach almost US$239bn by 2031.
DHL has committed a €2bn (US$2.29bn) global investment into LSHC, €500m (US$568.9m) of which is going towards the Asia Pacific Health Logistics expansion.
This will go across infrastructure, technology, storage, fulfilment, distribution, global transportation and last-mile delivery.
DHL’s Global Expansion
1969 - DHL was founded by Adrian Dalsey, Larry Hillblom and Robert Lynn
1979 - The company began to deliver parcels
2002 - Deutsche Post acquired DHL
2007 - The Group opens the DHL Innovation Center
2012 - DHL opens its biggest express hub in Asia
2025 - DHL Group commits to €2bn investment by 2030
DHL Global Forwarding is developing the DHL Singapore Coldchain Hub. It is a €15m (US$17m) facility, which will provide 3,047 sqm of GDP-aligned temperature-controlled infrastructure.
This will correctly store pharmaceuticals, vaccines and biologics, with dedicated handling environments across chilled and ambient temperatures.
It is designed to ensure the cold chain operates unbroken, preserving product integrity end-to-end and is expected to launch in late 2027.
DHL Singapore Coldchain Hub will support vaccines, biologics and medicines. Credit: DHL
Following the success of the Pharma Hub, first launched in Singapore in 2025, a second will be developed in order to support ambient storage capability across
pharmaceuticals
and medical devices.
The €5m (US$5.6m) facility will operate between 15°C and 25°C in temperature controlled environments, with a humidity control below 60%.
“Capacity on its own isn’t the goal. It’s what that capacity allows our customers to do,” adds
Eunis Hew
, Managing Director,
DHL Supply Chain
Singapore.
“As healthcare supply chains become more sophisticated, purpose-built infrastructure becomes increasingly important.”
Eunis Hew, Managing Director at DHL Supply Chain Singapore. Credit: Eunis Hew LinkedIn
Developing expertise
Every step of compliance and efficiency is being developed.
The South Asia Hub at Changi Airport has a GDP-compliant handling space to ensure the shipments move securely throughout the air logistics gateways.
“When it comes to healthcare shipments, every handoff matters,” adds
Christopher Ong
, Managing Director,
DHL Express
Singapore.
“By expanding GDP-compliant handling and storage capabilities within our South Asia Hub, we’re helping customers reduce risk during transit and maintain the integrity of temperature-sensitive products throughout their journey. That reliability is critical especially when those shipments support clinical trials, hospital treatments and patient care.”
Christopher Ong, Managing Director at DHL Express Singapore. Credit: Christopher Ong LinkedIn
Across its operations, teams in its Express, Global Forwarding and Supply Chain networks are gaining ongoing training for GDP requirements, temperature-controlled handling and quality management.
Employees are being equipped with evolving knowledge to keep up with the demands of
healthcare supply chains

The collaboration brings together Deloitte's consulting services and Sirion's AI platform to automate contract processes across supplier relationships. Through this, leaders could gain access to contract data that has traditionally remained siloed across departments and systems.
Supply chain organisations increasingly face pressure to demonstrate value through cost reduction and risk mitigation. Contract management represents a significant opportunity in both areas, yet many teams lack the tools to extract insights from existing agreements. The partnership addresses this gap by connecting contract intelligence
directly to supply chain workflows
Contract data remains disconnected
In recent years, supply chain operations have adopted digital tools across multiple functions. Contract management has lagged behind these efforts.
According to Sirion and World Commerce & Contracting, 54% of organisations lack automated data flow between contract management systems. The study launched in May 2026 found that 73% of respondents store contract data across multiple disconnected platforms.
Gaps in contract infrastructure
71% of North American respondents store contract data in shared drives
27% of organisations store all executed contracts exclusively in contract lifecycle management systems
54% have no automated data flow between systems
9% have two way synchronisation to keep contract data updated across platforms
42% are adopting or implementing AI in contracting processes
Teams are managing pricing negotiations, delivery schedules and renewal terms across supplier networks. When contract information sits in separate systems, tracking these commitments becomes difficult.
The fragmentation of contract data creates particular challenges for supply chain resilience. Procurement professionals may struggle to identify which suppliers hold critical commitments or where alternative sourcing arrangements exist. This lack of visibility can delay response times when supply disruptions occur or when organisations need to renegotiate terms quickly.
Supply chain visibility depends on access
"Contract lifecycle management is rapidly evolving from a back office function to a strategic enabler of business transformation," says Mark Ross, Legal Business Services Growth and Markets Leader at Deloitte. Organisations that cannot access contract data could miss supplier commitments or fail to respond to changing commercial conditions.
Supplier relationship management requires structured access to contractual terms. Supply chain teams need this information to
identify potential disruptions
before they affect operations.
AI contract lifecycle management platforms could help companies optimise supplier agreements and reduce costs. According to Sirion, the company has saved clients a combined total of more than US$2.2bn through its platform.
Modern supply chains operate across multiple tiers of suppliers, each with distinct contractual arrangements. Teams must track obligations across this network while maintaining compliance with regulatory requirements and internal policies. Without centralised contract intelligence, organisations risk exposure to supplier failures, price volatility and delivery delays that could have been anticipated through better data access.
Carin Giuliante, chair and CEO, Deloitte Tax
Procurement integration drives adoption
"As organisations accelerate their digital transformation journeys, the ability to manage contracts intelligently has become a strategic imperative, not just for legal teams, but for tax, finance, procurement and the broader enterprise," says Carin Giuliante, chair and CEO, Deloitte Tax. The alliance aims to embed contract intelligence into procurement workflows.
Sirion's platform uses conversational interfaces and AI agents to store,
create and manage contracts
. According to the company, it supports more than seven million contracts across more than 100 languages.
The platform can flag invoice discrepancies and monitor compliance across supplier agreements. It provides tools for each stage of the contract lifecycle from drafting through risk management.
"Sirion's AI first platform was built to handle the complexity of global supply chains and financial relationships," said Ajay Agrawal, CEO of Sirion. Deloitte will integrate contract intelligence into wider business processes using its Legal Business Services experience.
Operational resilience requires contract visibility
"Our partnership with Deloitte is about giving supply chain, procurement, legal, finance and delivery teams something they've rarely had, which is a real view into what their business has actually agreed to," explains Kanti Prabha, President, Chief Product & Technology Officer at Sirion. Supplier contracts often become inaccessible after execution.
Kanti Prabha, Co-Founder and President at Sirion (Credit: Sirion)
Finance teams could miss savings they negotiated. Operations might only learn about supplier problems after they disrupt production.
The partnership brings contract intelligence into finance, supply chain and enterprise resource planning systems. Teams can access this information through the platforms they use daily.
Deloitte serves almost 90% of the Fortune 500 through its finance and procurement network. The firm will apply this reach to help organisations integrate Sirion's platform.
Deloitte expands digital offerings
The Sirion alliance follows Deloitte's February 2026 launch of Enterprise AI Navigator. That solution helps organisations assess business processes and technology readiness for AI investments.
Enterprise AI Navigator supports development of AI agent prototypes and implementation roadmaps. According to Deloitte, the solution can reduce time required for
traditional AI strategy
work by up to 50%.
The firm launched Risk Clarity shortly before the Sirion partnership. The AI platform for risk management could offer efficiency gains of up to 30%, according to Deloitte.
"This alliance is about reimagining contract management as a driver of business value, insight and risk mitigation in an increasingly complex world," says Carin. The contract lifecycle management offering extends Deloitte's digital consultancy portfolio across the implementation process.

Its model aims to help those in the supply chain sector as they navigate the growing demand and increasing complexity in the modern market. It works to help companies with cost savings, efficiency, long-term resilience and business growth.
It embeds into its clients’ business operations and combines human and artificial talent in order to increase efficiency for its clients. It approaches each challenge with an integrated approach, looking at where human insight is critical and where AI agents can do the work.

title: Sphera AI Introduces Agentic AI Supply Chain Risk Tools
content:
Sphera AI Introduces Agentic AI Supply Chain Risk Tools
Prioritise Us
on Google
Sphera has launched new AI capabilities for Supply Chain Risk Management (SCRM)
Sphera CEO Paul Marushka outlines AI-powered supply chain risk management for faster supplier, product and operations decisions
Sphera has launched new AI capabilities for Supply Chain Risk Management (SCRM), designed to connect external risk signals with the suppliers, products and operations they could affect.
The new capabilities include agentic AI tools, conversational AI features and a Model Context Protocol (MCP), which allows organisations to pull insights directly from SCRM into compatible AI tools.
The Chicago-based company said the technology is intended to help organisations assess disruption impacts and coordinate responses in minutes rather than days.
The announcement follows the publication of Sphera research showing that external events - including supplier failures, port closures, material shortages and trade restrictions - are a major source of operational disruption.
Paul Marushka, CEO at Sphera
External risk is becoming operational risk
Across the US, UK, Germany, France and UAE, 58% of surveyed chief operating officers said their most significant disruptions originated at least as much outside their organisation as within it. The figure rose to 71% among respondents in the UAE.
The research surveyed 750 COOs. It found that the most difficult parts of disruption management were:
Identifying exposed suppliers or products: 33%
Selecting the right mitigation action: 30%
Quantifying potential business impact: 29%
The findings reflect a growing gap between risk detection and operational decision-making. Organisations may identify an external event quickly, but still struggle to determine which sites, products, suppliers or customer commitments are exposed.
“The boundary of the enterprise is no longer the boundary of operational risk. A disruption can begin with a supplier, a critical material or an event on the other side of the world, but its consequences are felt inside the business,” says Paul Marushka, CEO and President of Sphera.
"The challenge is connecting those external signals to the products and operations they affect quickly enough to make a better decision. Sphera AI helps close that gap, while keeping people in control of the decisions that matter most,” adds Paul.
Sphera notes 58% of surveyed chief operating officers said their most significant disruptions originated at least as much outside their organisation as within it.
Sphera AI connects signals to business impact
The new Sphera AI capabilities are designed to link external intelligence to internal business context.
Users can ask questions about supplier and supply chain risk in plain language and identify which suppliers, products and operations may be exposed. The aim is to reduce the need to compare multiple dashboards or manually trace relationships between an external event and the business processes it threatens.
The capabilities include: external risk signals, supplier exposure, product dependencies, operational impact, risk severity, mitigation decisions, response coordination, supply continuity, production protection and revenue protection.
Sphera’s Supply Chain Risk Management platform combines external risk intelligence with suppliers, products, commodities and multi-tier dependencies.
Model Context Protocol extends risk intelligence
Sphera has also added support for the Model Context Protocol (MCP).
MCP allows organisations to make selected SCRM insights available through compatible artificial intelligence tools. This means risk information can be accessed in the environments where teams already analyse data and make operational decisions.
The potential applications include querying supplier risk through compatible AI assistants, retrieving risk context without switching between systems, connecting external events to internal supplier records, supporting procurement and operations workflows, making trusted risk data available to authorised users and reducing time spent searching across separate applications.
The approach is intended to make risk intelligence more accessible while retaining organisational controls over data, workflows and decision-making.
AI agents support risk triage
Within Sphera’s Risk Response & Resolution Center, the recently introduced AI agents assess risk severity and supplier impact.
The system is designed to help teams distinguish urgent risks from lower-priority signals. By automating aspects of triage, Sphera said users can focus on the events most likely to affect production, supply continuity or revenue.
The Risk Response & Resolution Center provides a central workspace for triaging risks, assigning ownership, executing mitigation plans and tracking outcomes with an audit trail.
Sphera’s broader platform monitors more than 300,000 news sources each day and processes approximately 15 billion data points each month, according to company information.
Human control remains central
Sphera’s announcement positions artificial intelligence as a decision-support capability rather than an autonomous replacement for supply chain and procurement teams.
The company said every one of the 750 COOs surveyed identified at least one risk-management activity they would allow AI to progress automatically, provided appropriate rules and controls were in place.
This creates a governance model in which AI could detect relevant events, classify risk signals, summarise complex information, match events to suppliers, estimate potential exposure, prioritise response activity as well as potentially recommending next steps.
Human teams remain responsible for decisions involving suppliers, production, customer commitments, financial exposure and operational continuity.
Traditional supply chain risk management often stops at the alert. Sphera’s announcement focuses on the next stage: translating an alert into an operational response.
The workflows that follow the identification of such a disruption include: detecting a geopolitical, environmental or logistics event, identifying affected suppliers and sub-tier relationships, mapping impacted products and facilities and estimating operational and commercial consequences. These steps are then followed by the assignment of response ownership, the selection and execution of mitigation actions, and tracking whether an organisation's exposure has reduced.
Sphera describes this connection between risk signals, business impact and response workflows as a way to reduce decision latency across the disruption lifecycle.

Detecting a geopolitical, environmental or logistics event
Identifying affected suppliers and sub-tier relationships
Mapping impacted products and facilities
Estimating operational and commercial consequences
Assigning response ownership
Selecting and executing mitigation actions
Tracking whether exposure has reduced

title: CATL advances solid-state battery development to 20 Ah samples - electrive.com
content:
According to Chinese media, CATL has expanded the development of its solid-state battery from a 10-Ah-class validation platform to test runs with 20-Ah samples. The company continues to aim for small-scale production in 2027 and is reportedly targeting an energy density of around 500 Wh/kg.
Image: CATL
According to Chinese media, CATL published an update this week on its solid-state battery development in response to investor queries via the state-regulated online communication platform of the Shenzhen Stock Exchange (“Hudongyi Platform”). According to the update, test runs with 20 Ah samples are now underway, and the start of pilot production
remains planned for 2027
CATL also shared that the development team working on this project comprises more than 1,000 employees and that the programme aims to achieve an energy density of approximately 500 Wh/kg at the cell level. However,
Car News China
notes that CATL has not explicitly confirmed this figure as a specification for mass-produced cells, nor “disclosed expected trial output, automotive customers or a vehicle launch date tied to these cells”. The company is still aiming for large-scale production around 2030.
Solid-state batteries are widely regarded as a promising technology for the next generation of energy storage. Their defining feature is the replacement of the liquid or gel-like electrolyte in conventional lithium-ion batteries with a solid electrolyte based on sulphide, polymer, or oxide materials. This is expected to improve fire safety, increase energy density, enable faster charging times, extend service life, and enhance the range of EVs.
Little is yet known about CATL’s specific technology approach. Unconfirmed reports suggest the company is primarily focusing on sulphide-based solid-state batteries. However, CATL has not yet disclosed the intended anode configuration.
In addition to CATL, companies like BYD and Toyota, as well as promising startups such as
Factorial
QuantumScape
, are advancing the technology. However, in June,
CATL CEO Robin Zeng noted
that technical and manufacturing challenges mean that the deployment of solid-state batteries in the mass market is still several years away, and he does not expect volume production before 2030. Moreover, Zeng stated that solid-state batteries will likely initially be used only in premium automotive platforms.
CATL also stated in June that its solid-state technology is currently at level four on the nine-point Technology Readiness Level (TRL) scale. This classification means that CATL is still engaged in laboratory validation and prototype development for solid-state batteries this summer.

title: 1.5 GPa spider silk inspires new push for sustainable textile fibers
content: Spider silk can withstand a pulling force equivalent to 150 newtons per square millimeter of its cross-sectional area before breaking.They are investigating ways to produce spider silk artificially because spiders produce much less silk per animal.The key challenge is turning liquid silk protein in spiders’ specialized glands into an actual fiber.Strength like steelSpider silk is a biomaterial produced by these arachnids, and it is mostly in the form of threadlike fiber with high elasticity and strength comparable to steel.The interesting thing about this silk is that it comes in many forms, each with its own purpose. While thin threads are the most familiar form, which the spiders use to make webs, there are a few other forms as well that this animal uses – sometimes to catch a prey or to protect eggs, or to use it as a safety rope.Among its many properties, spider silk’s tensile strength is quite intriguing, reaching up to 1.5 billion pascals (GPa). That means it can withstand a pulling force equivalent to 150 newtons per square millimeter of its cross-sectional area before breaking. This is comparable to high-grade steel.Due to their tensile strength, toughness, light weight, and biodegradability, they have a potential for their usage, especially in the textile industry. Researchers are investigating ways to produce it artificially because spiders produce much less silk per animal, and they can’t be raised in large numbers like silkworms because they are cannibalistic.Scaling up is challengingUniversity of North Carolina (UNC) ‘s Sarah Stellwagen, who studies silk from arthropods (insects and arachnids) at the material and genetic levels, said in an interview that the challenge is turning liquid silk protein in spiders’ specialized glands into an actual fiber.“Researchers have made plenty of protein soup, as a spider does, but unlike spiders, they haven’t been able to spin that protein into solid threads at a scale that is relevant for the public,” said Stellwagen, who is an assistant professor in the Department of Biological Sciences at UNC Charlotte.The spider does this by passing the fluid from its gland through a narrow duct, changing its chemical environment and assembling it into a tightly packed structure called a beta-sheet. The fiber then emerges through its spinnerets in the solid form.However, there has been some progress as well. Researchers at the Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences (SLU) have shown that protein can be produced in larger quantities and more efficiently, which can also reduce production costs. Researchers Anna Rising and Benjamin Schmuck, who earlier this year received a grant of EUR 200,000 from H&M Foundation, are now working to produce fibers and yarn from protein for textile tests.The group is also exploring the fiber’s use for medical purposes.“The award (grant and support program) gives us the opportunity to take the next step: do more trials, improve the manufacturing process, and produce enough material to test yarn and textiles,” says Anna Rising, professor at the Department of Animal Biosciences.Earlier research from King’s College London and San Diego State University (SDSU) in California has decoded the “molecular stickers” that make spider silk stronger than steel and tougher than Kevlar.

title: 24,000-ton nuclear submarine launches 5,160-mile-range Bulava missile
content: Russia has test-fired a Bulava intercontinental ballistic missile from a submerged nuclear-powered submarine in the Sea of Okhotsk. The missile headed toward a designated test range in Russia’s Arkhangelsk region, according to the Russian Defense Ministry.The launch took place on October 28 as part of a scheduled combat training exercise. The submarine, Generalissimo Suvorov, belongs to Russia’s Pacific Fleet and carries weapons designed for the country’s sea-based nuclear deterrent.The test involved launching a strategic missile from beneath the surface, with the submarine operating in the Russian Far East. Its target lay thousands of miles away in northwestern Russia.Testing the Bulava missileThe Russian Defense Ministry said the crew launched the Bulava missile toward the Chizha test range in the Arkhangelsk region. The ministry did not disclose the missile’s flight time or provide detailed results from the test.Launching a ballistic missile from underwater requires careful coordination between the submarine and its weapon systems. The crew must follow the launch sequence while the vessel remains submerged, allowing it to fire without surfacing first.That capability is central to the role of ballistic missile submarines. Their ability to operate at sea gives them greater flexibility than fixed land-based launch sites.The Bulava serves as the primary weapon aboard Russia’s Borei-class strategic submarines. These missiles give the Russian Navy a sea-based option for delivering nuclear weapons as part of the country’s broader deterrent.Inside the Borei-A submarineThe Generalissimo Suvorov, also known as K-553, belongs to the Project 955A Borei-A class. Russia developed these nuclear-powered submarines to carry strategic missiles while improving on earlier submarine designs.The Generalissimo Suvorov measures around 558 feet long and displaces approximately 14,720 metric tons on the surface. Its submerged displacement rises to about 24,000 metric tons. Powered by a nuclear reactor, the Borei-A class submarine can reach speeds of around 15 knots on the surface and up to 29 knots underwater. It also carries 16 Bulava intercontinental ballistic missiles.The vessel incorporates updated equipment and technical systems. Its design also aims to reduce detectable physical signatures and improve protection during operations.Rubin Central Design Bureau for Marine Engineering, based in St. Petersburg, designed the submarine. Construction began at the Sevmash shipyard on December 26, 2014, and the Russian Navy commissioned the vessel in 2022.The submarine initially served with Russia’s Northern Fleet. It transferred to the Pacific Fleet in October 2023 and arrived at its permanent base in Kamchatka.That move placed the vessel within Russia’s Pacific submarine force, which operates across the country’s eastern maritime approaches. The Sea of Okhotsk provides an important operating area for Russian naval forces based in the region.Russia’s sea-based nuclear forceBorei and Borei-A class submarines carry 16 Bulava intercontinental ballistic missiles, according to the Russian report. Nuclear propulsion allows them to remain at sea for extended periods without the refueling needs of conventional submarines.The combination of underwater launch capability and long-range missiles makes these vessels an important part of Russia’s strategic arsenal. Submarines can operate away from fixed launch facilities, complicating efforts to track their movements.The latest test confirms that the Generalissimo Suvorov continues to participate in Russia’s combat training program. However, the ministry released few details about the missile’s performance or the exercise’s specific objectives.The launch also provides no indication of changes to the Bulava’s capabilities. Its significance lies in demonstrating the submarine’s continued role in training with one of Russia’s principal sea-based nuclear weapons.

title: 370,000 tons of CO₂ to be captured using innovative purification tech
content: A French company is set to deliver innovative CO₂ purification technology for UK’s first carbon capture plant at a waste-to-energy facility. Veolia has been awarded a significant contract by Kanadevia Inova AG to design and supply two CO₂ purification and dehydration units to be installed at Encyclis’ energy-from-waste facility near Ellesmere Port, Cheshire. Veolia’s cutting-edge purification and dehydration technology will support the capture and storage of 370,000 tons of CO₂ annually, which is equivalent to removing 200,000 petrol cars from the road.Facility will become a negative emitter“This pioneering project establishes Veolia at the forefront of industrial decarbonization and environmental security,” said Anne Le Guennec, CEO of Veolia’s water technology activities. “We are delivering on our promise to drive ecological transformation by enabling industries to transition toward net zero, in line with our GreenUp strategic program. With active carbon capture projects across Europe and the US, Veolia is the partner of choice for organizations seeking to decarbonize at scale, and we look forward to accelerating additional carbon capture, utilization and storage projects worldwide.”The Protos project, the UK’s first full-scale carbon capture facility integrated with an energy-from-waste plant, will process up to 500,000 tons of non-recyclable waste annually, generating up to 49.9 MW of baseload electricity for the National Grid while capturing approximately 370,000 tons of CO₂ each year. Once operational in mid-2029, the facility will become a negative emitter, with captured CO₂ transported via the HyNet North West pipeline network for permanent geological storage in depleted gas reservoirs beneath Liverpool Bay, according to a press release.Full-scale carbon capture marketThis contract marks Veolia’s entry into the full-scale carbon capture market and reinforces its commitment to accelerating industrial decarbonization and environmental security through innovative technology.Veolia’s compact, modular purification and dehydration units were specifically designed to fit within the constrained space of the Protos ERF building envelope. The technology will ensure the captured CO₂ meets the stringent purity standards required for safe transport and long-term storage, a critical factor in the project’s success and a testament to Veolia’s ability to deliver tailored decarbonization solutions for complex industrial challenges, as per the release.Carbon dioxide captured from industrial processes often requires further treatment before it can be transported through pipeline infrastructure or stored underground. Purification removes unwanted impurities, while dehydration reduces moisture content. Both processes are essential to ensure that the CO₂ meets the required specifications for transportation and storage.Veolia’s compact, modular systems have been specifically designed to accommodate the space constraints of the existing energy-from-waste facility. Their integration into the plant will help address the technical challenges associated with installing carbon capture infrastructure within an operational industrial site.The contract highlights the importance of specialized gas treatment and purification systems in making large-scale carbon capture projects technically viable.For the waste management sector, carbon capture could provide an additional pathway for reducing emissions from residual waste treatment, complementing waste prevention, reuse and recycling. It should not, however, replace efforts to reduce waste generation or improve material recovery.The Protos project offers an opportunity to assess how these approaches can be integrated into a broader environmental strategy.

title: 6,000-ton frigate that can launch missiles offered to US Navy
content: A London-based defense manufacturer has offered its powerful Arrowhead 140 frigates to the U.S. Navy. Developed by Babcock, these vessels could form a proposed fleet of the U.S. Navy.The Arrowhead 140 is a general-purpose frigate and its design is derived from Denmark’s Iver Huitfeldt-class warships. It was selected as the foundation of Britain’s five-ship Type 31 programme, which is being built at Babcock’s Rosyth shipyard in Scotland. The design has also been selected for export programmes in Poland and Indonesia, giving it a growing international footprint.Frigate integrates diesel propulsion, offers speeds exceeding 28 knots In its baseline configuration, the Arrowhead 140 is approximately 452-feet (138 metres long), has a beam of around 20 metres and displaces approximately 5,700-6,000 tons. It uses a conventional combined diesel-and-diesel propulsion system and is capable of speeds exceeding 28 knots.Babcock does not operate a shipyard in the United States, making an American industrial partner central to its proposal. Huntington Ingalls Industries is expected to be a potential partner because of its experience building warships for the U.S. Navy and its established industrial infrastructure.The two companies already have working relationships in the submarine sector, including activities associated with components supporting American and British nuclear-powered submarine programmes. These existing connections could provide a foundation for broader cooperation in surface shipbuilding.For the U.S., the Arrowhead 140 represents a potential route to broadening its frigate options and reducing dependence on lengthy new-design development. If the ship can be adapted economically and produced at scale, it could help the Navy expand its surface fleet while preserving larger combatants for more demanding missions.Recently, Babcock welcomed suppliers, industry partners and Indonesian and UK Government stakeholders to London for a UK-Indonesia Supplier Day, highlighting opportunities for British businesses to support the delivery of Indonesia’s ambitious Maritime Partnership Programme (MPP). The event reinforces our commitment to building a strong, collaborative supply chain that delivers economic growth, innovation and long-term maritime capability in both nations.“Strong partnerships are essential to delivering growth, innovation and capability. This Supplier Day demonstrates the momentum behind the Maritime Partnership Programme and our commitment to ensuring UK industry plays a meaningful role in its success,” said Harry Holt, Group CEO, Babcock. “The programme is about more than ships. It is about building long-term industrial partnerships, developing skills, supporting technology transfer and creating economic opportunities across both nations. By bringing together suppliers, industry leaders and government stakeholders, we are helping create the foundations for lasting collaboration and sustainable growth.”American frigate requirement has gained urgencyThe American frigate requirement has gained urgency following the cancellation of the Constellation-class programme. Originally intended to provide a modern, multi-mission frigate based on the European FREMM design, the programme encountered significant delays and escalating costs as the ship was extensively modified to meet U.S. Navy requirements.The experience highlighted a central problem in warship procurement; selecting an existing design does not necessarily guarantee faster or cheaper construction if the customer substantially changes its architecture.The U.S. Navy could use a frigate of Arrowhead 140 type for maritime security, escort operations, independent deployments and other missions that do not always require its more expensive destroyers. Such a division of responsibilities could allow Arleigh Burke-class destroyers to concentrate on demanding tasks such as area air defence, missile defence and long-range strike operations.
