title: No Batteries, No Plugs: Scientists Create a Tiny Sensor That Powers Itself
content:
Technology
Soldering a graphene-based sensor. Credit: Russell Cothren
Scientists have developed a tiny temperature sensor that harvests energy from magnetic fields near electrical wiring.
Electrical wiring produces weak electromagnetic fields that typically go unnoticed, but researchers have found a way to turn some of that energy into a power source for tiny electronic devices. Scientists at the
University of Arkansas (U of A)
University of Michigan
have developed a graphene-based energy harvester capable of powering an ultra-low-power temperature sensor without a conventional battery.
The prototype operates using energy collected from its immediate surroundings, consuming power measured in nanowatts, or billionths of a watt. It represents another advance toward the team’s goal of developing autonomous sensors that could function unattended for decades.
Turning Electrical Wiring Into a Power Source
The technology captures energy from magnetic fields generated by electrical wiring carrying alternating current. In the United States, electricity typically operates at 60 hertz, meaning the current changes direction 60 times each second. The researchers designed their sensor to harvest energy from these low-frequency fields.
A graphene inductor collects the energy and sends an alternating electrical signal to a custom circuit, which converts it into direct current. That electricity charges capacitors that store energy for the sensor to use. Unlike a battery, a capacitor stores energy in an electric field rather than through chemical reactions.
“The inductor adds charge to these capacitors at a slow rate,” explained University of Arkansas physics professor Paul Thibado, “but it’s faster than the rate the sensor uses up the charges from the capacitors.”
Because the sensor consumes energy more slowly than the system replenishes it, the capacitors can maintain an electrical reserve. Thibado estimates that this stored energy could keep the device operating for at least 24 hours during a power outage, potentially extending to a week.
Building Sensors That Can Power Themselves
The new device is the second graphene-powered temperature sensor developed by the research team. Their earlier work demonstrated that graphene-based solar cells could supply enough electricity to operate temperature sensors, establishing another possible source of energy for autonomous electronics.
Graphene, a material consisting of a single layer of carbon atoms, has electrical properties that make it useful in energy-harvesting technologies. Thibado has investigated these properties for more than a decade and invented the graphene energy harvesters used in the team’s research.
The researchers ultimately want to combine several methods of collecting environmental energy, including sunlight, heat, sound, motion, and ambient electromagnetic fields. A sensor equipped with multiple harvesting systems could continue operating when one energy source becomes unavailable, reducing its dependence on any single power supply.
Applications Beyond Temperature Monitoring
Although temperature measurement provides a practical demonstration, the technology could eventually support sensors used in agriculture, environmental monitoring, medical tracking, wearable electronics, and supply chain management. These applications often require devices to operate in locations where replacing batteries is expensive, inconvenient, or impractical.
Thibado describes the long-term vision as “set it and forget it,” with sensors designed to operate for extended periods without routine battery replacement. Eliminating disposable batteries could also reduce maintenance demands and electronic waste, although decades of reliable operation have not yet been demonstrated.
The research was published in the
Journal of Vacuum Science and Technology B
, with MD Rezaul Kabir, a doctoral candidate in materials science and engineering at the University of Arkansas, serving as first author. The project also involves researchers at the University of Michigan, including electrical engineering and computer science professor David Blaauw, whose work focuses on low-power wireless sensors and embedded systems.
Commercial Development and Future Possibilities
NTS Innovations, a nanotechnology company, holds the exclusive license to commercialize the graphene energy-harvesting technology. The company has supported patent development, business planning, and efforts to identify potential customers and commercial partners.
More than 60 parties have expressed interest in testing the technology and exploring ways to integrate it into products. Ongoing discussions are helping establish practical requirements, including the minimum electrical power needed for different applications.
The researchers envision networks of self-powered sensors that can collect information for years with little human intervention. Combining graphene-based energy harvesting with electronics that consume extremely small amounts of electricity could help make that goal achievable, particularly as connected devices become more common in homes, industries, and environmental monitoring systems.
Reference: “Graphene powerline energy harvester powers a batteryless sensor” by Md R. Kabir, Ashaduzzaman, T. B. Amin, J. M. Mangum, S. M. Rahman, H. Do, G. Carichner, D. Blaauw and P. M. Thibado, 20 October 2026,
Journal of Vacuum Science & Technology B

title: Scientists Discover 3 Strange Quantum Materials That Could Finally Reveal Dark Matter
content:
Dark matter is an invisible form of matter believed to account for about 85% of all matter in the universe. Although it does not emit, absorb, or reflect light, its gravitational influence helps hold galaxies together and shapes the large-scale structure of the cosmos. Credit: SciTechDaily.com
Scientists have identified three unusual quantum materials that could transform the search for dark matter.
Quantum simulations suggest that a material called titanium diselenide could make future detectors up to 1,000 times more sensitive to certain forms of light dark matter than current benchmark materials. The finding could help researchers search for particles whose interactions with ordinary matter are too faint for conventional detectors to register.
In a study published in
Physical Review Letters
, an international research team identified three promising materials: titanium diselenide (TiSe₂), strontium ruthenate (Sr₂RuO₄), and hole-doped diamond. Each has unusual electronic properties that could make it particularly effective at detecting the tiny energy transfers expected from lightweight dark matter particles.
Why Dark Matter Is So Difficult to Detect
Dark matter is thought to account for approximately 85% of all matter in the universe. Its gravitational effects help explain how galaxies move and how large cosmic structures form, yet no experiment has directly detected a dark matter particle. Because dark matter does not emit, absorb, or reflect light, scientists must search for other evidence of its interactions with ordinary matter.
One approach involves looking for small amounts of energy deposited when a dark matter particle encounters a detector. The challenge becomes greater for lighter particles, which may transfer so little energy that existing detector materials cannot reliably register the interaction.
Quantum Materials Could Reveal Previously Undetectable Signals
The three proposed materials contain collective electronic excitations known as plasmons. These involve coordinated movements of electrons and can respond to exceptionally small energy deposits. Their properties could allow detectors to register interactions that would otherwise produce signals too weak to measure.
Using advanced quantum mechanical simulations based on fundamental physical principles, the researchers calculated how each material would respond to hypothetical dark matter interactions. Their results indicate that these materials could outperform existing benchmark candidates across a broad range of particle masses, potentially reaching regions that current detection approaches cannot effectively explore.
The calculations identified titanium diselenide as particularly promising, with projected sensitivity improvements of two to three orders of magnitude. These gains remain theoretical and have not yet been demonstrated in working dark matter detectors.
Earth’s Rotation Could Help Identify Dark Matter Signals
Two of the materials also showed a potentially valuable property: directional sensitivity. Their predicted responses depend on the direction from which a dark matter particle enters relative to the crystal’s internal structure.
As Earth rotates, the orientation of a detector changes relative to the expected incoming dark matter flux. This could produce a repeating daily variation in the signal, helping researchers distinguish potential dark matter interactions from background events that do not follow the same directional pattern.
Toward a New Generation of Dark Matter Detectors
The proposed materials have practical advantages beyond their predicted sensitivity. All three can be produced using established synthesis techniques, while titanium diselenide appears particularly suitable for larger-scale manufacturing. Incorporating these materials into existing detector technologies could provide a route toward future experiments, although their performance must first be tested.
The research was conducted by Prof. Yonit Hochberg and Rotem Ovadia of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Dr. Dino Novko of the Institute of Physics in Croatia, and Prof. Antonio Politano of the University of L’Aquila.
“Dark matter remains one of the greatest mysteries in physics, and discovering its nature requires us to rethink not only the particles we are searching for, but also the materials we use to search for them,” said the researchers. “By identifying quantum materials that naturally amplify the tiny signals expected from light dark matter, we’ve uncovered a promising new path toward experiments that are significantly more sensitive than those available today.”
The calculations also suggest that the search need not be limited to these three candidates. Other quantum materials with suitable low-energy electronic excitations may offer additional opportunities to detect elusive dark matter particles.
Reference: “Unconventional Materials for Light Dark Matter Detection” by Yonit Hochberg, Dino Novko, Rotem Ovadia and Antonio Politano, 2 September 2026,
Physical Review Letters
DOI: 10.1103/jdw6-3556

title: Scientists Discover a New Dinosaur Species Hiding in Plain Sight for 25 Years
content:
A reconstruction of the iguanodontian dinosaur Paludohadros proudlovii walking through mud along the edge of a shallow body of water. In the distance, the large predatory dinosaur Baryonyx can be seen. Credit: Guilherme Gehr
A dinosaur fossil unearthed in England more than two decades ago has now been identified as an entirely new genus and species.
A dinosaur discovered in an English clay quarry 25 years ago has finally been recognized as an entirely new genus and species. Named
Paludohadros proudlovii
, the plant-eating dinosaur lived about 125 million years ago, when muddy wetlands covered much of southern England. Its identification is also prompting scientists to reconsider other fossils that have spent decades in museum collections.
The four-legged herbivore measured approximately 5 meters (16 feet) long and weighed an estimated 1.5 to 2 metric tons (3,300 to 4,400 pounds), making it comparable in size to a rhinoceros. However, its bones were not fully developed, suggesting that the individual was still young when it died. A mature
Paludohadros
might have grown to twice its size.
A Prehistoric Predator May Have Hunted This Dinosaur
Paludohadros
shared its Early Cretaceous environment with
Baryonyx walkeri
, a large, two-legged carnivore discovered at the same Surrey quarry in 1983. Although
Baryonyx
is particularly well known for eating fish, evidence of a young iguanodontian in its last meal suggests that other dinosaurs were also part of its diet.
Professor Susannah Maidment, a senior author of the research from the Natural History Museum, London, and the University of Birmingham, explains: “Paludohadros was found just 100 meters (about 330 feet) away from Baryonyx, whose fossils we also look after at the Natural History Museum. While Baryonyx is best known for eating fish, this dinosaur’s last meal also included a baby iguanodontian.”
“We can’t tell for certain which species this came from, so it’s possible that Baryonyx could have been scavenging on the remains of young Paludohadros or even hunting them when it had the opportunity.”
In situ skull bones Credit: Tim Burgess (Wienerberger Ltd)
Why Scientists Are Discovering New Dinosaurs in Old Fossils
Paludohadros
belonged to the iguanodontians, a widespread group of plant-eating dinosaurs distinguished in part by their characteristic thumb spikes. For many years, iguanodontian fossils from southern England were generally assigned to one of two genera:
Iguanodon
or its smaller relative,
Mantellisaurus
A detailed scientific reassessment of
Mantellisaurus
, published by Natural History Museum researchers in 2023, clarified anatomical differences that had previously been overlooked. These distinctions have helped paleontologists recognize several separate iguanodontian dinosaurs, including
Brighstoneus
Comptonatus
, the sail-backed
Istiorachis
, and now
Paludohadros
The latest identification has also led researchers back to older museum specimens. Several fossils collected as early as the 1950s have now been recognized as belonging to
Paludohadros
, suggesting that additional examples of the dinosaur were preserved long before scientists understood that it represented a separate genus.
A Dinosaur Named in Memory of a Quarry Manager
The original
Paludohadros
fossil was unearthed in 2001 at wienerberger’s Ewhurst brick and roof tile works (Ewhurst Works) in Surrey and subsequently donated to the Natural History Museum. Its genus name reflects the wetland environment it inhabited, drawing on the Latin word
, meaning “swamp.”
The species name,
proudlovii
, honors Will Proudlove, a former employee who worked his way up to become the quarry’s manager. Proudlove had a strong interest in the fossils exposed by quarrying operations but died at age 35, shortly before the dinosaur was discovered. He was survived by his wife, Rachael, and their young children, Ellie and Matt.
Rachael Proudlove says, “Will always had an interest in dinosaur fossils and was fascinated about what, if anything, would be uncovered each time a layer of clay was removed from the quarry. Sadly, this dinosaur was only discovered the year after he died, but its story has become a part of our lives since then.”
“We were invited to go and look at it being excavated back in 2001, so it’s amazing to hear all this time later that it’s not just a new species of dinosaur, but a new genus too. We’re absolutely overjoyed and honored that Will’s name and legacy will live on in this dinosaur.”
More Unknown Dinosaurs May Be Hiding in Museum Collections
The research was led by Ricardo Sacamoto, a PhD student at the Natural History Museum, London, and the University of São Paulo. He plans to continue examining the museum’s extensive collection of iguanodontian fossils, looking for anatomical differences that could identify additional unrecognized species.
Paludohadros
is the first species I’ve ever named and I’m honored to have been able to work on it. I still remember the incredible moment when I realized that this was a new species that no one had ever identified before,” Sacamoto says.
“I’m now going to go through the Natural History Museum’s iguanodontian collections to identify what’s there as part of my PhD. This could lead to the discovery of more new dinosaur species that haven’t yet been recognized.”

title: Scientists Separate Psilocybin’s Brain-Rewiring Power From Its Hallucinations
content:
Psilocybin, the naturally occurring psychedelic compound found in certain “magic mushrooms,” is gaining attention for its potential to treat depression and other mental health conditions. Credit: Stock
Mouse experiments suggest psilocybin’s ability to rebuild brain connections may be separable from its psychedelic effects, opening new possibilities for non-hallucinogenic psychiatric medications.
Chronic stress can strip away connections between brain cells, disrupting the circuits they form. Researchers at the
University of California, Santa Cruz
, found that psilocybin, the psychoactive compound in “magic mushrooms,” reshapes this wiring differently in healthy mice and those affected by stress.
The study, published on October 15 in
Nature Neuroscience
, also identified a group of brain cells that supported new connections without triggering a rodent behavior used as a proxy for hallucinogenic activity.
“I consider this work a major advance, particularly in our understanding of how psilocybin reshapes neural circuits and its potential implications for treating mental disorders,” said senior author Yi Zuo, professor of molecular, cell, and developmental biology at UC Santa Cruz.
Psilocybin’s effects depend on prior stress
Using two-photon microscopy, a high-resolution imaging technique, the team tracked individual dendritic spines on living mouse brain cells over several weeks. These tiny protrusions act as receiving docks, collecting signals from neighboring neurons at junctions called synapses. Within 24 hours of administering psilocybin, the researchers observed a rapid increase in new spine formation.
In mice subjected to unpredictable mild stress, a model that mimics aspects of human depressive states, psilocybin produced a significantly larger surge in new spines than in healthy controls. It also halted the excessive loss of existing connections. In healthy mice, the growth spurt was temporary. As some connections that predated treatment were removed over three weeks, connectivity gradually returned toward baseline, preserving structural stability while the wiring changed.
An artistic illustration of the dual effects of psilocybin, the psychedelic compound derived from “magic mushrooms,” on a mouse’s brain. Psilocybin promotes the formation and maturation of dendritic spines, tiny protrusions from the dendritic branches that serve as neuronal connection sites, here portrayed as little mushrooms. At the same time, psilocybin induced the mouse’s head to twitch rapidly, a proxy of hallucinations in humans. Credit: Illustration by Emily Kogan, UC Santa Cruz
“These findings challenge the prevailing view that psilocybin simply increases neural connectivity and suggest that its effects depend on the brain’s underlying condition,” Zuo added. “This provides a new perspective on how psychedelics might help restore neural circuits disrupted by stress, with potentially important implications for understanding their therapeutic effects in depression and other psychiatric disorders.”
In untreated mice, newly formed spines typically had an immature “stubby” shape and were unstable and short-lived. Psilocybin accelerated their development, with a significantly higher proportion quickly growing into large “mushroom” shapes. These mature, stable structures have abundant neurotransmitter receptors, which receive chemical messages from other neurons and help sustain strong signals involved in memory and mood.
“Psychedelics are fascinating compounds because they have the potential to profoundly transform who we are by reshaping the neural circuits in our brains,” said lead author Jacob Baker, a Ph.D. student in Zuo’s lab. “These newly formed connections can integrate into existing neural circuitry and persist over time, leaving a lasting structural trace of psilocybin’s effects on the brain.”
Psychedelic therapies reach the FDA’s agenda
Psychedelic research has changed course several times over the past century. Natural psychedelics entered Western scientific study in the mid-20th century, and researchers identified active compounds such as psilocybin and LSD that profoundly altered consciousness and mood. Early clinical investigations suggested potential uses in psychiatric care, but research largely stalled after passage of the federal Controlled Substances Act in 1970.
Renewed interest now focuses on psychedelics as “psychoplastogens,” compounds capable of rapidly stimulating changes in neural structure and function after a single dose. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) previously granted Breakthrough Therapy designations for substances including psilocybin and MDMA.
Last month, the FDA hosted a
public hearing
“Considerations for Potential Future Therapeutic Use of Psychedelic Drugs.”
Experts addressed standardized frameworks for provider credentialing, protocols for Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS), and clinical-trial designs as regulators consider how psychedelic-assisted therapies might fit into healthcare.
Brain rewiring without a marker of hallucinations
One question could shape the development of those treatments, according to Baker: whether lasting changes in brain connectivity require the psychedelic experience itself.
To investigate the cellular pathways involved, the team focused on serotonin 2A receptors, also called 5-HT2ARs. These proteins sit on cell membranes and help mediate psilocybin’s effects. They are particularly abundant on Layer 5 pyramidal neurons, principal output cells in the cerebral cortex. Using specialized mouse lines, the researchers manipulated the receptors specifically in those neurons.
When serotonin 2A receptors were restored exclusively in Layer 5 pyramidal neurons, psilocybin triggered new synapse formation and structural stabilization. Yet the mice did not show the head-twitch response, a rodent movement widely used to assess hallucinogenic activity. The reverse experiment produced the opposite pattern. Selectively deleting the receptors from those neurons prevented structural synapse growth, while leaving the head-twitch response fully intact.
In these experiments, serotonin 2A signaling in Layer 5 pyramidal neurons was both necessary and sufficient for psilocybin’s structural effects, but was not required for the head-twitch behavior. Whether this separation could support effective treatments for depression, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), or other psychiatric conditions in people remains to be tested.
“By showing that therapeutic circuit remodeling and hallucinogenic effects operate through distinct cellular pathways, our study provides a promising blueprint for designing non-hallucinogenic drug analogs,” Zuo said. “Such therapeutics could deliver the fast and lasting antidepressant benefits of psychedelics while eliminating hallucinogenic side effects—making neuroplasticity treatments safer, more scalable, and accessible to a broader patient population.”
Reference: “5-HT2A receptors in layer 5 pyramidal neurons mediate the neuroplastic but not the hallucinogenic effects of psilocybin” by Jacob J. Baker, Emily Kogan, Shaorong Ma, Ju Lu and Yi Zuo, 15 October 2026,
Nature Neuroscience
DOI: 10.1038/s41593-026-02490-y

title: Something Strange Is Happening to Barn Owls: They’re Changing Color
content:
Barn owls are nocturnal birds of prey known for their distinctive heart-shaped faces, pale feathers, and nearly silent flight. Credit: Shutterstock
DNA from more than 3,000 barn owls reveals natural selection at work, but the advantage behind their changing feathers may involve coping with stress rather than color itself.
Swiss barn owls have become more reddish-brown and more heavily spotted over the past 30 years. By tracking the DNA variants linked to their plumage, researchers have found evidence of natural selection acting over about ten generations, offering a detailed view of evolution unfolding in the wild.
The study, published in
Nature Communications
, was led by Dr. Tristan Cumer, a research fellow in the Department of Ecology and Evolution at the University of Lausanne (Unil)’s Faculty of Biology and Medicine. Working in Professor Jérôme Goudet’s team, Cumer and his colleagues examined how genetic variants associated with color and spotting became more or less common over time. The challenge was to distinguish changes that could occur randomly from those shaped by natural selection.
“We compared the changes observed in the population with simulations in which evolution was entirely random. A genetic variant associated with reddish-brown plumage became far more common than chance alone could explain. Only simulations that included natural selection reproduced the changes we observed,” explains Cumer, the paper’s first author.
Redder feathers may be a byproduct
The analysis depended on both extensive genetic sequencing and records collected through decades of fieldwork.
“Drawing on the exceptional volume of data collected by Alexandre Roulin and his group, who have monitored these birds of prey in the field for decades, we were able to sequence the complete genomes of more than 3,000 owls and identify the DNA variants associated with color and spotting. This is one of the most in-depth genetic analyses ever conducted on a wild population,” says Goudet, the study’s last author, who is also affiliated with the SIB Swiss Institute of Bioinformatics.
Barn owls. Credit: Quentin Fort
The researchers identified genetic regions that play a major role in the birds’ appearance. These include MC1R, a gene already known to affect pigmentation, and a region on a sex chromosome whose contribution to both color and spotting they clarified. Identifying these links, however, does not establish which trait natural selection is favoring.
“We also do not know whether plumage color is itself the trait directly favored by natural selection,” says Goudet. “MC1R plays a role in pigmentation, but it is part of the melanocortin system, which has also been linked to other traits, including stress responses and aggression. Selection may therefore be acting on one of these traits, with the change in the owls’ appearance simply arising as a consequence.”
Food and stress could shape plumage
Barn owl plumage ranges from pure white to deep reddish-brown, with shades of golden brown in between. Some birds have only a few faint dark spots on their chests, while others carry many more prominent markings. Research at Unil has linked this variation to aspects of the birds’ lives beyond their appearance.
Plumage color is associated with fertility, hunting strategies, and diet. White barn owls, for example,
use moonlight to their advantage when attacking prey
, as described in an earlier Unil report in French. Spotting is associated with immunity and the ability to cope with stress. Birds with large black spots appear better able to withstand certain stressful conditions, including food shortages and parasites.
These connections offer possible explanations for the recent changes, although the ecological factors driving them remain unidentified. Roulin, a professor in Unil’s Department of Ecology and Evolution and a co-author of the study, suggests that shifts in food supplies or environmental stress could be involved.
“A change in prey availability may have favored reddish-brown barn owls, which eat more voles, whereas white owls tend to feed more on wood mice. The increase in spotting could be linked to greater environmental stress. Despite the striking differences in color between individuals, it remains extremely difficult to determine which ecological factors explain these variations.”
Evolution tracked across ten owl generations
The study’s evidence for natural selection is clearer than the explanation for what is driving it.
“Conducted in collaboration with the Swiss Ornithological Institute in Sempach, this study is one of the rare cases in which the genetic basis of recent evolution has been traced with such precision in the wild. This kind of demonstration is much harder in animals living in their natural environment than in a laboratory,” adds Goudet.
For almost a decade, Goudet and his team have been working to decode the barn owl genome and establish the species as a model for studying evolution in the wild. Their work includes sequencing and assembling its
reference genome
, a DNA sequence that serves as a guide for genetic research, and reconstructing its
evolutionary history across Europe and the Mediterranean
. They have also investigated
genetic recombination
, which reshuffles DNA from one generation to the next, and studied
how mutations arise
and are passed on within populations.
“Research on this scale is possible because field teams, genomics specialists, and members of the Faculty of Biology and Medicine’s core facilities work together,” says Professor Goudet.
The changes documented in the owls show that detectable genetic evolution need not take millions of years. Cumer sees potential implications for how wild species respond to changing conditions, while the pressures acting on these owls remain unresolved.
“The study carries an encouraging message: it shows that species living in the wild can evolve over a short period. This capacity for rapid adaptation could help them cope with environmental change, including climate change,” says Cumer.
The team now plans to use computer analysis of photographs to measure color and spotting more precisely. Researchers also intend to reconstruct the plumage color of birds that died very young using their genetic data, allowing them to investigate whether particular plumage features are associated with better chances of survival.
Reference: “Genomic bases of short-term evolution in wild barn owls revealed by long-term monitoring and population-scale sequencing” by Tristan Cumer, Alexandros Topaloudis, Eleonore Lavanchy, Anne-Lyse Ducrest, Sonia Sarmiento Cabello, Anna Hewett, Paolo Becciu, Céline Simon, Julien Marquis, Aline Charpagne, Bettina Almasi, Alexandre Roulin and Jérôme Goudet, 12 October 2026,
Nature Communications

title: The Future of Electromagnetic Shields Could Be Lighter, Stronger, and Greener
content:
The review explores preparation methods, toughening mechanisms, and 1D, 2D, and 3D structural designs of MXene/nanocellulose composites, highlighting their excellent mechanical strength and electromagnetic shielding performance. Credit: Nano Research, Tsinghua University Press
Researchers are exploring a new generation of electromagnetic shielding materials that combine exceptional conductivity with improved strength and flexibility.
Electromagnetic shielding materials must block unwanted signals without adding excessive weight or sacrificing durability. Conventional options, including metals, conductive polymers, and carbon-based materials, can be heavy, inflexible, or expensive. Researchers are now exploring composites that combine exceptional electrical conductivity with the strength and flexibility needed for practical applications.
One promising approach pairs two-dimensional transition metal carbides and nitrides (MXenes) with nanocellulose, a lightweight material derived from natural biomass. MXenes offer excellent conductivity and chemical stability, but films made from them alone tend to be brittle. Adding nanocellulose can improve mechanical strength while preserving the electrical properties needed to shield electronics from electromagnetic interference.
How Material Structure Changes Electromagnetic Shielding
A research team led by Prof. Ming-Guo Ma of Beijing Forestry University in China has published a comprehensive review of MXene/nanocellulose composites, examining how their structure, fabrication methods, and strengthening mechanisms influence performance.
The researchers identified important differences between one-dimensional fibers, two-dimensional layered films, and three-dimensional networks. Dense films primarily block electromagnetic waves through reflection, while porous aerogels favor absorption by allowing waves to penetrate interconnected structures and interact with conductive surfaces. Hydrogels can provide a more balanced combination of reflection and absorption. Layered designs, including sandwich, Janus, and structures inspired by nature, offer additional ways to control shielding behavior.
Building Stronger, More Flexible Materials
Improving durability requires more than simply combining MXene sheets with cellulose fibers. The review examines several strengthening approaches, including physical interactions such as hydrogen bonding, fiber entanglement, and metal-ion crosslinking. Chemical techniques introduce stronger covalent bonds using agents such as polydopamine or PMDI.
Combining reversible physical bonds with permanent chemical networks can produce materials with greater strength, toughness, and stability. The researchers also compared manufacturing techniques, ranging from solution mixing and vacuum filtration to 3D printing, freeze-drying, electrospinning, and layer-by-layer assembly. Each method presents different trade-offs between mechanical properties, shielding effectiveness, and manufacturing complexity.
What Must Improve Before Widespread Use?
Despite encouraging laboratory results, several obstacles remain. MXene production needs more environmentally friendly synthesis methods, and composite materials must maintain their performance under prolonged exposure to humidity and high temperatures. Scaling manufacturing processes while retaining consistent mechanical and electrical properties also presents challenges.
Future research may expand shielding capabilities across a broader frequency range, from gigahertz to terahertz, while incorporating magnetic or temperature-responsive components. Such advances could support smart shielding materials that adjust their electromagnetic behavior in response to changing conditions.
“This review provides a holistic perspective that connects fabrication methods, toughening mechanisms, and structural architectures,” said Prof. Ming-Guo Ma, the corresponding author. “It will greatly advance the rational design and practical application of high-performance MXene/nanocellulose electromagnetic shielding composites.”
Reference: “Flexible multifunctional MXene/nanocellulose nanocomposites for mechanical and electromagnetic shielding performance” by Qi Liu, Jia-Qi Lang, Lei Chen, Chuanyin Xiong, Xiufu Hua and Ming-Guo Ma, 30 August 2026,
Nano Research
DOI: 10.26599/NR.2026.94908889
This work was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (22478036).

title: Why Are Octopuses So Smart? The Answer May Lie in How Their DNA Folds
content:
Octopuses, squid, and cuttlefish are among the most intelligent invertebrates, possessing remarkably sophisticated nervous systems. Octopuses can solve puzzles, navigate mazes, and manipulate objects, while cuttlefish demonstrate impressive learning and memory abilities. Credit: Shutterstock
The extraordinary intelligence of octopuses, squid, and cuttlefish may be linked to more than just their genes.
Octopuses can solve problems, squid can rapidly change their appearance, and cuttlefish display remarkably sophisticated behaviors. These abilities rely on unusually complex nervous systems, but how such biological complexity evolved remains an open question. A new study suggests that part of the answer may lie in the three-dimensional structure of DNA rather than in genes alone.
Scientists at the
University of Vienna
discovered evidence that extensive genome rearrangements hundreds of millions of years ago changed how different regions of DNA interact in cephalopods. Published in
Nature Communications
, the study suggests that these ancient changes may have helped establish new patterns of gene regulation, potentially contributing to the evolution of their elaborate nervous systems.
How Ancient Genome Changes Reshaped Gene Regulation
DNA is not arranged as a straight strand inside the cell nucleus. Instead, it folds into a complex three-dimensional structure that brings distant genetic regions close together. This positioning influences which regulatory elements can interact with genes and control their activity.
Californian two-spot octopus (Octopus bimaculoides). Embryo at the final stage before hatching. The species is named after the two prominent blue eyespots that can help deter predators. Credit: Natalie Grace Schulz
“The genome isn’t just a sequence of genes. It’s folded into a complex three-dimensional structure,” said lead author Dr. Thea Rogers. “Understanding how that structure evolves is becoming increasingly important for understanding how new forms of biological complexity arise.”
Why Some Parts of the Genome Change More Than Others
The study also found that different levels of genome organization have evolved at strikingly different rates. Large structural regions called chromatin domains remained relatively stable over evolutionary time, even as other features of the genome changed substantially.
Smaller structures known as chromatin loops showed much greater variation across species, tissues, and developmental stages. These loops bring distant sections of DNA into physical proximity, allowing regulatory elements to influence genes that may be far away along the DNA sequence. Many occurred near genes associated with distinctive cephalopod characteristics, including those linked to the nervous system.
The researchers propose that regulatory entanglement may allow genomes to develop new patterns of gene expression while preserving essential biological functions. Stable chromatin domains could help maintain existing regulatory organization, while more flexible loops provide opportunities for evolutionary changes.
The findings suggest that the physical arrangement of DNA may actively influence evolutionary processes rather than simply reflect changes that have already occurred.
Reference: “Genome reorganisation and expansion shape 3D genome architecture and define a distinct regulatory landscape in coleoid cephalopods” by Thea F. Rogers, Jessica Stock, Natalie Grace Schulz, Gözde Yalçin, Simone Rencken, Anton Weissenbacher, Tereza Clarence, Darrin T. Schultz, Clifton W. Ragsdale, Caroline B. Albertin and Oleg Simakov, 9 October 2026,
Nature Communications

title: At Peak Energy, the Focus is on Avoiding the Missteps of a Big Battery Industry Failure
content: General Motors–backed startup Peak Energy boasts that it’s on a pathway to undercut China’s dominance of the massive batteries that power AI data centers and the grid. Its approach involves deploying an entirely different chemistry from the lithium-based ones China controls. But success, Peak executives say, requires always keeping a dreaded word in mind: Northvolt. In one of modern history’s worst business failures, Swedish battery maker Northvolt went bankrupt last year after squandering some $13 billion in equity and debt its founders had raised with the goal of building a European battery behemoth. The collapse made Northvolt a cautionary tale in the battery industry. The company seemed to have the wind at its back: It had $55 billion in orders and the support of Volkswagen and BMW, in addition to the EU. Yet it never managed to reach commercial production. Northvolt’s failure is a particularly top-of-mind lesson for Peak Energy co-founder and CEO Landon Mossburg, former president of Northvolt’s North America arm and a former Tesla executive. Mossburg co-founded Peak in 2023 to build sodium-ion stationary storage batteries that would leapfrog the lithium-based ones currently dominating backup power for AI data centers, the grid and other industrial deployments. Last week, Peak announced that it had raised a $108 million Series B round, led by GM, to fund the build-out of the first stage of a 4-gigawatt-hour sodium-ion battery assembly plant in Sacramento, Calif., enough to power roughly 2.8 million homes for an hour. GM previously said its investment in Peak was approximately $30 million. The Sacramento plant plans to fulfill $1.1 billion in orders starting in the first quarter of next year. Eventually, Mossburg wants Peak, in a partnership with GM, to make multiple components of the battery, including the cathodes and cells as well as the raw powders that go into making them. Tesla has successfully begun manufacturing cathodes, along with battery cells, showing that it’s possible to carry out what Peak has in mind. But in a conversation this week, Mossburg seemed a lot less focused on that and far more mindful of Northvolt’s fatal missteps. Chief among those, in his view, was its attempt to do too much at once, which resulted in mastering little . “The contrast is very stark for me,” Mossburg told me, “because I went from Tesla to Northvolt. And one clearly worked, and the other one clearly didn’t.” Peak is hardly alone in its fixation. Since its collapse, Northvolt has become an industry byword for everything that could possibly go wrong in producing batteries. In 2017, two former Tesla executives, Peter Carlsson and Paolo Cerruti, launched Northvolt. They rapidly raised $13 billion for what they sold as a European battery champion that would compete on equal ground with industry giants, including Chinese behemoth Contemporary Amperex Technology Ltd. Carlsson and Cerruti began splashing around the cash, launching divisions to refine lithium, make cathodes, build complete cells and recycle them—all functions usually carried out by stand-alone companies. They also set out to build plants not only at home in Sweden but also in Germany, Poland, Norway and Canada. They acquired Cuberg, a California startup that was developing next-generation aviation batteries. By 2024, however, Northvolt was still unable to reliably make battery cells at its flagship Swedish plant, as I reported at the time . Northvolt’s “first cathode plant didn’t work pretty much at all,” Mossburg said. In summer 2025, Lyten—a relatively tiny San Jose, Calif., startup— scooped up most of Northvolt’s assets for pennies on the dollar. Mossburg said he is intent on avoiding these blunders. His business thesis is that sodium—1,000 times more prevalent in the Earth’s crust than lithium—will be cheaper than lithium once manufacturers scale up processing it. And if that processing occurs outside China, sodium would also reduce lithium’s geopolitical risks for the U.S. That’s if everything goes well. To avoid what happened to Northvolt, he said, Peak will do things one at a time. First, it will assemble batteries in Sacramento. Later, it will manufacture the sodium-ion cells it is currently developing alongside GM. Mossburg also intends to make cathodes. “We have told everybody who’s asked us to help catalyze the sodium-ion supply chain, which we’re very interested in doing, [that the] way to do it is sequentially and do it very, very fast sequentially. Don’t do it in parallel,” Mossburg said. Where things can go wrong for battery makers like Peak is when they try to do everything at the same time, he said. Invariably, hiccups arise in the development or supply of one component or more. “You have a whole supply chain that needs to run together, and it’s the first time all of these factories are going to come online,” he said. “They all have to come online at the exact same time, just like a concert. If anything’s delayed, the whole thing is delayed. And you’re going to have some stuff delayed, especially as you get into active material production. “Building three businesses at once like Northvolt did is pretty tough,” Mossburg said. “And you don’t have to, because you can do it just as fast. You just do it sequentially.”

title: CBS’ Bari Weiss Tells Critics to ‘Judge Us by the Journalism’
content: CBS News editor-in-chief Bari Weiss said critics of her leadership of the network should “judge us by the journalism” in a wide-ranging interview with Jessica Lessin of The Information Wednesday. Speaking at The Information’s WTF Summit , a gathering of senior women in the technology and finance industries, Weiss acknowledged the “unusual” and “exceptionally loud year” she’s had. Weiss has grabbed headlines for months over her efforts to reshape CBS News, including venerable programs like “60 Minutes.” “Change is hard,” she said. What has gotten much less attention about her efforts at CBS, she said, is that the majority of producers, journalists and correspondents at CBS “have shifted to a much more entrepreneurial mentality and culture.” Among the examples she cited were live events hosted by veteran correspondent Norah O’Donnell, the launch of Tony Dokoupil’s new podcast “Great Question” and coverage of the war in Ukraine by CBS correspondent Aidan Stretch. Weiss mentioned she’s also trying to get Elizabeth Holmes, the convicted founder of now-defunct blood-testing firm Theranos, to appear on CBS, floating the possibility of Holmes appearing live on the network’s free streaming app. Holmes was the subject of a lauded documentary by comedian and filmmaker Nathan Fielder released this month. Weiss vaulted into the spotlight last year when Skydance, the owner of CBS formerly known as Paramount Skydance, bought her publication The Free Press for more than $100 million and promoted Weiss to the top role at the broadcast network’s news division. A journalist and columnist known for attacking left-leaning bias in the media, Weiss has had to juggle the challenges of leading a legacy news organization suffering from ratings declines, an aging audience and broader shifts in media consumption away from television. At the same time, her critics have alleged that Weiss has injected her own political views into the network’s news coverage. Most recently, her editorial leadership came under scrutiny when Status’ Oliver Darcy reported that a CBS editor pushed back on including the number of Palestinians killed by Israel in a report on the anniversary of the October 7 Hamas attacks on Israel. CBS reported the Gaza death toll in a morning story about the Hamas attack, but not in its evening news report. Weiss, who noted that CBS has about 1,200 people in the newsroom, said she wasn’t involved in editing the stories. She likened the issue of including the Gaza death toll to how a news organization might cover the anniversary of the September 2001 al Qaeda terrorist attack on New York. She said it was “a question of taste” to focus on the victims of the Hamas attacks rather than the Palestinian victims of Israel’s bombings that followed. “You can make a legitimate argument on either side of that. It seemed like in the morning we went with one perspective. In the evening, we went with another,” Weiss said. “I don’t think there’s anything scandalous or controversial about that.” Weiss defended the network’s approach to covering national and world events, arguing that it is guided by a desire to ensure “the information that people are getting is accurate and fair, and again, reflects reality.” She pointed to Lesley Stahl’s investigative report on Israeli settler violence in the West Bank this month and the way correspondent Matt Gutman has covered the Israeli election. “The myth that anyone has a view from nowhere and is a perfectly blank slate, has been exploded by social media,” she said. “The question is whether or not you can strive to get outside of your own perspective to understand what your blind spots are and to make sure that the product, the information that people are getting, is accurate and fair.” Weiss indicated that CBS could test subscriptions after focusing on making content viewers would want to pay for. CBS doesn’t have such paywalls now, though its content is available on the subscription based Paramount+ streaming app. “I’m a total believer” in subscription-based pricing, Weiss said. “And so, obviously, that’s the future.” ‘Civilizational Role’ There’s been wide speculation that Skydance CEO David Ellison could seek to consolidate CBS and CNN following the completion of Skydance’s buyout this month of Warner Bros. Discovery, which owns CNN. That cable news network has around 3,000 employees worldwide, while CBS has far fewer staffers. Weiss didn’t address whether layoffs at the combined company’s news operations are on the table. She acknowledged misgivings over the topic among staffers, saying “everyone feels anxiety whether or not their company has just merged with another giant company as ours had.” Still, she spoke favorably about CNN’s potential. “The possibilities here are really, really incredible,” she said. “CNN is an unbelievable organization.” Asked whether she would want to run CNN, Weiss said: “I want to focus on doing CBS News, trust me. This is a big enough challenge.” CNN CEO Mark Thompson was previously the chief executive of The New York Times when Weiss was an opinion columnist and made a fiery exit, claiming that the newspaper’s staff was hostile to other political points of view. Weiss said she and Thompson recently laughed about the episode during a plane ride. Asked about declining ratings and her overhaul of CBS’ flagship show, “60 Minutes”—the network’s management has fired several prominent staffers, including longtime correspondent Scott Pelley, roiling the team—Weiss defended the changes she’s made to the show, which she said is doing “tremendously well.” “I am focused on transforming the business,” she said. In response to a question about the decline in ratings at “60 Minutes,” she said: “I could never build anything if I were focused on the precise number of people that happen to tune in to the second feature on 60 Minutes on a given Sunday.” Weiss dismissed the idea that Trump has been particularly sympathetic to CBS and Ellison, noting the U.S. president has called her a “gay dictator.” (Weiss is married to the journalist and The Free Press co-founder Nellie Bowles.) Weiss noted that the Trump administration has been a loud critic on social media of CBS’ work, including journalist Gianna Toboni’s reporting on the U.S. government’s deportations of immigrants to countries that aren’t their country of origin. Weiss said her “only way to function” as the leader of CBS is to “put the blinders on, tune out the noise and focus,” when discussing what it is like to be in the media spotlight. Otherwise her “entire life” would be devoted to being “a reply guy on the internet,” she said. She said of her new role, “I’m not doing anything I’m doing for popularity’s sake.” “Journalism and journalists have a civilizational role to play,” she said. “And that’s my focus.”

title: Encryption Under Siege? OpenAI, Anthropic Disprove Key Cryptography Theorem
content: Cryptographers who develop encryption technologies may not be sleeping very well these days. OpenAI and Anthropic both said Monday that their internal AI models had disproven the Exponential Time Hypothesis , a longstanding computer science theorem that predicts the minimum difficulty of solving a certain category of problems. Cryptographers had long assumed the hypothesis was true, and built other findings on the basis of that assumption. Disproving the Exponential Time Hypothesis won’t endanger any current encryption methods, said Matthew Green , professor of computer science at Johns Hopkins University and founder of encryption startup Zeutro . But the finding is a big theoretical step, showing that some problems are easier to solve than cryptographers had thought. That means cryptographers could also be wrong about other assumptions underlying core encryption methods such as elliptic curve encryption , a method underlying the majority of internet traffic, which would create a scramble to find new ways to keep information on the internet secure. “Our intuition about what‘s hard is very human, and what human beings think is hard doesn’t matter anymore,” Green said. OpenAI and Anthropic have contacted outside experts to review their results on the Exponential Time Hypothesis. The experts include academics working on complexity theory, a field of research that measures the complexity of certain math or science problems, and thus how difficult they are to solve. Ryan Williams , a professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology who is one of the outside experts reviewing OpenAI’s research, said the company told him it “didn’t necessarily find anything” that would impact existing encryption systems. But OpenAI’s Exponential Time Hypothesis result is “the kind of finding that would make one wonder about those things,” he said. The fact that a spokesperson for OpenAI did not have a comment to us about whether it’s tried to use its models to solve practical cryptography problems won’t make such researchers wonder any less! Yael Kalai , a professor of electrical engineering and computer science at MIT , said it was possible the finding could prompt the National Institute of Standards and Technology , a U.S. agency governing innovation and tech, to increase its recommended security strength for encryption. That would increase the costs of memory and computation needed for any organization that uses encryption processes, Kalai said. If OpenAI or Anthropic do end up finding flaws in existing encryption algorithms, we would imagine they would probably inform the National Security Agency first, long before disclosing it publicly. In other news… Harvey Acquires AI Sales Startup Aida Legal AI startup Harvey has acquired Aida , which develops AI assistants for sales reps to help them catch deals that may be falling through the cracks, the company told The Information exclusively. The deal, whose terms weren’t disclosed, marks Harvey’s fifth acquisition this year, following its most recent acquisitions of AI security startup Guardrails AI in September and Benchmark , which develops AI for investment firms, in July. With Aida’s tech, Harvey hopes to help its customers better organize their proprietary data, so its legal tools can make use of that data, which may be siloed in different organizations right now. Aida’s leaders have experience in this field, otherwise known as AI for enterprise search; its CEO, Piyush Prahladka , for example, was a cofounder at AI search startup Glean . It’s a sign of how AI application startups are hoping to differentiate themselves from model developers that are also releasing vertical-specific products by leveraging hard-to-access data from their customers.— Stephanie Palazzolo Moonshot’s Influencer Backlash Moonshot AI’s release of a new model last week was supposed to be a much-needed breakout moment for a Chinese firm aiming to go public soon. Instead, it was quickly overshadowed by allegations that the company asked influencers to promote the model without disclosing that it was paying them. Moonshot unveiled Kimi K3.1 Pro last Friday as an upgrade to its popular predecessor, Kimi K3 . Hours later, an X user with the account name of Elshayib , a software developer in Jordan who often comments on AI products, said he had boycotted Moonshot’s paid campaign for the new model because the company told him and other influencers not to label their posts as a paid sponsorship. Elshayib argued that doing so would violate X’s terms of service. Elshayib had the receipts: he posted screenshots that he said showed Moonshot’s instructions for influencers participating in the campaign. The instructions in his screenshots suggested that influencers had to use certain talking points , such as “Kimi K3.1 is literally Opus 5.5 open-source, but 5x cheaper” or “China just made Opus 5.5 free to use for everyone,” referring to Anthropic’s flagship Opus 5.5 closed-source model. Some of the recommended talking points put K3.1 Pro in the context of the U.S.-China tech rivalry. One of them said: “The U.S. cut China off from advanced chips, Kimi trained new [state of the art] model without the compute American labs take for granted.” Moonshot hasn’t addressed the allegations publicly, and a Moonshot spokesperson declined to comment. The PR crisis is the last thing the company, valued at $50 billion in a recent private funding round, needs as it moves toward a public listing in Hong Kong. The exact timeframe for its IPO is unclear, and the market sentiment for publicly traded Chinese AI firms, such as MiniMax and Z.ai , has soured in recent months. The controversy comes as closed-source developers such as Anthropic and OpenAI appear to have maintained their lead against open-source rivals when it comes to capabilities, despite recent rumblings that the gap was closing.— Juro Osawa Government Checks In on Anthropic’s Evaluators The White House has checked in with Anthropic about the company’s work with embedded evaluators, Anthropic head of public policy Sarah Heck said at The Information’s Women in Tech and Finance summit on Wednesday. Current evaluators include employees from AI research nonprofit METR and consulting company Accenture , who work inside the company with “employee-like” access to assess safety risks and practices. “We‘re frankly only a couple weeks into it, and I think we’re all learning,” Heck said at the conference. “I‘ve had many conversations with folks in the administration that want to know how it’s going. They want to know what they're seeing.” Here’s what else is going on… Overheard Areas of weakness are emerging within the broader AI market as the cost of capital is set to continue rising, Kim Posnett , Goldman Sachs ’ global co-head of investment banking, said at The Information’s WTF Summit on Tuesday. Posnett noted that while she’s “hugely bullish” on AI overall, investors are growing more discerning. Anthropic ’s highly anticipated megalisting has been looming over the broader initial public offering market, holding back other companies gearing up for debuts, Lynn Martin , president of the New York Stock Exchange Group , said at The Information’s WTF Summit on Wednesday. Earnings Report Oracle shares rose more than 10% Wednesday after the company sketched out a timeline for when it would begin to slow its capital spending for data centers and start generating cash again. Microsoft revenue rose 19% to $92.3 billion in the September quarter, 1 percentage point faster than the growth it reported in the second quarter. Accelerating sales in its Azure cloud unit, driven in part by server rental revenue from OpenAI, offset the slight revenue decreases in its Xbox and devices units. Google’s cloud sales surged in the latest quarter but overall revenue at parent Alphabet grew a slower-than-expected 25% to $127.6 billion, disappointing investors. ServiceNow shares dropped 19% after its third-quarter earnings. ServiceNow says adoption of its AI products is continuing to grow, but investors seem to remain wary of the potential threat AI could pose to its business. Here’s what else is going on… Deals and Debuts See The Information’s Generative AI Database for an exclusive list of private companies and their investors. Chipmaker Marvell Technologies has been in talks to buy data center optics maker Lumentum , The Information and others reported. A deal for Lumentum would rank as one of the largest semiconductor deals, as Lumentum has a market capitalization of more than $80 billion. The status of the deal couldn’t be learned, but Bloomberg reported that a transaction could be announced as soon as next week. Cognition , the AI coding startup behind Devin , is weighing a new funding round before year's end after receiving offers valuing it at $70 billion to $80 billion — up sharply from the $48 billion valuation it announced just weeks earlier, Business Insider reported. FuriosaAI , a South Korean company that designs AI chips for data-center inference, raised $620 million (KRW 820 billion) in a Series D funding round at a $2.9 billion valuation led by South Korea's National Growth Fund. Upwind Security , which provides security around cloud infrastructure and AI agents, raised $400 million in a Series C funding round at a $3.8 billion valuation led by Bessemer Venture Partners. BioGeometry , a Beijing-based AI-native biopharmaceutical company, raised more than $100 million across its Series A financing rounds, led by China Life Capital . Lumaril , which develops AI software for optimizing industrial production, raised $66 million in Series A funding led by Elad Gil . Casap , an AI agent platform for financial services, raised $56 million in a Series B funding round led by Base10 Partners. Fragment , which builds autonomous AI agents for purchasing and payment services, launched with $56 million in total funding: a Series A led by 8VC and an earlier seed round led by General Catalyst and A *. Broccoli AI , which sells AI agents that answer calls and book jobs for plumbing, HVAC and electrical contractors, disclosed $52 million in combined funding: a previously unannounced $22 million Series A and a new $30 million Series B, both led by Khosla Ventures. Easol , an AI platform for businesses like festivals and wellness retreats, raised $30 million in a Series A extension funding round with investors including Y Combinator . Circuit Mind , which uses agentic AI to design circuit boards, raised $25 million in new funding: an $18.5 million Series A led by Norwest and a previously unannounced seed round led by Third Prime. Plato , which builds simulated workplaces where AI models can practice real jobs, raised $16 million in a Series A funding round led by Nava Ventures. Sava , which builds agentic software infrastructure for the US trust and estate industry, raised $10 million in funding led by Gradient Ventures. AvalonX , an AI-powered security startup, emerged from 18 months in stealth with up to $10 million in funding from Ridown Capital . Google unveiled Gemini 4 Carbon , which it said is significantly more capable than the model it released less than a month ago, as the company steps up efforts to contend with the leading frontier labs. Shopify said it has added agentic payment technology created by Visa , Mastercard and American Express for its checkout feature, Shop Pay , a move that runs counter to how Stripe mainly handles agentic shopping and credit cards. Amazon has significantly expanded its Shop Direct program to list more than 250 million products from rivals, up from around 100 million in March, as rival AI agents make it easier to buy across retailers. title: Everyone’s Using AI But Divisions Are Growing:  WTF Highlights
content: Artificial intelligence has thoroughly infiltrated business and politics, but it’s also starting to divide companies and investors. That was the takeaway from leaders at The Information’s WTF Summit, a gathering of senior women in the technology and finance industries this week. Investors are increasingly picking AI winners and losers, and favoring companies that can train models and control the chips and data centers that undergird them, said Goldman Sachs’ global co-head of investment banking Kim Posnett . “What you’re seeing is not a change in AI sentiment,” she said, but “you’re seeing a repositioning and differentiation across the AI trade.” Meanwhile, the largest tech companies are starting to square off over essential policies that govern the progress of the technology, such as chip export control. Amanda Peterson Corio, Google’s global head of data center energy, warned that fast-moving cloud upstarts are prompting the need for new industry-wide standards and regulation around data centers’ use of resources. Leaders from these companies as well as NYSE Group, Goldman Sachs spoke at the conference, alongside CBS News Editor In Chief Bari Weiss and Bumble’s co-founder Whitney Wolfe Herd . Anthropic Policy Chief Hopeful ‘Compromise’ on Chip Export Controls Will Pass Anthropic Head of Public Affairs Sarah Heck said the chip export controls the AI lab has been lobbying to include in the U.S. government’s annual defense bill are the best chance to pass such controls before year end, though she emphasized that the legislation passing is “not assured.” The maker of Claude Code has advocated for stronger chip export controls, warning that without them, governments like China could use American technology to “cement authoritarianism .” Heck said Anthropic has been working with Republicans, Democrats and the White House to “get language that people feel they can live with” in the National Defense Authorization Act. Congress is still debating whether to include three bills that would curb the sale of chips and chipmaking equipment to China. Anthropic Head of Public Affairs Sarah Heck. Photo by Erin Beach. These bills have also divided the tech industry. In September, Anthropic quit a major tech trade group after the organization, which includes Nvidia and OpenAI as members, urged lawmakers not to include the chip export control bills in the NDAA. The group argued that some of the measures could slow the progress of American AI companies and turn some customers toward China because of the country’s relative lack of regulation. “This is an area where there has been a bit of compromise,” Heck added of the bill. “But if something gets passed, it will be the NDAA.” Heck was dismissive of the argument that China would be able to catch up or pass America’s AI lead without using American chips. “If you believe China is somewhere between six and 12 months behind us, they’re not going to be able to build chips fast enough to close that gap,” she said. Heck acknowledged that Anthropic and other U.S. AI companies may need to work with China on AI safety in the future, but said that could be possible even with chip exporting restrictions. “I think we can do both. I think we can walk and chew gum at the same time,” she said. — Jemima McEvoy AI is Accelerating Trading, NYSE President Says New York Stock Exchange President Lynn Martin. Photo by Erin Beach. AI is the latest technology to change the nature of trading itself, New York Stock Exchange President Lynn Martin said. It’s a far cry from when Martin started her career in financial services, when a trader’s physical stature influenced their effectiveness on the trading floor, she recalled. “A guy who was six foot eight could yell a lot louder over a woman who is five four. That actually mattered,” Martin said. That advantage shrank with the rise of electronic trading, which also made markets more liquid and more efficient. She said AI is accelerating that process. NYSE processes 1.2 trillion to 1.3 trillion incoming order messages every single day, according to Martin. She predicts AI will significantly increase the volume of inbound messages the exchange has to process. While technology can help manage that volume, Martin argued the increase will make the role of human intervention more important. “If the model is trading with [other] models, that’s not a good scenario, or if there’s a bug in the model’s code” and the model itself doesn’t have the judgment or discretion to react appropriately, “that’s not good for markets,” Martin said. “Having that human interacting with the AI is, in my mind, the optimal market.” Martin also noted Anthropic’s highly anticipated megalisting has been looming over the broader initial public offering market, holding back other companies gearing up for debuts.— Anita Ramaswamy Google Data Center Power Head: ‘I Live in 2031’ Amanda Peterson Corio. Photo by Erin Beach. The timeline for AI server chip production is much shorter than the time it takes to build out enough power to run AI data centers, said Amanda Peterson Corio, Google’s Global Head of Data Center Energy. That means Corio is thinking today about data centers that get built and switched on in 2031 or later. It takes five to ten years to build out new power on the grid, but Google churns out new versions of tensor processing units—the company’s AI chips—about once a year. “That inherently doesn’t work with a seven-year build out of power,” Corio said. To solve that mismatch and prevent a potential chip glut, Corio foresees a rise in power sources like gas generators or clean energy sources built directly on or near data center sites and bigger upfront capital commitments to fund the buildout of new grid and transmission infrastructure. Corio said she just returned from a trip to India to explore pumped hydropower solutions. Local community concerns are also a major factor in whether a data center is built and powered on time. Corio pushed back against broader concerns that data centers use too much water, don’t create enough jobs or pay enough in taxes. She also said that some newer entrants into the space are rushing to build data centers and don’t have the same “history or sophistication” as Google, making industry-wide regulation critically important. “We’re very supportive of that for the industry,” she said. — Phoebe Liu Goldman Sachs Investment Banking Co-Head Sees ‘Repositioning’ Amid AI Boom Goldman Sachs’ Kim Posnett. Photo by Erin Beach. Areas of weakness are emerging within the broader AI market as the cost of capital is set to continue rising, said Kim Posnett, Goldman Sachs’ global co-head of investment banking. Posnett said that while she’s “hugely bullish” on AI overall, investors are growing more discerning. Posnett noted that AI projects won’t drive expected returns should rates stay elevated for a long period. “While AI itself is not a bubble, I think you can have bubbles within that,” she said. Investors are starting to favor vertically integrated companies that produce frontier models, business applications and AI chips, Posnett added. Goldman is playing leading roles in major deals announced this week for some of the biggest AI companies, including SpaceX’s GPU financing , Meta’s stock offering and Anthropic’s planned initial public offering. Asked about circular financing across the AI ecosystem, Posnett said she’s thinking “more about demand” but acknowledged the risk in tech giants like Nvidia funding their own suppliers and customers. “It makes sense that they want to build closer partnerships with each other,” she said. “And I think it creates greater risk. I think both are true.”— Laura Bratton Flock Co-Founder: ‘Not Our Call’ if Police Share Footage With ICE Flock Safety co-founder and chief people officer Paige Todd said the “most challenging” part of running the startup has been navigating an early decision to not restrict law enforcement’s legal use of its technology. “I have a lot of personal beliefs on a lot of legislation out there, as does everyone. We decided it was not our call to actually decide how laws would be implemented with our technology,” said Todd. “If it is legal in a market to work with [U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement], then that is their decision.” Founded nine years ago, venture-backed Flock makes license plate recognition technology designed to help local officials enforce traffic laws and find criminals. As President Donald Trump sent more federal agents across the country to crack down on illegal immigration, some residents warned the cameras were aiding forced deportations. The company does not have a contract with ICE, said Todd, though “local law enforcement may choose to share their footage with Immigration.” “It’s not our call, because at the end of the day, we actually don’t own the footage ourselves,” she said. Todd added that, despite protests against Flock cameras, the company internally has “actually been pretty calm.” The company offered voluntary buyouts to its U.S.-based employees in September because “people were sitting at the dinner table with their family or going out with their friends on a weekend, and people were like, ‘I cannot believe you work there,’” Todd said. “And after a while, no matter how much they believe in what we’re doing, it just hurt.” — Julia Hornstein Arm, Nscale Executives: There is No Chip Glut Arm’s Ami Badani and Nscale’s Nidhi Chappell. Photo by Erin Beach. Some data center developers, market analysts and investors have become increasingly worried about a future glut of specialized AI server chips that don’t have a functional data center to plug into, due to delays in obtaining power, political pushback and technical issues. Ami Badani, chief marketing officer of semiconductor firm Arm, said she is not aware of any Arm-based chips currently sitting idle in warehouses due to a lack of power. Nidhi Chappell, president of AI infrastructure at data center and cloud company Nscale, said Nscale was also monitoring its supply chain to prevent such power and chip mismatches. In recent months, fears that a shortage of data centers connected to power could lead to chip deliveries going unused has prompted Nvidia to obsessively track power supply . Badani also said Arm was seeing more customer interest than ever in designing custom chips, called ASICs. Arm has helped design chips for Nvidia, Apple and all of the largest cloud computing providers. Designing your own chip can have higher up-front cost, but it can afford companies more control, according to Badani. Shifts in how consumers are using AI are also driving changes to chip demand, Chappell and Badani said. One trend is tighter integration between the different hardware components within a datacenter, which can include different types of chips specialized to different purposes, in order to make the best use of all components. Chips are also getting more specialized for specific types of work, such as training or running AI, Chappell said.  — Tiffany Li 23andMe’s Wojcicki: AI Can Find Medical Insights Anne Wojcicki. Photo by Erin Beach. Anne Wojcicki, who heads the 23andMe Research Institute, said she believes AI will help find new medical insights and concrete actions people can take to improve their health by mining the nonprofit’s huge DNA database. “It is the power of scale,” she said. Wojcicki recounted her personal journey co-founding 23andMe, which became a pioneer in the direct-to-consumer DNA testing market but never came up with a sustainable business model. The company ended up filing for bankruptcy in 2025. Wojcicki spent more than $300 million of her own money to buy the company back last year and turned it into a nonprofit research institute. At the summit, Wojcicki cited a recent scientific collaboration that demonstrated the potential for making new discoveries from the 23andMe database, which includes DNA from more than 3.3 million people who have agreed to participate in research. She said that researchers from Dana-Farber Cancer Institute in Boston and the 23andMe Research Institute identified a rare genetic mutation that puts people at exceptionally high risk of getting lung cancer. People who have never smoked but have the gene mutation are 60 times more likely to get lung cancer as people without the faulty gene. Wojcicki’s sister, Susan, the former CEO of YouTube, died in 2024 from lung cancer. “I care a lot about this cause,” Wojcicki said. Wojcicki said she met the Dana-Farber researchers at a scientific conference. They told her they were studying the gene mutation but only had 20 people and how difficult it was to find more patients. “Oh, I have 500 of these people with that genetic variant,” she told them. She said 23andMe can now contact the people and suggest they do screening to make sure they do not have cancer. “I can save these lives,” Wojcicki said. The 23andMe Research Institute is working on a new feature called the Health Summary that can use AI to find connections between people’s DNA and all the other health data they share to make health recommendations. “The more information we get,” she said, “we can give you insights.” — Amy Dockser Marcus
