title: The Jobs That Actually Exist Inside Data Centers
content:
On the whole, data centers do not create large numbers of
permanent jobs
once construction is complete. But limited staffing is not the same as no staffing. To understand data centers’ true impact on employment, it is necessary to look at the roles they do create, the skills those positions require, and who typically fills them.
With that in mind, here is a look at the jobs in a typical data center, focusing on roles that require in-person, on-site work. Data centers may also support a wider range of software development and IT jobs tied to the workloads they host, but those roles are rarely based inside the facilities where the hardware physically resides.
Data Center Technicians: The Core of On-Site Operations
Data center technician
” is a broad term for workers responsible for installing, maintaining, and troubleshooting IT equipment and supporting infrastructure inside a facility. Depending on the operator, technicians may rack and stack servers, run and label cables, replace failed hardware, monitor equipment health, and respond to incidents tied to physical infrastructure.
Related:
Data Center Pay Is Rising, but Turnover Remains High, Survey Finds
In many facilities, technicians make up the largest share of the on-site workforce. Smaller data centers may operate with relatively lean teams, while hyperscale campuses can employ much larger technician teams spread across multiple buildings and shifts.
Network Engineers: Building and Maintaining Connectivity
In a data center environment, network engineers are responsible for designing, implementing, and supporting the network infrastructure that connects servers, storage, and external connectivity. In some facilities, technicians handle portions of this work as well. But operators with more complex or performance-sensitive environments may rely on network specialists to manage switching, routing, redundancy, and optimization.
Because a data center’s core network architecture typically does not change dramatically once the facility is up and running, the permanent on-site footprint for network engineers is often fairly small. Some facilities may maintain only a limited number of network specialists on site, while others depend partly on centralized or remote teams.
HVAC Specialists: Keeping Cooling Systems Running
Cooling is fundamental to data center reliability, which makes HVAC expertise especially important. Whether a facility relies on chillers,
evaporative cooling systems
, CRAH units, or other thermal management technologies, it needs people who can maintain the equipment and respond to problems as they arise.
Related:
Build an AI Tool, Land a Job: Data Center Operator Launches Hiring Contest
Some operators outsource HVAC work to specialist firms. Even so, facilities with complex cooling systems or a very low tolerance for downtime are more likely to maintain dedicated on-site expertise or ensure regular on-site support from contracted specialists.
Electricians: Supporting Mission-Critical Power
Electrical infrastructure is another essential part of ongoing data center operations. Although the bulk of electrical work occurs during construction, operating facilities still need skilled electricians to inspect equipment, troubleshoot faults, support preventive maintenance, and perform repairs or upgrades to switchgear,
UPS systems
, backup power, and distribution infrastructure.
As with HVAC work, some electrical support may be outsourced. However, because data center power environments are highly specialized and downtime is expensive, operators often prefer electricians who understand the demands of mission-critical facilities.
Security Staff: Protecting the Physical Facility
Physical security
remains a core requirement in data centers. Hardened building design, surveillance systems, and access controls all help reduce risk, but they do not eliminate the need for trained personnel who can manage entry, monitor suspicious activity, and respond quickly to incidents.
Security staffing levels vary based on a facility’s size, location, and risk profile. In general, however, data centers maintain a dedicated on-site security presence, with larger or more isolated sites often requiring broader coverage across shifts and access points.
Data Center Managers: Overseeing Daily Operations
Most data centers also employ a small number of managers responsible for overseeing day-to-day operations. These leaders coordinate staffing, maintenance planning, incident response, vendor relationships, compliance requirements, and overall facility performance. In effect, they translate business priorities into operational execution and ensure teams remain aligned around uptime, efficiency, and safety.
Who Do Data Centers Hire?
Understanding the employment impact of data centers also requires looking at who fills these roles.
Available evidence suggests that many data center jobs are filled locally. The Brookings Institution, for example, has found that local employment rates tend to
increase
when data centers open in a community, even if the absolute number of permanent roles remains relatively modest. That pattern is not especially surprising. Many on-site data center jobs require technical skills and training, but they do not always demand rare expertise that would force operators to recruit exclusively from outside the region.
The result is a more nuanced employment picture than either critics or boosters sometimes suggest. A typical data center does not create a hiring bonanza once it is operational, and construction jobs are generally more numerous than long-term facility roles. Still, most data centers do require a core on-site workforce with expertise in hardware support, networking, cooling, electrical systems, physical security, and facility operations.

title: Batteries are big at All Energy Australia 2026 - Energy Storage
content: The sense of optimism within Australia’s renewable energy sector was on display at All Energy Australia 2026 conference and trade show in Melbourne on Oct. 28 and 29, where energy security, growing demand, and investment and market certainty featured prominently in discussions. Batteries were also a major topic of conversation with the strong presence of both grid and small-scale battery suppliers on the expanded exhibition floor showcasing a growing confidence in the market. RX Global, which organises All Energy alongside the Clean Energy Council (CEC), said more than 22,000 people attended the event this year – up about 5,000 on 2025 figures – and more than 490 national and international companies and organisations exhibited on the trade show floor. Batteries big and small were prominent among the displays with exhibitors keen to be part of the surging small and grid-scale markets. More than 550,000 residential battery systems have been installed by Australian homeowners in the 15 months since the launch of the federal government’s Cheaper Home Batteries program – that subsidises approximately 30% of the cost of an eligible home energy-storage system. The growth pattern has steadied since the initial boom in installations, but the industry is confident there is still plenty of upside in the small-scale sector. “Residential has stabilized over the past few months but there is still a lot of potential in that segment,” EP Cube Sales Manager Sudeesh V said. “Metropolitan areas like Melbourne and Sydney might be slowing but areas such as South Australia, Western Australia, Queensland, even the Northern Territory, there’s a lot of growth potential.” The large-scale battery sector is also experiencing record growth with nine projects representing 2.3 GW / 7.1 GWh of storage capacity switched on in the first six months of the year, surpassing the 2 GW / 5.1 GWh added during 2025. In addition, 13 projects totalling 1.6 GW / 6.5 GWh reached financial close in H1 2026. “We see a very, very significant penetration of battery storage and looking ahead, we’ll see this scaling up even more,” Rystad Energy Renewables and Power Vice President Sally Bogle said, adding that battery energy storage systems are serving as “a silver bullet for the power market.” “They have quite a multi-faceted role,” she said, highlighting their ability to mitigate the curtailment of daytime solar in our markets. “Asset performance wise, that is really, really valuable,” she said. “It allows a solar or wind facility to really maximise their asset and optimise the grid connection.” The outlook for Australia’s solar market is also buoyant with the federal government’s recent raising of the Small-scale Renewable Energy Scheme (SRES) eligibility cap from 100 kW to 1 MW tipped to drive growth in the commercial and industrial (C&I) segment. The expansion extends financial incentives through the Small-scale Technology Certificate (STC) mechanism, reducing the upfront cost of qualifying mid-scale systems by approximately 20%. “This will definitely unlock a lot of small to medium commercial projects,” said Charles Guo, Australian manager with module manufacturer Gorkin Solar. Government policy also appears to be accelerating large-scale solar development. Australia is targeting 82% renewables share in the National Electricity Market (NEM) by 2030 while Western Australia recently committed to a renewable energy target of 75% by 2031 for its main electricity grid. Australian Energy Market Operator data shows a record 80.9 GW of new generation and storage projects now in the pipeline but as ageing coal-fired power plants retire and electricity consumption forecast to grow by more than 40% over the next decade, getting new capacity built will be critical. Victorian Energy Minister Jaclyn Symes said capital is available, but providing investors with certainty is key. “Investors need clear policy, predictable approvals, and confidence that the infrastructure connecting projects will be delivered,” she said. title: Chile’s 840 MWh battery storage project targets 2028 start - Energy Storage
content: Qualitas Energy has secured $286 million in non-recourse financing for a Chilean renewable energy portfolio comprising 259 MW of generation capacity and 840 MWh of battery energy storage. The eight-asset portfolio includes a 154 MWp solar project paired with battery storage, with the solar, wind and storage facilities scheduled to enter commercial operation in 2028. The financing, provided by BNP Paribas and Banco Santander, covers all of Qualitas Energy’s Chilean assets held in Qualitas Energy Fund V (QE V). It combines the refinancing of operational facilities with funding for new projects under construction. The portfolio comprises eight assets across three renewable energy technologies: 66 MW of operational run-of-river hydropower plants, a 154 MWp solar photovoltaic project incorporating a battery energy storage system (BESS) with 840 MWh of capacity, and 39 MW of onshore wind facilities. The solar, wind and battery storage projects are under construction and are scheduled to begin commercial operations in 2028. Qualitas Energy has not disclosed the solar plant’s name or location, or the battery system’s power capacity in MW, which would be needed to establish its discharge duration at full power. Structured as green financing, the package includes non-recourse senior debt, letters of credit facilities and a facility to finance value-added tax (VAT). BNP Paribas acted as sole structuring bank, global coordinator and green financing coordinator. Banco Santander served as administrative agent, joint lead arranger and joint placement coordinator. Qualitas Energy was advised by White & Case and Philippi Prietocarrizosa Ferrero DU & Uría, while Milbank and SCLB Abogados advised the lenders. Qualitas Energy said the portfolio has long-term power purchase agreements (PPAs) with corporate offtakers that provide contracted revenues to support the financing. The company has not disclosed the counterparties, contracted energy volumes, prices or agreement terms. Qualitas Energy began operating in Chile in 2023, opening an office in Santiago and acquiring its first hydropower asset in the country. In July 2026, the company announced a tender for up to 517 GWh per year of electricity from its portfolio of small distributed generation projects (PMGD) and utility-scale assets in central Chile and the Coquimbo region. The tender covered physical and financial contracts, with baseload, solar and nighttime supply options and terms of 10, 12 and 15 years. title: Indian grid operator commissions 250 MW/500 MWh standalone BESS - Energy Storage
content: IndiGrid and EnerGrid have commissioned a 250 MW/500 MWh standalone battery energy storage system (BESS) project in Rajasthan, India, through a special purpose vehicle, Rajasthan BESS Private Ltd (RBPL). The commissioning marks IndiGrid’s third utility-scale BESS project to become operational. The project was awarded to IndiGrid by NTPC Vidyut Vyapar Nigam Ltd (NVVN) in November 2024. The scope of work includes the design, supply, installation, testing, commissioning, operation and maintenance of the 250 MW/500 MWh standalone BESS facility The project was awarded through a tariff-based competitive bidding (TBCB) process and is developed on a build-own-operate (BOO) basis. IndiGrid signed a battery energy storage service agreement (BESSA) with NVVN in December 2024 for a contract period of 12 years from the commercial operation date. Located in a key renewable energy generation hub, the RBPL project will provide peak power support and enhance grid flexibility, facilitating the integration of renewable energy into India’s power system. AmpereHour Energy served as the technology partner for the project. IndiGrid is India’s first and largest publicly listed infrastructure investment trust (InvIT) in the power sector. Established in 2016 and registered with the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI), it owns, operates and manages power transmission, renewable energy generation and energy storage assets. The platform is backed by KKR. EnerGrid is a joint venture platform backed by IndiGrid and co-founded with British International Investment and Norfund. It focuses on developing greenfield power infrastructure projects, complementing IndiGrid’s role in acquiring and operating established, cash-generating assets. title: Peak Energy CEO: 'Anywhere LFP ESS goes, we go - and we do it better' - Energy Storage
content: On 21 October, Peak Energy announced its oversubscribed Series B funding round which raised $108 million to advance its grid-scale passive cooling sodium-ion energy storage systems. GM Ventures led the round while other participants included LG Technology Ventures, Maverick Silicon, Infinite Capital, Eclipse and Xora Innovation. Peak didn’t disclose its valuation or the scale of GM Ventures’ contribution, but much of the Series B funding will be poured into the company’s factory in Sacramento, California, which opened in July with an annual production target of 4 GWh of Peak’s grid-scale sodium-ion battery energy storage systems (BESS). Earlier this year, Landon Mossburg, CEO at Peak Energy, sat down with ESS News for a wide-ranging interview covering Chinese battery manufacturing domination, sodium-ion’s advantages over LFP, data center customers and deployment of grid-scale sodium-ion battery projects. ESS News: Gigawatt-scale production of sodium-ion batteries is a big deal for a company like Peak which is only three years old. How do you plan to pull it off? Mossburg: We’re already shipping from our pilot line in Burlingame, California, and we can do around 30 systems a year out of there. Next year, the big factory in Sacramento will get into hundreds of systems per year. We’re just getting started and it will be one of the biggest sodium-ion systems factories in the world when we turn it on. It’s highly automated but there’s still plenty of jobs for folks to do. We take a very pragmatic approach which comes from experience – we’ve all built a lot of factories before, and a lot of the company is ex-Tesla. Over-automation early on is one of the failure modes we’re trying to avoid. The pilot line where we produced our first modules was mostly by hand – the laser weld was done with a handheld laser welder but now when you walk into that factory almost all the process steps are done by robots. Early next year we’ll probably commit to another round of large cap-ex investment. The next phase of scaling is automating material flows between stations and for that we need to bring in some of the production processes that we outsource today like stamping that are heavy cap-ex. The fundamental cell chemistry and design work that we do is based in Denver, Colorado, and it’s a small but very capable team of about 15 or so. They work closely with suppliers and partners to inform and test and be the fastest at bringing new technology into our systems and getting it out into the world. I think that speed is a super important part of being a leader in anything that incorporates sodium-ion for the next decade, just because there’s going to be so much innovation happening so quickly. The majority of the company, about 120 people, are in Burlingame at our pilot factory and the ESS R&D facilities. Most of our technology innovation happens at the system level, not at the cell level – ie. that’s where our passive cooling stuff is done – and that’s the special technology part of the company. We’re the only ones still to have ever done passive cooling in ESS in an application that is techno-economically viable. Now that we’ve proven what the core thesis of the company is we will continue to advance it and make our product and we’ll also announce some variants of our ESS product soon. I think others are still trying to catch up. If you unlock passive cooling at a grid scale what else is possible? We’ve been thinking about that for probably the past two years and working on some stuff quietly in the background that we’ll announce as well coming up around the end of the year, probably. Our first system was grid-connected last year, so we’re beating that goal, but to claim you’re moving the needle in this industry, you need to be doing gigawatt-hour-scale deployments, and we will be very close to a gigawatt-hour next year. We may cross it. It might be a little tough given scaling and project timelines but certainly in 2028 we’ll cross that milestone. What do your customers like about your technology? Why a sodium-ion battery over an LFP system? We’re delivering in Texas as we speak, from our pilot line, and we have other projects all over the country – in California, MISO, and PJM. Anywhere LFP ESS goes, we go – and we do it better. It’s exciting to think about all the niche applications that are unserved with current technologies. Customers in places like Canada, Alaska and the Yukon, can’t install LFP because for parts of the year these places are unpopulated. So, if you leave the batteries there, they freeze, and LFP needs auxiliary power. Our ESS doesn’t need any auxiliary power and that enables these local communities to make clean energy choices and drives the cost down. It’s the same for cities where we’re working with developers who’ve had their projects stranded because their permits have been challenged by community activists worried about fires. Those are concerns we need to listen to undoubtedly but if you’re choosing a good ESS, even if it’s LFP, your safety concerns are overblown. There are some caveats. There’s been a bit of backsliding on technology driven by the fact that China can’t access the market anymore. Generally, LFP is quite safe but we’re safer. Zinc and some flow batteries, at least on paper, have safety cases that solve these problems, but the economics are so poor that even at a large premium they struggle to make projects work. How will you scale in a way that LFP companies and other competitors didn’t? It’s a good position to be in to have a product that doesn’t need a massive premium to compete. We compete head-to-head on price with LFP systems and outperform them on total cost of ownership and project returns, but we also compete with them on safety and time to power and on life. The only thing we don’t compete on for regular energy projects is footprint – we’re probably about 15% less energy density at a site level. But for data center customers, they need high availability and LFP can’t provide that and the way they’re solving it is to overbuild. In the end, we’re more space efficient because you’re not having to build so much redundant capacity to serve the same load. So, on paper we are less energy efficient or energy dense at the site level but in reality we end up being better for most projects. The market is right at the inflection point, and the world is starting to change in terms of the way that folks are thinking about sodium-ion. Lots of different companies working on new technologies are starting to make predictions that sound very similar to what we say, which is by 2035, sodium-ion will do the same thing in ESS or in EVs that LFP did in those markets. The reason sodium-ion can win in these markets is for all the same reasons that LFP won 15 years ago: it’s cheaper, less constrained on the raw material side, longer life, better safety. Its only downside is energy density and that’s improving very quickly. It’s actually improving much faster than LFP did because it can benefit from a lot of the things we learned from bringing LFP efficiency up. As we do that, we need to look closer at other areas that need to be addressed now and that’s where we’re going to build capability and build products and start to go to market in those areas specifically. Storage is great is but without generation you don’t have anything to store, and I think the way we do grid scale ESS today is a product of the way the technology evolved and one of the key factors that drove the architectures for grid scale storage is the fact that you have to cool it and you can already see us disrupting there as our system doesn’t have any outer enclosure, for example, but there are principles to be broken in system building and there’s more disruption possible in the way storage is built into our grid as you start to think about sodium-ion not needing active cooling etc. It allows us to do things pretty differently in a lot of ways. Everything from increased speed of deployment, reliability of the grid, and affordability of energy but it also unlocks better techno-economics for clean energy sources and for intermittent power sources that are becoming increasingly limited by dispatchability. Storage obviously solves all that. If you look at solar plus storage, wind plus storage… that’s now relatively competitive even with cheap natural gas. But it’s not so competitive that it overcomes enough of the obstacles. You see a lot of data center customers choosing gas and it’s one of the ambitions of the company to make choosing storage so obvious that you can’t not choose it. What do you think the long-term outlook for sodium-ion battery manufacturing is in the US? The US has a lot of work to do. We’re in the lead position on the end application which is the most important part of the supply chain right now but we need to quickly start to bring a supply of cells and other components here domestically. China have got about a 15-year head start on us and they put export controls on the technology now at the cathode level and they have the structural supply chain benefit that comes from the way they make steel that makes their LFP cathode precursor cheaper than the US will ever make it so I think continuing to focus on LFP is a real risk. Can it ever be viable without a subsidy? I think that’s one of the reasons GM invested in us. They share the same view and that’s why they’re doing sodium-ion with us for ESS. We’ve got the largest proven natural reserves of soda ash which is the precursor equivalent of sodium carbonate or lithium carbonate for LFP and on the anode side we have advantages from our petrochemical industries which are the long-term target feedstock for it. The US has got to get in the game. We lost the first leg of the race and I’m encouraged by the fact we and others like Unigrid and Manna are making a lot of progress. But we need to see big industrial players invest now. I was in Northvolt before and one of the reasons Northvolt didn’t make it was because it tried to build the entire supply chain on its own in Europe and we’re not going to repeat that mistake here. We want to do this with partners. It’s a massive market and if we attract competitors it’s good for us for many years until we have to worry about competing with each other. There’s so much demand. China has the largest sodium-ion battery installations because they get a ton of subsidies, but we have to win entirely on merit, and it’s fun to think that a small, scrappy startup company like us can beat CATL to the largest installation again. We already beat them once in terms of getting the first product out there, but we’ll do it again next year with the biggest installation. China have got about a 15-year head start on us and they put export controls on the technology now at the cathode level and they have the structural supply chain benefit that comes from the way they make steel that makes their LFP cathode precursor cheaper than the US will ever make it so I think continuing to focus on LFP is a real risk. Can it ever be viable without a subsidy? One of our first investors was TDK Corp, which is a Japanese conglomerate but they’re the parent company of ATL which is the company that CATL spun out of. title: UK solar-plus-storage co-located project reaches financial close - Energy Storage
content: UK renewable energy developer OnPath Energy has achieved financial close on the Common Farm Solar Park, its first co-located solar and battery energy storage system (BESS) project. Located near the Todwick Road Industrial Estate in Dinnington, South Yorkshire, east of Sheffield, the project combines a 49 MW solar farm with a 50 MW / 100 MWh BESS. To secure debt financing, OnPath separated the commercial offtake structures for the generation and storage assets. The 49 MW solar farm is backed by a subsidy-free, long-term power purchase agreement (PPA) with an undisclosed “global technology firm,” whereas the 100 MWh battery will trade under a third-party optimization agreement. In June, the company moved to de-risk its storage portfolio via fixed-revenue offtake structures with SmartestEnerg , which may focus on this project. NatWest is providing financing for the development, with the financing package including a term loan and other ancillary facilities to support the project through construction and operations. Construction is already underway, with completion targeted for mid-2027. “While there are currently few co-located sites across the UK, especially at this scale, it makes technical and operational sense to place solar and battery technologies in the same location and allows for efficient use to be made of the available grid connections,” said Oliver Hartley, finance director at OnPath Energy. OnPath Energy said that infrastructure consultancy AECOM is serving as lead consultant on the project, while engineering firm Grupotec is responsible for engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) work, as well as operations and maintenance (O&M) services once the project enters operation. The Common Farm financing follows steady growth in OnPath Energy’s standalone storage pipeline. Formerly known as Banks Renewables before its acquisition by Brookfield Asset Management, the developer has accumulated roughly 250 MW of consented or under-construction battery storage across the UK, including planning approval for a 200 MW BESS in West Lothian, Scotland . . title: Harley-Davidson’s electric motorcycle brand LiveWire warns it may not survive
content:
Electric Motorcycles
LiveWire
Micah Toll
| Oct 30 2026 - 1:10 am PT
Harley-Davidson-born electric motorcycle maker
LiveWire
has issued a troubling warning about its financial future, announcing that it has substantial doubt about its ability to continue operating as a going concern. The news sent LiveWire’s stock plunging more than 40% on Thursday morning as the company withdrew its full-year financial guidance.
The announcement comes despite some signs of improving sales, with LiveWire reporting a 38% increase in third-quarter revenue to $7.9 million and a 21% rise in motorcycle unit sales. However, the company continues to burn through cash, reporting a net loss of $18.6 million for the quarter.
LiveWire’s cash reserves have also dwindled significantly, falling from $82.8 million at the end of 2025 to just $39.9 million as of September 30, 2026.
The company has now formed a special restructuring committee to explore potential financing arrangements, strategic partnerships, investments, or even a sale. It also withdrew its previous guidance projecting a $70 million to $80 million operating loss for 2026.
The financial warning comes at a particularly pivotal moment for LiveWire, which is
preparing to launch its most affordable electric motorcycles yet.
The upcoming LiveWire S4 Honcho series represents a major departure from the company’s existing premium electric motorcycles, offering smaller, lighter, and significantly more affordable models designed to attract a much broader audience of riders with a starting price below US $5,000.
LiveWire S4 Honcho Street electric motorcycle
The lower prices could dramatically increase LiveWire’s sales volumes, especially as the company attempts to move beyond the relatively small market for high-dollar electric motorcycles. The Honcho lineup is also expected to help lower the barrier to entry for new riders, with approachable electric motorcycles that eliminate the complexity of clutch and gear shifting.
LiveWire is also preparing to
showcase its latest developments at EICMA in Milan next week
, where it is expected to display new models and further expand its upcoming electric motorcycle lineup.
Whether those new motorcycles can arrive quickly enough to turn around the company’s financial situation remains to be seen.
Electrek’s Take
This is genuinely sad news to see. If there’s any legacy motorcycle manufacturer that deserves to succeed in the electric motorcycle space, it’s Harley-Davidson.
Make all the jokes you want about old dudes in leather jackets riding around on loud, chrome-covered motorcycles. But the fact is that Harley-Davidson was taking electric motorcycles seriously when most other major motorcycle manufacturers were still pretending they didn’t exist.
Harley-Davidson didn’t just dip its toes into electric motorcycles. It dove in headfirst, developing the original LiveWire electric motorcycle
well over a decade ago
and eventually bringing a highly acclaimed production bike to market in 2019. That’s right, Harley-Davidson had a legitimately impressive electric motorcycle on the road before COVID was even a thing. Meanwhile, most of its legacy competitors are only now starting to roll out their first serious electric offerings.
And that’s what makes this so frustrating. Harley-Davidson did the hard part. It invested early, developed excellent technology, received rave reviews, and proved that electric motorcycles could be thrilling, premium machines. But building great motorcycles and building a profitable electric motorcycle business have turned out to be two very different challenges.
The timing is especially unfortunate because I genuinely believe LiveWire’s upcoming S4 Honcho series could be exactly what the company needs. These smaller, significantly more affordable electric motorcycles could finally open LiveWire up to a younger audience that doesn’t have $15,000 to drop on a flagship motorcycle but still wants something fun, stylish, and electric for $5,000.
In many ways, that audience seems like a much more natural fit for LiveWire’s branding and ethos than the premium motorcycle market it has been chasing for years.
I really hope LiveWire can find what it needs to get through this difficult period. After spending more than a decade helping drag the legacy motorcycle industry kicking and screaming into the electric age, it would be a real shame to see the company stumble just as its most promising chapter might be about to begin.

title: Jasion Poki review: The Electric Minibike that packs heavy-duty fun
content:
Seth Weintraub
| Oct 30 2026 - 5:42 am PT
In our transportation reporting, we rarely come across something as fun as today’s review of the
Jasion Poki.
The Poki is a severely overpowered electric minibike that looks like it came from yesteryear. If the power isn’t enough, it also packs some cool tricks, and we’re not (just) talking about wheelies this time.
Jasion Poki by the numbers:
Massive peak power from its central mid-drive motor. There’s a 2kW label on our early review model, which we reviewed thinking something was up. Turns out we were right; this is a powerhouse.
260 N·m:
Raw, low-end torque to launch the bike forward. And Wheelies!
60V 30Ah:
The hefty lithium-ion battery capacity built into the base chassis. Under the seat with a relatively high center of gravity..
Jasion’s top speed. As a 200lber, I acheived 44mph crouched on flat ground. It shouldn’t even go this fast. I don’t think it would hit 50 without a 90-pounder wearing lycra behind the handlebars.
60 miles of range
: At 30-40mph, expect closer to half that range
137.5 lbs:
The substantial net weight of the bike, making it a heavy lift for manual transport.
So taking a look at this bad boy, it just screams fun. It is really low to the ground, has a big, wide seat large enough for 2 people as long as they are under 350lbs total, and has pegs for 2 people and a basket, great for carrying a picnic and an extra helmet.
Heavy duty
This thing is built like a tank, and it tips the scales accordingly. Getting this thing in my SUV ruptured a few discs in my back, though its compact nature means it fit quite well. Loosen the handlebars and it is downright compact. But that weight is strangely like 50lbs heavier than I would expect at close to 140lbs.
That also makes the built-in wheelies a little bit more suspect. My son, who is by now becoming an expert at wheelies, found this one to be a bit more difficult than the auto wheelies on bikes like the Anyland or new Yozma IN11.
The fun part
OK so not only does this little powerhouse get you (and your friend) around town in style and it also makes wheelies a bit easier; but it also has a huge Bluetooth speaker in the back that sounds like a Harley and is all synced up with the actual controller so it sounds real.
Sure, it is a gimmick, but it is a fun one, and it might actually make the low-down bike a little safer since it is going to be out of the sight of most cars.
Electrek’s take:
I love this thing. It is my favorite bike to go to the beach on (and it does well in the sand with those fat tires). But I think there are some big misses here. First of all, it has no business going over 40mph. Not only does it feel scary with those tiny wheels, but speed wobbles puts both the rider a possible second rider at significant risk here. This is a fun bike and it should top out at 20-28mph max. Keep all the torque, just cut out the power at a reasonable top speed.
Also it should weigh a lot less. At 140lbs, it is silly hard to get into the back of a car, which it easily fits in. Making the frame aluminum would go a long way here. Also, if this thing rolled on top of you, it would be a bad day.
Make this thing safer and more portable, and I’d recommend everyone with a beach commute to get one. As it stands, best for responsible adults with strong backs and a Peter Pan complex.

title: Volkswagen hits pause on the Golf EV as it faces an 'urgent need for action'
content:
Volkswagen
Peter Johnson
| Oct 30 2026 - 7:29 am PT
Volkswagen
has put the electric Golf on hold for now as it faces growing pressure to cut costs.
Volkswagen is suspending Golf EV development for now
“We cannot afford to lose any time and must act quickly and decisively,” Volkswagen Group CFO and COO Arno Antlitz warned after the company reported its largest quarterly loss since the “Dieselgate” scandal in 2015 on Thursday.
VW Group’s operating loss swelled to €5.9 billion ($6.5 billion) in the third quarter because of a write-down of its Porsche stake, weak sales in China, and lower profit margins on electric vehicles.
As part of its latest cost-control efforts, Volkswagen is pausing development of the all-electric Golf at its Wolfsburg plant in Germany.
“We simply can’t afford this work right now,” VW brand CEO Thomas Schäfer said in an internal memo
reviewed on Friday. The Wolfsburg plant, or the “heart of the VW brand,” is about €300 million ($334.5 million) short of its cost-cutting targets, the memo said.
Volkswagen Golf EV preview (Source: Volkswagen)
Schäfer said the “decision was really not an easy one for us,” knowing what the Golf means to Wolfsburg.
The decision comes after Volkswagen’s Supervisory Board approved its restructuring strategy, “Future Plan 2030,” last month, which includes reducing its global workforce by 100,000, trimming its lineup, and closing several plants in Germany.
Volkswagen initially planned to launch the Golf EV in 2028, but Schäfer confirmed earlier this year that the electric hatch
will be delayed
until closer to 2030.
Volkswagen Golf GTI Edition 50 (Source: Volkswagen)
Schäfer suggested the delay was because the SSP (Scalable Systems Platform), developed through its partnership with Rivian, was taking longer than expected.
The electric Golf, which is expected to arrive as the ID. Golf, will be one of the first vehicles based on the new platform.
While development is on hold, VW’s works council said the pause will not delay the Golf EV’s launch, promising to make up for lost time. It’s still expected to launch in 2030.
Volkswagen will begin building the electric Golf in Wolfsburg closer to the end of the decade, while production of the gas-powered model will move to Mexico in 2027.

title: Waymo picks Toyota bZ4X as its next robotaxi, starting in Japan in 2027
content:
Robotaxi
autonomous driving
Toyota bZ4X
Fred Lambert
| Oct 30 2026 - 6:22 am PT
Waymo is adding the Toyota bZ4X to its robotaxi lineup. Toyota will build a custom version of the electric SUV with the Waymo Driver integrated right on the line in Japan, and a test fleet will start operating there in 2027.
It’s the first actual vehicle to come out of the partnership the two companies signed last year. And it gives Waymo a Japanese-built car for its Tokyo launch, with the UK and other markets to follow.
When Waymo and Toyota
first announced their deal in April 2025
, it was a preliminary agreement to “explore” working together on autonomous driving, including in personally owned vehicles. Lots of intent, no product.
Now there’s a product. According to
Waymo’s announcement
, Toyota will produce the vehicles at its Takaoka plant in Toyota City, Aichi Prefecture, and Waymo’s self-driving hardware will be installed and integrated at that same site instead of being retrofitted somewhere else.
The robotaxi bZ4X gets a few rider-focused changes: extra rear legroom, automatic doors, a power liftgate, and ambient lighting. Waymo didn’t share sensor specs, unit volumes, or what each vehicle costs.
Operations in 2027 are about testing and validating the autonomous bZ4X fleet in Japan. The UK and “other Waymo markets” come in later years, with no dates attached.
The two companies also say they’ll keep working on autonomous tech for Toyota’s personal vehicles, plus safety projects with Woven by Toyota, the automaker’s software arm.
Waymo co-CEO Dmitri Dolgov said that “Toyota’s commitment to zero traffic accidents resonates deeply with us at Waymo.”
Waymo now has four vehicle platforms
The timing lines up with Waymo’s Japan plans. In September, Waymo said it’s
targeting fully driverless commercial rides in Tokyo in 2027
with taxi operator Nihon Kotsu and ride-hailing app GO, scaling to about 100 vehicles, pending regulatory approval.
In the US, Waymo’s fleet is still mostly made up of Jaguar I-Pace SUVs, a model Jaguar no longer produces. It’s been adding the Zeekr-built Ojai van and the Hyundai Ioniq 5, and Hyundai is reportedly in talks to
supply up to 50,000 Ioniq 5 robotaxis by 2028
The bZ4X makes four. It isn’t Toyota’s first robotaxi bZ4X either: Toyota and Pony.ai started mass-producing bZ4X-based robotaxis in China earlier this year.
For US readers, the refreshed model is sold here simply as the Toyota bZ, starting at $34,900. A cheap, high-volume base vehicle matters a lot when you’re trying to scale a fleet.
And Waymo is scaling. It now does over 500,000 paid rides a week across 15 US metros, and it
picked Toronto as its first Canadian city
earlier this month, with riders targeted for 2028.
Electrek’s Take
This is a big one, even if the bZ4X is about as exciting as a toaster.
Waymo’s biggest constraint right now is cars. It has been running a fleet built on a discontinued Jaguar, and every new automaker it signs adds manufacturing capacity it doesn’t have to build itself. Toyota is the world’s best-selling automaker. Having it build Waymo-ready vehicles on its own assembly line is exactly the kind of industrial partner Waymo needed.
Yes, the bZ4X had a rough start (Toyota recalled the first batch in 2022 because the wheels could come off). But it has come a long way now – becoming boring and reliable. And for a robotaxi, boring and reliable is the whole point.
Compare that with Tesla’s approach: a two-seat Cybercab with no steering wheel, built in-house, with a self-certified autonomy stack that still isn’t operating at anything close to Waymo’s scale. Waymo keeps plugging its driver into existing EVs from established automakers and expanding city by city. So far, that’s working.
The way it is looking now. It sounds like Toyota will take over manufacturing Waymo driver cars for right-hand-drive markets. But what interests me most is the personal-vehicle angle. Toyota and Waymo keep mentioning it, but there’s still nothing concrete. If Toyota actually puts the Waymo Driver in a car you can buy, Tesla’s FSD Supervised pitch gets a lot harder to sell. Will that happen before the end of the decade? Who knows.

title: 固态电池材料企业星科源完成融资，客户涉及宁德时代、比亚迪
content:
据10月29日报道，超细纳米硅材料企业星科源完成亿元级Pre-A轮融资。本轮融资由弘毅投资领投，厦门钨业产业基金、宜宾人才基金跟投，云道资本担任长期独家财务顾问。资金将主要用于产能扩张、设备及基地建设、团队建设、研发和市场开拓。
对于本轮投资，弘毅投资表示，看好固态电池发展带来的硅基负极材料机遇，认为星科源在超细纳米硅制备、客户适配及规模化生产方面已形成一定优势。厦门钨业产业基金则认为，星科源的超细纳米硅产业化能力，与其在锂电正极材料研发、规模制造及下游应用方面的积累具有互补性。
星科源成立于2022年，主要聚焦下一代固态电池用纳米硅材料，同时布局AI芯片用硅基光电材料。其自主研发化学气相沉积（CVD）设备及超细纳米硅原料，并围绕材料开展表面改性、二次造粒和客户应用方案开发。此外，星科源还将AI for Science（AI4S）技术引入材料研发及生产过程。
在技术及产能方面，星科源已实现小于30nm超细纳米硅的稳定制备，并具备粒径调节能力。据媒体报道，星科源位于杭州钱塘区的新厂房于今年5月20日全线投产，产能由此前的公斤级、吨级提升至百吨级。目前，星科源正推进头部客户验证及百吨级产线爬坡，部分国内项目已由认证导入阶段转向批量交付准备。
客户拓展方面，星科源已形成国内固态电池客户认证导入、液态电池体系产品拓展，以及日韩、北美产业客户联合开发的业务布局。据媒体报道，其客户包括宁德时代、比亚迪、广汽、贝特瑞、凯金等。
除电池材料外，星科源还布局AI芯片用硅基光电器件所需的纳米硅材料，尝试拓展在光电领域的应用，形成新的业务增长方向。

title: 小米拟出资17亿入股欣旺达动力
content:
集邦光储观察获悉，10月29日晚，欣旺达发布多条公告，涉及2026年第三季度业绩、动力电池子公司增资扩股及终止发行H股并在香港联交所主板上市等事项。
前三季度营收增长，净利润同比下滑
财务数据显示，2026年前三季度，欣旺达实现营业收入634.62亿元，同比增长45.78%；归母净利润6.13亿元，同比下降56.37%；扣非净利润2.27亿元，同比下降77.65%。
单季度来看，第三季度公司实现营业收入252.84亿元，同比增长52.78%；归母净利润1056.71万元，同比下降98.08%；扣非净利润1.29亿元，同比下降69.98%。
对于前三季度利润下滑的原因，欣旺达表示，主要受到消费电子下游需求承压、物料成本同比上行等因素影响，利润空间受到压缩。此外，人民币升值、出口退税税率下降及消费税等因素也对公司利润造成一定影响。
小米拟出资17亿元入股欣旺达动力
10月28日，欣旺达召开董事会会议，审议通过子公司欣旺达动力增资扩股事项。根据公告，小米旗下投资平台瀚星创投拟出资17亿元，认购欣旺达动力约8.98亿股新增股份，增资完成后持有欣旺达动力5.34%的股权。
本次增资完成后，欣旺达动力注册资本将由约159.15亿元增至约168.13亿元。欣旺达通过旗下欣旺达惠州新能源有限公司持有的欣旺达动力股份比例，将由24.06%降至22.78%。
值得关注的是，本次增资还涉及欣旺达动力的控制权及合并报表范围变化。根据公告，在增资及董事会换届选举完成后，欣旺达在欣旺达动力董事会中的席位将不超过半数，公司将不再拥有对欣旺达动力的控制权。届时，欣旺达动力将由控股子公司转为参股子公司，不再纳入欣旺达合并报表范围。
终止港股发行上市计划
此外，欣旺达还发布了关于公司终止发行H股股票并在香港联合交易所有限公司主板上市的公告。
据公告，欣旺达此前于2025年7月审议通过H股发行上市相关议案。经过综合考量当前市场环境、公司自身变化及发展规划等因素，公司于2026年10月28日召开董事会，审议通过终止H股发行上市的议案。
对于终止原因，欣旺达在投资者关系活动中表示，这是基于多方面因素作出的审慎决策。目前公司经营情况正常，该事项不会对经营活动和持续发展造成重大影响。

title: 晶澳/TCL中环/阿特斯3家光伏企业发布三季度业绩
content:
集邦光储观察获悉，近期，晶澳科技、TCL中环及阿特斯相继公布2026年三季度报告。
10月28日，晶澳科技披露2026年三季度报告。报告期内，公司前三季度营业收入为281.13亿元，同比减少23.62%；归母净利润亏损36.4亿元，亏损额较上年同期扩大2.32%；扣非净利润亏损41.37亿元，同比扩大19.81%。
其中，第三季度营业收入为106.16亿元，同比下降17.74%；归母净利润亏损9.74亿元，与去年同期基本持平；扣非净利润亏损11.14亿元，较上年同期有所收窄。
出货量方面，今年1—9月，晶澳科技电池组件合计出货36.22GW（含自用68MW），组件海外出货占比达到60.92%。
财务数据方面，前三季度公司财务费用同比大幅增加，主要与汇兑损失增加、利息支出上升及利息收入减少有关。此外，资产减值损失达到8.83亿元，较上年同期有所增加，主要来自存货跌价准备和固定资产减值准备增加。同期，公司营业外支出增多，为3.17亿元，主要由于履约索赔损失增加。
10月29日，TCL中环公布2026年第三季度报告。前三季度，公司营业收入为235.14亿元，同比增长9.01%；归母净利润亏损45.56亿元，同比减亏21.12%；扣非净利润亏损51.5亿元，同比减亏14.63%。
第三季度单季，公司营业收入为91.99亿元，同比增长12.55%；归母净利润亏损13.52亿元，同比减亏11.86%；扣非净利润亏损12.52亿元，同比减亏19.62%。
光伏业务方面，前三季度TCL中环新能源光伏业务销售收入为186.1亿元，其中组件业务收入占比为50.1%，较上半年提高3.2个百分点。
出货方面，1—9月，公司光伏硅片出货量为83.4GW，市占率位居行业第一，海外出货占比为13.8%，同比增长355%。同期，电池及组件销量合计14.5GW，同比增长43%，海外出货占比为20.6%，同比增长202%。
此外，TCL中环收购一道新能源控股权已于今年7月初完成交割。目前，公司已启动20GW电池和25GW组件BC技改项目，预计明年一季度陆续完成。项目完成后，公司电池产能预计达到20GW，组件产能达到50GW，其中BC电池及组件产能分别为20GW和25GW，另有25GW TOPCon组件产能。
10月29日，阿特斯发布2026年第三季度报告。前三季度，公司营业收入为186.47亿元，同比下降40.37%；归母净利润亏损9526.07万元，同比下降109.63%；扣非净利润亏损7.49亿元，同比下降166.92%。
第三季度，公司营业收入为58.63亿元，同比下降42.63%；归母净利润亏损3.95亿元，同比下降253.09%；扣非净利润亏损4.97亿元，同比下降275.10%。
对于业绩下滑的原因，阿特斯在报告中表示，行业竞争加剧、产品价格承压，对光伏板块业务造成影响。报告期内，储能板块业务虽有增长，但增量仍不足以弥补光伏板块业务量减少带来的影响，公司整体收入及利润因此下降。

title: 隆基推进滁州组件产线升级，规划6.8GW HPBC 2.0产能
content:
近期，隆基在安徽滁州推进两项光伏组件产线升级改造，计划将原有TOPCon产线调整为HPBC 2.0产线，涉及投资合计约10.6亿元。两项技改完成后，预计将形成6.8GW HPBC 2.0组件产能。
隆基S2项目升级2.8GW HPBC 2.0产能
根据环评资料，隆基S2新型单晶组件绿色化智能化装备升级项目位于滁州经济技术开发区淮安路19号，总投资3.2343亿元，建设单位为滁州隆基乐叶光伏科技有限公司。
该项目拟对二期厂区五车间、八车间进行改造。其中，五车间现有5条TOPCon产线将升级为2条HPBC 2.0产线，八车间现有4条TOPCon产线将升级为1条HPBC 2.0产线。
项目改造前，TOPCon组件产能为5GW；改造后，将形成2.8GW HPBC 2.0组件产能。
设备方面，项目将新增热压机、上料机、汇流条焊接机、丝印机、自动注胶机等设备，并对现有层压机、封边机、边框打胶机等进行改造，同时更新部分公辅配套设施。项目建成后，产品将调整为隆基Hi-MO10系列HPBC 2.0组件，搭载XBC高效电池。
滁州基地新增4GW HPBC 2.0产能
另一项技改项目为滁州隆基乐叶单晶组件产品升级改造及设备智能化提升项目。根据环评资料，该项目拟对现有组件生产线进行调整，将6条TOPCon产线中的3条升级改造为HPBC 2.0产线，其余3条产线拆除。
从产品方案来看，该项目改造前拥有4.5GW TOPCon组件产能，改造后将不再生产TOPCon组件，转而形成4GW HPBC 2.0组件产能。
此次改造还涉及生产设备及配套设施调整，新增串排叠设备、烘干炉、UV静置及固化设备等，以适配HPBC 2.0组件生产需求。

title: Consumer Appetite for Personal AI Goes Mainstream
content:
This article is brought to you by Qualcomm Technologies.
For many consumers, much of the promise and appeal of AI is personal. Consumers are looking past generic tools and want to know how these technologies will help them in their daily lives. These trends coincide with the advent of new classes of wearable devices that, in addition to being able to leverage powerful frontier models, feature built-in intelligence that understand the context of a user. Where are they? What are they seeing and hearing? What are their habits, their preferences, their schedules?
It’s an astonishing pivot, from passive accessories that served mostly to send users smartphone notifications to proactive, intelligent companions. The smartphone is no longer the center of that universe; though it’s still incredibly important, in this personal AI paradigm, the AI is the UI. And it shifts the focus toward you, the user.
These new technologies are exciting. But what do consumers really want?
A Personal AI report, commissioned by Qualcomm Technologies, built on a survey of more than 12,000 people across key geographies worldwide (the U.S., U.K., Germany, India, Brazil, and China) focused on the rise of personal AI in intelligent wearables looks deeply at these developments.
The smartphone is no longer the center of that universe; though it’s still incredibly important, in this personal AI paradigm, the AI is the UI.
Survey respondents are less interested in single devices and are responding more to the idea of connected ecosystems. As people expand their roster of devices, it only makes sense. Instead of relying entirely on a smartphone and a laptop, respondents also have connected technology in their cars, as well as intelligent wearables like smartwatches, smart glasses, hearables, and other wearables like rings, pins, and pendants. They want those devices to work in concert, and the way to do that is to decentralize any single one of them. Instead, the AI agent that knows the user and works across all of those devices becomes the unifying factor.
Consider a typical workday: A user’s watch detects it is time to leave for a meeting and, with permission, their AI agent factors in calendar details, real-time traffic and battery status across their devices. In the car, it suggests the best route and briefs them on their meeting agenda. As they arrive, smart glasses surface a discreet reminder, such as the meeting location or the name of a new contact, while the phone stays in their pocket. No one device has to do everything; each plays the role it is best suited for, coordinated by a personal AI agent that understands the user’s context and acts only at the user’s direction.
With this in mind, simply adding more hardware to the mix isn’t sufficient. Even though respondents will be open to new form factors, they’ll demand more from their ecosystem of devices. They’ll be sensitive to points of friction and needless complexity, and they’ll require each new device to bring something new to the table — “incremental intelligence, convenience, or contextual awareness that their existing devices cannot deliver on their own what the report,” reads the report.
The usage trends are up. The report found that those who own wearables are already using AI frequently (60 percent use it at least weekly), which indicates that it’s becoming less of a fun experiment for early adopters and more of a critical mass habit.
The “always-on” nature of intelligent wearables appears to be winning respondents, too. The report found the following statistics on average continuous wear among users:
- True wireless earbuds – 3 hours
- Wireless headphones – 3 hours
- Smart glasses – 5 hours
- Audio glasses – 6 hours
- Smartwatches – 9 hours
- Smart rings, necklaces and pendants – 8 hours
Consumers want AI that is personal and understands their context — they’re looking for smooth, intuitive experiences that are marked by privacy, security, and user control.
Consumer Trust Is Hard-Won
But for all the excitement and engagement around intelligent wearables, there’s a gating factor: trust. As use cases for intelligent wearables expands to more personal and persistent experiences, trust is a necessity for Personal AI.
The top reported issues around adoption are privacy, security, and user control. The data points to a certain amount of caution around deeply personal use cases, like voice, health, and location, as almost 60 percent of respondents want to keep data from their wearables private, or at least insist on gaining approval before it gets shared.
In other words, even though premium features like high-quality audio, perception sensing, battery life, and comfort whet consumer appetites (and agentic AI capabilities drive upgrade intent), true adoption will come only with consumer trust. They want security, privacy, transparency and control.
Notably, the report found that respondents expressed more interest in adopting intelligent wearables when Snapdragon was introduced as the enabling platform. This reinforces the value of having an established, trusted technology foundation in the mix.
The Industry Remains Fluid
The report shows that consumer appetite for AI is high, with 60-70 percent of those surveyed expressing interest in advanced AI as they consider a new device. That’s a constant. But remaining purchase drivers differed between device categories.
Audio playback quality is the most influential purchase driver for true wireless earbuds and headphones. For smartwatches, it’s display quality and responsiveness. Respondents are less concerned about technical specifications than aesthetics like materials and finish when it comes to devices like smart rings and pendants. And for smart glasses, it’s all about the type of control, whether it’s voice, gesture, or touch.
The Rise of Personal AI in Intelligent Wearables
Artificial intelligence is entering a new phase, one that is deeply personal, continuously present, and seamlessly embedded into the devices we wear every day. This evolution, which we define as “Personal AI”, represents a shift away from generic, cloud-only intelligence toward AI that understands individuals in context: their habits, preferences, environments, and intent, in real time.
Alongside these purchase drivers is another key finding: Consumer appetite for Personal AI agents has gone mainstream. The report says that 70 percent of respondents “express strong interest in an AI assistant that can interact naturally through voice and seamlessly manage devices, apps, and everyday tasks.” With each individual as the center of their own ecosystem, voice becomes the most critical, natural method for interacting with agents.
The Opportunity
The industry for intelligent wearables is exciting. It’s clear that consumer demand for Personal AI is high, and this report dives deeply into the specifics of what respondents want out of it. They want AI that is personal and understands their context, and they want it to be proactive and helpful instead of merely reactive. They’re looking for smooth, intuitive experiences that are marked by privacy, security, and user control.
Intelligent wearables comprise much of the hardware of this “ecosystem of you.” Consumers are interested in ecosystems instead of single devices, and they’re looking for agentic AI capabilities that understand and act on their behalf.
Yet so much of the industry remains undefined. OEMs and technology makers have an enormous opportunity right now to innovate and iterate on the strong technological foundations that platform makers are building. And the roadmap for what consumers want is clear.
All percentages, consumer behaviors, and attitudes stated in this report are based only on the responses of the individuals who participated in our survey.
Qualcomm Technologies is a global leader in communications and computing technologies, including leading-edge AI, high-performance, low-power computing, and connectivity solutions. Headquartered in San Diego, Calif., the company develops technologies for next-generation mobile networks and smart devices, and designs semiconductors such as mobile processors and AI chips.

title: Fiat's Tiny $15,000 EV Can Finally Hit American Streets
content:
Fiat's Tiny $15,000 EV Can Finally Hit American Streets
Get ready for your taste of la dolce vita, because the Fiat Topolino is street legal now.
Who doesn't want a Fiat Topolino? Sure, it's slow, has little range, and seems to have all the creature comforts of a plastic beach chair. But it's adorable, filled with character, and has a starting price of just $14,985 including a destination fee. And, I mean, just look at it.
When Fiat first launched the Topolino in the U.S. not too long ago, it wasn't legal to drive on public roads. Originally, Fiat's "little mouse" only had a top speed of 19 mph, since it wasn't designated as a Low-Speed Vehicle (LSV), which is what neighborhood EVs and street-legal golf carts are. Customers could still buy them, but they were only allowed on private properties. With the 2027 model year that launched on Thursday, the Topolino comes street legal right out of the box, with a top speed of 25 miles per hour.
For 2027, Fiat also brought a new "Open Air" model to the lineup, so you can live la dolce vita, al fresco.
For customers who already bought the non-streel-legal version, Fiat is offering a complimentary LSV upgrade.
There are now three different models: the standard Topolino, Dolce Vita, and the new Open Air. The standard car is just a two-door hardtop, while the Dolce Vita comes with a roll-off soft-top roof and fun stanchions instead of doors, like a Jeep Wrangler only cuter. The new Open Air is a combination of the two, with the Dolce Vita's roll-off roof but the normal car's doors. All models have the same $13,995 MSRP. All of them come with Fiat's new full-color digital gauge cluster, too.
The only option you can pick is the color, and there are only three choices. Verde Vita Mint is the only no-cost color, while Luna Greige and Corallo Orange cost $295. Fiat does offer one accessory, a $395 rear luggage rack.
Under that lovable design are some pretty underwhelming specs. But you also have to remember that this isn't a car in the traditional sense.
With only 46 miles of range, you aren't going very far, especially with its paltry 8 horsepower. But honestly, who cares? It's a joy to look at and is legal on roads with speed limits under 35 mph (depending on the jurisdiction). It's the perfect little beach town cruiser and it will likely be big hit wherever golf carts are popular.

title: Ford CEO Says Its New EV Tech Is 30% More Efficient Than BYD's
content:
Ford CEO Says Its New EV Tech Is 30% More Efficient Than BYD's
CEO Jim Farley says that its new motors, inverters, and EV gearboxes will maximize efficiency and keep costs down.
Ford has explicitly framed its Universal Electric Vehicle platform as a way to compete with Chinese cars on cost and technology. According to Ford CEO Jim Farley, the company has succeeded in at least one way: efficiency.
"There's another area that we really found to be quite advantaged relative to a BYD. And that is the efficiency of our motors, gearbox and inverters, which are about 30% more efficient than theirs and allows us to design a battery that's much less," Farley said today on the automaker's third-quarter earnings call. "I think that's really critical."
Farley says that's one of the keys to keeping costs down for the UEV platform, which debuts with the $28,350 Fathom pickup. The more efficient motor, gearbox, and drivetrain have allowed Ford to install a smaller battery, which is the biggest single cost in an EV. The company pitches its new platform—which features fewer parts, better efficiency, and overhauled manufacturing process—as a way to make EVs that are far more economically viable than the Mustang Mach-E and F-150 Lightning.
Ford hasn’t said exactly what the Fathom’s battery size is, but past reports have estimated somewhere in the 50 to 60 kWh battery range. For a workable range of more than 200 miles, Ford will need to take advantage of every efficiency gain it can and make the most out of its not-so-big battery. It also wasn't clear exactly which BYD powertrain Farley was comparing Ford's to.
It makes sense that Ford is targeting BYD in particular. China's biggest automaker surpassed the Blue Oval in global sales last year, and much of its success comes from deep vertical integration. It looks like Ford is taking that lesson to heart, bringing more of its own supply chain in-house and developing the UEV architecture from the ground up.
Ford is taking notes from other Chinese manufacturers too. Earlier in the call, Ford executives explained what it’s learning from its partnership with Geely in Europe: how to make cars more cheaply, and speed up product development.
Ford says the engineering improvements in the UEV platform won't be limited to EVs. Kumar Galhotra, Ford’s Chief Operating Officer, said that the company's hybrids will benefit from the same efficiency gains realized in the UEV platform.

title: Ford Fathom Pricing Will Stretch Into the 'High $30,000 Range'
content:
Ford Fathom Pricing Will Stretch Into the 'High $30,000 Range'
The Ford Fathom starts at under $29,000. Here's how much a nicely equipped one will cost you.
- You'll be able to spec out Ford's sub-$29,000 pickup to the "high $30,000 range."
- Ford hasn't revealed what options will be included, but says that it realizes that customers buying "nicer" trims care about the digital experience.
- This could mean recurring revenue through software subscriptions.
Ford's upcoming Fathom electric pickup is shaping up to be one of the cheapest EVs on the market. But its $28,350 starting price won't be the only bargain. Ford says even higher-end versions of the truck will come in below $40,000.
"The starting price of the $28,350 is just that," said Andrew Frick, president of Ford Blue and Model e, on Ford's third quarter earnings call on Thursday. "We'll have a range that goes to the high $30,000 range. And we'll have a couple of different offerings within that."
Ford Fathom Prototypes in Las Vegas
It's not clear whether high-$30,000s will be the starting price for higher-level trims, or whether a truly fully-loaded truck will come in below $40,000. Frick said that Ford will share more details about how the Fathom's offerings break down as it gets closer to launch. Pre-orders start early next year with first delivers slated for late 2027.
Ford discussed another trick it has up its sleeve to make money off of the relatively affordable Fathom: subscriptions. CEO Jim Farley said Ford realized that customers spending more on "nicer" trims of the Fathom really care about the digital experience that they are getting when buying an EV:
"We can offer at an incredibly low cost, very advanced ADAS, as well as digital camera, [and] dashboard," said Farley. He later continued: "[T]he digital suite, including the embedded Apple Maps, is really a game changer for any EV, let alone at this price. I think for me, personally, that is going to be the most exciting upsell opportunity. It's really the long-term subscription and digital experience for the customer."
Ford has been clear that it wants to move to more software-defined vehicles that it can monetize through digital features. In fact, its Q3 sales figures reveal that Ford has a whopping 1.7 million customers paying for subscriptions. That could be through Ford Pro, BlueCruise, or other digital services that Ford offers today—and it's a 40% increase compared to this time last year.
Farley mentioned in the opening remarks for the call that Ford found that retail customer retention can be up to 9 percentage points higher when combined with a software subscription. So if Ford can play the long-game by monetizing its low-cost vehicle, it could be a way for the automaker to earn more annual recurring revenue off of the Fathom.
For shoppers, the good news is that even a nicely equipped Fathom shouldn't break the bank. But Farley's comments also raise an interesting question: How much of the truck's most appealing technology will be included in the purchase price, and how much will cost extra every month?
That's something we'll be watching closely as Ford gets closer to revealing the finished truck.

title: Rivian's Amazon Van Got More Range And AWD To Cover More Routes
content:
Rivian's Amazon Van Got More Range And AWD To Cover More Routes
The lovable electric delivery van is now shipping with a longer-range battery, as well as an all-wheel-drive version with 710 hp.
- Rivian has expanded the powertrain options for its electric delivery van.
- The startup has added a larger-capacity battery and a dual-motor variant to the lineup.
- The additions apply to both the Amazon-branded EDV and the general-purpose RCV.
Rivian’s only commercial model has long been America’s best-selling electric van, thanks in no small part to the 100,000-strong order from Amazon. And now, the lovable EV is even more appealing, thanks to two big updates that are already shipping.
The Rivian Commercial Van (RCV), which is also known as the Electric Delivery Van (EDV), can be specced with a larger-capacity battery pack that increases the driving range by about 30% compared to the standard-range models. Additionally, a dual-motor option that adds an electric motor on the rear axle was added to the lineup, improving performance and usability on rough roads.
“In addition to the EDV standard pack variant already on the road, in early October we began delivering new variants that are specifically designed to expand route coverage into more rural networks, including an AWD configuration as well as a larger battery pack that offers a 30% increase in range,” Rivian said in its third-quarter earnings report.
According to EPA filings submitted by the California company, the Large battery pack has a usable energy capacity of 129 kilowatt-hours, up from the Standard pack’s 90 kWh, and is only available on the long-wheelbase versions of the van. The all-wheel drive option, which is also exclusive to the 700 body version, pairs two Enduro motors for a total output of 710 horsepower (530 kilowatts).
Rivian Commercial Van powertrain versions
The Large battery uses lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cells, just like the Standard model. Range-wise, the larger-capacity pack enables roughly 220 miles on the front-wheel-drive EDV 700 model, according to the EPA certification filing, which is 37% more than the standard-range version. Meanwhile, the EDV 700 with the Large battery and AWD should deliver approximately 200 miles of range on a full charge. Rivian has not revealed the final range figures for the newly added powertrain configurations yet.
The spec sheet suggests that the 129 kWh battery is roughly 1,000 pounds heavier than the standard-range pack, while the rear-mounted electric motor adds another 450 pounds to the mix. As a result, the fully-loaded long-wheelbase Rivian van has a curb weight of 8,677 lbs and a gross vehicle weight rating (GVWR) of 10,000 lbs. By contrast, the entry-level short-wheelbase model with the Standard battery and front-wheel drive weighs roughly 7,000 lbs and has a GVWR of 9,500 lbs.
All Rivian vans come from the factory with 19-inch wheels and a CCS1 charging port that can accept up to 100 kW from a DC fast charger. On AC charging, the electric delivery can take in up to 11 kW from a 240-volt, 48-ampere Level 2 charger. Rivian said it would provide NACS charging adapters as an opt-out option, enabling the van to use NACS fast chargers.
According to Cox Automotive data, Rivian sold 15,685 EDVs and RCVs from January through September, making it the best-selling electric commercial van in the United States by a wide margin.

title: Rivian's R2 Is Already Its Best-Selling EV. Now The Company Expects Even Bigger Sales
content:
Rivian's R2 Is Already Its Best-Selling EV. Now The Company Expects Even Bigger Sales
Rivian's Tesla Model Y rival is a hit among buyers, with Rivian increasing its annual delivery guidance again.
The R2 is already Rivian’s best-selling model just months after deliveries started, the California startup said in its third quarter earnings report Thursday. The midsize electric SUV already outsold the R1T, R1S, and its electric delivery van between July and September.
As a result, the company is now revising the baseline for its annual delivery target from 65,000-70,000 units to 67,000-70,000 units. After a record 19,751 deliveries in Q3, the company previously had already revised the baseline deliveries from 62,000 units to 65,000 units. Now that outlook is looking even more optimistic.
“We had great results with R2 becoming our best selling vehicle by volume in the third quarter," CEO RJ Scaringe said in a statement. "Customer and media feedback on R2 has been exceptional," he added.
The new guidance indicates Rivian is gearing up for its best-ever quarter of deliveries. To hit the low end of its target, the company would need to deliver at least 25,193 vehicles. On the automaker's earnings call, Rivian Interim CFO Derek Mulvey said the company expects the majority of those deliveries will be R2s.
Rivian's Q3 revenue grew 38% to $2.1 billion from the same period last year thanks to increase in deliveries, earnings from regulatory credits, and growth in its software and services division. Thanks to its partnership with the Volkswagen Group, its software and services revenue grew to 45% to $605 million. The startup is still not profitable though, reporting a net loss of $913 million for the quarter, an improvement from a $1.17 billion loss during the year-ago quarter.
It's betting that the R2 will help with its turnaround. The crossover is the company's make-or-break vehicle, one designed to go toe to toe with the Model Y and bring it much-needed scale. Rivian said on Thursday that it started a second shift of R2 production and expects its production run rate to increase over the coming quarters. The company said Thursday that it expects the R2's ramp to help it end the year with a positive automotive gross margin.
Rivian launched the R2 in June with a Performance Launch Edition trim that costs a little under $60,000. A Premium model costing $53,990 is supposed to hit the market this year, with a $44,990 Standard version joining the lineup in 2027.
The electric SUV will not only help fund the development and production of future models like the R3 and R4, but also the company's burgeoning autonomy ambitions.
Rivian's Amazon Prime electric delivery vans.
The company is working to release a more advanced driver assistance system to rival Tesla's Full-Self Driving (Supervised) system under its Autonomy+ offering. Currently, Autonomy+ includes hands-free driving on highways and automatic lane changes on command. The more advanced version of this will include point-to-point autonomous driving on city streets as well, and a limited rollout of that is expected begin by the end of this year.
Rivian also plans to deliver up to 50,000 robotaxis to Uber starting in 2028. It recently acquired U.K.-based synthetic data startup Third Dimension to help with those efforts.

title: Tesla's Cybercab Is Built In A Radical New Way. Here's How It Works
content:
Tesla's Cybercab Is Built In A Radical New Way. Here's How It Works
The Cybercab skips the paint shop and reaches final assembly mostly built. Tesla says it needs roughly half the factory space.
- Tesla builds and tests major Cybercab sections separately, then joins them with much of the wiring and interior already installed.
- Molded exterior panels eliminate the traditional paint shop, helping Tesla reduce factory space and production steps.
- Final assembly takes about 25 stations, while replaceable battery modules and easier component access simplify repairs.
For years, Tesla talked about throwing the typical car-making playbook out the window with its radical "unboxed" process for new cars. Now it's putting that idea to work at the Texas factory where it cranks out the Cybercab—and releasing new details about how it all works.
In a new video from the engineering firm Munro & Associates, Tesla engineering chief Lars Moravy and Cybercab lead Eric Earley tour the cab's production line and dive deep into its design and assembly process. Here's what we learned.
Traditional car production generally starts by putting together a body, painting it, then installing its mechanical parts, wiring, and interior as the partially-built vehicle transverses a long sequence of assembly stations. Tesla’s “unboxed” process instead uses separate lines to build and equip the front, rear, sides, and floor before joining them at the end. The idea is that instead of reaching inside a car to install things, workers and robots tackle smaller, more accessible assemblies, working faster and more efficiently. Tesla says the line is about 78% automated.
Ford is working on a similar process for its Universal Electric Vehicle platform, which kicks off with the $30,000 Fathom pickup. The company calls it an "assembly tree," rather than the typical assembly line.
Tesla Cybercab Unboxed Production Line
Tesla says the front module contains roughly half the car’s parts and content. Its drive unit, suspension, and thermal hardware sit on a positioning pallet. The front structure, already carrying the dashboard, is lowered over them. Meanwhile, workers can assemble the side sections flat, install overhead components at a comfortable height, and attach seats and carpet to the battery pack, whose top cover doubles as the cabin floor.
Those pre-assembled sections converge on the automated framing line, arriving with wiring, hoses, and other components already installed. Robots position and join them before the car enters a final assembly line of about 25 stations. Moravy says that for the Model Y, it's about 5-10 times that number. The wheels go on at the second-to-last station; the car first stands on its wheels as it rolls off the line near the end. Much of the work normally associated with final assembly happens elsewhere.
In the video, Moravy says the idea began about six years ago, when Tesla was stuck trying to automate existing designs and concluded the problem was the car. Breaking it into smaller sections gave robots better access and allowed stations to sit closer together.
Testing also happens in stages. They check individual components before building larger assemblies, then test them again. Tesla says the front module arrives with its computers connected and systems already checked. That reduces the chance of discovering a faulty component after it's been installed deep inside the vehicle.
Tesla Cybercab Unboxed Production Line
A conventional paint shop would interrupt the process by requiring Tesla to assemble the body earlier. Instead, the cab's plastic exterior panels are infused with color during molding. (Slate, too, decided to skip the expensive painting process by making its truck's exterior out of gray plastic.) The front and rear structural modules also skip electrocoating, although the steel side structures remain coated.
Tesla explored films and other alternatives before choosing this process. The engineers say scratches remain repairable much like conventional paint.
Moravy says the factory doesn’t run every day because Tesla can produce Cybercabs faster than it's deploying them. But that may say less about the factory's efficiency and more about the pace of Tesla's public Cybercab rollout.
If all goes Tesla's way, though, the factory will be working overtime. At full clip, Tesla says the Cybercab line can churn out 125,000 vehicles per year, and on the company's last earnings call Elon Musk set a lofty goal of 5 million annual vehicle deliveries by 2030—more than double what it does today.

title: Toyota Is Turning The bZ EV Into A Waymo Robotaxi, Starting in 2027
content:
Toyota Is Turning The bZ EV Into A Waymo Robotaxi, Starting in 2027
Toyota will build the driverless crossovers on the same assembly line as the regular version.
- The Toyota bZ EV is being turned into a Waymo robotaxi in Japan.
- Toyota will build the driverless EVs using Waymo’s hardware at its Takaoka plant.
- The first Toyota-made Waymos will hit Japanese streets next year.
Driverless Toyota bZ electric crossovers will start rolling off the same assembly line that builds the regular-flavoured bZ in Japan, thanks to a deeper partnership with Waymo.
The Japanese automaker will outfit the custom-built EVs with Waymo’s self-driving hardware at its Takaoka plant in Toyota City in Aichi Prefecture, with the first models scheduled to go through initial testing and validation in 2027.
Waymo Jaguar I-Pace in Japan
It’s a big step for Waymo, which currently outfits self-driving Jaguar I-Pace crossovers and the Zeekr-made Ojai minivans at its manufacturing site in Mesa, Arizona. Separately, Hyundai said it would build “tens of thousands” of robotaxis for Waymo at its factory in Georgia, but that hasn’t happened yet.
Following its introduction in Japan, where it’s still called the bZ4X, the Waymo-powered robotaxi will make its way to the United Kingdom and other markets where the Alphabet-owned rideshare company operates, with a rollout planned for the following years.
"We'll start with the right-hand drive markets in Japan and the UK," said Dmitri Dolgov, co-CEO of Waymo. "I think the vision and the strategic partnership is to extend that beyond that, but we don't have any other countries or timelines or specifics to share"
The custom-outfitted EVs will come from the factory with automatic doors, a power liftgate, and ambient lighting, making life as easy as possible for riders. Toyota said the move marks a major milestone in the expansion of Japan’s first fully autonomous ride-hailing service using mainstream, locally manufactured vehicles.
Neither Waymo nor Toyota said how many Japanese-made robotaxis would hit the road, and there’s no concrete timeline for a wide rollout. The American autonomous ride-hailing company already has a handful of left-hand drive Jaguar I-Pace EVs on the road in Tokyo, but they still have a safety operator behind the steering wheel, with a full-on unmanned commercial rollout scheduled for 2027.
“We chose Toyota because of our respect for the legendary safety, reliability, and quality of their vehicles, and we look forward to deepening our collaboration as we scale our fully autonomous Waymo Driver technology globally," Dolgov said.
Toyota and Waymo partnered in 2025 to develop a new autonomous vehicle platform, while also finding ways to integrate the ride-hailing company’s autonomous technology into Toyota’s next-generation passenger vehicles.
“We share a strong sense of purpose and a common vision with Waymo in advancing safety through automated driving technology, and we are confident this collaboration can help bring our solutions to more people around the world, moving us one step closer to a zero-accident society,” said Hiroki Nakajima, Member of the Board and Executive Vice President of Toyota Motor Corporation, when the partnership was signed in April 2025. “Our companies are taking an important step toward a future with greater safety and peace of mind for all.”
